It is true that there is no agreement on what is gained or on what is lost between the day of birth and that of death. Some have fixed on the continual increase in the volume of the protoplasm, from the birth of the cell to its death1. More plausible and more profound is the theory which places the decrease in the quantity of nutritive substance contained in the "internal environment" in which the organism renews itself, and the increase in the quantity of residual unexcreted substances which, accumulating in the body, end by "encrusting2" it. Must one nevertheless, with an eminent microbiologist, declare inadequate every explanation of ageing that does not take phagocytosis into account3? I am not qualified to decide the question. But the fact that the two theories agree in affirming the constant accumulation or the constant loss of a certain kind of matter, while in determining what is gained and what is lost they no longer have much in common, shows clearly enough that the frame of the explanation has been supplied a priori. We shall see this better and better as we advance in our study: it is not easy, when one thinks of time, to escape the image of the hourglass. The cause of ageing must lie deeper. I hold that there is unbroken continuity between the evolution of the embryo and that of the complete organism. The push by virtue of which the living being grows, develops and ages is the very one which made it pass through the phases of embryonic life. The development of the embryo is a perpetual change of form. Whoever wished to note all its successive aspects would lose himself in an infinity, as happens whenever one has to do with a continuity. Life is the prolongation of this prenatal evolution. The proof of this is that it is often impossible to say whether one has to do with an organism that is ageing or with an embryo that is continuing to evolve: such is the case with the larvae of Insects and Crustaceans, for example. On the other hand, in an organism like ours, crises such as puberty or the menopause, which bring about the complete transformation of the individual, are altogether comparable to the changes accomplished in the course of larval or embryonic life; yet they form an integral part of our ageing. Though they occur at a determinate age, and in a time that may be fairly short, no one will maintain that they then supervene ex abrupto, from outside, simply because a certain age has been reached, as the call to the colours comes to the man who has turned twenty. It is evident that a change like that of puberty is in preparation at every instant from birth and even before birth, and that the ageing of the living being up to this crisis consists, in part at least, in this gradual preparation. In short, what is properly vital in ageing is the insensible, infinitely divided continuation of the change of form. Phenomena of organic destruction accompany it, moreover, without any doubt. To these a mechanistic explanation of ageing will attach itself. It will note the facts of sclerosis, the gradual accumulation of residual substances, the growing hypertrophy of the protoplasm of the cell. But beneath these visible effects an inner cause lies hidden. The evolution of the living being, like that of the embryo, implies a continual recording of duration, a persistence of the past in the present, and consequently an appearance at least of organic memory. The present state of an inert body depends exclusively on what was happening at the preceding instant. The position of the material points of a system defined and isolated by science is determined by the position of these same points at the immediately preceding moment. In other words, the laws governing unorganised matter can be expressed, in principle, by differential equations in which time (in the sense in which the mathematician takes this word) would play the part of independent variable. Is it so with the laws of life? Does the state of a living body find its complete explanation in the immediately preceding state? Yes, if one agrees a priori to liken the living body to the other bodies of nature and to identify it, for the purposes of the argument, with the artificial systems on which the chemist, the physicist and the astronomer operate. But in astronomy, in physics and in chemistry, the proposition has a well-determined meaning: it signifies that certain aspects of the present, important for science, are calculable as a function of the immediate past. Nothing of the kind in the domain of life. Here calculation takes hold, at most, of certain phenomena of organic destruction. Of organic creation, on the contrary, of the evolutionary phenomena which properly constitute life, we do not even glimpse how we could subject them to mathematical treatment. It will be said that this inability is due only to our ignorance. But it may equally well express that the present moment of a living body does not find its reason for being in the immediately preceding moment, that one must add to that moment the whole past of the organism, its heredity, in short the whole of a very long history. In reality, it is the second of these two hypotheses that expresses the present state of the biological sciences, and even their direction. As for the idea that the living body could be subjected by some superhuman calculator to the same mathematical treatment as our solar system, it has issued little by little from a certain metaphysics which has taken a more precise form since the physical discoveries of Galileo, but which, - as I shall show, - was always the natural metaphysics of the human mind. Its apparent clarity, our impatient desire to find it true, the eagerness with which so many excellent minds accept it without proof, in short all the seductions it exercises over our thought, ought to put us on our guard against it. The attraction it has for us proves clearly enough that it satisfies an innate inclination. But, as will be seen further on, the intellectual tendencies, today innate, which life must have created in the course of its evolution, are made for something quite other than to furnish us with an explanation of life. It is against the opposition of this tendency that one comes up as soon as one wishes to distinguish between an artificial system and a natural system, between the dead and the living. It causes one to find it equally difficult to think that the organised endures and that the unorganised does not endure. What! it will be said, in affirming that the state of an artificial system depends exclusively on its state at the preceding moment, do you not bring time in, do you not put the system into duration? And, on the other hand, this past which, according to you, is one with the present moment of the living being, does not organic memory contract it entirely into the immediately preceding moment, which thereupon becomes the sole cause of the present state? - To speak thus is to misunderstand the capital difference separating concrete time, along which a real system develops, from the abstract time that enters into our speculations on artificial systems. When we say that the state of an artificial system depends on what it was at the immediately preceding moment, what do we mean by this? There is not, there cannot be, an instant immediately preceding an instant, any more than there is a mathematical point contiguous to a mathematical point. The "immediately preceding" instant is, in reality, the one which is connected with the present instant by the interval dt. All that we mean, then, is that the present state of the system is defined by equations into which there enter differential coefficients such as de/dt, dv/dt, that is to say, at bottom, present velocities and present accelerations. It is, then, finally only of the present that there is question, of a present taken, it is true, together with its tendency. And, in fact, the systems on which science operates are in an instantaneous present that is unceasingly renewed, never in the real, concrete duration in which the past is one with the present. When the mathematician calculates the future state of a system at the end of the time t, nothing prevents him from supposing that, between now and then, the material universe vanishes, to reappear all of a sudden. It is the t-th moment alone that counts, - something that will be a pure instantaneity. What will flow in the interval, that is to say real time, does not count and cannot enter into the calculation. If the mathematician says he places himself within this interval, it is always to a certain point, to a certain moment, I mean to the extremity of a time t', that he transports himself, and then it is the interval up to t' that is no longer in question. If he divides the interval into infinitely small parts by considering the differential dt, he thereby simply expresses that he will consider accelerations and velocities, that is to say numbers which note tendencies and which allow the state of the system at a given moment to be calculated; but it is always a given moment, I mean a stopped one, that is in question, and not time that flows. In short, the world on which the mathematician operates is a world that dies and is reborn at every instant, the very one Descartes was thinking of when he spoke of continued creation. But, in time so conceived, how is one to represent to oneself an evolution, that is to say the characteristic trait of life? Evolution, for its part, implies a real continuation of the past by the present, a duration which is a connecting link. In other words, the knowledge of a living being or natural system is a knowledge that bears on the very interval of duration, whereas the knowledge of an artificial or mathematical system bears only on the extremity. Continuity of change, preservation of the past in the present, true duration: the living being does seem, then, to share these attributes with consciousness. Can one go further, and say that life is invention, as conscious activity is, unceasing creation, as it is? It is not within my purpose to enumerate here the proofs of transformism. I wish only to explain in a few words why I shall accept it, in the present work, as a sufficiently exact and precise rendering of the known facts. The idea of transformism is already in germ in the natural classification of organised beings. The naturalist, in fact, brings together the organisms that resemble one another, then divides the group into sub-groups within which the resemblance is greater still, and so on: all along the operation, the characters of the group appear as general themes on which each of the sub-groups would perform its particular variations. Now, such is precisely the relation that we find, in the animal world and in the vegetable world, between what engenders and what is engendered: on the canvas that the ancestor transmits to its descendants, and which these possess in common, each puts its original embroidery. It is true that the differences between descendant and ascendant are slight, and that one may ask whether one and the same living matter has enough plasticity to assume successively forms as different as those of a Fish, a Reptile and a Bird. But to this question observation gives a peremptory answer. It shows us that, up to a certain period of its development, the embryo of the Bird is hardly distinguishable from that of the Reptile, and that the individual develops, through embryonic life in general, a series of transformations comparable to those by which, according to evolutionism, one would pass from one species to another. A single cell, obtained by the combination of the two cells, male and female, accomplishes this work by dividing. Every day, before our eyes, the highest forms of life issue from a very elementary form. Experience thus establishes that the most complex may have issued from the most simple by way of evolution. Now, did it in fact so issue? Palaeontology, despite the insufficiency of its records, invites us to believe so, for where it recovers with some precision the order of succession of species, this order is just the one that considerations drawn from comparative embryogeny and anatomy would have led us to suppose, and each new palaeontological discovery brings transformism a new confirmation. Thus the proof drawn from observation pure and simple keeps growing stronger, while, on the other hand, experiment removes the objections one by one: thus the curious experiments of H. de Vries, for example, by showing that important variations can occur suddenly and be transmitted regularly, dispose of some of the greatest difficulties the thesis raised. They allow us to shorten greatly the time that biological evolution seemed to require. They also make us less exacting towards palaeontology. So that, in sum, the transformist hypothesis appears more and more as an at least approximate expression of the truth. It is not rigorously demonstrable; but, beneath the certainty given by theoretical or experimental demonstration, there is that indefinitely increasing probability which stands in for evidence and tends towards it as towards its limit: such is the kind of probability that transformism presents. Let us admit, however, that transformism is convicted of error. Let us suppose that it comes to be established, by inference or by experiment, that species arose by a discontinuous process of which we have today no idea. Would the doctrine be affected in what is most interesting in it and, for us, most important? The classification would doubtless subsist in its main lines. The present data of embryology would subsist likewise. The correspondence between comparative embryogeny and comparative anatomy would subsist. In that case biology could and should continue to establish between living forms the same relations that transformism supposes today, the same kinship. It would be, it is true, an ideal kinship and no longer a material descent. But, since the present data of palaeontology would also subsist, one would indeed still be forced to admit that it is successively, and not simultaneously, that the forms between which an ideal kinship is revealed have appeared. Now the evolutionist theory, in what is important in it in the eyes of the philosopher, asks no more than this. It consists above all in establishing relations of ideal kinship and in maintaining that, where there is this relation of so to speak logical descent between forms, there is also a relation of chronological succession between the species in which these forms are materialised. This double thesis would subsist in any event. And in that case one would still have to suppose an evolution somewhere - either in a creative Thought in which the ideas of the various species would have engendered one another exactly as transformism will have it that the species themselves were engendered on the earth, - or in a plan of vital organisation immanent in nature, which would gradually make itself explicit, in which the relations of logical and chronological descent between the pure forms would be precisely those that transformism presents to us as relations of real descent between living individuals, - or finally in some unknown cause of life, which would develop its effects as if some engendered the others. One would thus simply have transposed evolution. One would have made it pass from the visible into the invisible. Almost everything that transformism tells us today would be preserved, even if it had to be interpreted in another way. Is it not better, then, to keep to the letter of transformism, as professed by the almost unanimous body of scientists? If one sets aside the question how far this evolutionism describes the facts and how far it symbolises them, there is nothing in it irreconcilable with the doctrines it has claimed to replace, even with that of separate creations, to which it is generally opposed. That is why I hold that the language of transformism is now binding on all philosophy, as the dogmatic affirmation of transformism is binding on science. But then one must no longer speak of life in general as of an abstraction, or as of a mere heading under which all living beings are entered. At a certain moment, at certain points of space, a clearly visible current has arisen: this current of life, passing through the bodies it has organised one after another, passing from generation to generation, has divided itself among species and scattered itself among individuals without losing anything of its force, intensifying rather as it advanced. It is known that, according to the thesis of the "continuity of the germ-plasm" maintained by Weismann, the sexual elements of the generating organism would transmit their properties directly to the sexual elements of the organism engendered. In this extreme form the thesis has seemed questionable, for it is only in exceptional cases that the sexual glands are seen to be sketched out as early as the segmentation of the fertilised ovum. But, if the cells generating the sexual elements do not, in general, appear from the very beginning of embryonic life, it is none the less true that they are always formed at the expense of those tissues of the embryo which have not yet undergone any particular functional differentiation and whose cells are made up of unmodified protoplasm1. In other words, the genetic power of the fertilised ovum weakens as it is distributed over the growing mass of the tissues of the embryo; but, while it is thus being diluted, it concentrates something of itself anew on a certain special point, on the cells from which the ova or the spermatozoa will be born. One might therefore say that, if the germ-plasm is not continuous, there is at least continuity of genetic energy, this energy being expended only for a few instants, just long enough to give the impulse to embryonic life, and recovering itself as soon as possible in new sexual elements in which, once again, it will bide its time. Regarded from this point of view, life appears as a current which passes from germ to germ through the medium of a developed organism. Everything happens as if the organism itself were only an excrescence, a bud caused to sprout by the old germ working to continue itself in a new germ. The essential thing is the continuity of progress which goes on indefinitely, an invisible progress on which each visible organism rides during the short interval of time that it is given to live. Now, the more one fixes one's attention on this continuity of life, the more one sees organic evolution draw near to that of a consciousness, in which the past presses against the present and causes a new form to spring forth from it, incommensurable with its antecedents. That the appearance of a vegetable or animal species is due to precise causes, no one will dispute. But this must be understood to mean that, if one knew the detail of these causes after the event, one would succeed in explaining by them the form that has been produced: of foreseeing it there could be no question2. Will it be said that one could foresee it if one knew, in all their detail, the conditions in which it will be produced? But these conditions are one with it and even make but one with it, being characteristic of the moment at which life then finds itself in its history: how can one suppose known in advance a situation which is unique of its kind, which has not yet occurred and will never occur again? Of the future one foresees only what resembles the past or what can be recomposed out of elements like those of the past. Such is the case with astronomical, physical and chemical facts, with all those that form part of a system in which elements supposed immutable are merely juxtaposed, in which only changes of position take place, in which there is no theoretical absurdity in imagining things put back in place, in which consequently the same total phenomenon, or at least the same elementary phenomena, can be repeated. But an original situation, which communicates something of its originality to its elements, that is to say to the partial views taken of it, how could one picture it as given before it is produced1? All that can be said is that it is explained, once produced, by the elements that analysis discovers in it. But what is true of the production of a new species is true also of that of a new individual, and more generally of any moment whatever of any living form whatever. For, though the variation must have reached a certain importance and a certain generality to give rise to a new species, it is taking place at every moment, continuous, insensible, in every living being. And the sudden mutations themselves, of which we are told today, are evidently possible only if a work of incubation, or better of maturing, has been accomplished through a series of generations which seemed not to change. In this sense one might say of life, as of consciousness, that at every instant it is creating something2. But against this idea of the absolute originality and unforeseeability of forms our whole intellect rises in revolt. Our intellect, as the evolution of life has moulded it, has as its essential function to light up our conduct, to prepare our action on things, to foresee, for a given situation, the favourable or unfavourable events that may follow from it. It therefore instinctively isolates, in a situation, whatever resembles the already known; it seeks the same, in order to be able to apply its principle that "the same produces the same". In this consists the foreseeing of the future by common sense. Science carries this operation to the highest possible degree of exactness and precision, but it does not alter its essential character. Like ordinary knowledge, science retains of things only the aspect of repetition. If the whole is original, it contrives to analyse it into elements or aspects which are more or less a reproduction of the past. It can operate only on what is supposed to repeat itself, that is to say on what is withdrawn, by hypothesis, from the action of duration. What is irreducible and irreversible in the successive moments of a history escapes it. To represent this irreducibility and this irreversibility to oneself, one must break with scientific habits which answer to the fundamental demands of thought, do violence to the mind, climb back up the natural slope of the intellect. But that is precisely the role of philosophy. That is why life may evolve before our eyes as a continuous creation of unforeseeable form, yet the idea always persists that form, unforeseeability and continuity are mere appearances, in which so many ignorances are reflected. What presents itself to the senses as a continuous history would break up, we shall be told, into successive states. What gives you the impression of an original state resolves itself, on analysis, into elementary facts each of which is the repetition of a known fact. What you call an unforeseeable form is only a new arrangement of old elements. The elementary causes whose totality determined this arrangement are themselves old causes repeating themselves while adopting a new order. Knowledge of the elements and of the elementary causes would have made it possible to sketch in advance the living form which is their sum and result. Having resolved the biological aspect of phenomena into physico-chemical factors, we shall leap, if need be, over physics and chemistry themselves: we shall go from masses to molecules, from molecules to atoms, from atoms to corpuscles; we shall indeed have to arrive at last at something that can be treated as a kind of solar system, astronomically. If you deny it, you dispute the very principle of scientific mechanism, and you declare arbitrarily that living matter is not made of the same elements as other matter. - I shall answer that I do not dispute the fundamental identity of inert matter and organised matter. The sole question is whether the natural systems we call living beings must be likened to the artificial systems that science cuts out of inert matter, or whether they ought not rather to be compared with that natural system which is the whole of the universe. That life is a kind of mechanism I am quite willing to grant. But is it the mechanism of the parts artificially isolable in the whole of the universe, or that of the real whole? The real whole might well be, I was saying, an indivisible continuity: the systems we cut out of it would then not be, properly speaking, parts of it; they would be partial views taken of the whole. And, with these partial views put end to end, you will not obtain even a beginning of the recomposition of the whole, any more than by multiplying photographs of an object, from a thousand different aspects, you will reproduce its materiality. So it is with life and with the physico-chemical phenomena into which one would claim to resolve it. Analysis will doubtless discover in the processes of organic creation an increasing number of physico-chemical phenomena. And that is what chemists and physicists will keep to. But it does not follow from this that chemistry and physics must give us the key to life. A very small element of a curve is almost a straight line. The smaller one takes it, the more it will resemble a straight line. At the limit, one may say, as one pleases, that it forms part of a straight line or of a curve. At each of its points, in fact, the curve coincides with its tangent. Thus "vitality" is tangent at any point whatever to physical and chemical forces; but these points are, after all, only the views of a mind which imagines stops at this or that moment of the movement that generates the curve. In reality, life is no more made of physico-chemical elements than a curve is composed of straight lines. Generally speaking, the most radical progress a science can accomplish consists in bringing the results already acquired into a new whole, in relation to which they become instantaneous and immobile views taken at intervals on the continuity of a movement. Such, for example, is the relation of the geometry of the moderns to that of the ancients. The latter, purely static, operated on figures once they had been described; the former studies the variation of a function, that is to say the continuity of the movement which describes the figure. One may no doubt, for greater rigour, eliminate from our mathematical procedures every consideration of movement; it is none the less true that the introduction of movement into the genesis of figures lies at the origin of modern mathematics. I believe that if biology could ever grasp its object as closely as mathematics grasps its own, it would become to the physico-chemistry of organised bodies what the mathematics of the moderns has proved to be to ancient geometry. The wholly superficial displacements of masses and molecules which physics and chemistry study would become, in relation to that vital movement which takes place in depth, which is transformation and no longer translation, what the stationary position of a moving body is to the movement of that body in space. And, so far as I can foresee it, the procedure by which one would pass from the definition of a certain vital action to the system of physico-chemical facts it implies would not be without analogy to the operation by which one goes from the function to its derivative, from the equation of the curve (that is to say, from the law of the continuous movement by which the curve is generated) to the equation of the tangent which gives its instantaneous direction. Such a science would be a mechanics of transformation, of which our mechanics of translation would become a particular case, a simplification, a projection on to the plane of pure quantity. And just as there exist an infinity of functions having the same differential, these functions differing from one another by a constant, so, perhaps, the integration of the physico-chemical elements of a properly vital action would determine that action only in part: a share would be left to indetermination. But at most one may dream of such an integration; I do not claim that the dream will ever become reality. I have only wished, by developing a certain comparison as far as possible, to show where my thesis comes close to pure mechanism, and how it is distinguished from it. One may, moreover, carry the imitation of the living by the unorganised fairly far. Not only does chemistry carry out organic syntheses, but one manages to reproduce artificially the external pattern of certain facts of organisation, such as the indirect division of the cell and protoplasmic circulation. It is well known that the protoplasm of the cell performs varied movements within its envelope. On the other hand, the so-called indirect division of the cell takes place through operations of extreme complexity, some of which concern the nucleus and others the cytoplasm. The latter begin with the doubling of the centrosome, a small spherical body situated beside the nucleus. The two centrosomes thus obtained move away from each other, draw to themselves the cut and likewise doubled segments of the filament which essentially made up the original nucleus, and end by forming two new nuclei around which are constituted the two new cells that will succeed the first. Now, it has been possible to imitate, in their broad outlines and in their external appearance, at least some of these operations. If one pulverises sugar or kitchen salt, adds some very old oil, and looks at a drop of the mixture under the microscope, one sees a foam of alveolar structure whose configuration resembles, according to certain theorists, that of protoplasm, and in which, in any case, movements take place that strongly recall those of protoplasmic circulation1. If, in a foam of the same kind, one extracts the air from an alveolus, one sees a cone of attraction take shape, analogous to those which form around the centrosomes and lead to the division of the nucleus2. Even the external movements of a unicellular organism, or at least of an Amoeba, are thought to be explicable mechanically. The displacements of the Amoeba in a drop of water would be comparable to the to-and-fro of a grain of dust in a room where open doors and windows set currents of air circulating. Its mass ceaselessly absorbs certain soluble substances contained in the surrounding water and gives back certain others to it; these continual exchanges, similar to those which take place between two vessels separated by a porous partition, would create around the little organism an ever-changing vortex. As for the temporary prolongations or pseudopodia which the Amoeba seems to give itself, they would be not so much sent out by it as drawn out of it by a kind of aspiration or suction of the surrounding medium3. Step by step, this mode of explanation will be extended to the more complex movements which the Infusorian itself executes with its vibratile cilia, which, moreover, are probably nothing but consolidated pseudopodia. Scientists, however, are far from agreeing among themselves on the value of explanations and schemata of this kind. Chemists have pointed out that, even if one considers only the organic, without going as far as the organised, science has so far reconstituted only the waste products of vital activity; the properly active, plastic substances remain refractory to synthesis. One of the most remarkable naturalists of our time has insisted on the opposition between the two orders of phenomena observed in living tissues, anagenesis on the one side and catagenesis on the other. The role of the anagenetic energies is to raise the lower energies to their own level by the assimilation of inorganic substances. They build up the tissues. On the contrary, the very functioning of life (with the exception, however, of assimilation, growth and reproduction) is of the catagenetic order, a descent of energy and no longer an ascent. It is only on these facts of the catagenetic order that physico-chemistry would get a hold, that is to say, in short, on the dead and not on the living4. And it is certain that the facts of the first kind seem refractory to physico-chemical analysis, even if they are not, in the proper sense of the word, anagenetic. As for the artificial imitation of the external appearance of protoplasm, ought one to attach any real theoretical importance to it, when one is not yet settled as to the physical configuration of this substance? Of recomposing it chemically there can be still less question for the moment. Finally, a physico-chemical explanation of the movements of the Amoeba, and a fortiori of the behaviour of an Infusorian, seems impossible to many of those who have observed these rudimentary organisms closely. Even in these humblest manifestations of life they perceive the trace of an effective psychological activity1. But what is most instructive of all is to see how often the thorough study of histological phenomena discourages, instead of strengthening, the tendency to explain everything by physics and chemistry. Such is the conclusion of the truly admirable book which the histologist E. B. Wilson has devoted to the development of the cell: "The study of the cell has on the whole seemed to widen rather than to narrow the enormous gap that separates even the lowest forms of life from the inorganic world2." In short, those who concern themselves only with the functional activity of the living being are inclined to believe that physics and chemistry will give us the key to biological processes3. They have to do chiefly, in fact, with the phenomena which are endlessly repeated in the living being, as in a retort. This explains in part the mechanistic tendencies of physiology. On the contrary, those whose attention is concentrated on the fine structure of living tissues, on their genesis and their evolution, histologists and embryologists on the one hand, naturalists on the other, are in the presence of the retort itself and no longer merely of its contents. They find that this retort creates its own form along a unique series of acts constituting a veritable history. These, histologists, embryologists or naturalists, are far from believing as readily as the physiologists in the physico-chemical character of vital actions. To tell the truth, neither of the two theses, neither the one which affirms nor the one which denies the possibility of ever producing an elementary organism chemically, can invoke the authority of experience. Both are unverifiable, the first because science has not yet advanced a single step towards the chemical synthesis of a living substance, the second because there exists no conceivable means of proving experimentally the impossibility of a fact. But I have set out the theoretical reasons which prevent me from assimilating the living being, a system closed by nature, to the systems which our science isolates. These reasons have less force, I admit, when it is a question of a rudimentary organism such as the Amoeba, which hardly evolves. But they gain more if one considers a more complex organism, which accomplishes a regulated cycle of transformations. The more duration marks the living being with its imprint, the more evidently the organism is distinguished from a mechanism pure and simple, over which duration glides without penetrating it. And the demonstration takes on its greatest force when it bears on the integral evolution of life from its humblest origins to its highest present forms, inasmuch as this evolution constitutes, through the unity and continuity of the animated matter which supports it, a single indivisible history. Hence I do not understand how the evolutionist hypothesis comes to pass, in general, for being akin to the mechanistic conception of life. Of this mechanistic conception I do not claim, of course, to offer a mathematical and definitive refutation. But the refutation which I draw from considerations of duration, and which is, in my opinion, the only possible refutation, gains in rigour and becomes more cogent the more frankly one places oneself within the evolutionist hypothesis. I must insist on this point. But let me first indicate, in clearer terms, the conception of life towards which I am making my way. Mechanistic explanations, I said, hold good for the systems which our thought artificially detaches from the whole. But of the whole itself, and of the systems which, within this whole, are naturally constituted in its image, one cannot admit a priori that they are explicable mechanically, for then time would be useless, and even unreal. The essence of mechanical explanations is in fact to regard the future and the past as calculable as functions of the present, and thus to claim that all is given. On this hypothesis, past, present and future would be visible at a single glance to a superhuman intellect capable of carrying out the calculation. And so the scientists who have believed in the universality and the perfect objectivity of mechanical explanations have made, consciously or unconsciously, a hypothesis of this kind. Laplace already formulated it with the greatest precision: "An intellect which, at a given instant, knew all the forces by which nature is animated and the respective situation of the beings which compose it, if moreover it were vast enough to submit these data to Analysis, would embrace in the same formula the movements of the greatest bodies of the universe and those of the lightest atom: nothing would be uncertain for it, and the future, like the past, would be present to its eyes1." And Du Bois-Reymond: "One can imagine the knowledge of nature arrived at a point where the universal process of the world would be represented by a single mathematical formula, by one immense system of simultaneous differential equations, from which could be derived, for each moment, the position, the direction and the velocity of every atom of the world2." Huxley, for his part, has expressed the same idea in a more concrete form: "If the fundamental proposition of evolution is true, namely that the entire world, animate and inanimate, is the result of the mutual interaction, according to definite laws, of the forces possessed by the molecules of which the primitive nebulosity of the universe was composed, then it is no less certain that the present world lay potentially in the cosmic vapour, and that a sufficient intellect could, knowing the properties of the molecules of that vapour, have predicted, for example, the state of the fauna of Great Britain in 1868, with as much certainty as when one says what will happen to the vapour of the breath on a cold winter's day." – In such a doctrine one still speaks of time, one pronounces the word, but one hardly thinks of the thing. For time is here deprived of efficacy, and, since it does nothing, it is nothing. Radical mechanism implies a metaphysics in which the totality of the real is posited en bloc, in eternity, and in which the apparent duration of things merely expresses the infirmity of a mind that cannot know everything at once. But duration is something quite other than this for our consciousness, that is to say, for what is most indisputable in our experience. We perceive duration as a stream which one cannot go back up. It is the ground of our being and, as we clearly feel, the very substance of the things with which we are in communication. In vain is the prospect of a universal mathematics made to shine before our eyes; we cannot sacrifice experience to the demands of a system. That is why I reject radical mechanism. But radical finalism seems to me quite as unacceptable, and for the same reason. The doctrine of finality, in its extreme form, such as we find it in Leibniz for example, implies that things and beings merely realise a programme traced once and for all. But if there is nothing unforeseen, no invention or creation in the universe, time again becomes useless. As in the mechanistic hypothesis, it is again supposed here that all is given. Finalism thus understood is only a mechanism in reverse. It draws on the same postulate, with this sole difference, that in the course of our finite intellects along the wholly apparent succession of things, it places in front of us the light with which it claims to guide us, instead of placing it behind. It substitutes the attraction of the future for the impulsion of the past. But succession remains none the less a mere appearance, as indeed does the course itself. In the doctrine of Leibniz, time is reduced to a confused perception, relative to the human point of view, which would vanish, like a mist that lifts, for a mind placed at the centre of things. Finalism, however, is not, like mechanism, a doctrine with fixed lines. It admits of as many inflections as one cares to impress upon it. The mechanistic philosophy is to be taken or left: it would have to be left if the smallest grain of dust, by deviating from the trajectory foreseen by mechanics, showed the slightest trace of spontaneity. The doctrine of final causes, on the contrary, will never be definitively refuted. If one form of it is set aside, it will take on another. Its principle, which is psychological in essence, is very supple. It is so extensible, and thereby so broad, that one accepts something of it as soon as one rejects pure mechanism. The thesis I shall set out in this book will therefore necessarily partake of finalism in a certain measure. That is why it is important to indicate precisely what I am going to take from it, and what I mean to leave. Let me say at once that it seems to me one goes astray when one attenuates Leibnizian finalism by breaking it up into infinitely many pieces. Yet such is the direction which the doctrine of finality has taken. It is clearly felt that if the universe as a whole is the realisation of a plan, this cannot be shown empirically. It is clearly felt, too, that even if one confines oneself to the organised world, it is hardly easier to prove that all is harmony there. The facts, if questioned, would say just as well the contrary. Nature sets living beings at grips with one another. It presents us everywhere with disorder beside order, regression beside progress. But might not what can be affirmed neither of matter as a whole nor of life as a whole be true of each organism taken separately? Does one not observe in it an admirable division of labour, a marvellous solidarity between the parts, perfect order in infinite complexity? In this sense, does not each living being realise a plan immanent in its substance? This thesis consists, at bottom, in breaking the ancient conception of finality into pieces. One does not accept, one even readily ridicules, the idea of an external finality by virtue of which living beings would be co-ordinated with one another: it is absurd, people say, to suppose that grass was made for the cow, the lamb for the wolf. But there is an internal finality: each being is made for itself, all its parts act in concert for the greatest good of the whole and organise themselves intelligently with a view to this end. Such is the conception of finality which was for a long time classical. Finalism has shrunk to the point of never embracing more than one living being at a time. In making itself smaller, it no doubt thought it would offer less surface to blows. The truth is that it exposed itself to them far more. However radical my thesis itself may appear, finality is external or it is nothing at all. Let us consider, in fact, the most complex and the most harmonious organism. All the elements, we are told, conspire for the greatest good of the whole. Granted; but let us not forget that each of the elements may itself, in certain cases, be an organism, and that in subordinating the existence of this small organism to the life of the large one we accept the principle of an external finality. The conception of a finality that is always internal thus destroys itself. An organism is composed of tissues each of which lives on its own account. The cells of which the tissues are made also have a certain independence. Strictly speaking, if the subordination of all the elements of the individual to the individual itself were complete, one might refuse to see organisms in them, reserve that name for the individual, and speak only of internal finality. But everyone knows that these elements can possess a genuine autonomy. Not to speak of the phagocytes, which push their independence so far as to attack the organism that nourishes them, nor of the germ cells, which have their own life beside the somatic cells, it suffices to mention the facts of regeneration: here an element or a group of elements suddenly reveals that if, in normal times, it submitted to occupying only a small place and accomplishing only a special function, it could do much more, it could even, in certain cases, regard itself as the equivalent of the whole. There lies the stumbling block of vitalist theories. I shall not reproach them, as is commonly done, with answering the question by the question itself. No doubt the "vital principle" does not explain much: at least it has the advantage of being a kind of label set on our ignorance, which may remind us of it on occasion1, whereas mechanism invites us to forget it. But the truth is that the position of vitalism is made very difficult by the fact that there is neither purely internal finality nor absolutely clear-cut individuality in nature. The organised elements that enter into the composition of the individual have themselves a certain individuality, and each will claim its own vital principle if the individual is to have its own. But, on the other hand, the individual itself is not independent enough, not isolated enough from the rest, for us to be able to grant it a "vital principle" of its own. An organism such as that of a higher Vertebrate is the most individuated of all organisms; yet if one notes that it is only the development of an ovum which formed part of its mother's body and of a spermatozoon which belonged to its father's body, that the egg (that is to say, the fertilised ovum) is a veritable connecting link between the two progenitors, since it is common to their two substances, one perceives that every individual organism, even that of a man, is a mere bud which has sprouted on the combined body of its two parents. Where, then, does the vital principle of the individual begin, where does it end? Step by step, one will go back to its remotest ancestors; one will find it bound up with each of them, bound up with that little mass of protoplasmic jelly which is no doubt at the root of the genealogical tree of life. Being one, in a certain measure, with this primitive ancestor, it is equally bound up with everything that has broken away from it by way of divergent descent: in this sense one may say that it remains united with the totality of the living by invisible bonds. It is therefore in vain that one claims to narrow finality down to the individuality of the living being. If there is finality in the world of life, it embraces the whole of life in a single indivisible embrace. This life common to all the living presents, without any doubt, many incoherences and many gaps, and on the other hand it is not so mathematically one that it cannot let each living being individualise itself in a certain measure. It forms none the less a single whole; and one must choose between the pure and simple negation of finality and the hypothesis which co-ordinates not only the parts of an organism with the organism itself, but also each living being with the totality of the others. It is not by pulverising finality that one will make it go down more easily. Either the hypothesis of a finality immanent in life must be rejected en bloc, or it is in quite another sense, I believe, that it must be modified. The error of radical finalism, as indeed that of radical mechanism, is to extend too far the application of certain concepts natural to our intellect. Originally, we think only in order to act. It is in the mould of action that our intellect has been cast. Speculation is a luxury, whereas action is a necessity. Now, in order to act, we begin by setting ourselves an aim; we make a plan, then we pass to the detail of the mechanism that will realise it. This last operation is possible only if we know what we can count on. We must have extracted from nature similarities which allow us to anticipate the future. We must therefore have applied, consciously or unconsciously, the law of causality. Moreover, the more sharply the idea of efficient causality takes shape in our mind, the more efficient causality takes the form of a mechanical causality. This latter relation, in its turn, is the more mathematical the more rigorous the necessity it expresses. That is why we have only to follow the bent of our mind to become mathematicians. But, on the other hand, this natural mathematics is only the unconscious support of our conscious habit of linking the same causes to the same effects; and this habit itself has as its ordinary object to guide actions inspired by intentions or, what comes to the same thing, to direct movements combined with a view to the execution of a model: we are born artisans as we are born geometers, and indeed we are geometers only because we are artisans. Thus the human intellect, in so far as it is fashioned to the demands of human action, is an intellect which proceeds at once by intention and by calculation, by the co-ordination of means to an end and by the representation of mechanisms of more and more geometrical form. Whether one pictures nature as an immense machine governed by mathematical laws or sees in it the realisation of a plan, one is only, in both cases, following to the end two tendencies of the mind which are complementary to each other and which have their origin in the same vital necessities. That is why radical finalism is very close to radical mechanism on most points. Both doctrines are averse to seeing in the course of things, or even simply in the development of life, an unforeseeable creation of form. Mechanism considers only the aspect of similarity or repetition in reality. It is therefore dominated by this law, that in nature there is only the same reproducing the same. The more clearly the geometry it contains comes out, the less it can admit that anything is created, were it only form. In so far as we are geometers, then, we reject the unforeseeable. We might accept it, assuredly, in so far as we are artists, for art lives on creation and implies a latent belief in the spontaneity of nature. But disinterested art is a luxury, like pure speculation. Long before being artists, we are artisans. And all manufacture, however rudimentary it may be, lives on similarities and repetitions, like the natural geometry which serves it as a point of support. It works on models which it sets itself to reproduce. And when it invents, it proceeds, or imagines it proceeds, by a new arrangement of known elements. Its principle is that "it takes the same to obtain the same". In short, the rigorous application of the principle of finality, like that of the principle of mechanical causality, leads to the conclusion that "all is given". The two principles say the same thing in their two languages, because they answer the same need. That is why they also agree in making a clean sweep of time. Real duration is the duration which bites into things and leaves on them the mark of its tooth. If everything is in time, everything changes inwardly, and the same concrete reality never repeats itself. Repetition is therefore possible only in the abstract: what is repeated is this or that aspect which our senses, and above all our intellect, have detached from reality, precisely because our action, towards which the whole effort of our intellect is bent, can move only among repetitions. Thus, concentrated on what is repeated, solely preoccupied with welding the same to the same, the intellect turns away from the vision of time. It is averse to the fluid and solidifies everything it touches. We do not think real time. But we live it, because life overflows the intellect. The feeling we have of our evolution and of the evolution of all things in pure duration is there, tracing around the intellectual representation properly so called an indistinct fringe that fades off into the night. Mechanism and finalism agree in taking account only of the luminous nucleus that shines at the centre. They forget that this nucleus has been formed at the expense of the rest by way of condensation, and that one would have to make use of everything, of the fluid as much as and more than of the condensed, to grasp again the inner movement of life. To tell the truth, if the fringe exists, however indistinct and blurred, it must be of even greater importance to the philosopher than the luminous nucleus it surrounds. For it is its presence that allows us to affirm that the nucleus is a nucleus, that pure intellect is a narrowing, by condensation, of a vaster power. And, precisely because this vague intuition is of no help to us in directing our action on things, an action wholly localised at the surface of the real, one may presume that it is exercised no longer merely on the surface, but in depth. As soon as we step out of the frames in which mechanism and radical finalism enclose our thought, reality appears to us as an uninterrupted upsurge of novelties, each of which has no sooner arisen to make the present than it has already receded into the past: at that precise instant it falls under the gaze of the intellect, whose eyes are eternally turned backwards. Such is already the case with our inner life. For each of our acts one will find without difficulty antecedents of which it would be, in a sense, the mechanical resultant. And one will say just as well that each action is the fulfilment of an intention. In this sense mechanism is everywhere, and finality everywhere, in the evolution of our conduct. But provided only that the action involves the whole of our person and is truly ours, it could not have been foreseen, even though its antecedents explain it once it is accomplished. And, while realising an intention, it differs, being a present and new reality, from the intention, which could only be a project of beginning again or rearranging the past. Mechanism and finalism are therefore here only external views taken of our conduct. They extract its intellectuality. But our conduct slips between the two and extends much further. This does not mean, once again, that the free action is the capricious, unreasonable action. To behave by caprice consists in oscillating mechanically between two or more ready-made courses and yet at last settling on one of them: it is not to have matured an inner situation, it is not to have evolved; it is, however paradoxical this assertion may seem, to have bent the will to imitate the mechanism of the intellect. On the contrary, a conduct truly ours is that of a will which does not seek to counterfeit the intellect and which, remaining itself, that is to say evolving, arrives by way of gradual maturation at acts which the intellect can resolve indefinitely into intelligible elements without ever quite getting there: the free act is incommensurable with the idea, and its "rationality" must be defined by this very incommensurability, which allows one to find in it as much intelligibility as one pleases. Such is the character of our inner evolution. And such too, no doubt, is that of the evolution of life. Our reason, incurably presumptuous, imagines that it possesses by right of birth or by right of conquest, innate or learned, all the essential elements of the knowledge of truth. Even where it admits that it does not know the object presented to it, it believes that its ignorance bears only on the question which of its old categories suits the new object. Into which drawer, ready to open, shall we put it? With which garment, already cut, are we going to clothe it? Is it this, or that, or something else? And "this" and "that" and "something else" are always for us the already conceived, the already known. The idea that we might have to create from scratch, for a new object, a new concept, perhaps a new method of thinking, is profoundly repugnant to us. Yet the history of philosophy is there, showing us the eternal conflict of systems, the impossibility of fitting the real once and for all into those ready-made garments which are our ready-made concepts, the necessity of working to measure. Rather than come to this extremity, our reason prefers to announce once and for all, with a proud modesty, that it will know only the relative and that the absolute is not within its competence: this preliminary declaration allows it to apply its habitual method of thinking without scruple and, on the pretext that it does not touch the absolute, to decide absolutely about all things. Plato was the first to set up as a theory that to know the real consists in finding its Idea, that is to say in fitting it into a pre-existing frame which would already be at our disposal, – as if we implicitly possessed universal science. But this belief is natural to the human intellect, always preoccupied with knowing under which old heading it will catalogue any new object whatever, and one might say, in a certain sense, that we are all born Platonists. Nowhere is the impotence of this method displayed so manifestly as in theories of life. If, in evolving in the direction of the Vertebrates in general, of man and the intellect in particular, Life has had to abandon on the way many elements incompatible with this particular mode of organisation and entrust them, as I shall show, to other lines of development, it is the totality of these elements that we shall have to seek out and fuse with the intellect proper, in order to grasp again the true nature of vital activity. We shall no doubt be helped in this, moreover, by the fringe of confused representation that surrounds our distinct, I mean intellectual, representation: what can this useless fringe be, in fact, if not the part of the evolving principle which has not shrunk to the special form of our organisation and which has been smuggled in? It is there, then, that we shall have to go to look for indications for dilating the intellectual form of our thought; it is from there that we shall draw the impetus needed to raise ourselves above ourselves. To represent to oneself the whole of life cannot consist in combining with one another simple ideas deposited in us by life itself in the course of its evolution: how could the part be equivalent to the whole, the content to the container, a residue of the vital operation to the operation itself? Such, however, is our illusion when we define the evolution of life as "the passage from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous", or by any other concept obtained by putting together fragments of intellect. We place ourselves at one of the terminal points of evolution, no doubt the principal one, but not the only one; and even at this point we do not take all that is to be found there, for we retain of the intellect only one or two of the concepts in which it expresses itself: and it is this part of a part that we declare representative of the whole, indeed of something that overflows the consolidated whole, I mean of the evolutionary movement of which this "whole" is only the present phase! The truth is that it would not be too much, it would not be enough here, to take the entire intellect. One would still have to bring together with it what we find at each other terminal point of evolution. And one would have to consider these diverse and divergent elements as so many extracts which are, or at least which were, in their humblest form, complementary to one another. Only then should we have an inkling of the real nature of the evolutionary movement; – and even then we should only have an inkling of it, for we should still have to do only with the evolved, which is a result, and not with evolution itself, that is to say with the act by which the result is obtained. Such is the philosophy of life towards which I am making my way. It claims to go beyond both mechanism and finalism; but, as I announced at the outset, it comes closer to the second doctrine than to the first. It will not be useless to insist on this point, and to show in more precise terms where it resembles finalism, and where it differs from it. Like radical finalism, though in a vaguer form, it will represent the organised world to us as a harmonious whole. But this harmony is far from being as perfect as has been claimed. It admits of many discords, because each species, even each individual, retains of the total impulse of life only a certain impetus, and tends to use this energy in its own interest; this is what adaptation consists in. The species and the individual thus think only of themselves, – whence a possible conflict with the other forms of life. Harmony does not therefore exist in fact; it exists rather in principle: I mean that the original impetus is a common impetus and that, the higher one goes back, the more the various tendencies appear complementary to one another. So the wind that rushes into a crossroads divides into divergent currents of air, which are all only one and the same breath. Harmony, or rather "complementarity", reveals itself only in the large, in tendencies rather than in states. Above all (and this is the point on which finalism has most gravely erred), harmony would be found behind rather than ahead. It is due to an identity of impulsion and not to a common aspiration. It is in vain that one would assign to life an aim, in the human sense of the word. To speak of an aim is to think of a pre-existing model which has only to be realised. It is therefore to suppose, at bottom, that all is given, that the future could be read in the present. It is to believe that life, in its movement and in its integrity, proceeds like our intellect, which is only a motionless and fragmentary view taken of it, and which naturally places itself always outside time. Life, for its part, progresses and endures. No doubt one will always be able, by casting a glance over the road once travelled, to mark its direction, to note it in psychological terms and to speak as if there had been the pursuit of an aim. This is how I shall speak myself. But of the road that was going to be travelled the human mind has nothing to say, for the road has been created step by step with the act that travelled it, being nothing but the direction of that act itself. Evolution must therefore admit at every moment of a psychological interpretation which is, from our point of view, the best explanation of it, but this explanation has value, and even meaning, only in the retroactive sense. Never must the finalist interpretation, such as I shall propose it, be taken for an anticipation of the future. It is a certain vision of the past in the light of the present. In short, the classical conception of finality postulates at once too much and too little. It is too broad and too narrow. In explaining life by the intellect, it narrows the meaning of life to excess; the intellect, at least as we find it in ourselves, has been fashioned by evolution in the course of the journey; it is cut out of something vaster, or rather it is only the necessarily flat projection of a reality which has relief and depth. It is this more comprehensive reality which true finalism ought to reconstitute, or rather embrace, if possible, in a simple vision. But, on the other hand, precisely because it overflows the intellect, the faculty of linking the same to the same, of perceiving and also of producing repetitions, this reality is no doubt creative, that is to say productive of effects in which it dilates and surpasses itself: these effects were therefore not given in it in advance, and consequently it could not take them for ends, even though, once produced, they admit of a rational interpretation, like that of the manufactured object which has realised a model. In short, the theory of final causes does not go far enough when it confines itself to putting intellect into nature, and it goes too far when it supposes a pre-existence of the future in the present in the form of an idea. The second thesis, which sins by excess, is moreover the consequence of the first, which sins by defect. For the intellect proper we must substitute the more comprehensive reality of which the intellect is only the narrowing. The future then appears as dilating the present. It was therefore not contained in the present in the form of a represented end. And nevertheless, once realised, it will explain the present as much as the present explained it, and even more; it will have to be regarded as an end as much as, and more than, as a result. Our intellect has the right to consider it abstractly from its habitual point of view, being itself an abstraction performed on the cause from which it emanates. It is true that the cause then seems to elude our grasp. Already the finalist theory of life escapes all precise verification. What will it be, people will say, if we go further than it in one of its directions? Here we are back, in fact, after a necessary digression, at the question I hold to be essential: can the insufficiency of mechanism be proved by the facts? I announced that, if this demonstration is possible, it is on condition that one places oneself frankly within the evolutionist hypothesis. The moment has come to establish that, if mechanism is not enough to account for evolution, the way to prove this insufficiency is not to stop at the classical conception of finality, still less to narrow or attenuate it, but on the contrary to go further than it. Let me indicate at once the principle of my demonstration. I said that life, from its origins, is the continuation of one and the same impetus which has divided itself among divergent lines of evolution. Something has grown, something has developed through a series of additions which have been so many creations. It is this very development that has caused tendencies to dissociate which could not grow beyond a certain point without becoming incompatible with one another. Strictly speaking, nothing would prevent one from imagining a single individual in whom, as a result of transformations spread over thousands of centuries, the evolution of life would have been accomplished. Or again, failing a single individual, one could suppose a plurality of individuals succeeding one another in a unilinear series. In both cases evolution would have had, if one may so express it, only one dimension. But evolution has in reality taken place through the intermediary of millions of individuals on divergent lines, each of which itself ended at a crossroads from which new paths radiated, and so on indefinitely. If my hypothesis is well founded, if the essential causes at work along these various paths are of a psychological nature, they must preserve something in common in spite of the divergence of their effects, as comrades long separated keep the same childhood memories. Bifurcations may well have occurred, side roads may have opened in which the dissociated elements unfolded independently; it is none the less by the primitive impetus of the whole that the movement of the parts continues. Something of the whole must therefore subsist in the parts. And this common element may be made perceptible to the eye in a certain way, perhaps by the presence of identical organs in very different organisms. Let us suppose, for a moment, that mechanism is the truth: evolution will have taken place through a series of accidents added to one another, each new accident being preserved by selection if it is advantageous to that sum of earlier advantageous accidents which the present form of the living being represents. What chance will there be that, through two entirely different series of accidents being added up, two entirely different evolutions should arrive at similar results? The more two lines of evolution diverge, the less probability there will be that accidental external influences or accidental internal variations should have determined on them the construction of identical apparatuses, especially if there was no trace of these apparatuses at the moment when the bifurcation took place. This similarity would be natural, on the contrary, something of the impulse received at the source. Pure mechanism would therefore be refutable, and finality, in the special sense in which I understand it, demonstrable in a certain respect, if one could establish that life manufactures certain identical apparatuses, by dissimilar means, on divergent lines of evolution. The force of the proof would moreover be proportional to the degree of separation of the lines of evolution chosen, and to the degree of complexity of the similar structures found on them. It will be alleged that the similarity of structure is due to the identity of the general conditions in which life has evolved. These lasting external conditions would have impressed the same direction on the forces constructing this or that apparatus, in spite of the diversity of transient external influences and of accidental internal variations. – I am not unaware, indeed, of the role which the concept of adaptation plays in contemporary science. Certainly, biologists do not all make the same use of it. For some, external conditions are capable of directly causing the variation of organisms in a definite direction, through the physico-chemical modifications they bring about in the living substance: such is the hypothesis of Eimer, for example. For others, more faithful to the spirit of Darwinism, the influence of conditions is exercised only in an indirect manner, by favouring, in the struggle for life, those representatives of a species whom the chance of birth has better adapted to the environment. In other words, some attribute to external conditions a positive influence and others a negative action: on the first hypothesis this cause would call forth variations, on the second it would only eliminate them. But in both cases it is supposed to bring about a precise adjustment of the organism to its conditions of existence. By this common adaptation one will no doubt try to explain mechanically the similarities of structure from which I believe the most formidable argument against mechanism could be drawn. That is why I must indicate at once in broad outline, before passing to the detail, why the explanations one would draw here from "adaptation" seem to me insufficient. Let us note first that, of the two hypotheses just formulated, the second is the only one that does not lend itself to equivocation. The Darwinian idea of an adaptation taking place through the automatic elimination of the unadapted is a simple and clear idea. On the other hand, and precisely because it attributes to the external cause directing evolution a wholly negative influence, it already has great difficulty in accounting for the progressive and rectilinear development of complex apparatuses such as those we are about to examine. What will it be when it seeks to explain the identity of structure of extraordinarily complicated organs on divergent lines of evolution? An accidental variation, however minute, implies the action of a host of small physical and chemical causes. An accumulation of accidental variations, such as is needed to produce a complicated structure, requires the concurrence of a number of infinitesimal causes that is, so to speak, infinite. How could these causes, all accidental, reappear the same, and in the same order, at different points of space and time? No one will maintain this, and the Darwinian himself will no doubt confine himself to saying that identical effects can arise from different causes, that more than one road leads to the same place. But let us not be the dupes of a metaphor. The place one arrives at does not trace the form of the road one has taken to arrive there, whereas an organic structure is the very accumulation of the small differences which evolution has had to pass through in order to attain it. The struggle for life and natural selection can be of no help to us in solving this part of the problem, for we are not concerned here with what has disappeared, we are simply looking at what has been preserved. Now, we see that on independent lines of evolution identical structures have taken shape through a gradual accumulation of effects added to one another. How can one suppose that accidental causes, presenting themselves in an accidental order, have several times arrived at the same result, the causes being infinitely numerous and the effect infinitely complicated? The principle of mechanism is that "the same causes produce the same effects". This principle does not always imply, it is true, that the same effects have the same causes; yet it entails this consequence in the particular case where the causes remain visible in the effect they produce and are its constituent elements. That two walkers who have set out from different points, and wander about the countryside as their whim takes them, should end by meeting, is nothing out of the ordinary. But that, in rambling thus, they should trace identical curves, exactly superposable on each other, is altogether improbable. The improbability will moreover be the greater, the more complicated the windings presented by the paths travelled on either side. And it will become impossibility if the zigzags of the two walkers are of infinite complexity. Now, what is this complication of zigzags beside that of an organ in which thousands of different cells, each of which is a kind of organism, are arranged in a certain order? Let us pass, then, to the second hypothesis, and see how it would solve the problem. Adaptation will no longer consist simply in the elimination of the unadapted. It will be due to the positive influence of external conditions which will have moulded the organism on their own form. It is indeed by the similarity of the cause that the similarity of the effects will be explained this time. We shall be, to all appearance, in pure mechanism. But let us look more closely. We shall see that the explanation is wholly verbal, that we are again the dupes of words, and that the artifice of the solution consists in taking the term "adaptation" in two quite different senses at the same time. If I pour into the same glass, in turn, water and wine, the two liquids will take the same form there, and the similarity of form will be due to the identity of adaptation of the content to the container. Adaptation does then mean mechanical insertion. The reason is that the form to which the matter adapts itself was already there, ready-made, and has imposed its own configuration on the matter. But when one speaks of the adaptation of an organism to the conditions in which it has to live, where is the pre-existing form awaiting its matter? The conditions are not a mould into which life will be inserted and from which it will receive its form: when one reasons thus, one is the dupe of a metaphor. There is as yet no form, and it will be for life to create for itself a form appropriate to the conditions imposed on it. It will have to turn these conditions to account, neutralise their drawbacks and use their advantages, in short respond to external actions by the construction of a machine which bears no resemblance to them. To adapt will here no longer consist in repeating, but in replying, which is quite different. If there is still adaptation, it will be in the sense in which one might say of the solution of a problem in geometry, for example, that it adapts itself to the conditions of the statement. I am quite willing to grant that adaptation so understood explains why different evolutionary processes arrive at similar forms; the same problem does indeed call for the same solution. But one will then have to bring in, as for the solution of a problem in geometry, an intelligent activity, or at least a cause which behaves in the same way. It is finality that one will be reintroducing, and a finality far too laden, this time, with anthropomorphic elements. In a word, if the adaptation spoken of is passive, a mere repetition in relief of what the conditions give in hollow, it will construct nothing of what one wants to make it construct; and if one declares it active, capable of responding with a calculated solution to the problem which the conditions set, one goes further than I do, indeed too far in my view, in the direction I indicated at the outset. But the truth is that one passes surreptitiously from one of these two senses to the other, and takes refuge in the first whenever one is about to be caught red-handed in finalism in the use of the second. It is the second which really serves the current practice of science, but it is the first which most often supplies it with its philosophy. In each particular case one expresses oneself as if the process of adaptation were an effort of the organism to construct a machine capable of getting the best possible advantage out of external conditions: then one speaks of adaptation in general as if it were the very imprint of circumstances, received passively by an indifferent matter. But let us come to the examples. It would be interesting, first, to institute here a general comparison between plants and animals. How can one fail to be struck by the parallel advances that have been accomplished, on both sides, in the direction of sexuality? Not only is fertilisation itself identical in the higher plants with what it is in the animal, since it consists, here as there, in the union of two half-nuclei which differed in their properties and their structure before coming together and which become, immediately afterwards, equivalent to each other; but the preparation of the sexual elements proceeds on both sides under similar conditions: it consists essentially in the reduction of the number of chromosomes and the rejection of a certain quantity of chromatic substance1. Yet plants and animals have evolved on independent lines, favoured by dissimilar circumstances, thwarted by different obstacles. Here are two great series which have gone on diverging. Along each of them, thousands upon thousands of causes have combined to determine the morphological and functional evolution. And yet these infinitely complicated causes have summed up, on both sides, in one and the same effect. Of this effect, moreover, one will hardly dare to say that it is a phenomenon of "adaptation": how can one speak of adaptation, how can one appeal to the pressure of external circumstances, when the very utility of sexual generation is not apparent, when it has been interpreted in the most diverse senses, and when excellent minds see in the sexuality of the plant, at least, a luxury which nature could have done without2? But I do not wish to dwell on facts so controversial. The ambiguity of the term "adaptation", the necessity of going beyond both the point of view of mechanical causality and that of anthropomorphic finality, will appear more clearly from simpler examples. At all times the doctrine of finality has made use of the marvellous structure of the sense organs to assimilate the work of nature to that of an intelligent workman.
