As, moreover, these organs are found in a rudimentary state in the lower animals, as nature offers us all the intermediaries between the pigment spot of the simplest organisms and the infinitely complicated eye of the Vertebrates, one may equally well bring in here the wholly mechanical play of natural selection bringing about an increasing perfection. Finally, if there is a case in which one seems to have the right to invoke adaptation, it is this one. For about the role and meaning of sexual generation, about the relation that binds it to the conditions in which it takes place, one may argue: but the relation of the eye to light is manifest, and when one speaks of adaptation here, one must know what one means. If, then, I could show, in this privileged case, the insufficiency of the principles invoked on either side, my demonstration would at once have reached a fairly high degree of generality. Let us consider the example on which the advocates of finality have always insisted: the structure of an eye such as the human eye. They have had no difficulty in showing that in this so complicated apparatus all the elements are marvellously co-ordinated with one another. In order that vision may take place, says the author of a well-known book on "Final Causes", "the sclerotic must become transparent at one point of its surface, so as to allow the luminous rays to pass through it...; the cornea must correspond precisely to the very opening of the orbit of the eye...; behind this transparent opening there must be converging media...; at the far end of the dark chamber there must be the retina...1; there must be, perpendicular to the retina, an innumerable quantity of transparent cones which allow only the light directed along their axis to reach the nervous membrane2, etc., etc." – To which the reply has been to invite the advocate of final causes to place himself within the evolutionist hypothesis. Everything seems marvellous, indeed, if one considers an eye such as ours, in which thousands of elements are co-ordinated to the unity of the function. But one ought to take the function at its origin, in the Infusorian, where it is reduced to the mere (almost purely chemical) impressionability of a pigment spot to light. This function, which was only an accidental fact at the beginning, may have brought about, either directly through some unknown mechanism, or indirectly, through the sole effect of the advantages it procured for the living being and of the hold it thus offered to natural selection, a slight complication of the organ, which will have carried with it an improvement of the function. Thus, through an indefinite series of actions and reactions between the function and the organ, and without bringing in any extra-mechanical cause, one would explain the progressive formation of an eye as well contrived as ours. The question is difficult to decide, indeed, if one puts it straight away between the function and the organ, as the doctrine of finality did, as mechanism itself does. For organ and function are two terms heterogeneous to each other, which condition each other so closely that it is impossible to say a priori whether, in stating their relation, it is better to begin with the first, as mechanism would have it, or with the second, as the thesis of finality would require. But the discussion would take quite another turn, I believe, if one first compared with each other two terms of the same nature, an organ with an organ, and no longer an organ with its function. This time one might make one's way little by little towards a more and more plausible solution. And one would have the better chance of arriving at it, the more resolutely one then placed oneself within the evolutionist hypothesis. Here, beside the eye of a Vertebrate, is that of a Mollusc such as the Pecten. There are, in the one and in the other, the same essential parts, composed of analogous elements. The eye of the Pecten presents a retina, a cornea, a lens of cellular structure like ours. One even observes in it that peculiar inversion of the retinal elements which is not met with, in general, in the retina of Invertebrates. Now, there is no doubt dispute about the origin of the Molluscs, but whatever opinion one adopts, it will be granted that Molluscs and Vertebrates separated from their common stock long before the appearance of an eye as complex as that of the Pecten. Whence, then, comes the analogy of structure? Let us question on this point, in turn, the two opposed systems of evolutionist explanation, the hypothesis of purely accidental variations, and that of a variation directed in a definite direction under the influence of external conditions. As regards the first, it is well known that it presents itself today in two rather different forms. Darwin had spoken of very slight variations which would add up through the effect of natural selection. He was not unaware of the facts of sudden variation; but these "sports", as he called them, gave in his view only monstrosities incapable of perpetuating themselves, and it was by an accumulation of insensible variations that he accounted for the genesis of species1. Such is still the opinion of many naturalists. It tends, however, to give way to the opposite idea: it would be all at once, through the simultaneous appearance of several new characters, rather different from the old ones, that a new species would be constituted. This latter hypothesis, already put forward by various authors, notably by Bateson in a remarkable book2, has taken on a profound significance and gained very great force since the fine experiments of Hugo de Vries. This botanist, working on Oenothera Lamarckiana, obtained, at the end of a few generations, a certain number of new species. The theory he draws from his experiments is of the highest interest. Species would pass through alternating periods of stability and transformation. When the period of "mutability" arrives, they would produce unexpected forms3. I shall not venture to take sides between this hypothesis and that of insensible variations. I wish simply to show that, small or great, the variations invoked are incapable, if they are accidental, of accounting for a similarity of structure such as the one I have pointed out. Let us first accept, then, the Darwinian thesis of insensible variations. Let us suppose small differences due to chance and continually adding up. It must not be forgotten that all the parts of an organism are necessarily co-ordinated with one another. It matters little to me whether the function is the effect or the cause of the organ: one point is incontestable, namely that the organ will be of service and give a hold to selection only if it functions. Should the fine structure of the retina develop and grow more complicated, this progress, instead of favouring vision, will no doubt disturb it, if the visual centres do not develop at the same time, as well as various parts of the visual organ itself. If the variations are accidental, it is only too evident that they will not come to an understanding among themselves so as to occur in all the parts of the organ at once, in such a way that it continues to perform its function. Darwin understood this well, and it is one of the reasons why he supposes the variation to be insensible4. The difference which arises accidentally at one point of the visual apparatus, being very slight, will not hinder the functioning of the organ; and from then on this first accidental variation can wait, in a sense, for complementary variations to come and add themselves to it and carry vision to a higher degree of perfection. Granted; but if the insensible variation does not hinder the functioning of the eye, neither does it serve it, so long as the complementary variations have not occurred: in that case, how could it be preserved through the effect of selection? Willy-nilly, one will reason as if the small variation were a toothing-stone set in place by the organism and reserved for a later construction. This hypothesis, so little in conformity with Darwin's principles, already seems hard to avoid when one considers an organ which has developed on a single great line of evolution, the eye of the Vertebrates for example. But it will impose itself absolutely if one notes the similarity of structure between the eye of the Vertebrates and that of the Molluscs. How, indeed, is one to suppose that the same small variations, incalculable in number, occurred in the same order on two independent lines of evolution, if they were purely accidental? And how were they preserved by selection and accumulated on both sides, the same ones in the same order, when each of them, taken separately, was of no use whatever? Let us pass, then, to the hypothesis of sudden variations, and see whether it will solve the problem. It lessens the difficulty, no doubt, on one point. On the other hand, it greatly aggravates it on another. If it is by a relatively small number of sudden leaps that the eye of the Molluscs, like that of the Vertebrates, has risen to its present form, I have less difficulty in understanding the similarity of the two organs than if this similarity were composed of an incalculable number of infinitesimal resemblances successively acquired: in both cases it is chance that operates, but in the second one does not ask of it the miracle it would have to perform in the first. Not only is the number of resemblances I have to add up reduced, but I understand better that each of them should have been preserved in order to be added to the others, for the elementary variation is large enough, this time, to secure an advantage for the living being and thus lend itself to the play of selection. Only, here another problem arises, no less formidable: how do all the parts of the visual apparatus, in suddenly changing, remain so well co-ordinated with one another that the eye continues to exercise its function? For the isolated variation of one part will make vision impossible, once this variation is no longer infinitesimal. All the parts must now change at once, and each must consult the others. I am quite willing to grant that a host of variations not co-ordinated with one another arose in less fortunate individuals, that natural selection eliminated them, and that only the viable combination, that is to say the one capable of preserving and improving vision, survived. Still this combination must have been produced. And, supposing chance to have granted this favour once, how can one admit that it repeats it in the course of the history of a species, so as to call forth each time, all at once, new complications, marvellously adjusted to one another, situated in the prolongation of the earlier complications? How, above all, can one suppose that, through a series of mere "accidents", these sudden variations occurred the same, in the same order, implying each time a perfect accord of more and more numerous and complex elements, along two independent lines of evolution? The law of correlation will be invoked, it is true, to which Darwin himself already appealed1. It will be alleged that a change is not localised at a single point of the organism, that it has its necessary repercussion at other points. The examples cited by Darwin have remained classic: white cats with blue eyes are generally deaf, hairless dogs have imperfect teeth, etc. Granted; but let us not now play on the sense of the word "correlation". A set of interdependent changes is one thing, a system of complementary changes is another, that is to say of changes co-ordinated with one another so as to maintain and even to improve the functioning of an organ under more complicated conditions. That an anomaly of the hair system should be accompanied by an anomaly of the teeth calls for no special principle of explanation: hair and teeth are similar formations2, and the same chemical alteration of the germ which hinders the formation of hair must no doubt interfere with that of teeth. It is probably to causes of the same kind that the deafness of white cats with blue eyes is to be attributed. In these various examples the "correlative" changes are only interdependent changes (not to mention that they are in reality lesions, I mean diminutions or suppressions of something, and not additions, which is very different). But when we are told of "correlative" changes occurring all of a sudden in the various parts of the eye, the word is taken in an entirely new sense: what is in question this time is a set of changes not only simultaneous, not only bound together by a community of origin, but also co-ordinated with one another in such a way that the organ continues to perform the same simple function, and even performs it better. That a modification of the germ which influences the formation of the retina should act at the same time also on that of the cornea, the iris, the lens, the visual centres, etc., I grant, strictly speaking, although these are formations far more heterogeneous to one another than hair and teeth no doubt are. But that all these simultaneous variations should take place in the direction of an improvement, or even simply of a maintenance, of vision, is what I cannot admit on the hypothesis of sudden variation, unless one brings in a mysterious principle whose role would be to watch over the interests of the function: but that would be to renounce the idea of an "accidental" variation. In reality, these two senses of the word "correlation" often interfere with each other in the mind of the biologist, just like those of the term "adaptation". And the confusion is almost legitimate in botany, precisely where the theory of the formation of species by sudden variation rests on the most solid experimental basis. In plants, indeed, function is far from being bound up with form as closely as in the animal. Profound morphological differences, such as a change in the shape of the leaves, have no appreciable influence on the exercise of the function and do not therefore require a whole system of complementary readjustments for the plant to remain viable. But it is not so in the animal, especially if one considers an organ such as the eye, of a very complex structure and at the same time of a very delicate functioning. Here one would seek in vain to identify variations that are merely interdependent with variations that are, in addition, complementary. The two senses of the word "correlation" must be carefully distinguished: one would commit a veritable paralogism in adopting one of them in the premisses of the reasoning, and the other in the conclusion. Yet this is just what is done when one invokes the principle of correlation in explanations of detail to account for complementary variations, and then speaks of correlation in general as if it were only any set of variations whatever brought about by any variation whatever of the germ. One begins by using the idea of correlation in current science as an advocate of finality might; one tells oneself that this is simply a convenient way of expressing oneself, that one will correct it and return to pure mechanism when one comes to explain oneself on the nature of principles and passes from science to philosophy. One does then return to mechanism, indeed; but it is on condition of taking the word "correlation" in a new sense, this time unsuited to the detail of explanations. In short, if the accidental variations which determine evolution are insensible variations, one will have to appeal to a good genius, – the genius of the future species, – to preserve and add up these variations, for it is not selection that will take care of it. If, on the other hand, the accidental variations are sudden, the old function will continue to be exercised, or a new function will replace it, only if all the changes that have occurred together complete one another with a view to the accomplishment of one and the same act: one will again have to resort to the good genius, this time to obtain the convergence of the simultaneous changes, as a moment ago to ensure the continuity of direction of the successive variations. Neither in the one case nor in the other can the parallel development of identical complex structures on independent lines of evolution be due to a mere accumulation of accidental variations. Let us come, then, to the second of the two great hypotheses I had to examine. Let us suppose that the variations are due no longer to accidental and internal causes, but to the direct influence of external conditions. Let us see how one would set about accounting for the similarity of structure of the eye in series independent from the phylogenetic point of view. If Molluscs and Vertebrates evolved separately, both have remained exposed to the influence of light. And light is a physical cause giving rise to determinate effects. Acting in a continuous way, it may have produced a continuous variation in a constant direction. No doubt it is improbable that the eye of the Vertebrates and that of the Molluscs were built up by a series of variations due to mere chance. Even granting that light then intervenes as an instrument of selection, so as to let only the useful variations survive, there is no chance that the play of chance, even when thus supervised from outside, should end, in the two cases, in the same juxtaposition of elements co-ordinated in the same way. But it would no longer be the same on the hypothesis that light acted directly on organised matter so as to modify its structure and adapt it, in a way, to its own form. The likeness of the two effects would this time be explained simply by the identity of the cause. The ever more complex eye would be something like the ever deeper imprint of light on a matter which, being organised, possesses a sui generis aptitude for receiving it. But can an organic structure be likened to an imprint? I have already pointed out the ambiguity of the term "adaptation". The gradual complication of a form which fits itself better and better into the mould of outward conditions is one thing; the ever more complex structure of an instrument which derives from these conditions an ever more advantageous benefit is another. In the first case, matter merely receives an imprint; but in the second it reacts actively, it solves a problem. Of these two senses of the word, it is evidently the second that is used when we say that the eye has become better and better adapted to the influence of light. But we pass more or less unconsciously from the second sense to the first, and a purely mechanistic biology will strive to make the passive adaptation of an inert matter, which undergoes the influence of its environment, coincide with the active adaptation of an organism, which derives from this influence an appropriate benefit. I acknowledge, moreover, that nature herself seems to invite our mind to confuse the two kinds of adaptation, for she usually begins with a passive adaptation where she is later to construct a mechanism that will react actively. Thus, in the case before us, it is incontestable that the first rudiment of the eye is found in the pigment spot of the lower organisms: this spot may very well have been produced physically by the very action of light, and we observe a host of intermediaries between the simple spot of pigment and a complicated eye like that of the Vertebrates. - But from the fact that we pass by degrees from one thing to another, it does not follow that the two things are of the same nature. From the fact that an orator first adopts the passions of his audience in order to come afterwards to master them, we shall not conclude that following is the same thing as leading. Now living matter seems to have no other means of turning circumstances to account than to adapt itself to them passively at first: where it is to take the direction of a movement, it begins by adopting it. Life proceeds by insinuation. It is all very well to show us all the intermediaries between a pigment spot and an eye; there will be between the two none the less the same interval as between a photograph and a photographic camera. The photograph has no doubt bent, little by little, in the direction of a photographic camera; but is it light alone, a physical force, that could have brought about this bending and converted an impression left by it into a machine capable of using it? It will be alleged that I am wrongly bringing in considerations of utility, that the eye is not made for seeing, but that we see because we have eyes, that the organ is what it is, and that "utility" is a word by which we designate the functional effects of the structure. But when I say that the eye "turns light to account", I do not mean by this merely that the eye is capable of seeing; I am alluding to the very precise relations that exist between this organ and the apparatus of locomotion. The retina of the Vertebrates is prolonged in an optic nerve, which is itself continued by cerebral centres connected with motor mechanisms. Our eye turns light to account in that it allows us to make use, by movements of reaction, of the objects we see to be advantageous, and to avoid those we see to be harmful. Now it will not be hard to show me that, if light has physically produced a spot of pigment, it can also physically determine the movements of certain organisms: ciliated Infusoria, for example, react to light. No one will maintain, however, that the influence of light has physically caused the formation of a nervous system, a muscular system, an osseous system, all things that are continuous with the apparatus of vision in the Vertebrates. To tell the truth, already when we speak of the gradual formation of the eye, and still more when we connect the eye with what is inseparable from it, we bring in something quite other than the direct action of light. We implicitly attribute to organised matter a certain sui generis capacity, the mysterious power of putting together very complicated machines to turn to account the simple excitation whose influence it undergoes. But this is precisely what people claim to do without. They want physics and chemistry to give us the key to everything. Eimer's major work is instructive in this respect. We know what penetrating effort this biologist made to demonstrate that transformation takes place, through the effect of a continuous influence of the outside on the inside, in a well-defined direction, and not, as Darwin would have it, through accidental variations. His thesis rests on observations of the highest interest, whose starting-point was the study of the course followed by the variation of skin colouring in certain Lizards. On the other hand, the already old experiments of Dorfmeister show that one and the same chrysalis, according as it is subjected to cold or to heat, gives rise to rather different butterflies, which had long been regarded as independent species, Vanessa levana and Vanessa prorsa: an intermediate temperature produces an intermediate form. We might set beside these facts the important transformations observed in a small Crustacean, Artemia salina, when the salinity of the water in which it lives is increased or diminished1. In these various experiments the external agent does seem to behave as a cause of transformation. But in what sense must the word cause be understood here? Without undertaking an exhaustive analysis of the idea of causality, I shall simply point out that three quite different senses of this term are commonly confused. A cause may act by impulsion, by release or by unrolling. The billiard ball that is thrown against another ball determines its movement by impulsion. The spark that brings about the explosion of the powder acts by release. The gradual relaxation of the spring that turns the phonograph unrolls the melody inscribed on the cylinder: if I take the melody being played for an effect, and the relaxation of the spring for the cause, I shall say that the cause here proceeds by unrolling. What distinguishes these three cases from one another is the greater or lesser solidarity between cause and effect. In the first, the quantity and quality of the effect vary with the quantity and quality of the cause. In the second, neither the quality nor the quantity of the effect varies with the quality and quantity of the cause: the effect is invariable. In the third, finally, the quantity of the effect depends on the quantity of the cause, but the cause has no influence on the quality of the effect: the longer the cylinder turns by the action of the spring, the longer will be the portion of the melody I shall hear, but the nature of the melody heard, or of the portion of it I hear, does not depend on the action of the spring. In reality, it is only in the first case that the cause explains its effect; in the other two, the effect is more or less given in advance, and the antecedent invoked is - in different degrees, it is true - its occasion rather than its cause. Now is it in the first sense that the word cause is taken when we say that the salinity of the water is the cause of the transformations of the Artemia, or that the degree of temperature determines the colour and markings of the wings that a certain chrysalis will assume on becoming a butterfly? Evidently not: causality has here a sense intermediate between those of unrolling and release. That is indeed how Eimer himself understands it, moreover, when he speaks of the "kaleidoscopic" character of variation1, or when he says that the variation of organised matter takes place in a definite direction just as inorganic matter crystallises in definite directions2. And that this is a purely physico-chemical process may be granted him, if need be, where changes in the colouring of the skin are concerned. But if this mode of explanation is extended to the case of the gradual formation of the eye of the Vertebrates, for example, we shall have to suppose that the physico-chemistry of the organism is such, here, that the influence of light has made it construct a progressive series of visual apparatuses, all extremely complex, yet all capable of seeing, and seeing better and better3. What more would the most resolute partisan of the doctrine of finality say to characterise this quite special physico-chemistry? And will not the position of a mechanistic philosophy become much more difficult still, once it has been pointed out to it that the egg of a Mollusc cannot have the same chemical composition as that of a Vertebrate, that the organic substance which evolved towards the first of the two forms cannot have been chemically identical with that which took the other direction, and that nevertheless, under the influence of light, it is the same organ that has been constructed in both cases? The more we reflect on it, the more we shall see how contrary this production of the same effect by two different accumulations of an enormous number of small causes is to the principles invoked by mechanistic philosophy. I have concentrated the whole effort of my discussion on an example drawn from phylogenesis. But ontogenesis would have furnished me with facts no less conclusive. At every moment, before our eyes, nature arrives at identical results, in species sometimes closely related to one another, by quite different embryogenic processes. Observations of "heteroblasty" have multiplied in recent years4, and the almost classical theory of the specificity of the embryonic layers has had to be abandoned. To keep, once again, to my comparison between the eye of the Vertebrates and that of the Molluscs, I shall point out that the retina of the Vertebrates is produced by an outgrowth put forth by the rudiment of the brain in the young embryo. It is a genuine nerve centre that has moved out towards the periphery. In the Molluscs, on the contrary, the retina derives from the ectoderm directly, and not indirectly through the medium of the embryonic encephalon. It is indeed, then, different evolutionary processes that end, in man and in the Pecten, in the development of one and the same retina. But even without going so far as to compare with each other two organisms so remote from one another, we should arrive at an identical conclusion by studying, in one and the same organism, certain very curious facts of regeneration. If the crystalline lens of a Triton is removed, we witness the regeneration of the lens by the iris1. Now the original lens had been built up out of the ectoderm, whereas the iris is of mesodermic origin. More than that: if, in the Salamandra maculata, the lens is removed while the iris is left intact, it is still from the upper part of the iris that the regeneration of the lens takes place; but if this upper part of the iris is itself removed, the regeneration is begun in the inner or retinal layer of the remaining region2. Thus parts differently situated, differently constituted, performing different functions in normal times, are capable of making the same substitutions and of manufacturing, when necessary, the same pieces of the machine. We have here indeed one and the same effect obtained by different combinations of causes. Willy-nilly, it is to an internal principle of direction that we shall have to appeal in order to obtain this convergence of effects. The possibility of such a convergence appears neither in the Darwinian, and above all neo-Darwinian, thesis of insensible accidental variations, nor in the hypothesis of sudden accidental variations, nor even in the theory that assigns definite directions to the evolution of the various organs by a kind of mechanical composition between external forces and internal forces. Let us come, then, to the only one of the present forms of evolutionism of which it remains for me to speak, neo-Lamarckism. It is well known that Lamarck attributed to the living being the faculty of varying in consequence of the use or disuse of its organs, and also of transmitting the variation thus acquired to its descendants. It is to a doctrine of the same kind that a certain number of biologists rally today. The variation that ends in producing a new species would not be an accidental variation inherent in the germ itself. Nor would it be governed by a sui generis determinism which would develop determinate characters in a determinate direction, independently of any concern for utility. It would arise from the very effort of the living being to adapt itself to the conditions in which it has to live. This effort might, moreover, be merely the mechanical exercise of certain organs, mechanically brought about by the pressure of external circumstances. But it might also imply consciousness and will, and it is in this latter sense that one of the most eminent representatives of the doctrine, the American naturalist Cope, seems to understand it3. Neo-Lamarckism is therefore, of all the present forms of evolutionism, the only one capable of admitting an internal and psychological principle of development, although it does not necessarily appeal to one. And it is also the only evolutionism that seems to me to account for the formation of identical complex organs on independent lines of development. It is conceivable, indeed, that the same effort to turn the same circumstances to account should arrive at the same result, especially if the problem posed by the external circumstances is one of those that admit of only one solution. It remains to be seen whether the term "effort" must not then be taken in a deeper sense, more psychological even than any neo-Lamarckian supposes. For a mere variation of size is one thing, a change of form another. That an organ can be strengthened and grow by exercise no one will dispute. But it is a long way from that to the progressive development of an eye like that of the Molluscs and the Vertebrates. If this effect is attributed to the prolongation of the influence of light, passively received, we fall back on the thesis I have just criticised. If, on the contrary, it is indeed an internal activity that is invoked, then it is a question of something quite other than what we usually call an effort, for never has effort produced before our eyes the slightest complication of an organ, and yet an enormous number of these complications, admirably co-ordinated with one another, was needed to pass from the pigment spot of the Infusorian to the eye of the Vertebrate. Let us grant, however, this conception of the evolutionary process for animals: how will it be extended to the world of plants? Here the variations of form do not seem always to imply or entail functional changes, and, if the cause of the variation is of a psychological order, it is difficult still to call it effort, unless the meaning of the word is singularly widened. The truth is that we must dig beneath effort itself and look for a deeper cause. We must do so above all, I believe, if we wish to arrive at a cause of regularly hereditary variations. I shall not enter here into the detail of the controversies relating to the transmissibility of acquired characters; still less should I wish to take sides too decidedly on a question that is not within my competence. I cannot, however, remain wholly indifferent to it. Nowhere is there more keenly felt the impossibility for philosophers today of keeping to vague generalities, the obligation upon them to follow scientists into the detail of experiments and to discuss the results with them. If Spencer had begun by putting to himself the question of the inheritance of acquired characters, his evolutionism would no doubt have taken quite another form. If (as seems to me probable) a habit contracted by the individual were transmitted to its descendants only in very exceptional cases, the whole of Spencer's psychology would have to be done over again, and a good part of his philosophy would collapse. Let me say, then, how the problem seems to me to be posed, and in what direction it seems to me that one might seek to solve it. After having been affirmed as a dogma, the transmissibility of acquired characters has been denied no less dogmatically, for reasons drawn a priori from the supposed nature of the germ cells. It is well known how Weismann was led, by his hypothesis of the continuity of the germ-plasm, to regard the germ cells - ova and spermatozoa - as almost independent of the somatic cells. Starting from this, it has been claimed, and many still claim, that the hereditary transmission of an acquired character would be something inconceivable. - But if by chance experience showed that acquired characters are transmissible, it would prove, by that very fact, that the germ-plasm is not as independent of the somatic environment as is said, and the transmissibility of acquired characters would ipso facto become conceivable: which amounts to saying that conceivability and inconceivability have nothing to do with such a matter, and that the question is solely one for experience. But it is precisely here that the difficulty begins. The acquired characters spoken of are most often habits or the effects of habit. And it is rare for there not to be a natural aptitude at the base of a contracted habit. So that one may always ask whether it is really the habit acquired by the soma of the individual that has been transmitted, or whether it might not rather be a natural aptitude, prior to the contracted habit: this aptitude would have remained inherent in the germen that the individual bears within it, as it was already inherent in the individual and consequently in its germ. Thus nothing proves that the Mole became blind because it took up the habit of living underground: it is perhaps because the eyes of the Mole were on the way to atrophy that it had to condemn itself to the subterranean life1. In that case the tendency to lose its sight would have been transmitted from germen to germen without anything having been acquired or lost by the soma of the Mole itself. From the fact that the son of a fencing master has become an excellent fencer much more quickly than his father, we cannot conclude that the habit of the parent has been transmitted to the child, for certain natural dispositions in course of growth may have passed from the producing germen of the father to the producing germen of the son, grown on the way by the effect of the original impetus, and ensured the son a greater suppleness than the father's, without concerning themselves, so to speak, with what the father was doing. So too with many examples drawn from the progressive domestication of animals. It is difficult to know whether it is the contracted habit that is transmitted, or whether it might not rather be a certain natural tendency, the very one that caused this or that particular species, or certain of its representatives, to be chosen for domestication. To tell the truth, when all the doubtful cases are eliminated, all the facts open to several interpretations, there remain hardly any absolutely incontestable examples of peculiarities acquired and transmitted save the famous experiments of Brown-Séquard, repeated and confirmed, moreover, by various physiologists2. By severing the spinal cord or the sciatic nerve in Guinea-pigs, Brown-Séquard brought about an epileptic state which they transmitted to their descendants. Lesions of this same sciatic nerve, of the restiform body, etc., produced in the Guinea-pig various disorders which its offspring could inherit, sometimes in a rather different form: exophthalmia, loss of toes, etc. - But it has not been demonstrated that in these various cases of hereditary transmission there was a genuine influence of the soma of the animal on its germen. Weismann had already objected that Brown-Séquard's operation might have introduced into the body of the Guinea-pig certain special microbes, which would find their nutritive medium in the nervous tissues and would transmit the disease by penetrating into the sexual elements3. This objection was set aside by Brown-Séquard himself4; but another, more plausible, might be made. It follows, indeed, from the experiments of Voisin and Peron that attacks of epilepsy are followed by the elimination of a toxic body capable of producing convulsive accidents in animals by injection5. Perhaps the trophic disorders consequent upon the nervous lesions that Brown-Séquard brought about are expressed precisely in the formation of this convulsive poison. In that case the toxin would pass from the Guinea-pig to its spermatozoon or its ovum, and would determine in the development of the embryo a general disorder, which might nevertheless produce visible effects only at this or that particular point of the organism once evolved. Things would happen here as in the experiments of Charrin, Delamare and Moussu. Pregnant guinea-pigs whose liver or kidney had been impaired transmitted this lesion to their offspring, simply because the impairment of the mother's organ had engendered specific "cytotoxins", which acted on the homologous organ of the foetus1. It is true that in these experiments, as indeed in an earlier observation by the same physiologists2, it is the already formed foetus that is influenced by the toxins. But other researches of Charrin's have succeeded in showing that the same effect can be produced, by an analogous mechanism, on the spermatozoa and the ova3. In short, the inheritance of an acquired peculiarity might be explained, in Brown-Séquard's experiments, by an intoxication of the germ. The lesion, however well localised it may seem, would be transmitted by the same process as the alcoholic taint, for example. But might not the same hold for every acquired peculiarity that becomes hereditary? There is one point, in fact, on which those who affirm and those who deny the transmissibility of acquired characters agree: namely, that certain influences, such as that of alcohol, can be exerted at once on the living being and on the germ-plasm of which it is the holder. In such a case there is inheritance of a taint, and everything happens as if the soma of the parent had acted on its germen, although in reality germen and soma have simply both undergone the action of one and the same cause. This being laid down, let us grant that the soma can influence the germen, as is believed when acquired characters are held to be transmissible. Is not the most natural hypothesis to suppose that things will happen in this second case as in the first, and that the direct effect of this influence of the soma will be a general alteration of the germ-plasm? If this were so, it would be by exception, and in a way by accident, that the modification of the descendant would be the same as that of the parent. It will be as with the inheritance of the alcoholic taint: this no doubt passes from father to children, but it may take a different form in each of the children, and in none of them resemble what it was in the father. Let us call C the change that has occurred in the plasm, C being, moreover, either positive or negative, that is to say representing either the gain or the loss of certain substances. The effect will reproduce its cause exactly, the modification of the germen brought about by a certain modification of a certain part of the soma will determine the same modification of the same part of the new organism in course of formation, only if all the other nascent parts of the latter enjoy, with respect to C, a kind of immunity: the same part will then be modified in the new organism because the formation of that part will have proved alone sensitive to the new influence; - and even so it may be modified in quite another direction than was the corresponding part of the generating organism. I should therefore propose to introduce a distinction between the inheritance of the deviation and that of the character. An individual that acquires a new character thereby deviates from the form it had, and which the germs, or more often the half-germs, of which it is the holder would have reproduced in developing. If this modification does not entail the production of substances capable of modifying the germen, or a general alteration of nutrition liable to deprive the germen of certain of its elements, it will have no effect on the individual's offspring. This is no doubt what happens most often. If, on the contrary, it has some effect, it is probably through the medium of a chemical change that it will have determined in the germ-plasm: this chemical change may, by exception, bring back the original modification in the organism that the germ is about to develop, but there are as many chances, and more, that it will do something else. In this latter case the engendered organism will perhaps deviate from the normal type as much as the generating organism, but it will deviate from it differently. It will have inherited the deviation and not the character. In general, then, the habits contracted by an individual probably have no repercussion on its offspring; and when they have, the modification that has occurred in the descendants may bear no visible resemblance to the original modification. Such at least is the hypothesis that seems to me most probable. In any case, until the contrary is proved, and as long as the decisive experiments called for by an eminent biologist1 have not been instituted, we must keep to the present results of observation. Now, putting things in the most favourable light for the thesis of the transmissibility of acquired characters, supposing that the alleged acquired character is not, in most cases, the more or less belated development of an innate character, the facts show us that hereditary transmission is the exception and not the rule. How are we to expect it to develop an organ such as the eye? When we think of the enormous number of variations, all directed in the same sense, that must be supposed accumulated one upon another in order to pass from the pigment spot of the Infusorian to the eye of the Mollusc and the Vertebrate, we wonder how heredity, as we observe it, could ever have determined this piling up of differences, even supposing that individual efforts could have produced each of them in particular. That is to say that neo-Lamarckism does not seem to me capable of solving the problem, any more than the other forms of evolutionism. In thus submitting the various present forms of evolutionism to a common test, in showing that they all come up against one and the same insurmountable difficulty, I have by no means the intention of dismissing them all alike. Each of them, on the contrary, supported by a considerable number of facts, must be true in its own way. Each of them must correspond to a certain point of view on the process of evolution. Perhaps, moreover, a theory must keep exclusively to a particular point of view in order to remain scientific, that is to say in order to give a precise direction to research in detail. But the reality of which each of these theories takes a partial view must go beyond them all. And this reality is the proper object of philosophy, which is in no way bound to the precision of science, since it aims at no application. Let me indicate, then, in a few words, what each of the three great present forms of evolutionism seems to me to contribute positively to the solution of the problem, what each of them leaves aside, and on what point, in my view, this threefold effort ought to be made to converge in order to obtain a more comprehensive, though by that very fact vaguer, idea of the evolutionary process. The neo-Darwinians are probably right, I believe, when they teach that the essential causes of variation are the differences inherent in the germ that the individual bears, and not the doings of this individual in the course of its career. Where I find it hard to follow these biologists is when they hold the differences inherent in the germ to be purely accidental and individual. I cannot help believing that they are the development of an impulse which passes from germ to germ across the individuals, that they are consequently not pure accidents, and that they might very well appear at the same time, in the same form, in all the representatives of one and the same species, or at least in a certain number of them. Already, moreover, the theory of mutations profoundly modifies Darwinism on this point. It says that at a given moment, after a long period has elapsed, the whole species is seized with a tendency to change. So the tendency to change is not accidental. Accidental, it is true, would be the change itself, if the mutation works, as De Vries would have it, in different directions in the different representatives of the species. But, in the first place, it will have to be seen whether the theory is confirmed on many other plant species (De Vries has verified it only on the Oenothera Lamarckiana1), and next it is not impossible, as I shall explain further on, that the part of chance is much greater in the variation of plants than in that of animals, because in the vegetable world function does not depend so closely on form. Be that as it may, the neo-Darwinians are on the way to admitting that the periods of mutation are determined. The direction of the mutation might therefore be so too, at least in animals, and to the extent that I shall have to indicate. We should thus arrive at a hypothesis like Eimer's, according to which the variations of the different characters would go on, from generation to generation, in definite directions. This hypothesis seems to me plausible, within the limits in which Eimer himself confines it. Certainly the evolution of the organic world cannot be predetermined as a whole. I maintain, on the contrary, that the spontaneity of life is manifested in it by a continual creation of forms succeeding other forms. But this indetermination cannot be complete: it must leave a certain part to determination. An organ such as the eye, for example, would have been built up precisely by a continuous variation in a definite direction. Indeed, I do not see how else the likeness of structure of the eye in species that have not at all the same history could be explained. Where I part company with Eimer is when he claims that combinations of physical and chemical causes suffice to ensure the result. I have tried, on the contrary, to establish, on the precise example of the eye, that if there is "orthogenesis" here, a psychological cause intervenes. It is precisely to a cause of a psychological order that certain neo-Lamarckians have recourse. Therein lies, in my view, one of the soundest points of neo-Lamarckism. But if this cause is only the conscious effort of the individual, it will be able to operate only in a rather restricted number of cases; it will intervene at most in the animal, and not in the vegetable world. In the animal itself it will act only on the points directly or indirectly subject to the influence of the will. Even where it does act, it is not clear how it could obtain a change so profound as an increase of complexity: at most this would be conceivable if acquired characters were transmitted regularly, so as to add themselves together; but this transmission seems to be the exception rather than the rule. A hereditary change in a definite direction, which goes on accumulating and compounding with itself so as to construct an ever more complicated machine, must no doubt be referred to some kind of effort, but to an effort far deeper than individual effort, far more independent of circumstances, common to most of the representatives of one and the same species, inherent in the germs they bear rather than in their substance alone, and thereby assured of being transmitted to their descendants. We thus come back, by a long detour, to the idea from which we started, that of an original impetus of life, passing from one generation of germs to the following generation of germs through the medium of the developed organisms that form the connecting link between the germs. This impetus, preserved along the lines of evolution among which it is divided, is the deep cause of variations, at least of those that are regularly transmitted, that add themselves together, that create new species. In general, when species have begun to diverge from a common stock, they accentuate their divergence as they advance in their evolution. Yet at definite points they may, and even must, evolve identically, if the hypothesis of a common impetus is accepted. This is what it remains for me to show in a more precise way on the very example I have chosen, the formation of the eye in the Molluscs and in the Vertebrates. The idea of an "original impetus" may, moreover, thereby become clearer. Two points are equally striking in an organ such as the eye: the complexity of its structure and the simplicity of its functioning. The eye is composed of distinct parts, such as the sclerotic, the cornea, the retina, the crystalline lens, etc. The detail of each of these parts would go on to infinity. To speak only of the retina, we know that it comprises three superposed layers of nervous elements - multipolar cells, bipolar cells, visual cells - each of which has its individuality and no doubt constitutes a very complex organism: and even this is only a simplified schema of the fine structure of this membrane. The machine that the eye is, is therefore composed of an infinity of machines, all of extreme complexity. Yet vision is a simple fact. As soon as the eye opens, vision takes place. Precisely because the functioning is simple, the slightest inattention on the part of nature in constructing the infinitely complicated machine would have made vision impossible. It is this contrast between the complexity of the organ and the unity of the function that disconcerts the mind. A mechanistic theory will be one that makes us witness the gradual construction of the machine under the influence of external circumstances, intervening directly by an action on the tissues or indirectly by the selection of the best adapted. But whatever form this thesis takes, supposing it to be worth something for the detail of the parts, it throws no light on their correlation. Then comes the doctrine of finality. It says that the parts have been assembled on a preconceived plan, with a view to an end. In this it likens the work of nature to that of the workman, who also proceeds by assembling parts with a view to realising an idea or imitating a model. Mechanism will therefore rightly reproach finalism with its anthropomorphic character. But it does not perceive that it itself proceeds according to this method, merely truncating it. No doubt it has made a clean sweep of the end pursued or of the ideal model. But it too will have it that nature has worked like the human workman, by assembling parts. A mere glance at the development of an embryo would, however, have shown it that life goes about it quite otherwise. It proceeds not by association and addition of elements, but by dissociation and division. We must therefore go beyond both points of view, that of mechanism and that of finalism, which are at bottom only points of view to which the human mind has been led by the spectacle of the work of man. But in what direction are we to go beyond them? I was saying that, from decomposition to decomposition, when we analyse the structure of an organ, we go on to infinity, although the functioning of the whole is a simple thing. This contrast between the infinite complication of the organ and the extreme simplicity of the function is precisely what ought to open our eyes. In general, when one and the same object appears on one side as simple and on the other as infinitely composite, the two aspects are far from having the same importance, or rather the same degree of reality. The simplicity then belongs to the object itself, and the infinity of complication to the views we take of the object in turning around it, to the juxtaposed symbols by which our senses or our intellect represent it to us, more generally to elements of a different order with which we try to imitate it artificially, but with which also it remains incommensurable, being of another nature than they. An artist of genius has painted a figure on the canvas. We can imitate his picture with many-coloured squares of mosaic. And we shall reproduce the curves and shades of the model the better, the smaller, the more numerous, the more varied in tone our squares are. But it would take an infinity of infinitely small elements, presenting an infinity of shades, to obtain the exact equivalent of this figure, which the artist conceived as a simple thing, which he meant to transfer as a whole on to the canvas, and which is the more finished the better it appears as the projection of an indivisible intuition. Now let us suppose our eyes so made that they cannot help seeing in the master's work an effect of mosaic. Or let us suppose our intellect so made that it cannot explain the appearance of the figure on the canvas otherwise than by a work of mosaic. We might then speak simply of an assemblage of little squares, and we should be in the mechanistic hypothesis. We might add that there was needed, besides the materiality of the assemblage, a plan on which the mosaic-worker worked: we should this time be expressing ourselves as finalists. But in neither case should we reach the real process, for there were no squares assembled. It is the picture, I mean the simple act projected on the canvas, which, by the mere fact of entering into our perception, has decomposed itself before our eyes into thousands upon thousands of little squares which present, as recomposed, an admirable arrangement. So the eye, with its marvellous complexity of structure, might be only the simple act of vision, inasmuch as it divides itself for us into a mosaic of cells, whose order seems marvellous to us once we have represented the whole to ourselves as an assemblage. If I raise my hand from A to B, this movement appears to me under two aspects at once. Felt from within, it is a simple, indivisible act. Perceived from without, it is the traversal of a certain curve AB. In this line I shall distinguish as many positions as I please, and the line itself may be defined as a certain co-ordination of these positions with one another. But the positions, infinite in number, and the order that connects the positions with one another, have issued automatically from the indivisible act by which my hand went from A to B. Mechanism would here consist in seeing only the positions. Finalism would take account of their order. But mechanism and finalism would both pass by the movement, which is reality itself. In a certain sense the movement is more than the positions and than their order, for it is enough to give it to oneself, in its indivisible simplicity, for the infinity of successive positions, as well as their order, to be given at one stroke, together with something more which is neither order nor position but which is the essential: mobility. But, in another sense, the movement is less than the series of positions with the order that connects them; for, to arrange points in a certain order, one must first represent the order to oneself and then realise it with points; there must be a work of assemblage and intellect is needed, whereas the simple movement of the hand contains nothing of all this. It is not intelligent, in the human sense of the word, and it is not an assemblage, for it is not made of elements. So too with the relation of the eye to vision. There is in vision more than the component cells of the eye and their reciprocal co-ordination: in this sense neither mechanism nor finalism goes as far as it should. But in another sense mechanism and finalism both go too far, for they attribute to nature the most formidable of the labours of Hercules in holding that it has raised up to the simple act of vision an infinity of infinitely complicated elements, whereas nature has had no more trouble in making an eye than I have in raising my hand. Its simple act has divided itself automatically into an infinity of elements which will be found co-ordinated to one and the same idea, just as the movement of my hand has let fall outside itself an infinity of points which are found to satisfy one and the same equation. But this is what we have great difficulty in understanding, because we cannot help representing organisation to ourselves as a manufacture. Yet to manufacture is one thing, to organise another. The first operation is peculiar to man. It consists in assembling parts of matter that have been cut in such a way that they can be fitted into one another and made to yield a common action. They are arranged, so to speak, around the action which is already their ideal centre. Manufacture therefore goes from the periphery to the centre or, as the philosophers would say, from the many to the one. The work of organisation, on the contrary, goes from the centre to the periphery. It begins at a point that is almost a mathematical point, and spreads around this point in concentric waves that go on ever widening. The work of manufacture is the more effective the greater the quantity of matter at its disposal. It proceeds by concentration and compression. The act of organisation, on the contrary, has something explosive about it: it needs at the start the least possible room, a minimum of matter, as if the organising forces entered space only reluctantly. The spermatozoon, which sets in motion the evolutionary process of embryonic life, is one of the smallest cells of the organism; and even so it is only a small portion of the spermatozoon that really takes part in the operation. But these are only superficial differences. By digging beneath them we should find, I believe, a deeper difference. The manufactured work traces out the form of the work of manufacture. I mean by this that the manufacturer finds again in his product exactly what he has put into it. If he wants to make a machine, he will cut out its pieces one by one, then assemble them: the finished machine will show both the pieces and their assemblage. The whole of the result here represents the whole of the work, and to each part of the work there corresponds a part of the result. Now I acknowledge that positive science can and must proceed as if organisation were a work of the same kind. Only on this condition will it have a hold on organised bodies. Its object is not, indeed, to reveal to us the bottom of things, but to furnish us with the best means of acting on them. Now physics and chemistry are already advanced sciences, and living matter lends itself to our action only in so far as we can treat it by the methods of our physics and our chemistry. Organisation will therefore be scientifically studiable only if the organised body has first been likened to a machine. The cells will be the pieces of the machine, the organism will be their assemblage. And the elementary works that have organised the parts will be deemed to be the real elements of the work that has organised the whole. That is the point of view of science. Quite different, in my view, is that of philosophy. For me, the whole of an organised machine does indeed represent, strictly speaking, the whole of the organising work (though this is true only approximately), but the parts of the machine do not correspond to parts of the work, for the materiality of this machine no longer represents a sum of means employed, but a sum of obstacles avoided - it is a negation rather than a positive reality. Thus, as I have shown in an earlier study, vision is a power which would reach, by right, an infinity of things inaccessible to our gaze. But such a vision would not be prolonged in action; it would suit a phantom and not a living being. The vision of a living being is an effective vision, limited to the objects on which the being can act: it is a canalised vision, and the visual apparatus simply symbolises the work of canalisation. Hence the creation of the visual apparatus is no more explained by the assembling of its anatomical elements than the digging of a canal would be explained by a bringing of earth that had made its banks. The mechanistic thesis would consist in saying that the earth was brought cartload by cartload; finalism would add that the earth was not dumped at random, that the carters followed a plan. But mechanism and finalism would both be mistaken, for the canal was made otherwise. More precisely, eye to the simple act by which we raise the hand. But I supposed that the hand met with no resistance. Let us imagine that, instead of moving through the air, my hand has to pass through iron filings which are compressed and resist in proportion as I advance. At a certain moment my hand will have exhausted its effort, and at that precise moment the grains of filings will have become juxtaposed and co-ordinated in a determinate form, that very form of the hand that stops and of a part of the arm. Now let us suppose that the hand and arm have remained invisible. The onlookers will seek in the grains of filings themselves, and in forces internal to the heap, the reason for the arrangement. Some will refer the position of each grain to the action that the neighbouring grains exert upon it: these will be mechanists. Others will have it that a plan of the whole presided over the detail of these elementary actions: they will be finalists. But the truth is that there has quite simply been one indivisible act, that of the hand passing through the filings: the inexhaustible detail of the movement of the grains, as well as the order of their final arrangement, expresses negatively, in a way, this undivided movement, being the overall form of a resistance and not a synthesis of elementary positive actions. That is why, if we give the name "effect" to the arrangement of the grains and that of "cause" to the movement of the hand, we may say, strictly speaking, that the whole of the effect is explained by the whole of the cause, but to parts of the cause there will in no way correspond parts of the effect. In other words, neither mechanism nor finalism will be in place here, and it is to a sui generis mode of explanation that we shall have to resort. Now, on the hypothesis I propose, the relation of vision to the visual apparatus would be roughly that of the hand to the iron filings which trace out, canalise and limit its movement. The greater the effort of the hand, the farther it goes into the filings. But wherever it stops, instantaneously and automatically the grains balance and co-ordinate with one another. So with vision and its organ. According as the undivided act which constitutes vision advances more or less far, the materiality of the organ is made up of a more or less considerable number of elements co-ordinated with one another, but the order is necessarily complete and perfect. It cannot be partial, because, once again, the real process that gives rise to it has no parts. This is what neither mechanism nor finalism takes into account, and it is what we do not heed either when we marvel at the wonderful structure of an instrument such as the eye. At the bottom of our wonder there is always this idea, that only a part of this order might have been realised, that its complete realisation is a kind of grace. This grace the finalists have dispensed to them all at once by the final cause; the mechanists claim to obtain it little by little through the effect of natural selection; but both alike see in this order something positive and in its cause, consequently, something divisible, admitting of every possible degree of completion. In reality the cause is more or less intense, but it can produce its effect only as a whole and in a completed manner. According as it goes more or less far in the direction of vision, it will give the simple pigmentary masses of a lower organism, or the rudimentary eye of a Serpula, or the already differentiated eye of the Alciope, or the marvellously perfected eye of a Bird; but all these organs, of very unequal complication, will necessarily present an equal co-ordination. That is why, however remote two animal species may be from each other, if on both sides the progress towards vision has gone equally far, there will be the same visual organ on both sides, for the form of the organ only expresses the degree to which the exercise of the function has been obtained. But in speaking of a progress towards vision, are we not coming back to the old conception of finality? It would be so, without any doubt, if this progress required the representation, conscious or unconscious, of an end to be attained. But the truth is that it is effected in virtue of the original impetus of life, that it is implied in this very movement, and that this is precisely why it is found again on independent lines of evolution. If I were now asked why and how it is implied in it, I should answer that life is, above all, a tendency to act on inert matter. The direction of this action is no doubt not predetermined: hence the unforeseeable variety of the forms that life, in evolving, sows along its path. But this action always presents, in a higher or lower degree, the character of contingency; it implies at the very least a rudiment of choice. Now a choice presupposes the anticipatory representation of several possible actions. Possibilities of action must therefore be outlined for the living being before the action itself. Visual perception is nothing else1: the visible outlines of bodies are the design of our eventual action on them. Vision will therefore be found again, in different degrees, in the most diverse animals, and it will manifest itself by the same complexity of structure wherever it has reached the same degree of intensity. I have dwelt on these likenesses of structure in general, and on the example of the eye in particular, because I had to define my attitude towards mechanism on the one hand and finalism on the other. It remains for me now to describe it more precisely in itself. This I shall do by considering the divergent results of evolution, no longer in what they present that is analogous, but in what is mutually complementary about them.

o: Le mouvement évolutif serait chose simple, nous aurions vite fait d'en déterminer la direction, si la vie décrivait une trajectoire unique, comparable à celle d'un boulet plein lancé par un canon. Mais nous avons affaire ici à un obus qui a tout de suite éclaté en fragments, lesquels, étant eux-mêmes des espèces d'obus, ont éclaté à leur tour en fragments destinés à éclater encore, et ainsi de suite pendant fort longtemps. Nous ne percevons que ce qui est le plus près de nous, les mouvements éparpillés des éclats pulvérisés. C'est en partant d'eux que nous devons remonter, de degré en degré, jusqu'au mouvement originel. Quand l'obus éclate, sa fragmentation particulière s'explique tout à la fois par la force explosive de la poudre qu'il renferme et par la résistance que le métal y oppose. Ainsi pour la fragmentation de la vie en individus et en espèces. Elle tient, croyons-nous, à deux séries de causes : la résistance que la vie éprouve de la part de la matière brute, et la force explosive - due à un équilibre instable de tendances - que la vie porte en elle. La résistance de la matière brute est l'obstacle qu'il fallut tourner d'abord. La vie semble y avoir réussi à force d'humilité, en se faisant très petite et très insinuante, biaisant avec les forces physiques et chimiques, consentant même à faire avec elles une partie du chemin, comme l'aiguille de la voie ferrée quand elle adopte pendant quelques instants la direction du rail dont elle veut se détacher. Des phénomènes observés dans les formes les plus élémentaires de la vie on ne peut dire s'ils sont encore physiques et chimiques ou s'ils sont déjà vitaux. Il fallait que la vie entrât ainsi dans les habitudes de la matière brute, pour entraîner peu à peu sur une autre voie cette matière magnétisée. Les formes animées qui parurent d'abord furent donc d'une simplicité extrême. C'étaient sans doute de petites masses de protoplasme à peine différencié, comparables du dehors aux Amibes que nous observons aujourd'hui, mais avec, en plus, la formidable poussée intérieure qui devait les hausser jusqu'aux formes supérieures de la vie. Qu'en vertu de cette poussée les premiers organismes aient cherché à grandir le plus possible, cela nous paraît probable : mais la matière organisée a une limite d'expansion bien vite atteinte. Elle se dédouble plutôt que de croître au delà d'un certain point. Il fallut, sans doute, des siècles d'effort et des prodiges de subtilité pour que la vie tournât ce nouvel obstacle. Elle obtint d'un nombre croissant d'éléments, prêts à se dédoubler, qu'ils restassent unis. Pair la division du travail elle noua entre eux un indissoluble lien. L'organisme complexe et quasi-discontinu fonctionne ainsi comme eût fait une masse vivante continue, qui aurait simplement grandi. Mais les causes vraies et profondes de division étaient celles que la vie portait en elle. Car la vie est tendance, et l'essence d'une tendance est de se développer en forme de gerbe, créant, par le seul fait de sa croissance, des directions divergentes entre lesquelles se partagera son élan. C'est ce que nous observons sur nous-mêmes dans l'évolution de cette tendance spéciale que nous appelons notre caractère. Chacun de nous, en jetant un coup d’œil rétrospectif sur son histoire, constatera que sa personnalité d'enfant, quoique indivisible, réunissait en elle des personnes diverses qui pouvaient rester fondues ensemble parce qu'elles étaient à l'état naissant : cette indécision pleine de promesses est même un des plus grands charmes de l'enfance. Mais les personnalités qui s'entrepénètrent deviennent incompatibles en grandissant, et, comme chacun de nous ne vit qu'une seule vie, force lui est de faire un choix. Nous choisissons en réalité sans cesse, et sans cesse aussi nous abandonnons beaucoup de choses. La route que nous parcourons dans le temps est jonchée des débris de tout ce que nous commencions d'être, de tout ce que nous aurions pu devenir. Mais la nature, qui dispose d'un nombre incalculable de vies, n'est point astreinte à de pareils sacrifices. Elle conserve les diverses tendances qui ont bifurqué en grandissant. Elle crée, avec elles, des séries divergentes d'espèces qui évolueront séparément. Ces séries pourront d'ailleurs être d'inégale importance. L'auteur qui commence un roman met dans son héros une foule de choses auxquelles il est obligé de renoncer à mesure qu'il avance. Peut-être les reprendra-t-il plus tard dans d'autres livres, pour composer avec elles des personnages nouveaux qui apparaîtront comme des extraits ou plutôt comme des compléments du premier ; mais presque toujours ceux-ci auront quelque chose d'étriqué en comparaison du personnage originel. Ainsi pour l'évolution de la vie. Les bifurcations, au cours du trajet, ont été nombreuses, mais il y a eu beaucoup d'impasses à côté de deux ou trois grandes routes ; et de ces routes elles-mêmes une seule, celle qui monte le long des Vertébrés jusqu'à l'homme, a été assez large pour laisser passer librement le grand souffle de la vie. Nous avons cette impression quand nous comparons les sociétés d'Abeilles ou de Fourmis, par exemple, aux sociétés humaines. Les premières sont admirablement disciplinées et unies, mais figées ; les autres sont ouvertes à tous les progrès, mais divisées, et en lutte incessante avec elles-mêmes. L'idéal serait une société toujours en marche et toujours en équilibre, mais cet idéal n'est peut-être pas réalisable : les deux caractères qui voudraient se compléter l'un l'autre, qui se complètent même à l'état embryonnaire, deviennent incompatibles en s'accentuant. Si l'on pouvait parler, autrement que par métaphore, d'une impulsion a la vie sociale, il faudrait dire que le gros de l'impulsion s'est porté le long de la ligne d'évolution qui aboutit à l'homme, et que le reste a été recueilli sur la voie conduisant aux Hyménoptères : les sociétés de Fourmis et d'Abeilles présenteraient ainsi l'aspect complémentaire des nôtres. Mais ce ne serait là qu'une manière de s'exprimer. Il n'y a pas eu d'impulsion particulière à la vie sociale. Il y a simplement le mouvement général de la vie, lequel crée, sur des lignes divergentes, des formes toujours nouvelles. Si des sociétés doivent apparaître sur deux de ces lignes, elles devront manifester la divergence des voies en même temps que la communauté de l'élan. Elles développeront ainsi deux séries de caractères, que nous trouverons vaguement complémentaires l'une de l'autre. L'étude du mouvement évolutif consistera donc à démêler un certain nombre de directions divergentes, à apprécier l'importance de ce qui s'est passé sur chacune d'elles, en un mot à déterminer la nature des tendances dissociées et à en faire le dosage. Combinant alors ces tendances entre elles, on obtiendra une approximation ou plutôt une imitation de l'indivisible principe moteur d'où procédait leur élan. C'est dire qu'on verra dans l'évolution tout autre chose qu'une série d'adaptations aux circonstances, comme le prétend le mécanisme, tout autre chose aussi que la réalisation d'un plan d'ensemble, comme le voudrait la doctrine de la finalité. Que la condition nécessaire de l'évolution soit l'adaptation au milieu, nous ne le contestons aucunement. Il est trop évident qu'une espèce disparaît quand elle ne se plie pas aux conditions d'existence qui lui sont faites. Mais autre chose est reconnaître que les circonstances extérieures sont des forces avec lesquelles l'évolution doit compter, autre chose soutenir qu'elles sont les causes directrices de l'évolution. Cette dernière thèse est celle du mécanisme. Elle exclut absolument l'hypothèse d'un élan originel, je veux dire d'une poussée intérieure qui porterait la vie, par des formes de plus en plus complexes, à des destinées de plus en plus hautes. Cet élan est pourtant visible, et un simple coup d'œil jeté sur les espèces fossiles nous montre que la vie aurait pu se passer d'évoluer, ou n'évoluer que dans des limites très restreintes, si elle avait pris le parti, beaucoup plus commode pour elle, de s'ankyloser dans ses formes primitives. Certains Foraminifères n'ont pas varié depuis l'époque silurienne. Impassibles témoins des révolutions sans nombre qui ont bouleversé notre planète, les Lingules sont aujourd'hui ce qu'elles étaient aux temps les plus reculés de l'ère paléozoïque. La vérité est que l'adaptation explique les sinuosités du mouvement évolutif, mais non pas les directions générales du mouvement, encore moins le mouvement lui-même1. La route qui mène à la ville est bien obligée de monter les côtes et de descendre les pentes, elle s'adapte aux accidents du terrain; mais les accidents de terrain ne sont pas cause de la route et ne lui ont pas non plus imprimé sa direction. A chaque moment ils lui fournissent l'indispensable, le sol même sur lequel elle se pose ; mais si l'on considère le tout de la route et non plus chacune de ses parties, les accidents de terrain n'apparaissent plus que comme des empêchements ou des causes de retard, car la route visait simplement la ville et aurait voulu être une ligne droite. Ainsi pour l'évolution de la vie et pour les circonstances qu'elle traverse, avec cette différence toutefois que l'évolution ne dessine pas une route unique, qu'elle s'engage dans des directions sans pourtant viser des buts, et qu'enfin elle reste inventive jusque dans ses adaptations. Mais, si l'évolution de la vie est autre chose qu'une série d'adaptations à des circonstances accidentelles, elle n'est pas davantage la réalisation d'un plan. Un plan est donné par avance. Il est représenté, ou tout au moins représentable, avant le détail de sa réalisation. L'exécution complète en peut être repoussée dans un avenir lointain, reculée même indéfiniment : l'idée n'en est pas moins formulable, dès maintenant, en termes actuellement donnés. Au contraire si l'évolution est une création sans cesse renouvelée, elle crée au fur et à mesure, non seulement les formes de la vie, mais les idées qui permettraient à une intelligence de la comprendre, les ternies qui serviraient à l'exprimer. C'est dire que son avenir déborde son présent et ne pourrait s'y dessiner en une idée. Là est la première erreur du finalisme. Elle en entraîne une autre, plus grave encore. Si la vie réalise un plan, elle devra manifester une harmonie plus haute à mesure qu'elle avancera plus loin. Telle, la maison dessine de mieux en mieux l'idée de l'architecte tandis que les pierres montent sur les pierres. Au contraire, si l'unité de la vie est tout entière dans l'élan qui la pousse sur la route du temps, l'harmonie n'est pas en avant, mais-en arrière. L'unité vient d'une vis a tergo : elle est donnée au début comme une impulsion, elle n'est pas posée au bout comme un attrait. L'élan se divise de plus en plus en se communiquant. La vie, au fur et à mesure de son progrès, s'éparpille en manifestations qui devront sans doute à la communauté de leur origine d'être complémentaires les unes des autres sous certains aspects, mais qui n'en seront pas moins antagonistes et incompatibles entre elles. Ainsi la désharmonie entre les espèces ira en s'accentuant. Encore n'en avons-nous signalé jusqu'ici que la cause essentielle. Nous avons supposé, pour simplifier, que chaque espèce acceptait l'impulsion reçue pour la transmettre à d'autres, et que, dans tous les sens où la vie évolue, la propagation s'effectuait en ligne droite.
