Of the phenomena observed in the most elementary forms of life we cannot say whether they are still physical and chemical or already vital. Life had thus to enter into the habits of inert matter, in order to draw this magnetised matter little by little on to another track. The animate forms that first appeared were therefore of extreme simplicity. They were no doubt little masses of barely differentiated protoplasm, comparable from without to the Amoebae we observe today, but with, in addition, the tremendous inner thrust that was to raise them up to the higher forms of life. That in virtue of this thrust the first organisms sought to grow as much as possible seems to me probable; but organised matter has a limit of expansion that is very quickly reached. It divides rather than grow beyond a certain point. No doubt centuries of effort and prodigies of subtlety were needed for life to get round this new obstacle. It induced an increasing number of elements, ready to divide, to remain united. By the division of labour it tied between them an indissoluble bond. The complex and quasi-discontinuous organism thus functions as a continuous living mass would have done that had simply grown. But the true and deep causes of division were those that life bore within itself. For life is tendency, and the essence of a tendency is to develop in the form of a sheaf, creating, by the mere fact of its growth, divergent directions among which its impetus will be divided. This is what we observe in ourselves in the evolution of that special tendency we call our character. Each of us, glancing back over his history, will find that his child personality, though indivisible, united in itself various persons, which could remain fused together because they were in the nascent state: this indecision so full of promise is even one of the greatest charms of childhood. But the interpenetrating personalities become incompatible in growing, and, as each of us lives only one life, he is forced to make a choice. We are in reality choosing unceasingly, and unceasingly too we abandon many things. The road we travel in time is strewn with the remains of all that we were beginning to be, of all that we might have become. But nature, which has at its disposal an incalculable number of lives, is in no way bound to such sacrifices. It preserves the various tendencies that have bifurcated in growing. With them it creates divergent series of species which will evolve separately. These series may, moreover, be of unequal importance. The author who begins a novel puts into his hero a host of things which he is obliged to give up as he goes on. Perhaps he will take them up again later in other books, to compose with them new characters who will appear as extracts from, or rather as complements of, the first; but almost always these will have something cramped about them in comparison with the original character. So with the evolution of life. The bifurcations along the way have been numerous, but there have been many blind alleys beside two or three great highways; and of these highways themselves only one, the one that climbs along the Vertebrates up to man, has been wide enough to let the great breath of life pass freely. We have this impression when we compare the societies of Bees or Ants, for example, with human societies. The former are admirably disciplined and united, but fixed; the latter are open to every progress, but divided, and in unceasing conflict with themselves. The ideal would be a society always on the march and always in equilibrium, but this ideal is perhaps not realisable: the two characters which would like to complete each other, which do complete each other in the embryonic state, become incompatible as they become more pronounced. If we could speak, otherwise than by metaphor, of an impulse towards social life, we should have to say that the bulk of the impulse was carried along the line of evolution that ends in man, and that the rest was gathered up on the track leading to the Hymenoptera: the societies of Ants and Bees would thus present the complementary aspect of ours. But this would be only a manner of speaking. There has been no particular impulse towards social life. There is simply the general movement of life, which creates, on divergent lines, ever new forms. If societies are to appear on two of these lines, they will have to manifest the divergence of the paths at the same time as the community of the impetus. They will thus develop two series of characters, which we shall find vaguely complementary to each other. The study of the evolutionary movement will therefore consist in disentangling a certain number of divergent directions, in appraising the importance of what has happened along each of them, in a word in determining the nature of the dissociated tendencies and in measuring out their proportions. Then, by combining these tendencies with one another, we shall obtain an approximation, or rather an imitation, of the indivisible motive principle from which their impetus proceeded. That is to say that we shall see in evolution something quite other than a series of adaptations to circumstances, as mechanism claims, and something quite other also than the realisation of a plan of the whole, as the doctrine of finality would have it. That adaptation to the environment is the necessary condition of evolution I do not in the least dispute. It is only too evident that a species disappears when it does not bend to the conditions of existence imposed on it. But to recognise that external circumstances are forces with which evolution must reckon is one thing; to maintain that they are the directing causes of evolution is another. This latter thesis is that of mechanism. It absolutely excludes the hypothesis of an original impetus, I mean of an inner thrust that would carry life, through ever more complex forms, towards ever higher destinies. Yet this impetus is visible, and a mere glance at fossil species shows us that life could have done without evolving, or could have evolved only within very narrow limits, if it had taken the course, much more convenient for it, of becoming anchylosed in its primitive forms. Certain Foraminifera have not varied since the Silurian epoch. Unmoved witnesses of the countless revolutions that have upheaved our planet, the Lingulae are today what they were in the remotest times of the Palaeozoic era. The truth is that adaptation explains the windings of the evolutionary movement, but not the general directions of the movement, still less the movement itself1. The road that leads to the town is indeed obliged to climb the hills and go down the slopes; it adapts itself to the unevenness of the ground; but the unevenness of the ground is not the cause of the road, nor has it impressed on it its direction. At every moment it furnishes the road with what is indispensable, the very soil on which it lies; but if we consider the whole of the road and no longer each of its parts, the unevenness of the ground appears only as so many hindrances or causes of delay, for the road aimed simply at the town and would have liked to be a straight line. So with the evolution of life and the circumstances through which it passes, with this difference, however, that evolution does not trace a single road, that it takes directions without for all that aiming at ends, and finally that it remains inventive even in its adaptations. But if the evolution of life is something other than a series of adaptations to accidental circumstances, no more is it the realisation of a plan. A plan is given in advance. It is represented, or at least representable, before the detail of its realisation. Its complete execution may be put off to a distant future, even postponed indefinitely: the idea of it is none the less formulable, here and now, in terms that are given at present. If, on the contrary, evolution is a creation unceasingly renewed, it creates as it goes not only the forms of life, but the ideas that would enable an intellect to understand it, the terms that would serve to express it. That is to say that its future overflows its present and could not be sketched out in it as an idea. Therein lies the first error of finalism. It entails another, graver still. If life realises a plan, it will have to manifest a higher harmony the farther it advances. Thus the house traces out the architect's idea better and better as stone rises upon stone. If, on the contrary, the unity of life lies wholly in the impetus that drives it along the road of time, the harmony is not ahead but behind. The unity comes from a vis a tergo: it is given at the start as an impulsion, it is not set at the end as an attraction. The impetus divides more and more in communicating itself. Life, in proportion to its progress, scatters itself in manifestations which will no doubt owe to the community of their origin their being complementary to one another in certain aspects, but which will none the less be antagonistic and incompatible with one another. Thus the disharmony among species will go on increasing. And so far I have indicated only its essential cause. I have supposed, for simplicity's sake, that each species accepted the impulsion received in order to transmit it to others, and that, in every direction in which life evolves, the propagation took place in a straight line. In fact there are species that come to a stop, and there are some that retrace their steps. Evolution is not only a movement forward; in many cases we observe a marking of time, and still more often a deviation or a turning back. It must be so, as I shall show further on, and the same causes that split up the evolutionary movement cause life, in evolving, often to become diverted from itself, hypnotised on the form it has just produced. But there results from this an increasing disorder. No doubt there is progress, if by progress we mean a continuous advance in the general direction that a first impulsion will determine; but this progress is accomplished only on the two or three great lines of evolution along which ever more complex, ever higher forms are outlined: between these lines run a host of secondary paths on which, on the contrary, deviations, halts and setbacks multiply. The philosopher who had begun by laying it down as a principle that every detail is connected with a plan of the whole goes from disappointment to disappointment on the day he comes to examine the facts; and as he had put everything on the same level, he now comes, for not having been willing to allow for accident, to believe that everything is accidental. We must begin, on the contrary, by allowing accident its share, which is very large. We must recognise that not everything in nature is coherent. We shall thereby be led to determine the centres around which the incoherence crystallises. And this very crystallisation will make the rest clear: the great directions will appear, in which life moves in developing the original impulsion. We shall not witness, it is true, the detailed accomplishment of a plan. There is more and better here than a plan being realised. A plan is a term assigned to a labour: it closes the future whose form it traces out. Before the evolution of life, on the contrary, the doors of the future remain wide open. It is a creation that goes on without end in virtue of an initial movement. This movement constitutes the unity of the organised world, a fecund unity, of infinite richness, superior to anything that any intellect could dream of, since the intellect is only one of its aspects or one of its products. But it is easier to define the method than to apply it. The complete interpretation of the evolutionary movement in the past, as I conceive it, would be possible only if the history of the organised world had been written. We are far from such a result. The genealogies proposed for the various species are, most often, problematic. They vary with their authors, with the theoretical views by which they are inspired, and they raise debates which the present state of science does not allow us to settle. But in comparing the various solutions with one another we shall see that the controversy bears on detail rather than on the main lines. By following the main lines as closely as possible, we shall therefore be sure of not going astray. They alone, moreover, matter to us, for I do not aim, as the naturalist does, at recovering the order of succession of the various species, but only at defining the principal directions of their evolution. And even these directions are not all of equal interest to us: it is with the path that leads to man that we must concern ourselves more particularly. I shall not lose sight, then, in following them one and all, of the fact that the main thing is to determine the relation of man to the animal kingdom as a whole, and the place of the animal kingdom itself in the organised world as a whole. To begin with the second point, let me say that no precise character distinguishes the plant from the animal. The attempts made to define the two kingdoms rigorously have always failed. There is not a single property of vegetable life that has not been found, in some degree, in certain animals, not a single characteristic trait of the animal that has not been observed in certain species, or at certain moments, in the vegetable world. It is understandable, then, that biologists enamoured of rigour should have held the distinction between the two kingdoms to be artificial. They would be right, if definition had to proceed here as in the mathematical and physical sciences, by certain static attributes which the object defined possesses and the others do not. Very different, in my view, is the kind of definition that suits the sciences of life. There is hardly any manifestation of life that does not contain, in a rudimentary, or latent, or virtual state, the essential characters of most other manifestations. The difference lies in the proportions. But this difference of proportion will suffice to define the group in which it is found, if it can be established that it is not accidental and that the group, as it evolved, tended more and more to lay stress on these particular characters. In a word, the group will no longer be defined by the possession of certain characters, but by its tendency to accentuate them. If we take up this point of view, if we take less account of states than of tendencies, we find that plants and animals can be defined and distinguished in a precise way, and that they do indeed correspond to two divergent developments of life. This divergence shows itself first in the mode of nutrition. It is well known that the plant takes directly from the air, the water and the soil the elements necessary for the maintenance of life, in particular carbon and nitrogen: it takes them in their mineral form. The animal, on the contrary, can seize upon these same elements only if they have already been fixed for it in organic substances by plants, or by animals which, directly or indirectly, owe them to plants, so that in the last resort it is the plant that feeds the animal. It is true that this law suffers many exceptions among plants. We do not hesitate to class among plants the Drosera, the Dionaea, the Pinguicula, which are insectivorous plants. On the other hand, the Fungi, which occupy so considerable a place in the vegetable world, feed like animals: whether they are ferments, saprophytes or parasites, it is from already formed organic substances that they draw their nourishment. No static definition, therefore, can be drawn from this difference which would automatically settle, in any case whatever, the question whether we are dealing with a plant or with an animal. But this difference can furnish the beginning of a dynamic definition of the two kingdoms, in that it marks the two divergent directions in which plants and animals have taken their flight. It is a remarkable fact that the Fungi, which are spread through nature in such extraordinary abundance, have not been able to evolve. They do not rise organically above the tissues which, in the higher plants, are formed in the embryo-sac of the ovule and precede the germinative development of the new individual1. They are, one might say, the abortions of the vegetable world. Their various species constitute so many blind alleys, as if, in renouncing the ordinary mode of nutrition of plants, they had stopped short on the great highway of vegetable evolution. As for the Droseras, the Dionaeas, and insectivorous plants in general, they feed like other plants through their roots, and they also fix, through their green parts, the carbon of the carbonic acid contained in the atmosphere. The faculty of capturing insects, of absorbing and digesting them, is a faculty that must have arisen in them late, in quite exceptional cases, where the soil, too poor, did not furnish them with sufficient nourishment. Generally speaking, if we attach ourselves less to the presence of characters than to their tendency to develop, and if we hold that tendency to be essential along which evolution has been able to continue indefinitely, we shall say that plants are distinguished from animals by the power of creating organic matter at the expense of mineral elements which they draw directly from the atmosphere, the soil and the water. But with this difference another is connected, a deeper one already. The animal, being unable to fix directly the carbon and nitrogen that are everywhere present, is obliged to seek, in order to feed on them, the plants that have already fixed these elements, or the animals that have themselves borrowed them from the vegetable kingdom. The animal is therefore necessarily mobile. From the Amoeba, which throws out its pseudopodia at random to seize the organic matter scattered in a drop of water, up to the higher animals, which possess sense organs to recognise their prey, locomotor organs to go and seize it, and a nervous system to co-ordinate their movements with their sensations, animal life is characterised, in its general direction, by mobility in space. In its most rudimentary form the animal presents itself as a little mass of protoplasm enveloped at most in a thin albuminoid film which leaves it full freedom to change shape and to move. The vegetable cell, on the contrary, surrounds itself with a cellulose membrane which condemns it to immobility. And from the bottom to the top of the vegetable kingdom there are the same ever more sedentary habits, the plant having no need to move and finding around it, in the atmosphere, in the water and in the soil where it is placed, the mineral elements which it appropriates directly. Certainly, phenomena of movement are also observed in plants. Darwin wrote a fine book on the movements of climbing plants. He studied the manoeuvres of certain insectivorous plants, such as the Drosera and the Dionaea, to seize their prey. The movements of the leaves of the Acacia, of the Sensitive Plant, etc., are well known. Moreover, the circulation of vegetable protoplasm to and fro within its envelope is there to bear witness to its kinship with the protoplasm of animals. Conversely, one would note in a host of animal species (generally parasites) phenomena of fixation analogous to those of plants2. Here again we should be mistaken if we claimed to make of fixity and mobility two characters that would enable us to decide, on simple inspection, whether we are in the presence of a plant or of an animal. But fixity, in the animal, most often appears as a torpor into which the species has fallen, as a refusal to evolve further in a certain direction: it is closely akin to parasitism, and is accompanied by characters that recall those of vegetable life. On the other hand, the movements of plants have neither the frequency nor the variety of those of animals. They usually involve only a part of the organism, and hardly ever extend to the whole organism. In the exceptional cases in which a vague spontaneity shows itself in them, it seems as if we were witnessing the accidental awakening of a normally dormant activity. In short, if mobility and fixity coexist in the vegetable world as in the animal world, the balance is manifestly tipped in favour of fixity in the one case and of mobility in the other. These two opposite tendencies so evidently direct the two evolutions that the two kingdoms might already be defined by them. But fixity and mobility, in their turn, are only the superficial signs of tendencies deeper still. Between mobility and consciousness there is an evident relation. No doubt, the consciousness of the higher organisms seems bound up with certain cerebral arrangements. The more the nervous system develops, the more numerous and the more precise become the movements among which it has the choice, and the more luminous, too, is the consciousness that accompanies them. But neither this mobility, nor this choice, nor consequently this consciousness has as its necessary condition the presence of a nervous system: the nervous system has only canalised in definite directions, and raised to a higher degree of intensity, a rudimentary and vague activity, diffused throughout the mass of the organised substance. The lower we go in the animal series, the more the nervous centres are simplified and also separated from one another; finally the nervous elements disappear, merged in the whole of a less differentiated organism. But the same is true of all the other apparatus, of all the other anatomical elements; and it would be as absurd to refuse consciousness to an animal because it has no brain as to declare it incapable of nourishing itself because it has no stomach. The truth is that the nervous system was born, like the other systems, of a division of labour. It does not create the function, it only raises it to a higher degree of intensity and precision by giving it the double form of reflex activity and voluntary activity. To accomplish a true reflex movement, a whole mechanism set up in the spinal cord or in the medulla is needed. To choose voluntarily among several definite courses of action, cerebral centres are needed, that is to say crossroads from which paths set out leading to motor mechanisms of diverse configuration and equal precision. But where there has not yet taken place a canalisation into nervous elements, still less a concentration of nervous elements into a system, there is something out of which, by way of splitting, both the reflex and the voluntary will come, something which has neither the mechanical precision of the former nor the intelligent hesitations of the latter, but which, partaking in an infinitesimal dose of both, is a reaction simply undecided and therefore already vaguely conscious. This amounts to saying that the humblest organism is conscious in the measure in which it moves freely. Is consciousness here, in relation to movement, the effect or the cause? In one sense it is cause, since its role is to direct locomotion. But in another sense it is effect, for it is motor activity that sustains it, and as soon as this activity disappears, consciousness atrophies or rather falls asleep. In Crustaceans such as the Rhizocephala, which must once have presented a more differentiated structure, fixity and parasitism accompany the degeneration and near disappearance of the nervous system: since, in such a case, the progress of organisation had localised all conscious activity in nervous centres, we may conjecture that consciousness is weaker still in animals of this kind than in organisms much less differentiated, which have never had nervous centres but have remained mobile. How then could the plant, which has fixed itself to the earth and finds its nourishment on the spot, have developed in the direction of conscious activity? The cellulose membrane in which the protoplasm wraps itself, at the same time as it immobilises the simplest vegetable organism, withdraws it in great part from those external excitations which act on the animal as irritants of sensibility and prevent it from falling asleep1. The plant is therefore generally unconscious. Here again we must beware of radical distinctions. Unconsciousness and consciousness are not two labels that can be stuck on mechanically, the one on every vegetable cell, the other on all animals. If consciousness falls asleep in the animal that has degenerated into an immobile parasite, conversely it doubtless awakes in the vegetable that has regained the freedom of its movements, and it awakes in the exact measure in which the vegetable has regained that freedom. Consciousness and unconsciousness nonetheless mark the directions in which the two kingdoms have developed, in this sense, that to find the best specimens of consciousness in the animal we must climb up to the highest representatives of the series, whereas to discover probable cases of vegetable consciousness we must go down as low as possible in the scale of plants, arrive at the zoospores of the Algae, for example, and more generally at those unicellular organisms of which it may be said that they hesitate between the vegetable form and animality. From this point of view, and in this measure, I would define the animal by sensibility and awakened consciousness, the vegetable by consciousness asleep and by insensibility. To sum up, the vegetable manufactures organic substances directly out of mineral substances: this aptitude generally dispenses it from moving and, by that very fact, from feeling. Animals, obliged to go in search of their food, have evolved in the direction of locomotor activity and consequently of a consciousness ever more ample, ever more distinct. Now, that the animal cell and the vegetable cell derive from a common stock, that the first living organisms oscillated between the vegetable form and the animal form, partaking of both at once, seems to me beyond doubt. We have just seen, in fact, that the characteristic tendencies of the evolution of the two kingdoms, although divergent, still coexist today, both in the plant and in the animal. Only the proportion differs. Ordinarily one of the two tendencies covers or crushes the other, but in exceptional circumstances the latter frees itself and regains the lost ground. The mobility and the consciousness of the vegetable cell are not so far asleep that they cannot awake when circumstances permit or require it. And, on the other hand, the evolution of the animal kingdom has been ceaselessly retarded, or arrested, or drawn backwards by the tendency it has kept towards vegetative life. However full, however overflowing the activity of an animal species may indeed appear, torpor and unconsciousness lie in wait for it. It keeps up its part only by an effort, at the price of fatigue. Along the road on which the animal has evolved, numberless failures have occurred, declines that are bound up for the most part with parasitic habits; they are so many switches on to the track of vegetative life. Thus everything leads us to suppose that the vegetable and the animal descend from a common ancestor which united, in the nascent state, the tendencies of both. But the two tendencies which mutually implied each other in this rudimentary form became dissociated as they grew. Hence the world of plants with its fixity and its insensibility, hence the animals with their mobility and their consciousness. There is no need, moreover, in order to explain this splitting, to bring in a mysterious force. It is enough to observe that the living being naturally inclines towards what is most convenient to it, and that vegetables and animals have opted, each on their own side, for two different kinds of convenience in the manner of procuring the carbon and nitrogen they needed. The former, continually and mechanically, draw these elements from a medium that ceaselessly supplies them. The latter, by an action that is discontinuous, concentrated in a few instants, conscious, go and seek these bodies in organisms which have already fixed them. They are two different ways of understanding work or, if one prefers, idleness. And so it seems to me doubtful that nervous elements will ever be discovered in the plant, however rudimentary one supposes them. What corresponds in the plant to the directing will of the animal is, I believe, the direction in which it bends the energy of solar radiation when it makes use of it to break the bonds of carbon with oxygen in carbonic acid. What corresponds in the plant to the sensibility of the animal is the quite special impressionability of its chlorophyll to light. Now, a nervous system being, above all, a mechanism which serves as intermediary between sensations and volitions, the true "nervous system" of the plant seems to me to be the mechanism, or rather the chemism sui generis, which serves as intermediary between the impressionability of its chlorophyll to light and the production of starch. Which amounts to saying that the plant should have no nervous elements, and that the same impetus which led the animal to give itself nerves and nervous centres must have issued, in the plant, in the chlorophyllian function1. This first glance cast over the organised world will allow us to determine in more precise terms what unites the two kingdoms, and also what separates them. Let us suppose, as I suggested in the preceding chapter, that at the root of life there is an effort to graft on to the necessity of physical forces the greatest possible amount of indetermination. This effort cannot result in creating energy, or, if it creates any, the quantity created does not belong to the order of magnitude on which our senses and our instruments of measurement, our experience and our science, have a hold. Everything will therefore happen as if the effort aimed simply at making the best use of a pre-existing energy which it finds at its disposal. It has only one means of succeeding in this: to obtain from matter such an accumulation of potential energy that it can, at a given moment, by working a trigger, obtain the work it needs in order to act. It itself possesses only this power of releasing. But the work of release, though always the same and always smaller than any given quantity, will be the more effective the heavier the weight it makes fall and the greater the height from which it falls, or, in other words, the more considerable the sum of potential energy accumulated and available. In fact, the principal source of the energy usable on the surface of our planet is the Sun. The problem was therefore this: to obtain from the Sun that here and there, on the surface of the earth, it should partially and provisionally suspend its incessant expenditure of usable energy, that it should store up a certain quantity of it, in the form of energy not yet used, in appropriate reservoirs from which it could afterwards flow out at the desired moment, at the desired place, in the desired direction. The substances on which the animal feeds are precisely reservoirs of this kind. Formed of very complex molecules which contain, in the potential state, a considerable sum of chemical energy, they constitute a kind of explosive, which needs only a spark to set free the stored-up force. Now, it is probable that life tended at first to obtain at one stroke both the manufacture of the explosive and the explosion that uses it. In that case the same organism that had directly stored up the energy of solar radiation would have spent it in free movements in space. And that is why we must presume that the first living beings sought, on the one hand, to accumulate unceasingly energy borrowed from the Sun and, on the other hand, to spend it in a discontinuous and explosive manner by movements of locomotion: the chlorophyll-bearing Infusoria, the Euglenae, perhaps still symbolise today, though in a cramped form incapable of evolving, this primordial tendency of life. Does the divergent development of the two kingdoms correspond to what might metaphorically be called the forgetting, by each kingdom, of one of the two halves of the programme? Or else, which is more probable, did the very nature of the matter that life found before it on our planet oppose the two tendencies' evolving very far together in one and the same organism? What is certain is that the vegetable has inclined chiefly in the first direction and the animal in the second. But if, from the beginning, the manufacture of the explosive had the explosion as its object, it is the evolution of the animal, far more than that of the vegetable, that indicates, on the whole, the fundamental direction of life. The "harmony" of the two kingdoms, the complementary characters they present, would then come, in the end, from their developing two tendencies at first fused in one. The more the original and single tendency grows, the harder it finds it to keep united in the same living being the two elements which, in the rudimentary state, are implied in each other. Hence a splitting, hence two divergent evolutions; hence also two series of characters which are opposed on certain points and complete each other on others, but which, whether they complete or oppose each other, always keep a family likeness between them. While the animal evolved, not without accidents along the road, towards an ever freer expenditure of discontinuous energy, the plant rather perfected its system of accumulation on the spot. I shall not dwell on this second point. Let it suffice to say that the plant must in its turn have been greatly served by a new splitting, analogous to the one that had taken place between plants and animals. If the primitive vegetable cell had by itself to fix both its carbon and its nitrogen, it was able almost to give up the second of these two functions on the day when microscopic vegetables inclined exclusively in that direction, specialising moreover in diverse ways in this still complicated work. The microbes which fix the nitrogen of the atmosphere and those which in turn convert ammoniacal compounds into nitrous compounds, and these into nitrates, have rendered to the whole of the vegetable world, by the same dissociation of an originally single tendency, the same kind of service that vegetables in general render to animals. If a special kingdom were created for these microscopic vegetables, it might be said that the microbes of the soil, the vegetables and the animals present to us the analysis, carried out by the matter that life had at its disposal on our planet, of all that life at first contained in a state of reciprocal implication. Is this, properly speaking, a "division of labour"? These words would not give an exact idea of evolution as I represent it. Where there is division of labour there is association, and there is also convergence of effort. On the contrary, the evolution I am speaking of is never accomplished in the direction of an association, but of a dissociation, never towards convergence but towards divergence of efforts. The harmony between terms which complete each other on certain points is not produced, in my view, on the way by a mutual adaptation; on the contrary, it is quite complete only at the start. It derives from an original identity. It comes from the fact that the evolutionary process, which opens out in the form of a sheaf, separates from one another, in proportion as they grow simultaneously, terms at first so well complementary that they were merged. It is far from being the case, moreover, that the elements into which a tendency dissociates all have the same importance, and above all the same power of evolving. I have just distinguished three different kingdoms, if one may so express it, in the organised world. Whereas the first comprises only micro-organisms that have remained in the rudimentary state, animals and vegetables have taken their flight towards very high fortunes. Now this is a fact that ordinarily occurs when a tendency analyses itself. Among the divergent developments to which it gives birth, some continue indefinitely, others come more or less quickly to the end of their tether. These latter do not proceed directly from the primitive tendency, but from one of the elements into which it has divided: they are residual developments, effected and deposited on the way by some truly elementary tendency which itself continues to evolve. As for these truly elementary tendencies, they bear, I believe, a mark by which they can be recognised. This mark is like the trace, still visible in each of them, of what was contained in the original tendency whose elementary directions they represent. The elements of a tendency are not comparable, in fact, to objects juxtaposed in space and mutually exclusive, but rather to psychological states, each of which, though it is first of all itself, yet partakes of the others and so virtually contains the whole personality to which it belongs. There is no essential manifestation of life, I said, that does not present to us, in the rudimentary or virtual state, the characters of the other manifestations. Conversely, when we meet on one line of evolution the recollection, so to speak, of what is developing along the other lines, we must conclude that we are dealing with the dissociated elements of one and the same original tendency. In this sense, vegetables and animals do indeed represent the two great divergent developments of life. If the plant is distinguished from the animal by fixity and insensibility, movement and consciousness slumber in it as recollections which can awake. Besides, alongside these normally sleeping recollections there are some that are awake and active. They are those whose activity does not hinder the development of the elementary tendency itself. This law might be stated: When a tendency analyses itself in developing, each of the particular tendencies thus born would wish to preserve and develop, of the primitive tendency, everything that is not incompatible with the work in which it has specialised. This would precisely explain the fact on which I dwelt at length in the preceding chapter, the formation of identical complex mechanisms on independent lines of evolution. Certain deep analogies between the vegetable and the animal probably have no other cause: sexual generation is perhaps only a luxury for the plant, but the animal had to come to it, and the plant must have been carried to it by the same impetus that drove the animal there, a primitive, original impetus, anterior to the splitting of the two kingdoms. I will say as much of the tendency of the vegetable towards increasing complexity. This tendency is essential to the animal kingdom, which is worked upon by the need of an ever more extended, ever more effective action. But vegetables, which have condemned themselves to insensibility and immobility, show the same tendency only because they received the same impulsion at the start. Recent experiments show them to us varying in any direction whatever when the period of "mutation" arrives; whereas the animal must have evolved, I believe, in much more definite directions. But I shall not dwell further on this original splitting of life. Let us come to the evolution of animals, which concerns us more particularly. What constitutes animality, I said, is the faculty of using a releasing mechanism to convert into "explosive" actions as great a sum as possible of accumulated potential energy. At the beginning the explosion takes place at random, without being able to choose its direction: thus the Amoeba thrusts out its pseudopodial prolongations in all directions at once. But as we rise in the animal series, we see the very form of the body trace out a certain number of well-determined directions along which the energy will travel. These directions are marked by so many chains of nervous elements placed end to end. Now the nervous element has gradually disengaged itself from the barely differentiated mass of organised tissue. We may therefore conjecture that it is in it and its appendages that the faculty of suddenly releasing accumulated energy is concentrated as soon as it appears. In truth, every living cell ceaselessly spends energy in maintaining itself in equilibrium. The vegetable cell, drowsy from the beginning, is wholly absorbed in this work of conservation, as if it took for an end what was at first to be only a means. But in the animal everything converges on action, that is to say on the use of energy for movements of translation. No doubt each animal cell spends a good part of the energy at its disposal, often even the whole of that energy, in living; but the organism as a whole would like to draw as much of it as possible to the points where the movements of locomotion are accomplished. So that, where there exists a nervous system with the sense organs and the motor apparatus that serve it as appendages, everything must happen as if the rest of the body had as its essential function to prepare for them, in order to transmit it to them at the desired moment, the force they will set free by a kind of explosion. The role of food in the higher animals is in fact extremely complex. It serves first to repair the tissues. It next supplies the animal with the heat it needs to make itself as independent as possible of variations in the external temperature. In this way it preserves, maintains and supports the organism in which the nervous system is inserted and on which the nervous elements must live. But these nervous elements would have no reason for existing if this organism did not pass on to them, to themselves and above all to the muscles they actuate, a certain energy to spend, and we may even conjecture that this is, on the whole, the essential and ultimate destination of food. This does not mean that the most considerable part of the food is employed in this work. A State may have to incur enormous expenses to secure the collection of taxes; the sum it will have at its disposal, once the costs of collection are deducted, will perhaps be minimal; it is nonetheless the reason for the tax and for everything that has been spent to obtain its collection. So it is with the energy that the animal asks of alimentary substances. Many facts seem to me to indicate that the nervous and muscular elements occupy this place with respect to the rest of the organism. Let us first glance at the distribution of alimentary substances among the various elements of the living body. These substances fall into two categories, the one quaternary or albuminoid, the other ternary, comprising the carbohydrates and the fats. The former are properly plastic, destined to remake the tissues, although by reason of the carbon they contain they may on occasion become energy-giving. But the energy-giving function is more especially assigned to the latter: these, being deposited in the cell rather than incorporated into its substance, bring it, in the form of chemical potential, an energy of power which will be converted directly into movement or into heat. In short, the role of the former is principally to remake the machine, while the latter supply it with energy. It is natural that the former should have no privileged place of election, since all the parts of the machine need to be maintained. But it is not so with the latter. The carbohydrates are distributed very unequally, and this inequality of distribution seems to me instructive in the highest degree. Carried by the arterial blood in the form of glucose, these substances are in fact deposited, in the form of glycogen, in the various cells that make up the tissues. We know that one of the principal functions of the liver is to keep the glucose content of the blood constant, thanks to the reserves of glycogen that the hepatic cell elaborates. Now, in this circulation of glucose and this accumulation of glycogen, it is easy to see that everything happens as if the entire effort of the organism were employed in supplying with potential energy the elements of muscular tissue and also those of nervous tissue. It proceeds differently in the two cases, but it arrives at the same result. In the first, it ensures the cell a considerable reserve, deposited in it in advance; the quantity of glycogen that the muscles contain is in fact enormous in comparison with what is found in the other tissues. In nervous tissue, on the contrary, the reserve is small (the nervous elements, whose role is simply to liberate the potential energy stored in the muscle, never, moreover, need to furnish much work at a time): but, remarkably, this reserve is restored by the blood at the very moment it is spent, so that the nerve recharges itself with potential energy instantaneously. Muscular tissue and nervous tissue are therefore indeed privileged, the one in being provided with a considerable reserve of energy, the other in being always served at the instant it needs it, and in the exact measure in which it needs it. More particularly, it is from the sensori-motor system that the call for glycogen, that is to say for potential energy, comes here, as if the rest of the organism were there to pass force on to the nervous system and to the muscles that the nerves actuate. Certainly, when we think of the part played by the nervous system (even the sensori-motor system) as regulator of organic life, we may ask whether, in this exchange of good offices between it and the rest of the body, it is truly a master whom the body serves. But we shall already incline to this hypothesis if we consider, in the static state so to speak, the distribution of potential energy among the tissues; and we shall come round to it entirely, I believe, if we reflect on the conditions in which energy is spent and restored. Let us suppose, in fact, that the sensori-motor system is a system like the others, of the same rank as the others. Borne by the organism as a whole, it will wait until a surplus of chemical potential has been supplied to it before it accomplishes work. In other words, it is the production of glycogen that will regulate the consumption of it by the nerves and muscles. Let us suppose, on the contrary, that the sensori-motor system is truly dominant. The duration and the extent of its action will be independent, in some measure at least, of the reserve of glycogen it contains, and even of that which the organism as a whole contains. It will furnish work, and the other tissues will have to manage as best they can to bring it potential energy. Now this is precisely how things happen, as is shown in particular by the experiments of Morat and Dufourt1. If the glycogenic function of the liver depends on the action of the excitatory nerves that govern it, the action of these nerves is subordinate to that of the nerves which set the locomotor muscles in motion, in this sense, that the latter begin by spending without counting, thus consuming glycogen, impoverishing the blood of glucose, and finally causing the liver, which will have had to pour into the impoverished blood part of its reserve of glycogen, to manufacture more. It is therefore indeed from the sensori-motor system, on the whole, that everything starts, it is on it that everything converges, and we may say, without metaphor, that the rest of the organism is at its service. Let us reflect further on what happens in prolonged fasting. It is a remarkable fact that in animals that have died of hunger the brain is found almost intact, while the other organs have lost a greater or smaller part of their weight and their cells have undergone profound alterations1. It seems as though the rest of the body had sustained the nervous system to the last extremity, treating itself as a mere means of which the nervous system is the end. To sum up, if we agree, for brevity's sake, to call "sensori-motor system" the cerebro-spinal nervous system together with the sensory apparatus in which it is prolonged and the locomotor muscles it governs, we may say that a higher organism is essentially constituted by a sensori-motor system installed on apparatus of digestion, respiration, circulation, secretion, etc., whose role is to repair it, to cleanse it, to protect it, to create for it a constant internal medium, and finally and above all to pass on to it potential energy to be converted into locomotor movement2. It is true that the more the nervous function is perfected, the more the functions destined to sustain it have to develop, and the more exacting, consequently, they become on their own account. As nervous activity emerged from the protoplasmic mass in which it was merged, it must have called up around itself activities of every kind on which to rest: these could develop only on other activities, which implied yet others, indefinitely. Thus it is that the complication of functioning in the higher organisms goes on to infinity. The study of one of these organisms therefore makes us go round in a circle, as if everything in it served as a means to everything else. This circle nonetheless has a centre, which is the system of nervous elements stretched between the sense organs and the apparatus of locomotion. I shall not dwell here on a point I treated at length in an earlier work. Let me only recall that the progress of the nervous system has taken place at once in the direction of a more precise adaptation of movements and in that of a greater latitude left to the living being to choose among them. These two tendencies may appear antagonistic, and so indeed they are. A nervous chain, even in its most rudimentary form, nevertheless succeeds in reconciling them. On the one hand, in fact, it traces a well-determined line between one point of the periphery and another, the first sensory and the second motor. It has therefore canalised an activity that was at first diffused in the protoplasmic mass. But on the other hand the elements composing it are probably discontinuous; in any case, even supposing that they anastomose with one another, they present a functional discontinuity, for each of them ends in a kind of crossroads where, no doubt, the nervous impulse can choose its route. From the humblest Monera up to the best-endowed Insects, up to the most intelligent Vertebrates, the progress achieved has been above all a progress of the nervous system, with, at each stage, all the creations and complications of parts that this progress required. As I intimated from the very beginning of this work, the role of life is to insert indetermination into matter. Indeterminate, I mean unforeseeable, are the forms it creates in the course of its evolution. Ever more indeterminate also, I mean ever more free, is the activity to which these forms are to serve as vehicle. A nervous system, with neurones placed end to end in such a way that at the extremity of each of them multiple paths open up, where as many questions present themselves, is a veritable reservoir of indetermination. That the essential part of the vital thrust has gone into the creation of apparatus of this kind is what a mere glance over the organised world as a whole seems to me to show. But concerning this very thrust of life a few clarifications are indispensable. We must not forget that the force which evolves throughout the organised world is a limited force, which always seeks to surpass itself, and always remains inadequate to the work it tends to produce. From the failure to recognise this point have sprung the errors and puerilities of radical finalism. It has represented the whole of the living world as a construction, and as a construction analogous to our own. All its parts would be arranged with a view to the best possible functioning of the machine. Each species would have its reason for existing, its function, its destination. Together they would give a great concert, in which the apparent dissonances would serve only to bring out the fundamental harmony. In short, everything would happen in nature as in the works of human genius, where the result obtained may be minimal, but where there is at least perfect adequacy between the manufactured object and the work of manufacture. Nothing of the kind in the evolution of life. The disproportion there between the work and the result is striking. From bottom to top of the organised world it is always one great effort; but more often than not this effort stops short, now paralysed by contrary forces, now distracted from what it should do by what it is doing, absorbed by the form it is busy taking, hypnotised by it as by a mirror. Even in its most perfect works, when it seems to have triumphed over external resistances and also over its own, it is at the mercy of the materiality it has had to give itself. This is what each of us can experience in himself. Our freedom, in the very movements by which it asserts itself, creates the nascent habits that will stifle it if it does not renew itself by a constant effort: automatism lies in wait for it. The most living thought will freeze in the formula that expresses it. The word turns against the idea. The letter kills the spirit. And our most ardent enthusiasm, when it is externalised in action, sometimes congeals so naturally into a cold calculation of interest or vanity, the one so easily adopts the form of the other, that we might confuse them together, doubt our own sincerity, deny goodness and love, if we did not know that the dead still keep for a while the features of the living. The deep cause of these dissonances lies in an irremediable difference of rhythm. Life in general is mobility itself; the particular manifestations of life accept this mobility only reluctantly and constantly lag behind it. The former always goes forward; the latter would like to mark time. Evolution in general would take place, as far as possible, in a straight line; each special evolution is a circular process. Like eddies of dust raised by the passing wind, the living turn upon themselves, borne up by the great breath of life. They are therefore relatively stable, and counterfeit immobility so well that we treat them as things rather than as progressions, forgetting that the very permanence of their form is only the outline of a movement. Sometimes, however, the invisible breath that bears them is materialised before our eyes in a fleeting apparition. We have this sudden illumination before certain forms of maternal love, so striking and also so touching in most animals, observable even in the solicitude of the plant for its seed. This love, in which some have seen the great mystery of life, would perhaps deliver its secret to us. It shows us each generation bending over the one that will follow it. It allows us to glimpse that the living being is above all a place of passage, and that the essence of life lies in the movement that transmits it. This contrast between life in general and the forms in which it manifests itself presents everywhere the same character. It might be said that life tends to act as much as possible, but that each species prefers to give the smallest possible sum of effort. Regarded in what is its very essence, that is to say as a transition from species to species, life is an ever-growing action. But each of the species through which life passes aims only at its own convenience. It goes towards what demands the least trouble. Absorbed in the form it is about to take, it enters into a half-sleep, in which it is almost wholly ignorant of the rest of life; it shapes itself with a view to the easiest possible exploitation of its immediate surroundings. Thus the act by which life moves towards the creation of a new form, and the act by which this form takes shape, are two different and often antagonistic movements. The first is prolonged into the second, but it cannot be prolonged into it without being distracted from its direction, as would happen to a jumper who, in order to clear the obstacle, was obliged to turn his eyes away from it and look at himself. Living forms are, by their very definition, viable forms. In whatever way the adaptation of the organism to its conditions of existence is explained, this adaptation is necessarily sufficient as soon as the species subsists. In this sense each of the successive species described by palaeontology and zoology was a success won by life. But things take on quite another aspect when we compare each species with the movement that deposited it on its way, and no longer with the conditions into which it has been inserted. Often this movement has deviated, very often too it has been stopped short; what was to have been only a place of passage has become the terminus. From this new point of view failure appears as the rule, success as exceptional and always imperfect. We shall see that, of the four great directions in which animal life engaged itself, two have led to blind alleys, and that on the other two the effort has generally been out of proportion to the result. We lack the documents to reconstruct the detail of this history. We can nevertheless disentangle its main lines. I said that animals and vegetables must have separated fairly soon from their common stock, the vegetable falling asleep in immobility, the animal on the contrary waking more and more and setting out on the conquest of a nervous system. It is probable that the effort of the animal kingdom resulted in creating organisms still simple, but endowed with a certain mobility, and above all sufficiently undecided in form to lend themselves to every future determination. These animals may have resembled some of our Worms, with this difference however, that the Worms living today with which we might compare them are the emptied and fixed specimens of the infinitely plastic forms, pregnant with an indefinite future, which were the common stock of the Echinoderms, the Molluscs, the Arthropods and the Vertebrates. One danger lay in wait for them, an obstacle which doubtless came near to arresting the upward flight of animal life. There is a peculiarity by which one cannot help being struck when one glances at the fauna of primary times. It is the imprisonment of the animal in a more or less hard envelope, which must have hampered and often even paralysed its movements. The Molluscs of that time had a shell more universally than those of today. The Arthropods in general were provided with a carapace; they were Crustaceans. The most ancient Fishes had a bony envelope of extreme hardness1. The explanation of this general fact must be sought, I believe, in a tendency of soft organisms to defend themselves against one another by making themselves, as far as possible, undevourable. Each species, in the act by which it constitutes itself, goes towards what is most convenient to it. Just as, among primitive organisms, some had turned towards animality by giving up manufacturing the organic out of the inorganic and borrowing ready-made organic substances from the organisms already switched on to the track of vegetable life, so among the animal species themselves many contrived to live at the expense of other animals. An organism which is animal, that is to say mobile, can in fact take advantage of its mobility to go in search of defenceless animals and feed on them, quite as well as on vegetables. Thus the more mobile the species became, the more voracious, no doubt, and the more dangerous to one another they became. From this there must have resulted an abrupt arrest of the whole animal world in the progress that was carrying it towards an ever higher mobility; for the hard, calcareous skin of the Echinoderm, the shell of the Mollusc, the carapace of the Crustacean and the ganoid cuirass of the ancient Fishes probably had as their common origin an effort of animal species to protect themselves against hostile species. But this cuirass, behind which the animal took shelter, hampered it in its movements and sometimes immobilised it. If the vegetable renounced consciousness in wrapping itself in a cellulose membrane, the animal that shut itself up in a citadel or in armour condemns itself to a half-sleep. It is in this torpor that the Echinoderms and even the Molluscs live to this day. Arthropods and Vertebrates were doubtless threatened with it as well. They escaped it, and on this fortunate circumstance depends the present flowering of the highest forms of life. In two directions, in fact, we see the thrust of life towards movement regain the upper hand. The Fishes exchange their ganoid cuirass for scales. Long before, the Insects had appeared, they too rid of the cuirass that had protected their ancestors. For the insufficiency of their protective envelope both made up by an agility which enabled them to escape their enemies and also to take the offensive, to choose the place and the moment of the encounter. It is a progress of the same kind that we observe in the evolution of human armament. The first impulse is to seek shelter; the second, which is the better, is to make oneself as supple as possible for flight and above all for attack, attack being still the most effective means of defence. Thus the heavy hoplite was supplanted by the legionary, the knight clad in iron had to give way to the foot-soldier free in his movements, and, in a general way, in the evolution of life as a whole, as in that of human societies, as in that of individual destinies, the greatest successes have gone to those who accepted the greatest risks. The well-understood interest of the animal was therefore to make itself more mobile. As I said with regard to adaptation in general, the transformation of species can always be explained by their particular interest. In this way the immediate cause of variation will be given. But often only the most superficial cause will be given in this way. The deep cause is the impulsion which launched life into the world, which made it divide between vegetables and animals, which switched animality on to suppleness of form, and which, at a certain moment, in the animal kingdom threatened with drowsiness, obtained, on a few points at least, that it should wake up and go forward. On the two paths along which the Vertebrates and the Arthropods evolved separately, development (setting aside the regressions connected with parasitism or any other cause) has consisted above all in a progress of the sensori-motor nervous system. Mobility is sought, suppleness is sought, variety of movements is sought, through much groping, and not without first falling into an exaggeration of mass and brute force. But this search itself has been made in divergent directions. A glance at the nervous system of the Arthropods and at that of the Vertebrates apprises us of the differences. In the former, the body is formed of a more or less long series of juxtaposed rings; motor activity is then distributed among a variable, sometimes considerable, number of appendages, each of which has its speciality. In the others, activity is concentrated on two pairs of limbs only, and these organs perform functions that depend much less strictly on their form1. The independence becomes complete in man, whose hand can carry out any work whatever. That at least is what we see. Behind what we see there is now what we divine, two powers immanent in life and at first merged, which must have dissociated as they grew. To define these powers, we must consider, in the evolution of the Arthropods and in that of the Vertebrates, the species which mark the culminating point on either side. How is this point to be determined? Here again we shall go astray if we aim at geometrical precision. There exists no single and simple sign by which we can recognise that one species is more advanced than another on the same line of evolution. There are multiple characters, which must be compared with one another and weighed in each particular case, to know how far they are essential or accidental, and in what measure they should be taken into account. It is not disputable, for example, that success is the most general criterion of superiority, the two terms being, up to a certain point, synonymous with each other. By success we must understand, when it is a question of the living being, an aptitude to develop in the most diverse media, through the greatest possible variety of obstacles, so as to cover the widest possible extent of the earth. A species which claims the whole earth for its domain is truly a dominating and consequently a superior species. Such is the human species, which will represent the culminating point of the evolution of the Vertebrates. But such also, in the series of the Articulata, are the Insects, and in particular certain Hymenoptera. It has been said that the Ants are masters of the subsoil of the earth, as man is master of the soil. On the other hand, a group of species that appeared late may be a group of degenerates, but for that a special cause of regression must have intervened. By right, this group would be superior to the group from which it derives, since it would correspond to a more advanced stage of evolution. Now man is probably the latest comer among the Vertebrates1. And in the series of the Insects there is nothing later than the Hymenoptera but the Lepidoptera, that is to say, no doubt, a kind of degenerate, a veritable parasite of flowering plants. Thus, by different roads, we are led to the same conclusion. The evolution of the Arthropods would have reached its culminating point with the Insect and in particular with the Hymenoptera, as that of the Vertebrates did with man. Now, if we observe that nowhere is instinct so developed as in the world of Insects, and that in no group of Insects is it so marvellous as in the Hymenoptera, we may say that the whole evolution of the animal kingdom, setting aside the regressions towards vegetative life, has been accomplished on two divergent paths, one of which led to instinct and the other to intellect. Vegetative torpor, instinct and intellect, these then, at last, are the elements which coincided in the vital impulsion common to plants and animals, and which, in the course of a development in which they manifested themselves in the most unforeseen forms, dissociated by the mere fact of their growth. The cardinal error, the one which, handed down since Aristotle, has vitiated most philosophies of nature, is to see in vegetative life, in instinctive life and in rational life three successive degrees of one and the same developing tendency, whereas they are three divergent directions of an activity that split as it grew. The difference between them is not a difference of intensity, nor more generally of degree, but of nature. It is important to go more deeply into this point. We have seen how vegetable life and animal life complete each other and how they are opposed. It is now a matter of showing that intellect and instinct too are opposed and complete each other. But let us first say why we are tempted to see in them activities of which the first would be superior to the second and superimposed upon it, whereas in reality they are not things of the same order, nor things that have succeeded one another, nor things to which ranks can be assigned. The reason is that intellect and instinct, having begun by interpenetrating, retain something of their common origin. Neither is ever met with in the pure state. I said that in the plant the consciousness and mobility of the animal, which have fallen asleep in it, can awake, and that the animal lives under the constant threat of being switched on to the track of vegetative life. The two tendencies of the plant and the animal at first interpenetrated so thoroughly that there has never been a complete break between them: the one continues to haunt the other; everywhere we find them mingled; it is the proportion that differs. So it is with intellect and instinct. There is no intellect in which traces of instinct are not to be discovered, above all no instinct that is not surrounded by a fringe of intellect. It is this fringe of intellect that has been the cause of so many misunderstandings. From the fact that instinct is always more or less intelligent, it has been concluded that intellect and instinct are things of the same order, that there is between them only a difference of complication or of perfection, and above all that one of the two is expressible in terms of the other. In reality they accompany each other only because they complete each other, and they complete each other only because they are different, what is instinctive in instinct being opposite in direction to what is intelligent in intellect. No one will be surprised if I insist on this point. I hold it to be of capital importance. Let me say first that the distinctions I am going to make will be too sharply drawn, precisely because I wish to define, of instinct, what is instinctive in it, and of intellect, what is intelligent in it, whereas every concrete instinct is mixed with intellect, as every real intellect is penetrated by instinct. Moreover, neither intellect nor instinct lends itself to rigid definitions; they are tendencies and not ready-made things. Finally, it must not be forgotten that in the present chapter I am considering intellect and instinct as they issue from the life that deposits them along its course. Now the life manifested by an organism is, in my eyes, a certain effort to obtain certain things from inert matter. No one will be surprised, then, if it is the diversity of this effort that strikes me in instinct and in intellect, and if I see in these two forms of psychical activity, above all, two different methods of action on inert matter. This somewhat narrow way of regarding them will have the advantage of furnishing us with an objective means of distinguishing them. On the other hand, it will give us, of intellect in general and of instinct in general, only the mean position above and below which both constantly oscillate. That is why what follows must be taken only as a schematic drawing, in which the respective outlines of intellect and of instinct will be more strongly marked than they should be, and in which I shall have neglected the shading that comes at once from the indecision of each of them and from their mutual encroachment upon each other. In so obscure a subject, one cannot make too great an effort towards the light. It will always be easy afterwards to make the forms more blurred, to correct whatever is too geometrical in the drawing, and finally to substitute for the stiffness of a schema the suppleness of life. To what date do we trace back the appearance of man on the earth? To the time when the first weapons, the first tools, were manufactured. The memorable quarrel that arose over Boucher de Perthes's discovery in the quarry of Moulin-Quignon has not been forgotten. The question was whether one was dealing with genuine axes or with fragments of flint broken by accident. But that, if they were hatchets, one was indeed in the presence of an intellect, and more particularly of the human intellect, no one doubted for a single instant. Let us open, on the other hand, a collection of anecdotes on the intelligence of animals. We shall see that, alongside many acts explicable by imitation or by the automatic association of images, there are some that we do not hesitate to declare intelligent; foremost among them figure those which bear witness to a thought of manufacture, whether the animal manages to fashion a crude instrument for itself or uses for its own profit an object manufactured by man. The animals that are classed immediately after man from the point of view of intelligence, the Apes and the Elephants, are those which know how to employ, on occasion, an artificial instrument. Below them, but not very far below, will be placed those which recognise a manufactured object: the Fox, for example, which knows very well that a trap is a trap. No doubt there is intellect wherever there is inference; but inference, which consists in a bending of past experience in the direction of present experience, is already a beginning of invention. Invention becomes complete when it is materialised in a manufactured instrument. It is towards this that the intellect of animals tends, as towards an ideal. And if, ordinarily, it does not yet succeed in fashioning artificial objects and making use of them, it prepares itself for this by the very variations it performs on the instincts furnished by nature. As regards the human intellect, it has not been sufficiently noticed that mechanical invention was from the first its essential step, that even today our social life gravitates around the manufacture and use of artificial instruments, that the inventions which mark out the road of progress have also traced its direction. We have difficulty in perceiving this, because the modifications of humanity ordinarily lag behind the transformations of its equipment. Our individual and even social habits survive for quite a long time the circumstances for which they were made, so that the deep effects of an invention make themselves noticed when we have already lost sight of its novelty. A century has passed since the invention of the steam engine, and we are only beginning to feel the deep shock it gave us. The revolution it brought about in industry has nonetheless overturned the relations between men. New ideas are arising. New feelings are on the point of blossoming. In thousands of years, when the distance of the past will allow only its main lines to be perceived, our wars and our revolutions will count for little, supposing they are still remembered; but of the steam engine, with the inventions of every kind that attend it, people will perhaps speak as we speak of bronze or of chipped stone; it will serve to define an age1. If we could strip ourselves of all pride, if, to define our species, we kept strictly to what history and prehistory present to us as the constant characteristic of man and of intellect, we should perhaps say not Homo sapiens, but Homo faber. In short, intellect, considered in what seems to be its original step, is the faculty of manufacturing artificial objects, in particular tools for making tools, and of varying their manufacture indefinitely. Now, does an unintelligent animal also possess tools or machines? Yes, certainly, but here the instrument forms part of the body that uses it. And, corresponding to this instrument, there is an instinct that knows how to make use of it. No doubt it is far from being the case that all instincts consist in a natural faculty of using an innate mechanism. Such a definition would not apply to the instincts which Romanes called "secondary", and more than one "primary" instinct would escape it. But this definition of instinct, like the one I am provisionally giving of intellect, determines at least the ideal limit towards which the very numerous forms of the object defined are moving. It has very often been pointed out that most instincts are the prolongation, or better the completion, of the work of organisation itself. Where does the activity of instinct begin? where does that of nature end? It is impossible to say. In the metamorphoses of the larva into nymph and perfect insect, metamorphoses which often require appropriate steps and a kind of initiative on the part of the larva, there is no sharp line of demarcation between the instinct of the animal and the organising work of living matter. We may say, as we please, that instinct organises the instruments it is going to use, or that organisation is prolonged into the instinct that is to use the organ. The most marvellous instincts of the Insect do no more than develop its special structure into movements, to such a point that, where social life divides labour among the individuals and thus imposes different instincts on them, a corresponding difference of structure is observed: the polymorphism of Ants, Bees, Wasps and certain Pseudoneuroptera is well known. Thus, if we consider only the limiting cases in which we witness the complete triumph of intellect and of instinct, we find between them an essential difference: instinct perfected is a faculty of using and even of constructing organised instruments; intellect perfected is the faculty of manufacturing and employing unorganised instruments. The advantages and drawbacks of these two modes of activity leap to the eye. Instinct finds the appropriate instrument within its reach: this instrument, which manufactures and repairs itself, which presents, like all the works of nature, an infinite complexity of detail and a marvellous simplicity of functioning, does at once, at the desired moment, without difficulty, with a perfection often admirable, what it is called upon to do. On the other hand, it keeps an almost invariable structure, since its modification does not take place without a modification of the species. Instinct is therefore necessarily specialised, being only the use, for a determinate object, of a determinate instrument. The instrument intelligently manufactured, on the contrary, is an imperfect instrument. It is obtained only at the price of an effort. It is almost always laborious to handle. But, since it is made of unorganised matter, it can take any form whatever, serve any purpose whatever, free the living being from every new difficulty that arises, and confer on it an unlimited number of powers. Inferior to the natural instrument for the satisfaction of immediate needs, it has all the more advantage over it the less pressing the need. Above all, it reacts on the nature of the being that manufactured it, for, in calling on it to exercise a new function, it confers on it, so to speak, a richer organisation, being an artificial organ which prolongs the natural organism. For every need it satisfies, it creates a new need, and so, instead of closing, as instinct does, the circle of action within which the animal will move automatically, it opens to this activity an indefinite field into which it pushes it ever further and makes it ever more free. But this advantage of intellect over instinct appears only late, and when intellect, having carried manufacture to its higher degree of power, is already manufacturing machines for manufacturing. At the beginning, the advantages and drawbacks of the manufactured instrument and of the natural instrument balance so well that it is difficult to say which of the two will secure the living being a greater empire over nature. We may conjecture that they began by being implied in each other, that the original psychical activity partook of both at once, and that if we went back far enough into the past we should find instincts closer to intellect than those of our Insects, an intellect nearer to instinct than that of our Vertebrates: elementary intellect and instinct, moreover, prisoners of a matter they do not succeed in mastering. If the force immanent in life were an unlimited force, it would perhaps have developed instinct and intellect indefinitely in the same organisms. But everything seems to indicate that this force is finite, and that it is exhausted fairly quickly in manifesting itself. It is difficult for it to go far in several directions at once. It must choose. Now it has the choice between two ways of acting on inert matter. It can furnish this action immediately by creating for itself an organised instrument with which it will work; or else it can give it mediately in an organism which, instead of possessing the required instrument naturally, will manufacture it itself by fashioning inorganic matter.
