Hence intellect and instinct, which diverge more and more as they develop, but which never separate entirely from each other. On the one hand, in fact, the most perfect instinct of the Insect is accompanied by some glimmers of intellect, were it only in the choice of the place, the moment and the materials of construction: when, exceptionally, Bees build their nests in the open air, they invent new and truly intelligent arrangements to adapt themselves to these new conditions1. But on the other hand intellect has even more need of instinct than instinct has of intellect, for fashioning inert matter already presupposes in the animal a higher degree of organisation, to which it could rise only on the wings of instinct. And so, while nature has evolved frankly towards instinct in the Arthropods, we witness in almost all the Vertebrates the seeking rather than the flowering of intellect. It is still instinct that forms the substratum of their psychical activity, but intellect is there, aspiring to supplant it. It does not succeed in inventing instruments: at least it makes the attempt by performing as many variations as possible on instinct, which it would like to do without. It takes full possession of itself only in man, and this triumph is attested by the very insufficiency of the natural means at man's disposal for defending himself against his enemies, against cold and hunger. This insufficiency, when one seeks to decipher its meaning, acquires the value of a prehistoric document: it is the final dismissal that instinct receives from intellect. It is nonetheless true that nature must have hesitated between two modes of psychical activity, the one assured of immediate success but limited in its effects, the other hazardous but one whose conquests, if it attained independence, could extend indefinitely. The greatest success, moreover, was here again won on the side where the greatest risk lay. Instinct and intellect therefore represent two divergent solutions, equally elegant, of one and the same problem. Hence, it is true, profound differences of internal structure between instinct and intellect. I shall dwell only on those that concern the present study. Let me say, then, that intellect and instinct imply two radically different kinds of knowledge. But some clarifications are first necessary on the subject of consciousness in general. It has been asked how far instinct is conscious. I shall answer that there is here a multitude of differences and degrees, that instinct is more or less conscious in some cases, unconscious in others. The plant, as we shall see, has instincts: it is doubtful whether these instincts are accompanied in it by feeling. Even in the animal there is scarcely a complex instinct to be found that is not unconscious in at least a part of its steps. But we must point out here a difference, too little noticed, between two kinds of unconsciousness, the one consisting in a consciousness that is nil and the other arising from a consciousness that is annulled. Consciousness nil and consciousness annulled are both equal to zero; but the first zero expresses that there is nothing, the second that we are dealing with two equal quantities of opposite sign which compensate and neutralise each other. The unconsciousness of a falling stone is a consciousness that is nil: the stone has no feeling of its fall. Is it the same with the unconsciousness of instinct in the extreme cases in which instinct is unconscious? When we mechanically perform a habitual action, when the somnambulist automatically acts out his dream, the unconsciousness may be absolute; but it is due, this time, to the fact that the representation of the act is held in check by the performance of the act itself, which is so perfectly similar to the representation and fits into it so exactly that no consciousness can overflow any longer. The representation is stopped up by the action. The proof is that if the accomplishment of the act is arrested or hindered by an obstacle, consciousness may spring forth. It was therefore there, but neutralised by the action which filled the representation. The obstacle has created nothing positive; it has simply made a void, it has unstopped an opening. This inadequacy of the act to the representation is precisely what we here call consciousness. On going more deeply into this point, we should find that consciousness is the light immanent in the zone of possible actions or of virtual activity that surrounds the action actually performed by the living being. It signifies hesitation or choice. Where many equally possible actions are sketched out without any real action (as in a deliberation that comes to nothing), consciousness is intense. Where the real action is the only possible action (as in activity of the somnambulistic or, more generally, automatic kind), consciousness becomes nil. Representation and knowledge nonetheless exist in this latter case, if it is established that we find in it a whole of systematised movements of which the last is already preformed in the first, and that consciousness can moreover spring from it at the shock of an obstacle. From this point of view the consciousness of the living being might be defined as an arithmetical difference between virtual activity and real activity. It measures the gap between representation and action. We may then presume that intellect will be oriented rather towards consciousness, instinct towards unconsciousness. For where the instrument to be handled is organised by nature, the point of application furnished by nature, the result to be obtained willed by nature, little is left to choice: the consciousness inherent in the representation will therefore be counterbalanced, in proportion as it tends to disengage itself, by the performance of the act, identical with the representation, which acts as a counterweight to it. Where it appears, it illuminates less the instinct itself than the thwartings to which instinct is subject: it is the deficit of instinct, the distance from the act to the idea, that will become consciousness; and consciousness will then be no more than an accident. It essentially marks only the initial step of instinct, the one that releases the whole series of automatic movements. Deficit, on the contrary, is the normal state of intellect. To suffer thwartings is its very essence. Having as its primitive function the manufacture of unorganised instruments, it must, through a thousand difficulties, choose for this work the place and the moment, the form and the matter. And it cannot wholly satisfy itself, because every new satisfaction creates new needs. In short, if instinct and intellect both involve knowledge, the knowledge is rather acted and unconscious in the case of instinct, rather thought and conscious in the case of intellect. But this is a difference of degree rather than of nature. So long as we attend only to consciousness, we close our eyes to what is, from the psychological point of view, the capital difference between intellect and instinct. To arrive at the essential difference, we must, without stopping at the more or less vivid light that illuminates these two forms of inner activity, go straight to the two objects, profoundly distinct from each other, which are their points of application. When the Horse Bot-fly lays its eggs on the legs or shoulders of the animal, it acts as if it knew that its larva must develop in the horse's stomach, and that the horse, in licking itself, will carry the newly hatched larva into its digestive tract. When a paralysing Hymenopteran strikes its victim at the precise points where nervous centres lie, so as to immobilise it without killing it, it proceeds as a learned entomologist would who was also a skilful surgeon. But what must not the little beetle whose story has so often been told, the Sitaris, know? This Coleopteran lays its eggs at the entrance of the underground galleries dug by a species of Bee, the Anthophora. The larva of the Sitaris, after a long wait, lies in wait for the male Anthophora as it comes out of the gallery, clings to it, and stays attached to it until the "nuptial flight"; there it seizes the opportunity of passing from the male to the female, and waits quietly until she lays her eggs. It then leaps on to the egg, which is to serve it as a support in the honey, devours the egg in a few days, and, installed on the shell, undergoes its first metamorphosis. Now organised to float on the honey, it consumes this store of food and becomes a nymph, then a perfect insect. Everything happens as if the larva of the Sitaris, from the moment it hatched, knew that the male Anthophora will come out of the gallery first, that the nuptial flight will furnish it with the means of transporting itself on to the female, that she will lead it to a store of honey capable of feeding it when it has been transformed, that, until this transformation, it will have gradually devoured the egg of the Anthophora, so as to nourish itself, to keep itself up on the surface of the honey, and also to suppress the rival that would have come out of the egg. And everything happens equally as if the Sitaris itself knew that its larva will know all these things. The knowledge, if knowledge there be, is only implicit. It is externalised in precise steps instead of being internalised in consciousness. It is nonetheless true that the conduct of the Insect outlines the representation of determinate things, existing or occurring at precise points of space and time, which the Insect knows without having learned them. Now, if we regard intellect from the same point of view, we find that it too knows certain things without having learned them. But this is knowledge of a very different order. I should not wish to revive here the old quarrel of the philosophers on the subject of innateness. Let us confine ourselves, then, to recording the point on which everyone agrees, namely that the little child immediately understands things that the animal will never understand, and that in this sense intellect, like instinct, is a hereditary function, and therefore innate. But this innate intellect, although it is a faculty of knowing, knows no object in particular. When the newborn child seeks its nurse's breast for the first time, thus bearing witness that it has the knowledge (unconscious, no doubt) of a thing it has never seen, it will be said, precisely because the innate knowledge is here that of a determinate object, that this is instinct and not intellect. Intellect therefore brings the innate knowledge of no object. And yet, if it knew nothing naturally, it would have nothing innate. What then can it know, it, which is ignorant of all things? Besides things, there are relations. The newborn child knows neither determinate objects nor a determinate property of any object; but on the day when a property is applied before him to an object, an epithet to a substantive, he will understand at once what this means. The relation of attribute to subject is therefore grasped by him naturally. And the same might be said of the general relation that the verb expresses, a relation so immediately conceived by the mind that language can leave it understood, as happens in rudimentary languages that have no verb. Intellect therefore naturally makes use of the relations of equivalent to equivalent, of content to container, of cause to effect, etc., which are implied in every sentence in which there is a subject, an attribute and a verb, expressed or understood. Can it be said to have innate knowledge of each of these relations in particular? It is for the logicians to inquire whether these are so many irreducible relations, or whether they could not be resolved into relations more general still. But in whatever way the analysis of thought is carried out, one will always arrive at one or more general frames, of which the mind possesses innate knowledge since it makes a natural use of them. Let us say, then, that if we consider in instinct and in intellect what they contain of innate knowledge, we find that this innate knowledge bears in the first case on things and in the second on relations. Philosophers distinguish between the matter of our knowledge and its form. The matter is what is given by the faculties of perception, taken in the raw state. The form is the whole of the relations established between these materials to constitute a systematic knowledge. Can form without matter already be the object of a knowledge? Yes, no doubt, on condition that this knowledge resembles less a thing possessed than a habit contracted, less a state than a direction; it will be, if you will, a certain natural bent of attention. The schoolboy who knows that a fraction is about to be dictated to him draws a line before he knows what the numerator and the denominator will be; he therefore has present to his mind the general relation between the two terms, although he knows neither of them; he knows the form without the matter. So it is with the frames, prior to all experience, into which our experience comes to be inserted. Let us therefore adopt here the words consecrated by usage. I shall give the distinction between intellect and instinct this more precise formula: intellect, in what it has of the innate, is the knowledge of a form; instinct implies that of a matter. From this second point of view, which is that of knowledge and no longer that of action, the force immanent in life in general again appears to us as a limited principle, in which, at the outset, two different and even divergent ways of knowing coexist and interpenetrate. The first reaches determinate objects immediately, in their very materiality. It says: "here is what is". The second reaches no object in particular; it is only a natural power of relating an object to an object, or a part to a part, or an aspect to an aspect, in short of drawing conclusions when one possesses premisses and of proceeding from what one has learnt to what one does not know. It no longer says "this is"; it says only that if the conditions are such, such will be the conditioned. In short, the first kind of knowledge, instinctive in nature, would be formulated in what philosophers call categorical propositions, whereas the second, intellectual in nature, is always expressed hypothetically. Of these two faculties, the first seems at first much preferable to the other. And so indeed it would be, if it extended to an indefinite number of objects. But in fact it never applies to anything but one special object, and even to a restricted part of that object. At least it has an inward and full knowledge of it, not explicit, but implied in the action accomplished. The second, on the contrary, naturally possesses only an outward and empty knowledge; but, for that very reason, it has the advantage of supplying a frame in which an infinity of objects will be able to find a place in turn. Everything happens as if the force that evolves through living forms, being a limited force, had had the choice, in the domain of natural or innate knowledge, between two kinds of limitation, the one bearing on the extension of knowledge, the other on its comprehension. In the first case, knowledge may be substantial and full, but it will then confine itself to a determinate object; in the second, it no longer limits its object, but that is because it no longer contains anything, being only a form without matter. The two tendencies, at first implied in one another, had to separate in order to grow. Each went off on its own side to seek its fortune in the world. They ended in instinct and in intellect. Such, then, are the two divergent modes of knowledge by which intellect and instinct will have to be defined, if it is from the point of view of knowledge, and no longer of action, that one takes one's stand. But knowledge and action are here only two aspects of one and the same faculty. It is easy to see, indeed, that the second definition is only a new form of the first. If instinct is, par excellence, the faculty of using a natural organised instrument, it must involve innate knowledge (virtual or unconscious, it is true) both of this instrument and of the object to which it applies. Instinct is therefore innate knowledge of a thing. But intellect is the faculty of manufacturing unorganised, that is to say artificial, instruments. If, through it, nature gives up endowing the living being with the instrument that will serve it, it is so that the living being may vary its manufacture according to circumstances. The essential function of the intellect will therefore be to make out, in any circumstances whatever, the means of getting out of difficulty. It will seek what can best serve, that is to say, fit into the frame proposed. It will bear essentially on the relations between the given situation and the means of utilising it. What it will have that is innate, then, is the tendency to establish relations, and this tendency implies the natural knowledge of certain very general relations, a veritable stuff which the activity proper to each intellect will cut into more particular relations. Where activity is directed towards manufacture, knowledge therefore necessarily bears on relations. But this wholly formal knowledge of the intellect has an incalculable advantage over the material knowledge of instinct. A form, just because it is empty, can be filled in turn, at will, by an indefinite number of things, even by those that are of no use. So that a formal knowledge is not limited to what is practically useful, even though it is with a view to practical utility that it made its appearance in the world. An intelligent being carries within itself the means of going beyond itself. It will go beyond itself, however, less than it would like, less also than it imagines it does. The purely formal character of the intellect deprives it of the ballast it would need in order to settle on the objects that would be of the most powerful interest to speculation. Instinct, on the contrary, would have the requisite materiality, but it is incapable of going so far afield in search of its object: it does not speculate. We are touching on the point that most concerns my present inquiry. The difference that I am about to point out between instinct and intellect is the one that the whole of my analysis tended to bring out. I would formulate it thus: There are things that intellect alone is capable of seeking, but which, by itself, it will never find. These things instinct alone would find; but it will never seek them. It is necessary here to go into some provisional details about the mechanism of the intellect. I have said that the function of the intellect was to establish relations. Let us determine more precisely the nature of the relations that the intellect establishes. On this point one remains in vagueness or in arbitrariness so long as one sees in the intellect a faculty intended for pure speculation. One is then reduced to taking the general frames of the understanding for some indefinable absolute, irreducible and inexplicable. The understanding would have fallen from heaven with its form, as each of us is born with his face. This form is defined, no doubt, but that is all one can do, and there is no asking why it is what it is rather than anything else. Thus it will be taught that the intellect is essentially unification, that all its operations have as their common object to introduce a certain unity into the diversity of phenomena, etc. But, in the first place, "unification" is a vague term, less clear than that of "relation" or even that of "thought", and it says no more. Moreover, one might ask whether the function of the intellect were not to divide, even more than to unite. Finally, if the intellect proceeds as it does because it wishes to unite, and if it seeks unification simply because it needs it, our knowledge becomes relative to certain requirements of the mind which might, no doubt, have been quite other than they are. For an intellect differently shaped, knowledge would have been different. The intellect no longer hanging on anything, everything then hangs on it. And so, through having placed the understanding too high, one ends by putting too low the knowledge it gives us. This knowledge becomes relative, from the moment the intellect is a kind of absolute. I, on the contrary, hold the human intellect to be relative to the necessities of action. Posit action, and the very form of the intellect can be deduced from it. This form is therefore neither irreducible nor inexplicable. And, precisely because it is not independent, it can no longer be said that knowledge depends on it. Knowledge ceases to be a product of the intellect and becomes, in a certain sense, an integral part of reality. Philosophers will reply that action is accomplished in an ordered world, that this order is already thought, and that I am begging the question in explaining the intellect by action, which presupposes it. In which they would be right, if the point of view I adopt in the present chapter were to be my definitive point of view. I should then be the dupe of an illusion like that of Spencer, who believed that the intellect was sufficiently explained when it was reduced to the imprint left in us by the general characters of matter: as if the order inherent in matter were not intellect itself! But I reserve for the next chapter the question how far, and by what method, philosophy might attempt a true genesis of the intellect together with that of matter. For the moment, the problem that occupies me is of a psychological order. I am asking which portion of the material world our intellect is specially adapted to. Now, to answer this question, there is no need to opt for a system of philosophy. It is enough to take the point of view of common sense. Let us start, then, from action, and lay it down as a principle that the intellect aims first of all at manufacturing. Manufacture is exercised exclusively on inert matter, in the sense that, even if it employs organised materials, it treats them as inert objects, without concerning itself with the life that has informed them. Of inert matter itself it retains scarcely anything but the solid: the rest escapes by its very fluidity. If, then, the intellect tends to manufacture, we may foresee that what is fluid in the real will partly escape it, and that what is properly vital in the living will escape it altogether. Our intellect, as it comes from the hands of nature, has the unorganised solid as its principal object. If we passed the intellectual faculties in review, we should see that the intellect feels at ease, that it is quite at home, only when it operates on inert matter, in particular on solids. What is the most general property of inert matter? It is extended; it presents us with objects external to other objects and, in these objects, with parts external to parts. No doubt it is useful to us, with a view to our later manipulations, to consider each object as divisible into arbitrarily cut parts, each part being further divisible as we please, and so on to infinity. But it is above all necessary for us, for the present manipulation, to take the real object we are dealing with, or the real elements into which we have resolved it, as provisionally final, and to treat them as so many units. It is to the possibility of decomposing matter as much as we please, and in whatever way we please, that we allude when we speak of the continuity of material extension; but this continuity, as we see, comes down for us to the faculty that matter leaves us of choosing the mode of discontinuity we shall find in it: it is always, in short, the mode of discontinuity once chosen that appears to us as effectively real and that fixes our attention, because it is by it that our present action is regulated. Thus discontinuity is thought for its own sake, it is thinkable in itself, we represent it to ourselves by a positive act of our mind, whereas the intellectual representation of continuity is rather negative, being, at bottom, only the refusal of our mind, before any system of decomposition actually given, to hold it as the only one possible. The intellect represents clearly to itself only the discontinuous. On the other hand, the objects on which our action is exercised are, without any doubt, moving objects. But what matters to us is to know where the moving body is going, where it is at any moment of its course. In other words, we attach ourselves above all to its present or future positions, and not to the progress by which it passes from one position to another, a progress which is movement itself. In the actions we accomplish, which are systematised movements, it is on the goal or the meaning of the movement, on its overall design, in a word on the motionless plan of execution, that we fix our mind. What is moving in the action interests us only in so far as the whole of it might be advanced, delayed or prevented by some incident occurring on the way. From mobility itself our intellect turns away, because it has no interest in concerning itself with it. If it were intended for pure theory, it is in movement that it would install itself, for movement is no doubt reality itself, and immobility is never anything but apparent or relative. But the intellect is intended for something quite different. Unless it does violence to itself, it follows the inverse course: it always starts from immobility, as if this were the ultimate reality or the element; when it wishes to represent movement to itself, it reconstructs it with immobilities that it juxtaposes. This operation, whose illegitimacy and danger in the speculative order I shall show (it leads to dead ends and artificially creates insoluble philosophical problems), is justified without difficulty when one refers it to its destination. The intellect, in its natural state, aims at a practically useful end. When it substitutes juxtaposed immobilities for movement, it does not claim to reconstitute movement as it is; it simply replaces it by a practical equivalent. It is the philosophers who are mistaken when they carry over into the domain of speculation a method of thinking that is made for action. But I propose to return to this point. Let us confine ourselves to saying that the stable and the unchanging are what our intellect attaches itself to by virtue of its natural disposition. Our intellect represents clearly to itself only immobility. Now, to manufacture consists in cutting the form of an object out of some matter. What matters above all is the form to be obtained. As for the matter, one chooses the one that suits best; but, in order to choose it, that is to say to go and look for it among many others, one must have tried, at least in imagination, to endow every kind of matter with the form of the object conceived. In other words, an intellect that aims at manufacturing is an intellect that never stops at the present form of things, that does not regard it as final, that holds all matter, on the contrary, to be cuttable at will. Plato compares the good dialectician to the skilful cook who carves the beast without breaking its bones, by following the articulations marked out by nature1. An intellect that always proceeded thus would indeed be an intellect turned towards speculation. But action, and in particular manufacture, requires the inverse turn of mind. It requires that we consider every present form of things, even natural ones, as artificial and provisional, that our thought efface from the object perceived, be it organised and living, the lines that mark its internal structure on the outside, in short that we hold its matter to be indifferent to its form. The whole of matter will therefore have to appear to our thought as an immense stuff in which we can cut out whatever we wish, to sew it together again as we please. Let us note in passing: it is this power that we affirm when we say that there is a space, that is to say a homogeneous and empty medium, infinite and infinitely divisible, lending itself indifferently to any mode of decomposition whatever. A medium of this kind is never perceived; it is only conceived. What is perceived is coloured, resistant extension, divided according to the lines traced by the outlines of real bodies or of their real elementary parts. But when we represent to ourselves our power over this matter, that is to say our faculty of decomposing and recomposing it as we please, we project, all together, all these possible decompositions and recompositions behind real extension, in the form of a homogeneous, empty and indifferent space which would underlie it. This space is therefore, above all, the schema of our possible action on things, even though things have a natural tendency, as I shall explain further on, to enter into a schema of this kind: it is a view of the mind. The animal probably has no idea of it, even when it perceives extended things as we do. It is a representation that symbolises the manufacturing tendency of the human intellect. But this point will not detain us for the moment. Let it suffice to say that the intellect is characterised by the unlimited power of decomposing according to any law whatever and of recomposing into any system whatever. I have enumerated some of the essential features of the human intellect. But I have taken the individual in the isolated state, without taking account of social life. In reality, man is a being who lives in society. If it is true that the human intellect aims at manufacturing, it must be added that it associates itself, for this and for the rest, with other intellects. Now, it is difficult to imagine a society whose members do not communicate with one another by signs. The societies of Insects no doubt have a language, and this language must be adapted, like that of man, to the necessities of life in common. It makes common action possible. But these necessities of common action are not at all the same for an ant-hill and for a human society. In the societies of Insects there is generally polymorphism, the division of labour is natural, and each individual is riveted by its structure to the function it performs. In any case, these societies rest on instinct, and consequently on certain actions or manufactures that are more or less bound up with the form of the organs. If, then, the Ants, for example, have a language, the signs composing this language must be in a well-determined number, and each of them must remain invariably attached, once the species is constituted, to a certain object or to a certain operation. The sign adheres to the thing signified. In a human society, on the contrary, manufacture and action are of variable form, and, moreover, each individual has to learn his part, not being predestined to it by his structure. What is needed, therefore, is a language that allows one, at every moment, to pass from what one knows to what one does not know. What is needed is a language whose signs, which cannot be infinite in number, are extensible to an infinity of things. This tendency of the sign to transfer itself from one object to another is characteristic of human language. It can be observed in the little child, from the day it begins to speak. At once, and naturally, it extends the meaning of the words it learns, taking advantage of the most accidental connexion or the remotest analogy to detach and carry elsewhere the sign that had been attached in its presence to an object. "Anything can designate anything": such is the latent principle of children's language. It has been a mistake to confuse this tendency with the faculty of generalising. Animals themselves generalise, and besides, a sign, even an instinctive one, always represents, more or less, a genus. What characterises the signs of human language is not so much their generality as their mobility. The instinctive sign is an adherent sign, the intelligent sign is a mobile sign. Now, this mobility of words, made so that they may go from one thing to another, has allowed them to extend from things to ideas. Certainly, language would not have given the faculty of reflecting to an intellect wholly externalised, incapable of turning back upon itself. An intellect that reflects is an intellect that had, over and above the practically useful effort, a surplus of force to spend. It is a consciousness that has already, virtually, won itself back. But still the virtuality must pass into act. It is to be presumed that, without language, the intellect would have been riveted to the material objects that it was in its interest to consider. It would have lived in a state of somnambulism, outside itself, hypnotised on its work. Language has done much to set it free. The word, made to go from one thing to another, is in fact essentially displaceable and free. It will therefore be able to extend, not only from one perceived thing to another perceived thing, but also from the perceived thing to the recollection of that thing, from the precise recollection to a more fleeting image, from a fleeting but still represented image to the representation of the act by which one represents it to oneself, that is to say to the idea. Thus there will open before the eyes of the intellect, which was looking outward, a whole inner world, the spectacle of its own operations. It was, moreover, only waiting for this opportunity. It takes advantage of the fact that the word is itself a thing in order to penetrate, carried by it, into the interior of its own work. Its first business may well have been to manufacture instruments; this manufacture is possible only through the use of certain means which are not cut to the exact measure of their object, which go beyond it, and which thus allow the intellect a supplementary, that is to say disinterested, work. From the day when the intellect, reflecting on its proceedings, perceives itself as a creator of ideas, as a faculty of representation in general, there is no object of which it does not wish to have the idea, even one without direct relation to practical action. That is why I said that there are things that intellect alone can seek. It alone, indeed, troubles itself about theory. And its theory would like to embrace everything, not only inert matter, on which it naturally has a hold, but also life and thought. With what means, what instruments, in short what method it will approach these problems, we can guess. Originally, it is adapted to the form of inert matter. Language itself, which has enabled it to extend its field of operations, is made to designate things and nothing but things: it is only because the word is mobile, because it travels from one thing to another, that the intellect was bound sooner or later to take it up on the way, while it was resting on nothing, in order to apply it to an object that is not a thing and that, hidden until then, was waiting for the help of the word in order to pass from the shade into the light. But the word, in covering this object, converts it once more into a thing. Thus the intellect, even when it no longer operates on inert matter, follows the habits it has contracted in that operation: it applies forms that are the very forms of unorganised matter. It is made for this kind of work. This kind of work alone satisfies it fully. And that is what it expresses in saying that only thus does it attain distinctness and clarity. It will therefore have, in order to think itself clearly and distinctly, to perceive itself in the form of discontinuity. Concepts are, indeed, external to one another, like objects in space. And they have the same stability as the objects on the model of which they were created. Taken together they constitute an "intelligible world" which resembles the world of solids in its essential characters, but whose elements are lighter, more diaphanous, easier for the intellect to handle than the pure and simple image of concrete things; they are no longer, indeed, the perception itself of things, but the representation of the act by which the intellect fixes itself upon them. They are therefore no longer images, but symbols. Our logic is the set of rules that must be followed in the manipulation of symbols. As these symbols derive from the consideration of solids, as the rules for the composition of these symbols with one another do little more than translate the most general relations between solids, our logic triumphs in the science that takes the solidity of bodies for its object, that is to say in geometry. Logic and geometry engender each other reciprocally, as we shall see a little further on. It is from the extension of a certain natural geometry, suggested by the general and immediately perceived properties of solids, that natural logic has issued. It is from this natural logic, in its turn, that scientific geometry has issued, which extends indefinitely the knowledge of the external properties of solids1. Geometry and logic are rigorously applicable to matter. There they are at home, there they can walk entirely on their own. But, outside this domain, pure reasoning needs to be watched over by good sense, which is something quite different. Thus all the elementary forces of the intellect tend to transform matter into an instrument of action, that is to say, in the etymological sense of the word, into an organ. Life, not content with producing organisms, would like to give them as an appendage inorganic matter itself, converted into an immense organ by the industry of the living being. Such is the task it first assigns to the intellect. That is why the intellect still behaves invariably as if it were fascinated by the contemplation of inert matter. It is life looking outward, externalising itself in relation to itself, adopting in principle, in order to direct them in fact, the ways of unorganised nature. Hence its astonishment when it turns towards the living and finds itself face to face with organisation. Whatever it then does, it resolves the organised into the unorganised, for it could not, without reversing its natural direction and without twisting round upon itself, think true continuity, real mobility, reciprocal interpenetration and, in a word, that creative evolution which is life. Is it a question of continuity? The aspect of life that is accessible to our intellect, as indeed to the senses that our intellect prolongs, is the one that offers a hold to our action. In order that we may modify an object, we must perceive it as divisible and discontinuous. From the point of view of positive science, an incomparable advance was made on the day when organised tissues were resolved into cells. The study of the cell, in its turn, has revealed in it an organism whose complexity seems to increase the more deeply it is examined. The further science advances, the more it sees the number of heterogeneous elements grow which are juxtaposed, external to one another, to make up a living being. Does it thereby close in more nearly on life? Or, on the contrary, does not what is properly vital in the living seem to recede in proportion as the detail of the juxtaposed parts is pushed further? Already there is showing itself among scientists a tendency to regard the substance of the organism as continuous, and the cell as an artificial entity2. But, supposing this view finally prevails, it can only end, as it deepens itself, in another mode of analysis of the living being, and consequently in a new discontinuity, though one less remote, perhaps, from the real continuity of life. The truth is that this continuity cannot be thought by an intellect that abandons itself to its natural movement. It implies at once the multiplicity of the elements and the reciprocal penetration of all by all, two properties that can scarcely be reconciled on the ground where our industry, and consequently our intellect too, is exercised. Just as we separate in space, we fix in time. The intellect is not made to think evolution, in the proper sense of the word, that is to say the continuity of a change that would be pure mobility. I shall not dwell here on this point, which I propose to examine more deeply in a special chapter. Let us say only that the intellect represents becoming to itself as a series of states, each of which is homogeneous with itself and consequently does not change. Is our attention called to the internal change of one of these states? At once we decompose it into another succession of states which, taken together, will constitute its inner modification. These new states will each be invariable, or else their internal change, if it strikes us, is at once resolved into a new series of invariable states, and so on indefinitely. Here again, to think consists in reconstituting, and, naturally, it is with given elements, and consequently with stable elements, that we reconstitute. So that, do what we may, we shall be able to imitate the mobility of becoming by the indefinite progress of our addition, but becoming itself will slip through our fingers when we think we hold it. Just because it always seeks to reconstitute, and to reconstitute with what is given, the intellect lets slip what is new at each moment of a history. It does not admit the unforeseeable. It rejects all creation. That determinate antecedents should bring about a determinate consequent, calculable as a function of them: that is what satisfies our intellect. That a determinate end should call forth determinate means for attaining it: this too we understand. In both cases we have to do with the known combining with the known and, in short, with the old repeating itself. Our intellect is at ease there. And, whatever the object, it will abstract, separate, eliminate, so as to substitute for the object itself, if need be, an approximate equivalent in which things will happen in this way. But that each instant should be a fresh contribution, that something new should ceaselessly spring forth, that a form should be born of which it will no doubt be said, once produced, that it is an effect determined by its causes, but of which it was impossible to suppose that what it would be had been foreseen, seeing that here the causes, unique of their kind, form part of the effect, took body at the same time as it, and are determined by it as much as they determine it: that is something we can feel within ourselves and divine by sympathy outside ourselves, but cannot express in terms of pure understanding nor, in the narrow sense of the word, think. We shall not be astonished at this if we consider the destination of our understanding. The causality it seeks and finds everywhere expresses the very mechanism of our industry, in which we recompose indefinitely the same whole with the same elements, in which we repeat the same movements to obtain the same result. Finality par excellence, for our understanding, is that of our industry, in which one works on a model given in advance, that is to say old or composed of known elements. As for invention properly so called, which is nevertheless the starting point of industry itself, our intellect does not succeed in grasping it in its springing forth, that is to say in what is indivisible in it, nor in its genius, that is to say in what is creative in it. To explain it always consists in resolving it, unforeseeable and new as it is, into known or old elements, arranged in a different order. The intellect no more admits complete novelty than radical becoming. That is to say that here again it lets slip an essential aspect of life, as if it were not made to think such an object. All my analyses bring me back to this conclusion. But there was no need to go into such long details about the mechanism of intellectual work: it would suffice to consider its results. We should see that the intellect, so skilful in handling the inert, displays its clumsiness as soon as it touches the living. Whether it is a matter of treating the life of the body or that of the mind, it proceeds with the rigour, the stiffness and the brutality of an instrument that was not intended for such a use. The history of hygiene and of pedagogy would have much to tell in this respect. When we think of the capital, pressing and constant interest we have in preserving our bodies and in raising our souls, of the special facilities given here to each of us for experimenting ceaselessly on ourselves and on others, of the palpable damage by which the defectiveness of a medical or pedagogical practice manifests itself and is paid for, we remain confounded at the crudeness and above all at the persistence of the errors. Their origin would easily be discovered in our obstinacy in treating the living like the inert and in thinking all reality, however fluid it may be, in the form of a solid definitively fixed. We are at ease only in the discontinuous, in the motionless, in the dead. The intellect is characterised by a natural inability to understand life. It is on the very form of life, on the contrary, that instinct is moulded. While the intellect treats all things mechanically, instinct proceeds, if one may so speak, organically. If the consciousness that slumbers in it were to awake, if it were to be internalised into knowledge instead of being externalised into action, if we knew how to question it and it could reply, it would yield up to us the most intimate secrets of life. For it only continues the work by which life organises matter, so much so that we could not say, as has very often been shown, where organisation ends and where instinct begins. When the little chick breaks its shell with a peck of its beak, it acts by instinct, and yet it merely follows the movement that has carried it through embryonic life. Conversely, in the course of embryonic life itself (especially when the embryo lives freely in the form of a larva) many proceedings are carried out that must be ascribed to instinct. The most essential of the primary instincts are therefore really vital processes. The virtual consciousness that accompanies them is most often actualised only in the initial phase of the act, and leaves the rest of the process to accomplish itself unaided. It would only have to expand more widely, and then to deepen itself completely, in order to coincide with the generative force of life. When we see, in a living body, thousands of cells working together towards a common end, sharing out the task, each living for itself at the same time as for the others, preserving themselves, feeding themselves, reproducing themselves, responding to threats of danger with appropriate defensive reactions, how can we help thinking of so many instincts? And yet these are natural functions of the cell, the constitutive elements of its vitality. Conversely, when we see the Bees of a hive form a system so closely organised that none of the individuals can live in isolation beyond a certain time, even if it is supplied with lodging and food, how can we fail to recognise that the hive is really, and not metaphorically, a single organism, of which each Bee is a cell united to the others by invisible bonds? The instinct that animates the Bee is therefore one with the force by which the cell is animated, or merely prolongs it. In extreme cases like this one, it coincides with the work of organisation. Certainly there are many degrees of perfection in the same instinct. Between the Bumble-bee and the Bee, for example, the distance is great, and one would pass from the one to the other through a host of intermediaries, which correspond to so many complications of social life. But the same diversity would be found in the functioning of histological elements belonging to different tissues, more or less related to one another. In both cases there are manifold variations played on one and the same theme. The constancy of the theme is none the less manifest, and the variations only adapt it to the diversity of circumstances. Now, in the one case as in the other, whether it be the instincts of the animal or the vital properties of the cell, the same knowledge and the same ignorance are manifested. Things happen as if the cell knew of the other cells what concerns it, the animal of the other animals what it will be able to use, all the rest remaining in the shade. It seems that life, as soon as it has contracted into a determinate species, loses contact with the rest of itself, except, however, at one or two points that concern the species just born. How can we fail to see that life proceeds here like consciousness in general, like memory? We drag behind us, without noticing it, the totality of our past; but our memory pours into the present only the two or three recollections that will complete our present situation in some respect. The instinctive knowledge that one species possesses of another species on a certain particular point therefore has its root in the very unity of life, which is, to use the expression of an ancient philosopher, a whole sympathetic to itself. It is impossible to consider certain special instincts of the animal and of the plant, evidently born in extraordinary circumstances, without comparing them to those recollections, apparently forgotten, which spring up suddenly under the pressure of an urgent need. No doubt a host of secondary instincts, and many modalities of primary instinct, admit of a scientific explanation. Yet it is doubtful whether science, with its present methods of explanation, will ever succeed in analysing instinct completely. The reason is that instinct and intellect are two divergent developments of one and the same principle which, in the one case, remains internal to itself and, in the other, externalises itself and becomes absorbed in the utilisation of inert matter: this continued divergence bears witness to a radical incompatibility and to the impossibility for the intellect of reabsorbing instinct. What is essential in instinct cannot be expressed in intellectual terms, nor consequently be analysed. A man born blind who had lived among others born blind would not admit that it was possible to perceive a distant object without having passed through the perception of all the intermediate objects. Yet vision performs this miracle. One may, it is true, side with the man born blind and say that vision, having its origin in the stimulation of the retina by the vibrations of light, is nothing else, in short, than a retinal touch. That, I grant, is the scientific explanation, for the role of science is precisely to translate every perception into terms of touch; but I have shown elsewhere that the philosophical explanation of perception must be of another nature, supposing one can still speak of explanation here1. Now instinct, too, is a knowledge at a distance. It is to the intellect what vision is to touch. Science will be unable to do otherwise than translate it into terms of intellect; but in so doing it will construct an imitation of instinct rather than penetrate into instinct itself. We shall be convinced of this by studying here the ingenious theories of evolutionist biology. They reduce to two types, which moreover often interfere with each other. Sometimes, according to the principles of neo-Darwinism, instinct is seen as a sum of accidental differences preserved by selection: some useful proceeding, naturally performed by the individual by virtue of an accidental predisposition of the germ, would have been transmitted from germ to germ, waiting for chance to come and add new improvements to it by the same process. Sometimes instinct is made into a degraded intellect: the action judged useful by the species or by some of its representatives would have engendered a habit, and the habit, hereditarily transmitted, would have become instinct. Of these two systems, the first has the advantage of being able to speak of hereditary transmission without raising any serious objection, for the accidental modification that it places at the origin of instinct would not be acquired by the individual but inherent in the germ. On the other hand, it is quite incapable of explaining instincts as expert as those of most Insects. No doubt these instincts did not reach all at once the degree of complexity they have today; they have probably evolved. But, on a hypothesis like that of the neo-Darwinians, the evolution of instinct could only come about through the progressive addition of new pieces, so to speak, which happy accidents would come to fit into the old ones like cogs. Now it is evident that, in most cases, it is not by way of simple accretion that instinct can have been perfected: each new piece required, in fact, on pain of spoiling everything, a complete recasting of the whole. How can such a recasting be expected from chance? I grant that an accidental modification of the germ will be transmitted hereditarily and may wait, so to speak, for new accidental modifications to come and complicate it. I grant too that natural selection will eliminate all those of the more complicated forms that are not viable. Still, for the life of instinct to evolve, viable complications will have to be produced. Now they will be produced only if, in certain cases, the addition of a new element brings about the correlative change of all the old elements. No one will maintain that chance can accomplish such a miracle. In one form or another, appeal will be made to intellect. It will be supposed that it is by a more or less conscious effort that the living being develops a higher instinct in itself. But it will then have to be admitted that a contracted habit can become hereditary, and that it does so regularly enough to ensure an evolution. The thing is doubtful, to say no more. Even if the instincts of animals could be ascribed to a habit hereditarily transmitted and intelligently acquired, it is not clear how this mode of explanation would extend to the vegetable world, where effort is never intelligent, supposing it is sometimes conscious. And yet, seeing with what sureness and precision climbing plants use their tendrils, what marvellously combined manoeuvres the Orchids perform in order to get themselves fertilised by Insects1, how can we help thinking of so many instincts? This does not mean that the thesis of the neo-Darwinists must be given up altogether, any more than that of the neo-Lamarckians. The former are no doubt right when they hold that evolution takes place from germ to germ rather than from individual to individual, the latter when they happen to say that at the origin of instinct there is an effort (though it is something quite other, I believe, than an intelligent effort). But the former are probably wrong when they make the evolution of instinct an accidental evolution, and the latter when they see in the effort from which instinct proceeds an individual effort. The effort by which a species modifies its instincts, and modifies itself as well, must be a much deeper thing, and one that does not depend solely on circumstances or on individuals. It does not depend solely on the initiative of individuals, although individuals collaborate in it, and it is not purely accidental, although accident has a large place in it. Let us compare, indeed, the various forms of the same instinct in various species of Hymenoptera. The impression we get is not always that which would be given us by an increasing complexity obtained through elements added successively to one another, or by an ascending series of arrangements ranged, so to speak, along a ladder. We think rather, in many cases at least, of a circumference from the various points of which these various varieties would have started, all looking towards the same centre, all making an effort in that direction, but each of them approaching it only in the measure of its means, in the measure also in which the central point was lit up for it. In other words, instinct is everywhere complete, but it is more or less simplified, and above all it is simplified in different ways. On the other hand, where a regular gradation is observed, instinct growing more complicated in one and the same direction, as if it were climbing the rungs of a ladder, the species that their instinct thus ranges in a linear series are far from always being related to one another by kinship. Thus the comparative study that has been made in recent years of the social instinct in the various Apidae establishes that the instinct of the Meliponinae is intermediate, as regards complexity, between the still rudimentary tendency of the Bombinae and the consummate science of our Bees: yet between the Bees and the Meliponinae there can be no relation of filiation2. In all likelihood, the greater or lesser complication of these various societies is not due to a greater or smaller number of elements added together. We are much rather in the presence of a certain musical theme which would first have transposed itself, as a whole, into a certain number of keys, and on which, also as a whole, various variations would then have been played, some very simple, others infinitely elaborate. As for the original theme, it is everywhere and nowhere. It would be vain to try to note it down in terms of representation: it was no doubt, at the origin, something felt rather than something thought. We have the same impression before the paralysing instinct of certain Wasps. It is known that the various species of paralysing Hymenoptera lay their eggs in Spiders, Beetles, Caterpillars which will go on living motionless for a certain number of days, and which will thus serve as fresh food for the larvae, having first been subjected by the Wasp to an expert surgical operation. In the sting they give to the nerve centres of their victim in order to immobilise it without killing it, these various species of Hymenoptera regulate themselves by the various species of prey they respectively have to deal with. The Scolia, which attacks a larva of the Rose-chafer, stings it at one point only, but at that point the motor ganglia are concentrated, and those ganglia only; the stinging of other ganglia might bring about death and putrefaction, which must be avoided1. The yellow-winged Sphex, which has chosen the Cricket for its victim, knows that the Cricket has three nerve centres which animate its three pairs of legs, or at least it acts as if it knew this. It stings the insect first under the neck, then behind the prothorax, and finally near the base of the abdomen2. The hairy Ammophila gives nine successive strokes of its sting to nine nerve centres of its Caterpillar, and finally seizes its head and chews it, just enough to bring about paralysis without death3. The general theme is "the necessity of paralysing without killing": the variations are subordinate to the structure of the subject operated on. No doubt the operation is far from always being performed perfectly. It has been shown recently that the Ammophila Sphex sometimes kills the Caterpillar instead of paralysing it, and that sometimes, too, it only half paralyses it4. But because instinct is fallible like intellect, because it too is liable to show individual deviations, it by no means follows that the instinct of the Sphex was acquired, as has been claimed, by intelligent groping. Supposing that, in the course of time, the Sphex had come to recognise one by one, by groping, the points of its victim that must be stung in order to immobilise it, and the special treatment that must be inflicted on the brain in order that paralysis may come without bringing death, how can we suppose that the so special elements of so precise a knowledge were transmitted regularly, one by one, by heredity? If there were, in the whole of our present experience, a single indisputable example of a transmission of this kind, the inheritance of acquired characters would be contested by no one. In reality, the hereditary transmission of the contracted habit takes place in an imprecise and irregular way, supposing it ever really occurs at all. But the whole difficulty arises from our wishing to translate the science of the Hymenopteran into terms of intellect. We are then compelled to assimilate the Sphex to the entomologist, who knows the Caterpillar as he knows all other things, that is to say from outside, without having on that side any special and vital interest. The Sphex would then have to learn one by one, like the entomologist, the positions of the nerve centres of the Caterpillar, or at least to acquire the practical knowledge of these positions by trying out the effects of its sting. But this would no longer be so if one supposed between the Sphex and its victim a sympathy (in the etymological sense of the word) which informed it from within, so to speak, about the vulnerability of the Caterpillar. This feeling of vulnerability might owe nothing to external perception, and might result from the mere bringing together of the Sphex and the Caterpillar, considered no longer as two organisms but as two activities. It would express in a concrete form the relation of the one to the other. Certainly a scientific theory cannot appeal to considerations of this kind. It must not put action before organisation, sympathy before perception and knowledge. But, once more, either philosophy has nothing to do here, or its role begins where that of science ends. Whether it makes instinct a "compound reflex", or a habit intelligently contracted and turned into automatism, or a sum of small accidental advantages accumulated and fixed by selection, in every case science claims to resolve instinct completely either into intelligent proceedings or into mechanisms built up piece by piece, like those our intellect contrives. I grant that science is here within its role. It will give us, failing a real analysis of the object, a translation of that object into terms of intellect. But how can we fail to notice that science itself invites philosophy to take things from another angle? If our biology were still at the stage of Aristotle, if it held the series of living beings to be unilinear, if it showed us life as a whole evolving towards intellect and passing, to that end, through sensibility and instinct, we should have the right, we intelligent beings, to turn back towards the earlier and consequently lower manifestations of life and to claim to make them fit, without distorting them, into the frames of our intellect. But one of the clearest results of biology has been to show that evolution has taken place along divergent lines. It is at the extremity of two of these lines, the two principal ones, that we find intellect and instinct in their approximately pure forms. Why then should instinct be resolvable into intelligent elements? Why even into wholly intelligible terms? Is it not plain that to think here of the intelligent, or of the absolutely intelligible, is to go back to the Aristotelian theory of nature? No doubt it would still be better to go back to it than to stop short before instinct as before an unfathomable mystery. But, though it does not belong to the domain of the intellect, instinct is not situated outside the limits of mind. In phenomena of feeling, in unreflecting sympathies and antipathies, we experience in ourselves, in a much vaguer form, and one too much penetrated with intellect besides, something of what must go on in the consciousness of an insect acting by instinct. Evolution has only drawn apart from each other, in order to develop them to the end, elements that interpenetrated at the origin. More precisely, the intellect is, above all, the faculty of relating one point of space to another point of space, one material object to another material object; it applies to all things, but remains outside them, and it never perceives of a deep cause anything but its diffusion into juxtaposed effects. Whatever the force that expresses itself in the genesis of the nervous system of the Caterpillar, we reach it, with our eyes and our intellect, only as a juxtaposition of nerves and nerve centres. It is true that we thus reach its whole external effect. The Sphex, for its part, no doubt grasps only a little of it, just what concerns it; but at least it grasps it from within, quite otherwise than by a process of knowledge, by an intuition (lived rather than represented) which no doubt resembles what in us is called divinatory sympathy. It is a remarkable fact, this to-and-fro of scientific theories of instinct between the intelligent and the merely intelligible, I mean between the assimilation of instinct to a "lapsed" intellect and the reduction of instinct to a pure mechanism1. Each of these two systems of explanation triumphs in its criticism of the other, the first when it shows us that instinct cannot be a pure reflex, the second when it says that it is something other than intellect, even lapsed into unconsciousness. What does this mean, if not that these are two symbolisms equally acceptable in some respects and, in others, equally inadequate to their object? The concrete explanation, no longer scientific but metaphysical, must be sought along quite another path, no longer in the direction of intellect but in that of "sympathy". Instinct is sympathy. If this sympathy could extend its object and also reflect upon itself, it would give us the key to vital operations, just as intellect, developed and set straight, introduces us into matter. For, I cannot repeat it too often, intellect and instinct are turned in two opposite directions, the former towards inert matter, the latter towards life. The intellect, through the medium of science, which is its work, will deliver to us more and more completely the secret of physical operations; of life it brings us, and indeed claims to bring us, only a translation in terms of inertia. It goes all round it, taking from outside the greatest possible number of views of this object, which it draws into its own home instead of entering into the object's. But it is to the very interior of life that intuition would lead us, I mean instinct become disinterested, conscious of itself, capable of reflecting upon its object and of enlarging it indefinitely. That an effort of this kind is not impossible is shown already by the existence in man of an aesthetic faculty alongside normal perception. Our eye perceives the features of the living being, but juxtaposed with one another and not organised among themselves. The intention of life, the simple movement that runs through the lines, that binds them to one another and gives them a meaning, escapes it. It is this intention that the artist aims at regaining, by placing himself back within the object through a kind of sympathy, by lowering, through an effort of intuition, the barrier that space interposes between him and the model. It is true that this aesthetic intuition, like external perception for that matter, attains only the individual. But we can conceive an inquiry directed in the same sense as art which would take life in general for its object, just as physical science, by following to the end the direction marked out by external perception, prolongs individual facts into general laws. No doubt this philosophy will never obtain of its object a knowledge comparable to that which science has of its own. Intellect remains the luminous nucleus around which instinct, even enlarged and purified into intuition, forms only a vague nebulosity. But, failing knowledge properly so called, which is reserved to pure intellect, intuition will be able to make us grasp what is insufficient here in the data of the intellect and let us glimpse the means of completing them. On the one hand, indeed, it will use the very mechanism of the intellect to show how the intellectual frames no longer find their exact application here, and, on the other, by its own work, it will suggest to us at least the vague feeling of what must be put in the place of the intellectual frames. Thus it will be able to bring the intellect to recognise that life does not fit wholly into the category of the many, nor into that of the one, that neither mechanical causality nor finality gives a sufficient translation of the vital process. Then, by the sympathetic communication it will establish between us and the rest of the living, by the dilatation of our consciousness that it will obtain, it will introduce us into the proper domain of life, which is reciprocal interpenetration, creation indefinitely continued. But if by this it goes beyond the intellect, it is from the intellect that the jolt will have come which made it rise to the point where it is. Without the intellect, it would have remained, in the form of instinct, riveted to the special object that interests it practically, and externalised by it into movements of locomotion. How the theory of knowledge must take account of these two faculties, intellect and intuition, and how too, for want of establishing a sufficiently clear distinction between intuition and intellect, it becomes involved in inextricable difficulties, creating phantoms of ideas to which phantoms of problems will attach themselves, is what I shall try to show a little further on. It will be seen that the problem of knowledge, taken from this angle, is one with the metaphysical problem, and that both then fall within the province of experience. On the one hand, indeed, if intellect is tuned to matter and intuition to life, we shall have to press them both in order to extract from them the quintessence of their object; metaphysics will therefore hang on the theory of knowledge. But, on the other hand, if consciousness has thus split into intuition and intellect, it is through the necessity of applying itself to matter at the same time as following the current of life. The doubling of consciousness would thus be due to the double form of the real, and the theory of knowledge would have to hang on metaphysics. In truth, each of these two inquiries leads to the other; they form a circle, and the circle can have for its centre only the empirical study of evolution. It is only by watching consciousness run through matter, lose itself there and find itself again, divide and reconstitute itself, that we shall form an idea of the opposition of the two terms to each other, as also, perhaps, of their common origin. But, on the other hand, by dwelling on this opposition of the two elements and on this community of origin, we shall no doubt bring out more clearly the meaning of evolution itself. Such will be the object of my next chapter. But already the facts we have just passed in review would suggest to us the idea of linking life either to consciousness itself or to something that resembles it. Throughout the whole extent of the animal kingdom, I said, consciousness appears proportional to the power of choice the living being has at its disposal. It lights up the zone of virtualities that surrounds the act. It measures the interval between what is done and what might be done. Viewed from outside, then, it might be taken for a mere auxiliary of action, for a light that action kindles, a fleeting spark that would flash out from the friction of real action against possible actions. But it must be remarked that things would happen in exactly the same way if consciousness, instead of being effect, were cause. It might be supposed that, even in the most rudimentary animal, consciousness covers by right an enormous field, but that it is in fact compressed in a kind of vice: each advance of the nerve centres, by giving the organism the choice among a greater number of actions, would send out a call to the virtualities capable of surrounding the real, would thus loosen the vice, and would let consciousness pass more freely. On this second hypothesis, as on the first, consciousness would indeed be the instrument of action; but it would be still truer to say that action is the instrument of consciousness, for the complication of action with itself and the setting of action at grips with action would be, for imprisoned consciousness, the only possible means of freeing itself. How are we to choose between the two hypotheses? If the first were true, consciousness would trace exactly, at each instant, the state of the brain; the parallelism (in so far as it is intelligible) between the psychological state and the cerebral state would be rigorous. On the second hypothesis, on the contrary, there would indeed be solidarity and interdependence between brain and consciousness, but not parallelism: the more complicated the brain becomes, thus increasing the number of possible actions among which the organism has the choice, the more consciousness will have to overflow its physical concomitant. Thus the recollection of one and the same spectacle at which they have both been present will probably modify a dog's brain and a man's brain in the same way, if the perception has been the same; yet the recollection must be something quite different in a man's consciousness from what it is in a dog's consciousness. In the dog, the recollection will remain captive to the perception; it will awake only when an analogous perception comes to recall it by reproducing the same spectacle, and it will then show itself in the recognition, acted rather than thought, of the present perception much more than in a true revival of the recollection itself. Man, on the contrary, is capable of calling up the recollection at will, at any moment whatever, independently of present perception. He does not confine himself to acting his past life; he represents it to himself and he dreams it. The local modification of the brain to which the recollection is attached being the same on both sides, the psychological difference between the two recollections cannot have its reason in some difference of detail between the two cerebral mechanisms, but in the difference between the two brains taken as wholes: the more complex of the two, by setting a greater number of mechanisms at grips with one another, will have allowed consciousness to disengage itself from the grip of them all and to attain independence. That things do indeed happen thus, that the second of the two hypotheses is the one for which we must opt, is what I tried to prove, in an earlier work, by the study of the facts that bring out best the relation of the conscious state to the cerebral state, the facts of normal and pathological recognition, in particular the aphasias1. But reasoning would have allowed us to foresee it just as well. I have shown on what self-contradictory postulate, on what confusion of two mutually incompatible symbolisms, the hypothesis of an equivalence between the cerebral state and the psychological state rests2. The evolution of life, viewed from this side, takes on a clearer meaning, even though it cannot be subsumed under a true idea. Everything happens as if a broad current of consciousness had penetrated into matter, laden, like all consciousness, with an enormous multiplicity of interpenetrating virtualities. It has drawn matter on to organisation, but its movement has been at once infinitely slowed down and infinitely divided. On the one hand, indeed, consciousness has had to fall into a doze, like the chrysalis in the envelope in which it prepares its wings, and on the other hand the manifold tendencies it contained were distributed among divergent series of organisms, which, moreover, externalised these tendencies in movements rather than internalising them in representations. In the course of this evolution, while some fell more and more deeply asleep, others awoke more and more completely, and the torpor of the ones served the activity of the others. But the awakening could take place in two different ways. Life, that is to say consciousness launched through matter, fixed its attention either on its own movement or on the matter it was passing through. It thus turned either in the direction of intuition or in that of intellect. Intuition, at first sight, seems far preferable to intellect, since in it life and consciousness remain internal to themselves. But the spectacle of the evolution of living beings shows us that it could not go very far. On the side of intuition, consciousness found itself so compressed by its envelope that it had to narrow intuition down into instinct, that is to say embrace only the very small portion of life that concerned it; and even this it embraces in the dark, touching it while scarcely seeing it. On this side the horizon closed at once. On the contrary, consciousness determining itself as intellect, that is to say concentrating itself first on matter, thus seems to externalise itself in relation to itself; but, just because it adapts itself to the objects outside, it succeeds in moving about among them, in getting round the barriers they set up against it, in enlarging its domain indefinitely. Once set free, moreover, it can turn back inward and awaken the virtualities of intuition that still slumber within it. From this point of view, not only does consciousness appear as the motive principle of evolution, but also, among conscious beings themselves, man comes to occupy a privileged place. Between the animals and him there is no longer a difference of degree, but of kind. Until this conclusion emerges from my next chapter, let me show how my preceding analyses suggest it. It is a fact worthy of remark, the extraordinary disproportion between the consequences of an invention and the invention itself. I said that the intellect is modelled on matter and that it aims first at manufacture. But does it manufacture for the sake of manufacturing, or might it not be pursuing, involuntarily and even unconsciously, something quite different? To manufacture consists in informing matter, in making it supple and bending it, in converting it into an instrument in order to become its master. It is this mastery that benefits humanity, much more even than the material result of the invention itself. If we derive an immediate advantage from the manufactured object, as an intelligent animal might do, if this advantage is even all the inventor was seeking, it is a slight thing in comparison with the new ideas, the new feelings that the invention may call forth on every side, as if its essential effect were to raise us above ourselves and thereby to enlarge our horizon. Between the effect and the cause the disproportion is here so great that it is difficult to regard the cause as productive of its effect. It releases it, while assigning it, it is true, its direction. Everything happens, in short, as if the intellect's laying hold of matter had as its principal object to let something pass that matter stops. The same impression emerges from a comparison between the brain of man and that of the animals. The difference seems at first to be only a difference of volume and complexity. But there must be something quite different besides, to judge by the functioning. In the animal, the motor mechanisms that the brain succeeds in setting up, or, in other words, the habits that its will contracts, have no other object and no other effect than to accomplish the movements traced out in these habits, stored up in these mechanisms. But in man the motor habit may have a second result, incommensurable with the first. It can hold other motor habits in check and thereby, by mastering automatism, set consciousness free. We know what vast territories language occupies in the human brain.
