L'ensemble du monde organisé devient comme l'humus sur lequel devait pousser ou l'homme lui-même ou un être qui, moralement, lui ressemblât. Les animaux, si éloignés, si ennemis même qu'ils soient de notre espèce, n'en ont pas moins été d'utiles compagnons de route, sur lesquels la conscience s'est déchargée de ce qu'elle traînait d'encombrant, et qui lui ont permis de s'élever, avec l'homme, sur les hauteurs d'où elle voit un horizon illimité se rouvrir devant elle. Il est vrai qu'elle n'a pas seulement abandonné en route un bagage embarrassant. Elle a dû renoncer aussi à des biens précieux. La conscience, chez l'homme, est surtout intelligence. Elle aurait pu, elle aurait dû, semble-t-il, être aussi intuition. Intuition et intelligence représentent deux directions opposées du travail conscient : l'intuition marche dans le sens même de la vie, l'intelligence va en sens inverse, et se trouve ainsi tout naturellement réglée sur le mouvement de la matière. Une humanité complète et parfaite serait celle où ces deux formes de l'activité consciente atteindraient leur plein développement. Entre cette humanité et la nôtre on conçoit d'ailleurs bien des intermédiaires possibles, correspondant à tous les degrés imaginables de l'intelligence et de l'intuition. Là est la part de la contingence dans la structure mentale de notre espèce. Une évolution autre eût pu conduire à une humanité ou plus intelligente encore, ou plus intuitive. En fait, dans l'humanité dont nous faisons partie, l'intuition est à peu près complètement sacrifiée à l'intelligence. Il semble qu'à conquérir la matière, et à se reconquérir sur elle-même, la conscience ait dû épuiser le meilleur de sa force. Cette conquête, dans les conditions particulières où elle s'est faite, exigeait que la conscience s'adaptât aux habitudes de la matière et concentrât toute son attention sur elles, enfin se déterminât plus spécialement en intelligence. L'intuition est là cependant, mais vague et surtout discontinue. C'est une lampe presque éteinte, qui ne se ranime que de loin en loin, pour quelques instants à peine. Mais elle se ranime, en somme, là où un intérêt vital est en jeu. Sur notre personnalité, sur notre liberté, sur la place que nous occupons dans l'ensemble de la nature, sur notre origine et peut-être aussi sur notre destinée, elle projette une lumière vacillante et faible, mais qui n'en perce pas moins l'obscurité de la nuit où nous laisse l'intelligence. De ces intuitions évanouissantes, et qui n'éclairent leur objet que de distance en distance, la philosophie doit s'emparer, d'abord pour les soutenir, ensuite pour les dilater et les raccorder ainsi entre elles. Plus elle avance dans ce travail, plus elle s'aperçoit que l'intuition est l'esprit même et, en un certain sens, la vie même : l'intelligence s'y découpe par un processus imitateur de celui qui a engendré la matière. Ainsi apparaît l'unité de la vie mentale. On ne la reconnaît qu'en se plaçant dans l'intuition pour aller de là à l'intelligence, car de l'intelligence on ne passera jamais à l'intuition. La philosophie nous introduit ainsi dans la vie spirituelle. Et elle nous montre en même temps la relation de la vie de l'esprit à celle du corps. La grande erreur des doctrines spiritualistes a été de croire qu'en isolant la vie spirituelle de tout le reste, en la suspendant dans l'espace aussi haut que possible au-dessus de terre, elles la mettaient à l'abri de toute atteinte : comme si elles ne l'exposaient pas simplement ainsi à être prise pour un effet de mirage ! Certes, elles ont raison d'écouter la conscience, quand la conscience affirme la liberté humaine , - mais l'intelligence est là, qui dit que la cause détermine son effet, que le même conditionne le même, que tout se répète et que tout est donné. Elles ont raison de croire à la réalité absolue de la personne et à son indépendance vis-à-vis de la matière ; - mais la science est là, qui montre la solidarité de la vie consciente et de l'activité cérébrale. Elles ont raison d'attribuer à l'homme une place privilégiée dans la nature, de tenir pour infinie la distance de l'animal à l'homme; - mais l'histoire de la vie est là, qui nous fait assister à la genèse des espèces par voie de transformation graduelle et qui semble ainsi réintégrer l'homme dans l'animalité. Quand un instinct puissant proclame la survivance probable de la personne, elles ont raison de ne pas fermer l'oreille à sa voix; -mais s'il existe ainsi des « âmes » capables d'une vie indépendante, d'où viennent-elles ? quand, comment, pourquoi entrent-elles dans ce corps que nous voyons, sous nos yeux, sortir très naturellement d'une cellule mixte empruntée aux corps de ses deux parents ? Toutes ces questions resteront sans réponse, une philosophie d'intuition sera la négation de la science, tôt ou tard elle sera balayée par la science, si elle ne se décide pas à voir la vie du corps là où elle est réellement, sur le chemin qui mène à la vie de l'esprit. Mais ce n'est plus alors à tels ou tels vivants déterminés qu'elle aura affaire. La vie entière, depuis l'impulsion initiale qui la lança dans le monde, lui apparaîtra comme un flot qui monte, et que contrarie le mouvement descendant de la matière. Sur la plus grande partie de sa surface, à des hauteurs diverses, le courant est converti par la matière en un tourbillonnement sur place. Sur un seul point il passe librement, entraînant avec lui l'obstacle, qui alourdira sa marche mais ne l'arrêtera pas. En ce point est l'humanité ; là est notre situation privilégiée. D'autre part, ce flot qui monte est conscience, et, comme toute conscience, il enveloppe des virtualités sans nombre qui se compénètrent, auxquelles ne conviennent par conséquent ni la catégorie de l'unité ni celle de la multiplicité, faites pour la matière inerte. Seule, la matière qu'il charrie avec lui, et dans les interstices de laquelle il s'insère, peut le diviser en individualités distinctes. Le courant passe donc, traversant les générations humaines, se subdivisant en individus : cette subdivision était dessinée en lui vaguement, mais elle ne se fût pas accusée sans la matière. Ainsi se créent sans cesse des âmes, qui cependant, en un certain sens, préexistaient. Elles ne sont pas autre chose que les ruisselets entre lesquels se partage le grand fleuve de la vie, coulant a travers le corps de l'humanité. Le mouvement d'un courant est distinct de ce qu'il traverse, bien qu'il en adopte nécessairement les sinuosités. La conscience est distincte de l'organisme qu'elle anime, bien qu'elle en subisse certaines vicissitudes. Comme les actions possibles, dont un état de conscience contient le dessin, reçoivent à tout instant, dans les centres nerveux, un commencement d'exécution, le cerveau souligne à tout instant les articulations motrices de l'état de conscience ; mais la se borne l'interdépendance de la conscience et du cerveau ; le sort de la conscience n'est pas lié pour cela au sort de la matière cérébrale. Enfin, la conscience est essentiellement libre ; elle est la liberté même : mais elle ne peut traverser la matière sans se poser sur elle, sans s'adapter à elle : cette adaptation est ce qu'on appelle l'intellectualité ; et l'intelligence, se retournant vers la conscience agissante, C'est-à-dire libre, la fait naturellement entrer dans les cadres où elle a coutume de voir la matière s'insérer. Elle apercevra donc toujours la liberté sous forme de nécessité ; toujours elle négligera la part de nouveauté ou de création inhérente à l'acte libre, toujours elle substituera à l'action elle-même une imitation artificielle, approximative, obtenue en composant l'ancien avec l'ancien et le même avec le même. Ainsi, aux yeux d'une philosophie qui fait effort pour réabsorber l'intelligence dans l'intuition, bien des difficultés s'évanouissent ou s'atténuent. Mais une telle doctrine ne facilite pas seulement la spéculation. Elle nous donne aussi plus de force pour agir et pour vivre. Car, avec elle, nous ne nous sentons plus isolés dans l'humanité, l'humanité ne nous semble pas non plus isolée dans la nature qu'elle domine. Comme le plus petit grain de poussière est solidaire de notre système solaire tout entier, entraîné avec lui dans ce mouvement indivisé de descente qui est la matérialité même, ainsi tous les êtres organisés, du plus humble au plus élevé, depuis les premières origines de la vie jusqu'au temps où nous sommes, et dans tous les lieux comme dans tous les temps, ne font que rendre sensible aux yeux une impulsion unique, inverse du mouvement de la matière et, en elle-même, indivisible. Tous les vivants se tiennent, et tous cèdent a la même formidable poussée. L'animal prend son point d'appui sur la plante, l'homme chevauche sur l'animalité, et l'humanité entière, dans l'espace et dans le temps, est une immense armée qui galope à côté de chacun de nous, en avant et en arrière de nous, dans une charge entraînante capable de culbuter toutes les résistances et de franchir bien des obstacles, même peut-être la mort.  ## Chapitre IV. Le mécanisme cinématographique de la pensée et l'illusion1 mécanistique. Coup d'œil sur l'histoire des systèmes. Le devenir réel et le faux évolutionnisme.
e: In the course of my first chapter, I drew a line of demarcation between the inorganic and the organised, but I indicated that the cutting up of matter into unorganised bodies is relative to our senses and to our intellect, and that matter, regarded as an undivided whole, must be a flux rather than a thing. In this way I was preparing the way for a rapprochement between the inert and the living. On the other hand, I showed in my second chapter that the same opposition is found again between intellect and instinct, the latter tuned to certain determinations of life, the former modelled on the configuration of inert matter. But instinct and intellect, I added, both stand out against a single background, which might be called, for want of a better word, Consciousness in general, and which must be coextensive with universal life. In this way I gave a glimpse of the possibility of engendering the intellect, starting from the consciousness that envelops it. The moment would therefore have come to attempt a genesis of the intellect together with a genesis of bodies, two undertakings evidently correlative with each other, if it is true that the main lines of our intellect trace the general form of our action on matter, and that the detail of matter is regulated by the requirements of our action. Intellectuality and materiality would have been constituted, in detail, by reciprocal adaptation. Both would derive from a wider and higher form of existence. It is there that we should have to put them back, in order to see them issue from it. Such an attempt will appear at first sight to surpass in temerity the boldest speculations of the metaphysicians. It would claim to go further than psychology, further than cosmogonies, further than traditional metaphysics, for psychology, cosmology and metaphysics begin by taking the intellect for granted in what is essential to it, whereas here it is a question of engendering it, in its form and in its matter. The undertaking is in reality much more modest, as I shall show. But let us first say in what respect it is distinguished from the others. To begin with psychology, we must not believe that it engenders the intellect when it follows its progressive development through the animal series. Comparative psychology teaches us that the more intelligent an animal is, the more it tends to reflect on the actions by which it uses things and thus to draw near to man; but its actions already adopted, of themselves, the principal lines of human action, they made out in the material world the same general directions that we make out in it, they rested on the same objects linked together by the same relations, so that the animal intellect, although it does not form concepts properly so called, already moves in a conceptual atmosphere. Absorbed at every moment by the acts and attitudes that issue from it, drawn outward by them, thus externalising itself in relation to itself, it no doubt acts out representations rather than thinking them; at least this play already traces in rough outline the schema of the human intellect1. To explain the intellect of man by that of the animal therefore consists simply in developing an embryo of humanity into the human. One shows how a certain direction has been followed further and further by more and more intelligent beings. But from the moment one posits the direction, one takes the intellect for granted. One takes it for granted also, as one takes matter for granted at the same stroke, in a cosmogony like that of Spencer. We are shown matter obeying laws, objects linked to objects and facts to facts by constant relations, consciousness receiving the imprint of these relations and these laws, thus adopting the general configuration of nature and determining itself as intellect. But how can we fail to see that the intellect is presupposed as soon as objects and facts are posited? A priori, apart from any hypothesis about the essence of matter, it is evident that the materiality of a body does not stop at the point where we touch it. It is present wherever its influence makes itself felt. Now its attractive force, to speak of that alone, is exerted on the sun, on the planets, perhaps on the entire universe. The more physics advances, moreover, the more it effaces the individuality of bodies and even of the particles into which the scientific imagination began by decomposing them; bodies and corpuscles tend to melt into a universal interaction. Our perceptions give us the design of our possible action on things much more than that of things themselves. The outlines we find in objects simply mark what we can reach and modify in them. The lines we see traced through matter are the very lines along which we are called upon to move. Outlines and roads have become marked in proportion as the action of consciousness on matter was being prepared, that is to say, in short, in proportion as the intellect was being constituted. It is doubtful whether animals built on another plan than ours, a Mollusc or an Insect for example, cut up matter according to the same articulations. It is not even necessary that they should break it up into bodies. To follow the indications of instinct, there is no need to perceive objects; it suffices to distinguish properties. The intellect, on the contrary, even in its humblest form, already aspires to make matter act on matter. If, on some side, matter lends itself to a division into agents and patients, or more simply into coexistent and distinct fragments, it is to that side that the intellect will look. And the more it busies itself with dividing, the more it will spread out in space, in the form of extension juxtaposed with extension, a matter that no doubt tends towards spatiality, but whose parts are nevertheless still in a state of reciprocal implication and interpenetration. Thus the same movement that leads the mind to determine itself as intellect, that is to say into distinct concepts, brings matter to break up into objects clearly external to one another. The more consciousness intellectualises itself, the more matter spatialises itself. That is to say that the evolutionist philosophy, when it represents to itself in space a matter cut up along the very lines that our action will follow, takes for granted in advance, ready-made, the intellect that it claimed to engender. Metaphysics devotes itself to a labour of the same kind, but subtler and more conscious of itself, when it deduces the categories of thought a priori. The intellect is compressed, brought back to its quintessence, made to fit into a principle so simple that one might believe it empty: from this principle one then draws what one has put into it potentially. In this way one no doubt shows the coherence of the intellect with itself, one defines the intellect, one gives its formula, but one does not at all retrace its genesis. An undertaking like that of Fichte, though more philosophical than that of Spencer in that it respects more the true order of things, scarcely takes us any further. Fichte takes thought in a state of concentration and expands it into reality. Spencer starts from external reality and condenses it again into intellect. But in the one case as in the other, one must begin by taking the intellect for granted, either contracted or expanded, grasped in itself by a direct vision or perceived by reflection in nature, as in a mirror. The agreement of most philosophers on this point comes from their concurring in affirming the unity of nature, and in representing this unity to themselves under an abstract and geometrical form. Between the organised and the unorganised they do not see, they will not see, the break. Some start from the inorganic and claim, by compounding it with itself, to reconstitute the living; others posit life first and make their way towards inert matter by a skilfully managed decrescendo; but, for the one party and for the other, there are in nature only differences of degree – degrees of complexity in the first hypothesis, degrees of intensity in the second. Once this principle is admitted, the intellect becomes as vast as the real, for it is indisputable that whatever is geometrical in things is entirely accessible to the human intellect; and, if the continuity is perfect between geometry and the rest, all the rest becomes equally intelligible, equally intelligent. Such is the postulate of most systems. One will easily be convinced of this by comparing with one another doctrines that seem to have no point of contact between them, no common measure, those of a Fichte and of a Spencer for example – two names that chance has just led me to set side by side. At the bottom of these speculations there are, then, the two convictions (correlative and complementary) that nature is one and that the function of the intellect is to embrace it in its entirety. The faculty of knowing being supposed coextensive with the totality of experience, there can no longer be any question of engendering it. One takes it as given and makes use of it, as one uses sight to take in the horizon. It is true that opinions will differ on the value of the result: for some, it is reality itself that the intellect grasps, for others it is only its phantom. But, phantom or reality, what the intellect seizes is held to be the totality of what can be seized. This explains the exaggerated confidence of philosophy in the powers of the individual mind. Whether it be dogmatic or critical, whether it consent to the relativity of our knowledge or claim to install itself in the absolute, a philosophy is generally the work of a philosopher, a single and global vision of the whole. It is to be taken or left. More modest, and also the only one capable of completing and perfecting itself, is the philosophy I am calling for. The human intellect, as I conceive it, is not at all the one that Plato showed us in the allegory of the cave. Its function is no more to watch empty shadows pass by than to turn round and contemplate the dazzling sun behind it. It has something else to do. Harnessed, like oxen at the plough, to a heavy task, we feel the play of our muscles and our joints, the weight of the plough and the resistance of the soil: to act and to know oneself acting, to come into contact with reality and even to live it, but only in so far as it concerns the work being accomplished and the furrow being dug – that is the function of the human intellect. Yet a beneficent fluid bathes us, from which we draw the very strength to work and to live. From this ocean of life, in which we are immersed, we are constantly drawing something in, and we feel that our being, or at least the intellect that guides it, was formed in it by a kind of local solidification. Philosophy can only be an effort to dissolve itself anew into the whole. The intellect, reabsorbed into its principle, will live its own genesis over again in reverse. But the undertaking can no longer be completed at one stroke; it will necessarily be collective and progressive. It will consist in an exchange of impressions which, correcting one another and also superimposing themselves on one another, will end by expanding humanity within us and by obtaining that it transcend itself. But this method has against it the most inveterate habits of the mind. It at once suggests the idea of a vicious circle. In vain, we shall be told, do you claim to go further than the intellect: how will you do so, except with the intellect itself? All that is lit up in your consciousness is intellect. You are inside your thought, you will not get out of it. Say, if you like, that the intellect is capable of progress, that it will see more and more clearly into a greater and greater number of things. But do not speak of engendering it, for it is with your intellect again that you would carry out its genesis. The objection naturally presents itself to the mind. But with such reasoning one could just as well prove the impossibility of acquiring any new habit whatever. It is of the essence of reasoning to shut us up within the circle of the given. But action breaks the circle. If you had never seen a man swim, you would perhaps tell me that swimming is an impossible thing, inasmuch as, to learn to swim, one would have to begin by keeping oneself up in the water, and consequently already know how to swim. Reasoning will always nail me, in fact, to dry land. But if, quite simply, I throw myself into the water without being afraid, I shall at first keep myself up on the water after a fashion by struggling against it, and little by little I shall adapt myself to this new medium, I shall learn to swim. Thus, in theory, there is a kind of absurdity in wishing to know otherwise than by the intellect; but, if one frankly accepts the risk, action will perhaps cut the knot that reasoning has tied and will not untie. The risk will, moreover, seem less great the more one adopts the point of view at which I place myself. I have shown that the intellect detached itself from a vaster reality, but that there was never a clean break between the two: around conceptual thought there remains an indistinct fringe that recalls its origin. More than that, I compared the intellect to a solid nucleus that had been formed by way of condensation. This nucleus does not differ radically from the fluid that envelops it. It will be reabsorbed into it only because it is made of the same substance. He who throws himself into the water, having never known anything but the resistance of dry land, would drown at once if he did not struggle against the fluidity of the new medium; he is obliged to cling to whatever, so to speak, solidity the water still offers him. Only on this condition does one end by accommodating oneself to the fluid in what it has of the unsubstantial. So it is with our thought, once it has resolved to make the leap. But it must leap, that is to say, leave its own medium. Never will reason, reasoning about its powers, succeed in extending them, even though this extension does not appear at all unreasonable once it has been accomplished. You may execute thousands upon thousands of variations on the theme of walking, you will not draw from them a rule for swimming. Go into the water, and, when you know how to swim, you will understand that the mechanism of swimming is connected with that of walking. The first prolongs the second, but the second would not have introduced you into the first. Thus, you may speculate as intelligently as you please on the mechanism of the intellect, you will never, by this method, succeed in going beyond it. You will obtain something more complicated, but not something higher, or even simply something different. Things must be forced, and, by an act of will, the intellect must be pushed out of its home. The vicious circle, then, is only apparent. It is, on the contrary, real, I believe, with every other way of philosophising. This is what I should like to show in a few words, if only to prove that philosophy cannot, must not, accept the relation established by pure intellectualism between the theory of knowledge and the theory of the known, between metaphysics and science. At first sight it may seem prudent to leave the consideration of facts to positive science. Physics and chemistry will occupy themselves with inert matter, the biological and psychological sciences will study the manifestations of life. The philosopher's task is then sharply circumscribed. He receives the facts and the laws from the hands of the scientist, and, whether he seeks to go beyond them in order to reach their deeper causes, or whether he believes it impossible to go further and proves this by the very analysis of scientific knowledge, in both cases he has for the facts and for the relations, such as science transmits them to him, the respect that is owed to a matter already judged. Upon this knowledge he will superimpose a critique of the faculty of knowing and also, should the occasion arise, a metaphysics: as for knowledge itself, in its materiality, he holds it to be the business of science and not of philosophy. But how can one fail to see that this so-called division of labour amounts to muddling and confusing everything? The metaphysics or the critique that the philosopher reserves to himself to make, he is going to receive ready-made from positive science, already contained in the descriptions and the analyses whose entire charge he has left to the scientist. For not having wished to intervene, from the outset, in questions of fact, he finds himself reduced, in questions of principle, to formulating purely and simply, in more precise terms, the unconscious and therefore inconsistent metaphysics and critique that are sketched out by the very attitude of science towards reality. Let us not be deceived by an apparent analogy between natural things and human things. We are not here in the judicial domain, where the description of the fact and the judgement on the fact are two distinct things, for the very simple reason that there is then above the fact, independent of it, a law enacted by a legislator. Here the laws are internal to the facts and relative to the lines that have been followed in cutting up the real into distinct facts. One cannot describe the aspect of the object without prejudging its inner nature and its organisation. The form is no longer altogether isolable from the matter, and he who began by reserving questions of principle for philosophy, and who wished thereby to set philosophy above the sciences as a Court of Cassation is set above the assize courts and the courts of appeal, will be led, step by step, to make of it no more than a mere court of registration, charged at most with drafting in more precise terms sentences that reach it already irrevocably pronounced. Positive science, in fact, is the work of pure intellect. Now, whether one accepts or rejects my conception of the intellect, there is one point that everyone will grant me, namely that the intellect feels most at home in the presence of unorganised matter. Of this matter it makes better and better use by mechanical inventions, and mechanical inventions become the easier for it the more mechanically it thinks matter. It carries within it, in the form of natural logic, a latent geometrism that is released in proportion as it penetrates further into the intimacy of inert matter. It is attuned to this matter, and that is why the physics and the metaphysics of inert matter are so close to each other. Now, when the intellect approaches the study of life, it necessarily treats the living like the inert, applying to this new object the same forms, carrying over into this new domain the same habits that have succeeded so well for it in the old. And it is right to do so, for only on this condition will the living offer our action the same hold as inert matter. But the truth that is thus arrived at becomes wholly relative to our faculty of acting. It is no longer anything but a symbolic truth. It cannot have the same value as physical truth, being only an extension of physics to an object of which we agree a priori to consider only the external aspect. The duty of philosophy would therefore be to intervene actively here, to examine the living without any ulterior thought of practical use, freeing itself from the forms and the habits that are properly intellectual. Its own object is to speculate, that is to say, to see; its attitude towards the living could not be that of science, which aims only at acting, and which, being able to act only through the intermediary of inert matter, considers the rest of reality under this single aspect. What will happen, then, if it leaves biological facts and psychological facts to positive science alone, as it has left to it, rightly, the physical facts? A priori it will accept a mechanistic conception of the whole of nature, a conception unreflecting and even unconscious, issuing from material need. A priori it will accept the doctrine of the simple unity of knowledge, and of the abstract unity of nature. From then on philosophy is ready-made. The philosopher has no longer any choice but between a metaphysical dogmatism and a metaphysical scepticism, which rest, at bottom, on the same postulate, and which add nothing to positive science. He may hypostatise the unity of nature or, what comes to the same thing, the unity of science, in a being that will be nothing since it will do nothing, in an ineffectual God who will simply sum up in himself all that is given, or in an eternal Matter, from whose bosom the properties of things and the laws of nature would pour forth, or again in a pure Form which would seek to seize an unseizable multiplicity and which will be, as one pleases, the form of nature or the form of thought. All these philosophies will say, in various languages, that science is right to treat the living like the inert, and that there is no difference of value, no distinction to be made, between the results at which the intellect arrives in applying its categories, whether it be resting in inert matter or attacking life. Yet, in many cases, one feels the frame cracking. But, since one did not begin by distinguishing between the inert and the living, the one adapted in advance to the frame into which it is inserted, the other unable to hold in it except by a convention that eliminates what is essential in it, one is reduced to casting an equal suspicion on everything that the frame contains. A metaphysical dogmatism, which set up as an absolute the factitious unity of science, will now be succeeded by a scepticism or a relativism that will universalise and extend to all the results of science the artificial character of certain of them. Thus philosophy will henceforth oscillate between the doctrine that holds absolute reality to be unknowable and the doctrine which, in the idea it gives us of that reality, says nothing more than science said. For having wished to forestall all conflict between science and philosophy, one will have sacrificed philosophy without science having gained much thereby. And for having claimed to avoid the apparent vicious circle that would consist in using the intellect to go beyond the intellect, one will go round in a very real circle, that which consists in laboriously rediscovering, in metaphysics, a unity that one began by positing a priori, a unity that one admitted blindly, unconsciously, by the mere fact that one was leaving the whole of experience to science and the whole of the real to the pure understanding. Let us begin, on the contrary, by drawing a line of demarcation between the inert and the living. We shall find that the first enters naturally into the frames of the intellect, that the second lends itself to them only artificially, and that from then on one must adopt a special attitude towards the latter and examine it with eyes that are not those of positive science. Philosophy thus invades the domain of experience. It meddles in many things that, until now, were none of its concern. Science, theory of knowledge and metaphysics are going to find themselves carried on to the same ground. At first a certain confusion among them will result. All three will at first believe they have lost something by it. But all three will end by profiting from the encounter. Scientific knowledge, in fact, could pride itself on the fact that a uniform value was attributed to its affirmations over the entire domain of experience. But, precisely because all of them found themselves placed in the same rank, all of them ended by being tainted there with the same relativity. It will no longer be so once one has begun by making the distinction that, in my view, is called for. The understanding is at home in the domain of inert matter. It is on this matter that human action is essentially exercised, and action, as I said above, cannot move in the unreal. Thus, provided that one considers only the general form of physics, and not the detail of its realisation, one may say that it touches the absolute. On the contrary, it is by accident – chance or convention, as you will – that science obtains on the living a hold analogous to that which it has on inert matter. Here the application of the frames of the understanding is no longer natural. I do not mean that it is no longer legitimate, in the scientific sense of the word. If science is to extend our action on things, and if we can act only with inert matter as our instrument, science can and must continue to treat the living as it treated the inert. But it will be understood that, the further it penetrates into the depths of life, the more symbolic the knowledge it furnishes us becomes, relative to the contingencies of action. On this new ground philosophy will therefore have to follow science, in order to superimpose on scientific truth a knowledge of another kind, which may be called metaphysical. From then on all our knowledge, scientific or metaphysical, is raised up again. In the absolute we are, we move and we live. The knowledge we have of it is incomplete, no doubt, but not external or relative. It is being itself, in its depths, that we reach by the combined and progressive development of science and philosophy. By thus renouncing the factitious unity that the understanding imposes on nature from without, we shall perhaps rediscover its true unity, inner and living. For the effort we make to go beyond the pure understanding introduces us into something vaster, out of which our understanding is cut and from which it must have detached itself. And, as matter regulates itself on the intellect, as there is between them an evident agreement, one cannot engender the one without carrying out the genesis of the other. An identical process must have cut out matter and the intellect at the same time from a stuff that contained them both. Into this reality we shall place ourselves back more and more completely, in proportion as we strive the more to transcend pure intellect. Let us concentrate, then, on what we have that is at once most detached from the external and least penetrated with intellectuality. Let us seek, in the deepest depths of ourselves, the point where we feel ourselves most inside our own life. It is into pure duration that we then plunge back, a duration in which the past, always on the march, is swelling unceasingly with a present that is absolutely new. But, at the same time, we feel the spring of our will stretched to its utmost limit. We must, by a violent contraction of our personality upon itself, gather up our past which is slipping away, in order to thrust it, compact and undivided, into a present that it will create by entering into it. Very rare are the moments when we take hold of ourselves to this degree: they are one with our truly free actions. And, even then, we never hold ourselves entirely. Our feeling of duration, I mean the coincidence of our self with itself, admits of degrees. But, the deeper the feeling and the more complete the coincidence, the more the life into which they put us back absorbs intellectuality by going beyond it. For the essential function of the intellect is to link the same with the same, and the only facts entirely adaptable to the frame of the intellect are those that repeat themselves. Now, on the real moments of real duration the intellect no doubt finds a hold after the event, by reconstituting the new state with a series of views taken of it from outside, which resemble as closely as possible what is already known: in this sense, the state contains intellectuality "potentially", so to speak. It overflows it, however; it remains incommensurable with it, being indivisible and new. Let us now relax, let us interrupt the effort that thrusts into the present the greatest possible part of the past. If the relaxation were complete, there would no longer be either memory or will: which is to say that we never fall into this absolute passivity, any more than we can make ourselves absolutely free. But, at the limit, we catch a glimpse of an existence made of a present that would begin again unceasingly – no more real duration, nothing but the instantaneous which dies and is born again indefinitely. Is that the existence of matter? Not altogether, no doubt, for analysis resolves it into elementary vibrations, the shortest of which are of a very slight duration, almost vanishing, but not nil. One may nevertheless presume that physical existence inclines in this second direction, as psychical existence does in the first. At the bottom of "spirituality" on the one hand, and of "materiality" together with intellectuality on the other, there would thus be two processes of opposite direction, and one would pass from the first to the second by way of inversion, perhaps even of simple interruption, if it is true that inversion and interruption are two terms that must be held here to be synonymous, as I shall show in detail a little further on. This presumption will be confirmed if one considers things from the point of view of extension, and no longer only from that of duration. The more we become conscious of our progress in pure duration, the more we feel the various parts of our being enter into one another and our whole personality concentrate itself in a point, or rather in a sharp edge, which inserts itself into the future, cutting into it unceasingly. Therein consist free life and free action. Let us, on the contrary, let ourselves go; instead of acting, let us dream. At one stroke our self is scattered; our past, which until then was gathered up upon itself in the indivisible impulse that it communicated to us, breaks up into thousands upon thousands of recollections that become external to one another. They cease to interpenetrate in proportion as they become more fixed. Our personality thus descends again in the direction of space. It skirts space constantly, moreover, in sensation. I shall not dwell here on a point that I have gone into elsewhere. Let me merely recall that extension admits of degrees, that every sensation is extensive in some measure, and that the idea of unextended sensations, artificially localised in space, is a mere view of the mind, suggested by an unconscious metaphysics much rather than by psychological observation. No doubt we take only the first steps in the direction of extension, even when we let ourselves go as much as we can. But let us suppose, for a moment, that matter consists in this same movement pushed further, and that the physical is simply the psychical inverted. We should then understand why the mind feels so much at home, and moves so naturally, in space, as soon as matter suggests to it a more distinct representation of it. Of this space it had the implicit representation in the very feeling it had of its possible relaxation, that is to say, of its possible extension. It finds it again in things, but it would have obtained it without them if it had had an imagination powerful enough to push to the end the inversion of its natural movement. On the other hand, we should thus explain to ourselves why matter accentuates its materiality still further under the gaze of the mind. Matter began by helping the mind to go down matter's own slope, it gave the mind the impulse. But the mind continues, once launched. The representation it forms of pure space is only the schema of the term in which this movement would end. Once in possession of the form of space, it uses it as a net whose meshes can be made and unmade at will, a net which, thrown over matter, divides it as the needs of our action require. Thus the space of our geometry and the spatiality of things engender each other by the reciprocal action and reaction of two terms that are of the same essence, but that move in opposite directions. Neither is space as foreign to our nature as we imagine it to be, nor is matter as completely extended in space as our intellect and our senses represent it. I have dealt with the first point elsewhere. As regards the second, I shall confine myself to observing that perfect spatiality would consist in a perfect externality of the parts in relation to one another, that is to say, in a complete reciprocal independence. Now, there is no material point that does not act on every other material point. If one notes that a thing is truly where it acts, one will be led to say (as Faraday did1) that all the atoms interpenetrate and that each of them fills the world. On such a hypothesis, the atom, or more generally the material point, becomes a mere view of the mind, the one at which we arrive by carrying far enough the work (wholly relative to our faculty of acting) by which we subdivide matter into bodies. Yet it is indisputable that matter lends itself to this subdivision, and that, in supposing it divisible into parts external to one another, we construct a science sufficiently representative of the real. It is indisputable that, though there is no altogether isolated system, science nevertheless finds the means of cutting up the universe into systems relatively independent of one another, and that it does not thereby commit any appreciable error. What does this mean, if not that matter extends itself in space without being absolutely extended in it, and that, in holding it to be decomposable into isolated systems, in attributing to it quite distinct elements that change in relation to one another without changing themselves (that "are displaced", we say, without being altered), in conferring on it, in short, the properties of pure space, one transports oneself to the term of the movement of which matter merely sketches the direction? What the Transcendental Aesthetic of Kant seems to me to have established in a definitive manner is that extension is not a material attribute comparable to the others. On the notion of heat, on that of colour or of weight, reasoning will not work indefinitely: in order to know the modalities of weight, or of heat, one will have to resume contact with experience. It is not so with the notion of space. Supposing it to be furnished to us empirically by sight and touch (and Kant never disputed this), it has this remarkable feature, that the mind, speculating on it with its own forces alone, cuts out within it a priori figures whose properties it will determine a priori: experience, with which it has not kept in contact, nevertheless follows it through the infinite complications of its reasonings and invariably proves them right. That is the fact. Kant brought it fully to light. But the explanation of the fact must be sought, I believe, along quite another path than the one on which Kant set out. The intellect, as Kant represents it to us, is bathed in an atmosphere of spatiality to which it is as inseparably united as the living body to the air it breathes. Our perceptions reach us only after having passed through this atmosphere. They have been impregnated in it in advance with our geometry, so that our faculty of thinking merely rediscovers, in matter, the mathematical properties that our faculty of perceiving deposited there in advance. Thus we are assured of seeing matter bend docilely to our reasonings; but this matter, in what it has of the intelligible, is our work: of reality "in itself" we know nothing and shall never know anything, since we seize of it only its refraction through the forms of our faculty of perceiving. If we claim to affirm anything of it, at once the contrary affirmation arises, equally demonstrable, equally plausible: the ideality of space, proved directly by the analysis of knowledge, is proved indirectly by the antinomies to which the opposite thesis leads. Such is the guiding idea of the Kantian critique. It inspired Kant with a peremptory refutation of the so-called "empiricist" theories of knowledge. It is, in my view, definitive in what it denies. But does it bring us, in what it affirms, the solution of the problem? It takes space as given, as a ready-made form of our faculty of perceiving – a veritable deus ex machina of which one sees neither how it arises nor why it is what it is rather than anything else. It takes as given "things in themselves" of which it claims that we can know nothing: by what right, then, does it affirm their existence, even as "problematic"? If the unknowable reality projects into our faculty of perceiving a sensible manifold capable of fitting into it exactly, is it not, by that very fact, known in part? And, in examining this fitting more deeply, shall we not be led, on one point at least, to suppose between things and our mind a pre-established agreement – a lazy hypothesis, which Kant was right to wish to do without? At bottom, it is for not having distinguished degrees in spatiality that Kant had to take space as given ready-made – whence the question of knowing how the "sensible manifold" adapts itself to it. It is for the same reason that he believed matter to be entirely unfolded into parts absolutely external to one another: hence antinomies, of which one would easily see that the thesis and the antithesis suppose the perfect coincidence of matter with geometrical space, but which vanish as soon as one ceases to extend to matter what is true of pure space. Hence, finally, the conclusion that there are three alternatives, and three only, among which to choose for the theory of knowledge: either the mind regulates itself on things, or things regulate themselves on the mind, or one must suppose between things and the mind a mysterious concordance. But the truth is that there is a fourth, which Kant does not seem to have thought of – first because he did not think that the mind overflowed the intellect, and secondly (and this is, at bottom, the same thing) because he did not attribute an absolute existence to duration, having put time a priori on the same line as space. This solution would consist, first, in considering the intellect as a special function of the mind, essentially turned towards inert matter. It would consist, next, in saying that neither does matter determine the form of the intellect, nor does the intellect impose its form on matter, nor have matter and the intellect been regulated on each other by some pre-established harmony or other, but that the intellect and matter have progressively adapted themselves to each other so as to come to rest at last in a common form. This adaptation would, moreover, have come about quite naturally, because it is the same inversion of the same movement that creates at once the intellectuality of the mind and the materiality of things. From this point of view, the knowledge of matter given us by our perception, on the one side, and by science, on the other, appears to us as approximate, no doubt, but not as relative. Our perception, whose role is to light up our actions, effects a sectioning of matter that will always be too sharp, always subordinated to practical demands, always, consequently, in need of revision. Our science, which aspires to take the mathematical form, accentuates the spatiality of matter more than it should; its schemata will therefore be, in general, too precise, and moreover always to be made over again. For a scientific theory to be definitive, the mind would have to be able to embrace the totality of things as a whole and situate them exactly in relation to one another; but in reality we are obliged to pose problems one by one, in terms that are by that very fact provisional terms, so that the solution of each problem will have to be indefinitely corrected by the solution that will be given to the problems that follow, and so that science, as a whole, is relative to the contingent order in which the problems have been posed in turn. It is in this sense, and in this measure, that science must be held to be conventional; but the conventionality is one of fact, so to speak, and not of right. In principle, positive science bears on reality itself, provided that it does not go beyond its own domain, which is inert matter. Scientific knowledge, thus considered, is raised. On the other hand, the theory of knowledge becomes an infinitely difficult undertaking, and one that exceeds the powers of the pure intellect. It is no longer enough, in fact, to determine the categories of thought by an analysis conducted with prudence; the task is to engender them. As regards space, one would have, by an effort of the mind sui generis, to follow the progression, or rather the regression, of the extra-spatial degrading itself into spatiality. By placing ourselves first as high as possible in our own consciousness, and then letting ourselves fall little by little, we do indeed have the feeling that our self is extending itself into inert recollections externalised in relation to one another, instead of tensing itself into an indivisible and active willing. But this is only a beginning. Our consciousness, in sketching the movement, shows us its direction and lets us glimpse the possibility of its continuing to the end; it does not itself go so far. On the other hand, if we consider matter, which at first seems to us to coincide with space, we find that, the more our attention fixes on it, the more the parts that we called juxtaposed enter into one another, each of them undergoing the action of the whole, which is consequently present to it in some manner. Thus, although it unfolds in the direction of space, matter does not quite reach it: from which one may conclude that it merely continues much further the movement that consciousness could sketch in us in the nascent state. We hold, then, the two ends of the chain, although we do not succeed in seizing the other links. Will they always escape us? It must be considered that philosophy, as I define it, has not yet become completely conscious of itself. Physics understands its role when it pushes matter in the direction of spatiality; but has metaphysics understood its own when it simply fell into step behind physics, with the chimerical hope of going further in the same direction? Would not its proper task be, on the contrary, to climb back up the slope that physics descends, to bring matter back to its origins, and progressively to constitute a cosmology that would be, if one may so speak, an inverted psychology? All that appears positive to the physicist and the geometer would become, from this new point of view, an interruption or inversion of the true positivity, which would have to be defined in psychological terms. Certainly, if one considers the admirable order of mathematics, the perfect agreement of the objects with which it deals, the logic immanent in numbers and figures, the certainty we have, however diverse and complex our reasonings on the same subject, of always coming back to the same conclusion, one will hesitate to see in properties so positive in appearance a system of negations, the absence rather than the presence of a true reality. But it must not be forgotten that our intellect, which observes this order and admires it, is directed in the very sense of the movement that ends in the materiality and the spatiality of its object. The more complication it puts into its object by analysing it, the more complicated is the order it finds there. And this order and this complication necessarily strike it as a positive reality, being of the same direction as itself. When a poet reads me his verses, I can be interested enough in him to enter into his thought, insert myself into his feelings, live over again the simple state that he has scattered in sentences and words. I then sympathise with his inspiration, I follow it with a continuous movement that is, like the inspiration itself, an undivided act. Now, I need only slacken my attention, relax what was tense in me, for the sounds, hitherto drowned in the sense, to appear to me distinctly, one by one, in their materiality. For this I have nothing to add; it is enough that I take something away. In proportion as I let myself go, the successive sounds will become more individualised: as the sentences had broken up into words, so the words will be scanned into syllables that I shall perceive in turn. Let us go further still in the direction of the dream: it is the letters that will become distinct from one another, and that I shall see file past, interlaced, on an imaginary sheet of paper. I shall then admire the precision of the interlacings, the marvellous order of the procession, the exact insertion of the letters into the syllables, of the syllables into the words and of the words into the sentences. The further I have advanced in the wholly negative direction of slackening, the more extension and complication I shall have created; the more the complication, in its turn, increases, the more admirable will seem to me the order that continues to reign, unshaken, among the elements. Yet this complication and this extension represent nothing positive: they express a deficiency of will. And, on the other hand, order must needs increase with complication, since it is only an aspect of it: the more parts one perceives symbolically in an indivisible whole, the more the number of relations that the parts have among themselves necessarily increases, since the same undividedness of the real whole continues to hover over the growing multiplicity of symbolic elements into which the scattering of attention has decomposed it. A comparison of this kind will make it understood, in some measure, how the same suppression of positive reality, the same inversion of a certain original movement, can create at one and the same time extension in space and the admirable order that our mathematics discovers there. There is no doubt this difference between the two cases, that words and letters were invented by a positive effort of humanity, whereas space arises automatically, as the remainder of a subtraction arises once the two terms are posited1. But in the one case as in the other, the infinite complication of the parts and their perfect coordination with one another are created at one stroke by an inversion that is, at bottom, an interruption, that is to say, a diminution of positive reality. All the operations of our intellect tend towards geometry, as towards the term in which they find their perfect completion. But, since geometry is necessarily prior to them (since these operations will never succeed in reconstructing space and cannot do otherwise than take it as given), it is evident that it is a latent geometry, immanent in our representation of space, that is the mainspring of our intellect and that makes it go. One will be convinced of this by considering the two essential functions of the intellect, the faculty of deducing and that of inducing. Let us begin with deduction. The same movement by which I trace a figure in space engenders its properties: they are visible and tangible in this very movement; I feel, I live in space the relation of the definition to its consequences, of the premisses to the conclusion. All the other concepts whose idea experience suggests to me are only partly reconstitutable a priori; their definition will therefore be imperfect, and the deductions into which these concepts enter, however rigorously one links the conclusion to the premisses, will share in this imperfection. But when I trace roughly in the sand the base of a triangle, and begin to form the two angles at the base, I know with certainty and I understand absolutely that, if these two angles are equal, the sides will be equal too, the figure then being able to turn over upon itself without anything in it being changed. I know it long before having learned geometry. Thus, prior to learned geometry, there is a natural geometry whose clarity and evidence surpass those of the other deductions. These others bear on qualities and no longer on magnitudes. They are therefore doubtless formed on the model of the first, and must borrow their force from the fact that, beneath the quality, we confusedly see magnitude showing through. Let us note that questions of position and of magnitude are the first that present themselves to our activity, those that the intellect externalised in action resolves even before reflective intellect has appeared: the savage is better than the civilised man at estimating distances, at determining a direction, at retracing from memory the often complex schema of the route he has travelled and thus returning, in a straight line, to his point of departure1. If the animal does not deduce explicitly, if it does not explicitly form concepts, neither does it represent to itself a homogeneous space. You cannot take this space as given without introducing, at the same stroke, a virtual geometry that will of itself degrade into logic. All the repugnance of philosophers to considering things from this angle comes from the fact that respects the relation that Plotinus supposes (in developments by which M. Ravaisson was to be inspired), when he makes extension not, to be sure, an inversion of original Being, but an enfeeblement of its essence, one of the last stages of the procession. (See in particular: Enn., IV, III, 9-11 and III, VI, 17-18.) Ancient philosophy, however, did not see what consequences resulted from this for mathematics, for Plotinus, like Plato, set up the mathematical essences as absolute realities. Above all, it let itself be deceived by the wholly external analogy of duration with extension. It treated the former as it had treated the latter, considering change as a degradation of immutability, the sensible as a fall from the intelligible. Hence, as I shall show in the next chapter, a philosophy that misunderstands the real function and scope of the intellect. the logical work of the intellect represents in their eyes a positive effort of the mind. But if by spirituality one means a march forward to ever new creations, to conclusions incommensurable with the premisses and indeterminable in relation to them, one will have to say of a representation that moves among relations of necessary determination, through premisses that contain their conclusion in advance, that it follows the inverse direction, that of materiality. What appears, from the point of view of the intellect, as an effort, is in itself a letting go. And whereas, from the point of view of the intellect, there is a begging of the question in making geometry issue automatically from space, and logic from geometry itself, on the contrary, if space is the ultimate term of the mind's movement of relaxation, one cannot take space as given without thereby positing logic and geometry, which lie along the path of which pure spatial intuition is the term. It has not been sufficiently noticed how slight is the reach of deduction in the psychological and moral sciences. From a proposition verified by the facts one can here draw verifiable consequences only up to a certain point, in a certain measure. Very soon one must appeal to good sense, that is to say, to the continuous experience of the real, in order to inflect the consequences deduced and bend them along the windings of life. Deduction succeeds in moral matters only metaphorically, so to speak, and in the exact measure in which the moral is transposable into the physical, I mean translatable into spatial symbols. The metaphor never goes very far, any more than the curve lets itself be confused for long with its tangent. How can one fail to be struck by what is strange, and even paradoxical, in this weakness of deduction? Here is a pure operation of the mind, accomplished by the sole force of the mind. It seems that if anywhere it ought to feel at home and move about at its ease, it is among the things of the mind, in the domain of the mind. Not at all; it is there that it is at once at the end of its tether. On the contrary, in geometry, in astronomy, in physics, where we have to do with things external to us, deduction is all-powerful! Observation and experiment are no doubt necessary here in order to arrive at the principle, that is to say, to discover the aspect under which things had to be considered; but, strictly speaking, with a great deal of luck, one could have found it at once; and, as soon as one possesses this principle, one draws from it, far enough, consequences that experience will always verify. What is to be concluded from this, if not that deduction is an operation regulated on the proceedings of matter, modelled on the mobile articulations of matter, implicitly given, in short, with the space that underlies matter? So long as it rolls along in space or in spatialised time, it has only to let itself go. It is duration that puts a spoke in its wheels. Deduction, then, does not go without a lurking thought of spatial intuition. But the same could be said of induction. Certainly it is not necessary to think as a geometer, nor even to think at all, in order to expect from the same conditions the repetition of the same fact. The consciousness of the animal already does this work, and, independently of all consciousness, the living body itself is already constructed to extract from the successive situations in which it finds itself the similarities that concern it, and thus to respond to stimuli by appropriate reactions. But it is a long way from a mechanical expectation and reaction of the body to induction properly so called, which is an intellectual operation. This rests on the belief that there are causes and effects, and that the same effects follow the same causes. Now, if one examines this double belief more deeply, here is what one finds. It implies, first, that reality is decomposable into groups that can practically be held to be isolated and independent. If I boil water in a saucepan placed on a stove, the operation and the objects that sustain it are, in reality, bound up with a multitude of other objects and a multitude of other operations: step by step, one would find that our entire solar system is concerned in what is taking place at this point of space. But, in a certain measure, and for the special end I am pursuing, I may admit that things happen as if the group water–saucepan–lighted stove were an independent microcosm. That is what I affirm first. Now, when I say that this microcosm will always behave in the same way, that the heat will necessarily bring about, at the end of a certain time, the boiling of the water, I admit that, if I take as given a certain number of elements of the system, this suffices for the system to be complete: it completes itself automatically, I am not free to complete it in thought as I please. The lighted stove, the saucepan and the water being posited, together with a certain interval of duration, the boiling, which experience showed me yesterday to be what the system lacked in order to be complete, will complete it tomorrow, at any time whatever, always. What lies at the bottom of this belief? It must be noted that it is more or less assured according to the case, and that it takes on the character of an absolute certainty when the microcosm considered contains nothing but magnitudes. If I posit two numbers, in fact, I am no longer free to choose their difference. If I take as given two sides of a triangle and the included angle, the third side arises of itself, the triangle completes itself automatically. I can, anywhere and at any time, trace the same two sides enclosing the same angle; it is evident that the new triangles thus formed could be superposed on the first, and that consequently the same third side will have come to complete the system. Now, if my certainty is perfect in the case where I reason on pure spatial determinations, must I not suppose that, in the other cases, it is the more so the nearer it approaches this limiting case? Indeed, might it not be the limiting case that shows through all the others1 and that colours them, according to their greater or lesser transparency, with a more or less marked tinge of geometrical necessity? In fact, when I say that my water placed on my stove is going to boil today as it did yesterday, and that this is of absolute necessity, I feel confusedly that my imagination is transporting the stove of today on to that of yesterday, the saucepan on to the saucepan, the water on to the water, the duration that is flowing on to the duration that is flowing, and that the rest then seems bound to coincide as well, for the same reason that makes the third sides of two triangles that are superposed coincide if the first two already coincide with each other. But my imagination proceeds in this way only because it shuts its eyes to two essential points. For the system of today to be superposable on that of yesterday, the latter would have had to wait for the former, time would have had to stop, and everything would have had to become simultaneous with everything: that is what happens in geometry, but in geometry only. Induction therefore implies, first, that in the world of the physicist, as in that of the geometer, time does not count. But it implies also that qualities can be superposed on one another like magnitudes. If I ideally transport today's lighted stove on to yesterday's, I no doubt observe that the form has remained the same; for that it is enough that the surfaces and the edges coincide; but what is the coincidence of two qualities, and how can they be superposed on each other in order to make sure that they are identical? Yet I extend to the second order of reality all that applies to the first. The physicist will later legitimise this operation by reducing, as far as possible, differences of quality to differences of magnitude; but, prior to all science, I incline to assimilate qualities to quantities, as if I perceived behind the former, by transparency, a geometrical mechanism1. The more complete this transparency, the more necessary the repetition of the same fact in the same conditions appears to me. Our inductions are certain, in our eyes, in the exact measure in which we make the qualitative differences melt into the homogeneity of the space that underlies them, so that geometry is the ideal limit of our inductions as well as of our deductions. The movement at whose term lies spatiality deposits along its path the faculty of inducing as well as that of deducing – intellectuality in its entirety. It creates them in the mind. But it also creates, in things, the "order" that our induction, aided by deduction, rediscovers. This order, on which our action leans and in which our intellect recognises itself, seems marvellous to us. Not only do the same gross causes always produce the same overall effects, but, beneath the visible causes and effects, our science discovers an infinity of infinitesimal changes that fit more and more exactly into one another the further the analysis is pushed: so much so that, at the term of this analysis, matter would be, it seems to us, geometry itself. Certainly the intellect rightly admires here the increasing order in the increasing complexity: the one and the other have for it a positive reality, being of the same direction as itself. But things change their aspect when one considers the whole of reality as an undivided march forward to creations that succeed one another. One then divines that the complication of the material elements, and the mathematical order that binds them together, must arise automatically as soon as a partial interruption or inversion occurs within the whole. Since, moreover, the intellect is cut out of the mind by a process of the same kind, it is attuned to this order and this complication, and admires them because it recognises itself in them. But what is admirable in itself, what would deserve to provoke astonishment, is the ceaselessly renewed creation that the whole of the real, undivided, accomplishes as it advances; for no complication of the mathematical order with itself, however elaborate one supposes it, will introduce one atom of novelty into the world, whereas, once this power of creation is posited (and it exists, since we become conscious of it in ourselves, at least, when we act freely), it has only to be distracted from itself in order to relax, to relax in order to extend, to extend in order that the mathematical order presiding over the disposition of the elements thus distinguished, and the inflexible determinism that binds them, may manifest the interruption of the creative act; they are one, moreover, with this very interruption. It is this wholly negative tendency that the particular laws of the physical world express. None of them, taken by itself, has objective reality: it is the work of a scientist who has considered things from a certain angle, isolated certain variables, applied certain conventional units of measurement. And nevertheless there is an approximately mathematical order immanent in matter, an objective order, which our science approaches in proportion as it progresses. For if matter is a slackening of the unextended into the extended and, thereby, of freedom into necessity, then, although it does not altogether coincide with pure homogeneous space, it has been constituted by the movement that leads to it, and from then on it is on the road to geometry. It is true that laws of mathematical form will never apply to it completely. For that it would have to be pure space, and to step out of duration. One can never insist enough on what is artificial in the mathematical form of a physical law, and consequently in our scientific knowledge of things1. Our units of measurement are conventional and, if one may so speak, foreign to the intentions of nature: how can one suppose that nature has referred all the modalities of heat to the expansions of one and the same mass of mercury, or to the changes of pressure of one and the same mass of air kept at a constant volume? But this is not saying enough. In a general way, measuring is a wholly human operation, which implies that one really or ideally superposes two objects on each other a certain number of times. Nature never thought of this superposition. It does not measure, nor does it count. Yet physics counts, measures, relates "quantitative" variations to one another in order to obtain laws, and it succeeds. Its success would be inexplicable if the movement constitutive of materiality were not the very movement which, prolonged by us to its term, that is to say, to homogeneous space, ends in making us count, measure, follow in their respective variations terms that are functions of one another. To effect this prolongation, our intellect has, moreover, only to prolong itself, for it goes naturally to space and to mathematics, intellectuality and materiality being of the same nature and being produced in the same way. If the mathematical order were a positive thing, if there were, immanent in matter, laws comparable to those of our codes, the success of our science would be little short of a miracle. What chance would we have, in fact, of rediscovering nature's standard and of isolating precisely, in order to determine their reciprocal relations, the variables that nature had chosen? But the success of a science of mathematical form would be no less incomprehensible if matter did not have all that is needed to enter into our frames. Only one hypothesis, therefore, remains plausible: that the mathematical order has nothing positive about it, that it is the form towards which a certain interruption tends of itself, and that materiality consists precisely in an interruption of this kind. We shall thus understand how our science can be contingent, relative to the variables it has chosen, relative to the order in which it has successively posed the problems, and yet succeed. It might, as a whole, have been quite different and still have succeeded. This is precisely because no definite system of mathematical laws lies at the basis of nature, and because mathematics in general simply represents the direction in which matter falls back. Put one of those little cork dolls with leaden feet in any posture you like, lay it on its back, turn it upside down, throw it into the air: it will always stand itself up again, automatically. So it is with matter: we can take it by any end and handle it in any way, it will always fall back into one or other of our mathematical frames, because it is ballasted with geometry. But the philosopher will perhaps refuse to found a theory of knowledge on such considerations. He will be reluctant to do so, because the mathematical order, being order, will seem to him to contain something positive. In vain do I say that this order is produced automatically by the interruption of the inverse order, that it is this very interruption. The idea nonetheless persists that there might be no order at all, and that the mathematical order of things, being a conquest over disorder, possesses a positive reality. By examining this point more deeply, one would see what a capital role the idea of disorder plays in the problems relating to the theory of knowledge. It does not appear there explicitly, and that is why no one has concerned himself with it. Yet it is with the critique of this idea that a theory of knowledge ought to begin, for if the great problem is to know why and how reality submits to an order, it is because the absence of every kind of order seems possible or conceivable. This absence of order the realist and the idealist both believe they are thinking of: the realist when he speaks of the regulation that "objective" laws actually impose on a possible disorder of nature, the idealist when he supposes a "sensible manifold" that would be coordinated – being consequently without order – under the organising influence of our understanding. The idea of disorder, taken in the sense of an absence of order, is therefore the one that would have to be analysed first. Philosophy borrows it from everyday life. And it is indisputable that, ordinarily, when we speak of disorder, we are thinking of something. But of what are we thinking? It will be seen, in the next chapter, how difficult it is to determine the content of a negative idea, and to what illusions one exposes oneself, into what inextricable difficulties philosophy falls, for not having undertaken this work. Difficulties and illusions usually arise from accepting as definitive a manner of expression that is essentially provisional. They arise from carrying over into the domain of speculation a procedure made for practice. If I choose a volume at random from my library, I may, after glancing into it, put it back on the shelves saying: "This is not verse." Is that really what I perceived in leafing through the book? Obviously not. I have not seen, I shall never see, an absence of verse. I have seen prose. But since it is poetry I want, I express what I find as a function of what I am looking for, and, instead of saying "here is prose", I say "this is not verse". Conversely, if I take a fancy to read prose and I come upon a volume of verse, I shall exclaim: "this is not prose", thus translating the data of my perception, which shows me verse, into the language of my expectation and my attention, which are fixed on the idea of prose and will hear of nothing else. Now, if M. Jourdain were listening to me, he would no doubt infer from my double exclamation that prose and poetry are two forms of language reserved for books, and that these learned forms have been superimposed on a raw language which was neither prose nor verse. Speaking of this thing which is neither verse nor prose, he would, moreover, believe he was thinking of it: yet this would be only a pseudo-representation. Let us go further: the pseudo-representation might create a pseudo-problem, if M. Jourdain were to ask his professor of philosophy how the form of prose and the form of poetry came to be added on to what possessed neither the one nor the other, and if he wanted to be given the theory, as it were, of the imposition of these two forms on this simple matter. His question would be absurd, and the absurdity would come from his having hypostatised as the common substratum of prose and poetry the simultaneous negation of both, forgetting that the negation of the one consists in the positing of the other. Now, let us suppose that there are two kinds of order, and that these two orders are two contraries within one and the same genus. Let us suppose also that the idea of disorder arises in our mind whenever, in looking for one of the two kinds of order, we encounter the other. The idea of disorder would then have a clear meaning in the ordinary practice of life; it would objectify, for the convenience of language, the disappointment of a mind that finds before it an order different from the one it needs, an order with which it has nothing to do for the moment and which, in this sense, does not exist for it. But it would admit of no theoretical use. If we nevertheless claim, in spite of everything, to introduce it into philosophy, we shall infallibly lose sight of its true meaning. It noted the absence of a certain order, but to the advantage of another (with which one had no need to concern oneself); only, since it applies to each of the two in turn, and even goes back and forth between the two unceasingly, we shall catch it on the way, or rather in mid-air, like the shuttlecock between the two battledores, and we shall treat it as if it represented, no longer the absence of the one or the other order indifferently, but the absence of both together – a thing that is neither perceived nor conceived, a mere verbal entity. Thus would arise the problem of knowing how order imposes itself on disorder, form on matter. By analysing the idea of disorder thus spirited away, one would see that it represents nothing at all, and at the same stroke the problems that had been raised around it would vanish. It is true that one would have to begin by distinguishing, and even by opposing to each other, two kinds of order that are usually confused together. Since this confusion has created the principal difficulties of the problem of knowledge, it will not be useless to dwell once more on the features by which the two orders are distinguished. In a general way, reality is ordered in the exact measure in which it satisfies our thought. Order is therefore a certain agreement between subject and object. It is the mind finding itself again in things. But the mind, as I said, can move in two opposite directions.
