Sometimes it follows its natural direction: it is then progress in the form of tension, continuous creation, free activity. Sometimes it inverts it, and this inversion, pushed to the end, would lead to extension, to the necessary reciprocal determination of elements externalised in relation to one another, and finally to geometrical mechanism. Now, whether experience seems to us to adopt the first direction or to be oriented in the sense of the second, in both cases we say that there is order, for in both processes the mind finds itself again. The confusion between them is therefore natural. To escape it, one would have to give the two kinds of order different names, and that is not easy, because of the variety and the variability of the forms they take. The order of the second kind could be defined by geometry, which is its extreme limit: more generally, it is this order that is in question whenever one finds a relation of necessary determination between causes and effects. It evokes ideas of inertia, of passivity, of automatism. As for the order of the first kind, it no doubt oscillates around finality: it could not, however, be defined by finality, for sometimes it is above it, sometimes below. In its highest forms it is more than finality, for of a free action or a work of art one may say that they manifest a perfect order, and yet they are expressible in terms of ideas only after the event and approximately. Life as a whole, considered as a creative evolution, is something analogous: it transcends finality, if by finality one means the realisation of an idea conceived or conceivable in advance. The frame of finality is therefore too narrow for life in its integrity. On the other hand, it is often too wide for this or that manifestation of life taken by itself. However that may be, it is always with the vital that we have to do here, and the whole of the present study tends to establish that the vital lies in the direction of the voluntary. One might therefore say that this first kind of order is that of the vital or of the willed, in opposition to the second, which is that of the inert and the automatic. Common sense, moreover, instinctively makes the distinction between the two kinds of order, at least in extreme cases: instinctively, too, it brings them together. Of astronomical phenomena one will say that they manifest an admirable order, meaning thereby that they can be foreseen mathematically. And one will find an order no less admirable in a symphony of Beethoven, which is genius, originality and consequently unforeseeability itself. But it is only by exception that order of the first kind takes on so distinct a form. In general, it presents itself with characters that it is in our every interest to confuse with those of the opposite order. It is quite certain, for example, that if we considered the evolution of life as a whole, the spontaneity of its movement and the unforeseeability of its proceedings would force themselves on our attention. But what we meet with in our ordinary experience is this or that determinate living being, these or those special manifestations of life, which repeat more or less forms and facts already known: indeed, the similarity of structure that we observe everywhere between what engenders and what is engendered, a similarity that allows us to enclose an indefinite number of living individuals in the same group, is in our eyes the very type of the generic, the inorganic genera seeming to us to take the living genera as their model. It thus turns out that the vital order, such as it offers itself to us in the experience that breaks it up, presents the same character and performs the same function as the physical order: both make our experience repeat itself, both allow our mind to generalise. In reality, this character has entirely different origins in the two cases, and even opposite meanings. In the second, it has for its type, for its ideal limit, and also for its foundation, the geometrical necessity by virtue of which the same components give an identical resultant. In the first, it implies, on the contrary, the intervention of something that arranges itself so as to obtain the same effect, even when the elementary causes, infinitely complex, may be entirely different. I insisted on this last point in my first chapter, when I showed how identical structures are met with on independent lines of evolution. But, without seeking so far afield, one may presume that the mere reproduction of the type of the ancestor by its descendants is already something quite other than the repetition of one and the same composition of forces that would sum themselves up in an identical resultant. When one thinks of the infinity of infinitesimal elements and infinitesimal causes that concur in the genesis of a living being, when one reflects that the absence or the deviation of one of them would suffice for nothing to work any longer, the first impulse of the mind is to have this army of little workmen supervised by a shrewd foreman, the "vital principle", who would at every moment repair the mistakes committed, correct the effect of moments of inattention, put things back in their place: in this way one tries to translate the difference between the physical order and the vital order, the former making the same combination of causes give the same overall effect, the latter ensuring the stability of the effect even when there is some wavering in the causes. But this is only a translation: on reflection, one finds that there can be no foreman, for the very simple reason that there are no workmen. The causes and the elements that physico-chemical analysis discovers are real causes and elements, no doubt, for the facts of organic destruction; they are then limited in number. But vital phenomena properly so called, or facts of organic creation, open up to us, when we analyse them, the prospect of a progress to infinity: from which it may be inferred that multiple causes and elements are here only views of the mind attempting an indefinitely approximate imitation of the operation of nature, whereas the operation imitated is an indivisible act. The resemblance between individuals of one and the same species would thus have quite another meaning, quite another origin, than the resemblance between complex effects obtained by the same composition of the same causes. But in the one case as in the other there is resemblance, and consequently possible generalisation. And since that is all that interests us in practice, since our daily life is necessarily an expectation of the same things and the same situations, it was natural that this common character, essential from the point of view of our action, should bring the two orders together, in spite of a wholly internal diversity which concerns only speculation. Hence the idea of a general order of nature, the same everywhere, hovering at once over life and over matter. Hence our habit of designating by the same word, and representing to ourselves in the same way, the existence of laws in the domain of inert matter and that of genera in the domain of life. That this confusion lies, moreover, at the origin of most of the difficulties raised by the problem of knowledge, among the ancients as among the moderns, does not seem to me doubtful. Indeed, the generality of laws and that of genera being designated by the same word, subsumed under the same idea, the geometrical order and the vital order were from then on confused together. According to the point of view one adopted, the generality of laws was explained by that of genera, or that of genera by that of laws. Of the two theses thus defined, the first is characteristic of ancient thought; the second belongs to modern philosophy. But in both philosophies the idea of "generality" is an equivocal idea, which unites in its extension and in its comprehension objects and elements incompatible with one another. In both, two kinds of order are grouped under the same concept, which resemble each other merely by the facility they give to our action on things. Two terms are brought together by virtue of a wholly external similarity, which no doubt justifies their designation by the same word in practice, but which does not in the least authorise us, in the speculative domain, to confuse them in the same definition. The ancients, in fact, did not ask themselves why nature submits to laws, but why it orders itself according to genera. The idea of genus corresponds above all to an objective reality in the domain of life, where it expresses an indisputable fact, heredity. There can, moreover, be genera only where there are individual objects: now, if the organised being is cut out of the whole of matter by its very organisation, I mean by nature, it is our perception that breaks up inert matter into distinct bodies, guided by the interests of action, guided by the nascent reactions that our body sketches out, that is to say, as has been shown elsewhere1, by the virtual genera that aspire to constitute themselves: genera and individuals here, then, determine each other by a semi-artificial operation, wholly relative to our future action on things. Nevertheless, the ancients did not hesitate to put all genera on the same rank, to attribute to them the same absolute existence. Reality thus becoming a system of genera, it was to the generality of genera (that is to say, in short, to the generality expressive of the vital order) that the generality of laws had to be reduced. It would be interesting, in this respect, to compare the Aristotelian theory of falling bodies with the explanation furnished by Galileo. Aristotle is solely preoccupied with the concepts of "high" and "low", of "proper place" and borrowed place, of "natural movement" and "forced movement"2: the physical law by virtue of which the stone falls expresses for him that the stone regains the "natural place" of all stones, namely the earth. The stone, in his eyes, is not quite a stone so long as it is not in its normal place; in falling back into this place it aims at completing itself, like a living being that grows, and at thus fully realising the essence of the genus stone3. If this conception of physical law were correct, the law would no longer be a mere relation established by the mind, and the subdivision of matter into bodies would no longer be relative to our faculty of perceiving: all bodies would have the same individuality as living bodies, and the laws of the physical universe would express relations of real kinship between real genera. We know what physics came of this, and how, for having believed in the possibility of a single and definitive science, embracing the totality of the real and coinciding with the absolute, the ancients had in fact to rest content with a more or less crude translation of the physical into the vital. But the same confusion is found again among the moderns, with this difference, that the relation between the two terms is inverted, that laws are no longer reduced to genera, but genera to laws, and that science, supposed once again to be one, becomes wholly relative, instead of being wholly, as the ancients would have it, in coincidence with the absolute. The eclipse of the problem of genera in modern philosophy is a remarkable fact. Our theory of knowledge turns almost exclusively on the question of laws: genera will have to find some means of coming to terms with laws, no matter how. The reason for this is that our philosophy has its point of departure in the great astronomical and physical discoveries of modern times. The laws of Kepler and of Galileo have remained, for it, the ideal and unique type of all knowledge. Now, a law is a relation between things or between facts. More precisely, a law of mathematical form expresses that a certain magnitude is a function of one or more other variables, suitably chosen. Now, the choice of the variable magnitudes, the distribution of nature into objects and into facts, already has something contingent and conventional about it. But let us admit that the choice is clearly indicated, even imposed, by experience: the law will nonetheless remain a relation, and a relation consists essentially in a comparison; it has objective reality only for an intellect that represents several terms to itself at the same time. This intellect may be neither mine nor yours; a science that bears on laws may therefore be an objective science, which experience contained in advance and which we merely make it disgorge: it is nonetheless true that the comparison, if it is not the work of anyone in particular, is effected at least impersonally, and that an experience made up of laws, that is to say, of terms related to other terms, is an experience made up of comparisons, which, by the time we gather it, must already have passed through an atmosphere of intellectuality. The idea of a science and an experience wholly relative to the human understanding is therefore implicitly contained in the conception of a single and integral science that would be composed of laws: Kant merely brought it to light. But this conception results from an arbitrary confusion between the generality of laws and that of genera. If an intellect is needed to condition terms in relation to one another, it is conceivable that, in certain cases, the terms themselves may exist in an independent manner. And if, alongside the relations of term to term, experience also presented us with independent terms, the living genera being something quite other than systems of laws, one half at least of our knowledge would bear on the "thing in itself", on reality itself. This knowledge would be very difficult, precisely because it would no longer construct its object and would be obliged, on the contrary, to submit to it; but, however little it cut into it, it would have bitten into the absolute itself. Let us go further: the other half of knowledge would no longer be as radically, as definitively relative as certain philosophers say, if it could be established that it bears on a reality of the inverse order, a reality that we always express in mathematical laws, that is to say, in relations that imply comparisons, but which lends itself to this work only because it is ballasted with spatiality and consequently with geometry. However that may be, it is the confusion of the two kinds of order that one finds behind the relativism of the moderns, as it already lay beneath the dogmatism of the ancients. I have said enough to mark the origin of this confusion. It comes from the fact that the "vital" order, which is essentially creation, manifests itself to us less in its essence than in some of its accidents: these imitate the physical and geometrical order; like it, they present us with repetitions that make generalisation possible, and that is all that matters to us. There is no doubt that life, as a whole, is an evolution, that is to say an unceasing transformation. But life can progress only by means of the living, which are its depositaries. Thousands upon thousands of them, nearly alike, must repeat one another in space and in time, in order that the novelty they are elaborating may grow and ripen. So a book might make its way towards its recasting by passing through thousands of printings of thousands of copies each. There is, however, this difference between the two cases, that the successive printings are identical, and identical too the simultaneous copies of the same printing, whereas the representatives of one and the same species are never quite alike, either at the various points of space or at the various moments of time. Heredity transmits not only characters; it transmits also the impetus by virtue of which the characters are modified, and this impetus is vitality itself. That is why I say that the repetition which serves as the basis of our generalisations is essential in the physical order, accidental in the vital order. The former is an "automatic" order; the latter is, I will not say voluntary, but analogous to the "willed" order. Now, as soon as we have clearly represented to ourselves the distinction between the "willed" order and the "automatic" order, the equivocation on which the idea of disorder lives is dispelled, and with it one of the principal difficulties of the problem of knowledge. The capital problem of the theory of knowledge is, in fact, to know how science is possible, that is to say, in short, why there is order, and not disorder, in things. Order exists; that is a fact. But, on the other hand, disorder, which seems to us to be less than order, would, it seems, be by right. The existence of order would therefore be a mystery to be cleared up, in any case a problem to be posed. More simply, as soon as we undertake to found order, we hold it to be contingent, if not in things, at least in the eyes of the mind: of a thing that we did not judge contingent we should ask no explanation. If order did not appear to us as a conquest over something, or as an addition to something (which would be the "absence of order"), neither would ancient realism have spoken of a "matter" to which the Idea was added, nor would modern idealism have posited a "sensible manifold" which the understanding organised into nature. And it is indisputable, in fact, that all order is contingent and conceived as such. But contingent in relation to what? The answer, in my view, is not in doubt. An order is contingent, and appears to us contingent, in relation to the inverse order, as verse is contingent in relation to prose and prose in relation to verse. But, just as all speech that is not prose is verse and is necessarily conceived as verse, just as all speech that is not verse is prose and is necessarily conceived as prose, so every manner of being that is not one of the two orders is the other, and is necessarily conceived as the other. But we may not realise what we are conceiving, and may perceive the idea really present to our mind only through a mist of affective states. We shall be convinced of this by considering the use we make of the idea of disorder in everyday life. When I enter a room and judge it to be "in disorder", what do I mean by that? The position of each object is explained by the automatic movements of the person who sleeps in the room, or by the efficient causes, whatever they may be, that have put each piece of furniture, each garment, etc., in the place where they are: the order, in the second sense of the word, is perfect. But it is order of the first kind that I am expecting, the order that a tidy person consciously puts into his life, in short the willed order and not the automatic. I then call the absence of this order disorder. At bottom, all that is real, perceived and even conceived in this absence of one of the two orders is the presence of the other. But the second is indifferent to me here, I am interested only in the first, and I express the presence of the second in terms of the first, instead of expressing it, so to speak, in terms of itself, by saying that it is disorder. Conversely, when we claim to be representing to ourselves a chaos, that is to say a state of things in which the physical world no longer obeys laws, what are we thinking of? We imagine facts that would appear and disappear capriciously. We begin by thinking of the physical universe as we know it, with effects and causes well proportioned to one another; then, by a series of arbitrary decrees, we increase, diminish, suppress, so as to obtain what we call disorder. In reality we have substituted willing for the mechanism of nature; we have replaced the "automatic order" by a multitude of elementary wills, as many as the appearances and disappearances of phenomena that we imagine. No doubt, for all these little wills to constitute a "willed order", they would have to have accepted the direction of a higher will. But, on looking closely, we shall see that this is just what they do: our will is there, objectifying itself in turn in each of these capricious wills, taking good care not to link the same with the same, not to let the effect be proportional to the cause, in short making a simple intention hover over the whole of the elementary volitions. Thus the absence of one of the two orders here too consists in the presence of the other. - By analysing the idea of chance, a close relative of the idea of disorder, we should find the same elements in it. Whether the wholly mechanical play of the causes that stop the roulette wheel at a number makes me win, and consequently operates as a good genius mindful of my interests would have done, or whether the wholly mechanical force of the wind tears a tile from the roof and hurls it at my head, that is to say acts as an evil genius conspiring against my person would have done, in both cases I find a mechanism where I should have looked for, where I ought, it seems, to have met with, an intention; that is what I express by speaking of chance. And of an anarchic world, in which phenomena succeeded one another as their caprice pleased, I shall again say that it is the reign of chance, meaning by that that I find before me wills, or rather decrees, when it was mechanism that I was expecting. Thus is explained the singular wavering of the mind when it tries to define chance. Neither the efficient cause nor the final cause can furnish it with the definition it seeks. It oscillates, unable to settle, between the idea of an absence of final cause and that of an absence of efficient cause, each of these two definitions sending it back to the other. The problem remains insoluble, in fact, so long as the idea of chance is held to be a pure idea, unmixed with feeling. But in reality chance merely objectifies the state of mind of one who expected one of the two kinds of order and meets with the other. Chance and disorder are therefore necessarily conceived as relative. If we wish to represent them to ourselves as absolute, we perceive that we are going to and fro like a shuttle, involuntarily, between the two kinds of order, passing into the one at the precise moment at which we should catch ourselves in the other, and that the supposed absence of all order is in reality the presence of both, together with the swaying of a mind that settles definitively on neither the one nor the other. Neither in things nor in our representation of things can there be any question of making this disorder the substratum of order, since it implies the two kinds of order and is made of their combination. But our intellect passes this by. By a simple sic jubeo (thus I command), it posits a disorder that would be an "absence of order". It thus thinks a word or a juxtaposition of words, nothing more. Let it try to put an idea under the word: it will find that disorder may well be the negation of an order, but that this negation is then the implicit recognition of the presence of the opposite order, a recognition to which we shut our eyes because it does not interest us, or which we evade by denying the second order in its turn, that is to say, at bottom, by re-establishing the first. How, then, can we speak of an incoherent manifold which an understanding would organise? It is no use saying that no one supposes this incoherence realised or realisable: from the moment one speaks of it, one believes one is thinking of it; now, on analysing the idea actually present, one will find in it, once again, only the disappointment of the mind before an order that does not interest it, or an oscillation of the mind between two kinds of order, or finally the pure and simple representation of the empty word that one has created by attaching the negative prefix to a word that signified something. But it is this analysis that one neglects to make. One omits it, precisely because one does not think of distinguishing two kinds of order irreducible to one another. I was saying, in fact, that all order necessarily appears as contingent. If there are two kinds of order, this contingency of order is explained: one of the forms is contingent in relation to the other. Where I find the geometrical, the vital was possible; where the order is vital, it might have been geometrical. But let us suppose that order is everywhere of the same kind and simply admits of degrees, ranging from the geometrical to the vital. A determinate order continuing to appear to me as contingent, and no longer able to be so in relation to an order of another kind, I shall necessarily believe that order is contingent in relation to an absence of itself, that is to say in relation to a state of things "in which there would be no order at all". And this state of things I shall believe I am thinking of, because it is implied, it seems, in the very contingency of order, which is an indisputable fact. I shall therefore place at the top of the hierarchy the vital order, then, as a diminution or a lesser complication of it, the geometrical order, and finally, at the very bottom, the absence of order, incoherence itself, on which order would be superposed. That is why incoherence will strike me as a word behind which there must be something, if not realised, at least thought. But if I notice that the state of things implied by the contingency of a determinate order is simply the presence of the contrary order, if by that very fact I posit two kinds of order, each the inverse of the other, I perceive that between the two orders no intermediate degrees can be imagined, and that neither can one descend from these two orders towards the "incoherent". Either the incoherent is only a word void of meaning, or, if I give it a signification, it is on condition of putting incoherence midway between the two orders, and not below both of them. There is not first the incoherent, then the geometrical, then the vital: there is simply the geometrical and the vital, and then, by a swaying of the mind between the one and the other, the idea of the incoherent. To speak of an uncoordinated manifold to which order is superadded is therefore to commit a veritable petitio principii, for in imagining the uncoordinated one really posits an order, or rather one posits two. This long analysis was necessary to show how the real might pass from tension to extension and from freedom to mechanical necessity by way of inversion. It was not enough to establish that this relation between the two terms is suggested to us at once by consciousness and by sensible experience. It had to be proved that the geometrical order needs no explanation, being purely and simply the suppression of the inverse order. And for that it was indispensable to establish that suppression is always a substitution, and even that it is necessarily conceived as such: only the demands of practical life suggest to us here a way of speaking that deceives us both about what goes on in things and about what is present to our thought. We must now examine more closely the inversion whose consequences I have just described. What, then, is the principle that has only to relax in order to extend itself, the interruption of the cause here amounting to a reversal of the effect? For want of a better word, I have called it consciousness. But it is not a question of that diminished consciousness which functions in each of us. Our own consciousness is the consciousness of a certain living being, placed at a certain point of space; and, though it does go in the same direction as its principle, it is ceaselessly drawn the opposite way, obliged, though it walks forward, to look backward. This retrospective vision is, as I have shown, the natural function of the intellect and consequently of distinct consciousness. For our consciousness to coincide with something of its principle, it would have to detach itself from the ready-made and attach itself to what is in the making. The faculty of seeing would have to turn round and twist back upon itself, and become one with the act of willing. A painful effort, which we can make suddenly by doing violence to nature, but cannot sustain beyond a few moments. In free action, when we contract our whole being in order to thrust it forward, we have a more or less clear consciousness of the motives and impelling causes, and even, at a pinch, of the becoming by which they organise themselves into an act; but pure willing, the current that runs through this matter communicating life to it, is something we barely feel, which at most we brush against in passing. Let us try to install ourselves in it, were it only for a moment: even then it is an individual, fragmentary willing that we shall grasp. To reach the principle of all life, as also of all materiality, we should have to go further still. Is it impossible? Certainly not; the history of philosophy is there to bear witness. There is no lasting system that is not, in some at least of its parts, vivified by intuition. Dialectic is necessary to put intuition to the test, necessary also in order that intuition may be refracted into concepts and propagated to other men; but very often it does no more than develop the result of that intuition which goes beyond it. In truth, the two procedures run in opposite directions: the same effort by which we link ideas to ideas makes the intuition vanish which the ideas were meant to store up. The philosopher is obliged to abandon intuition once he has received its impetus, and to rely on himself to continue the movement, now pushing concepts one after another. But very soon he feels he has lost his footing; a fresh contact becomes necessary; the greater part of what had been done will have to be undone. In sum, dialectic is what ensures the agreement of our thought with itself. But by dialectic, - which is only a relaxation of intuition, - many different agreements are possible, and yet there is only one truth. Intuition, if it could be prolonged beyond a few moments, would ensure not only the agreement of the philosopher with his own thought, but also that of all philosophers with one another. Such as it exists, fleeting and incomplete, it is, in each system, what is worth more than the system and what survives it. The object of philosophy would be attained if this intuition could sustain itself, generalise itself, and above all secure external landmarks so as not to go astray. For that, a continual coming and going between nature and mind is necessary. When we put our being back into our willing, and our willing itself back into the impulsion it prolongs, we understand, we feel that reality is a perpetual growth, a creation pursued without end. Our will already performs this miracle. Every human work that contains a share of invention, every voluntary act that contains a share of freedom, every movement of an organism that manifests spontaneity, brings something new into the world. These, it is true, are only creations of form. How could they be anything else? We are not the vital current itself; we are this current already loaded with matter, that is to say with congealed parts of its substance which it carries along its course. In the composition of a work of genius as in a simple free decision, we may stretch the spring of our activity to the utmost and thus create what no mere assemblage of materials could have given (what juxtaposition of known curves will ever be equivalent to the pencil stroke of a great artist?), but there are none the less elements here that pre-exist and survive their organisation. But if a mere arrest of the action that generates form could constitute its matter (are not the original lines drawn by the artist already, in themselves, the fixation and as it were the congealing of a movement?), a creation of matter would be neither incomprehensible nor inadmissible. For we grasp from within, we live at every instant, a creation of form, and it is precisely there, in the cases where the form is pure and where the creative current is momentarily interrupted, that there would be a creation of matter. Let us consider all the letters of the alphabet that enter into the composition of everything that has ever been written: we do not conceive that other letters should spring up and come to add themselves to these to make a new poem. But that the poet creates the poem and that human thought is enriched by it, this we understand very well: this creation is a simple act of the mind, and the action has only to make a pause, instead of continuing itself in a new creation, for it to scatter of itself into words which dissociate into letters, which will be added to all the letters there already were in the world. Thus, that the number of atoms composing the material universe at a given moment should increase runs counter to our habits of mind and contradicts our experience. But that a reality of quite another order, which stands out against the atom as the poet's thought stands out against the letters of the alphabet, should grow by sudden additions is not inadmissible; and the reverse side of each addition might well be a world, which we represent to ourselves, symbolically moreover, as a juxtaposition of atoms. The mystery that hangs over the existence of the universe comes in large part, in fact, from our wanting its genesis to have taken place all at once, or else all matter to be eternal. Whether we speak of creation or posit an uncreated matter, in both cases it is the totality of the universe that we call in question. By probing this habit of mind, we should find in it the prejudice that I shall analyse in my next chapter, the idea, common to materialists and their opponents, that there is no really active duration, and that the absolute - matter or mind - cannot take its place in concrete time, in the time we feel to be the very stuff of our life: from which it would follow that everything is given once for all, and that we must posit from all eternity either material multiplicity itself, or the act creative of this multiplicity, given en bloc in the divine essence. Once this prejudice is uprooted, the idea of creation becomes clearer, for it merges with that of growth. But then it is no longer of the universe in its totality that we shall have to speak. Why should we speak of it? The universe is an assemblage of solar systems which we have every reason to believe analogous to our own. No doubt these systems are not absolutely independent of one another. Our sun radiates heat and light beyond the farthest planet, and, on the other hand, our solar system as a whole moves in a definite direction, as though it were drawn there. There is therefore a bond between the worlds. But this bond may be regarded as infinitely loose in comparison with the solidarity that unites the parts of one and the same world with one another. So that it is not artificially, for reasons of mere convenience, that we isolate our solar system; nature itself invites us to isolate it. As living beings, we depend on the planet on which we are and on the sun that feeds it, but on nothing else. As thinking beings, we may apply the laws of our physics to our own world, and no doubt also extend them to each of the worlds taken in isolation, but nothing says that they still apply to the entire universe, nor even that such an assertion has a meaning, for the universe is not made, but is ceaselessly in the making. It grows, no doubt, indefinitely by the addition of new worlds. Let us then extend to the whole of our solar system, but limit to this relatively closed system, as to the other relatively closed systems, the two most general laws of our science, the principle of the conservation of energy and that of degradation. Let us see what will result. It must first be noted that these two principles do not have the same metaphysical bearing. The first is a quantitative law, and consequently relative, in part, to our methods of measurement. It says that in a system supposed closed the total energy, that is to say the sum of the kinetic and potential energies, remains constant. Now, if there were only kinetic energy in the world, or even if there were, besides kinetic energy, only a single kind of potential energy, the artifice of measurement would not suffice to make the law artificial. The law of the conservation of energy would indeed express that something is conserved in constant quantity. But there are in reality energies of diverse nature1, and the measure of each of them has evidently been chosen in such a way as to justify the principle of the conservation of energy. The share of convention inherent in this principle is therefore fairly large, although there is no doubt, between the variations of the various energies composing one and the same system, a solidarity which is precisely what has made possible the extension of the principle by suitably chosen measures. If, then, the philosopher applies this principle to the whole of the solar system, he will at least have to blur its outlines. The law of the conservation of energy will no longer be able to express here the objective permanence of a certain quantity of a certain thing, but rather the necessity for every change that occurs to be counterbalanced, somewhere, by a change in the opposite direction. That is to say that, even if it governs the whole of our solar system, the law of the conservation of energy informs us about the relation of one fragment of this world to another fragment rather than about the nature of the whole. It is otherwise with the second principle of thermodynamics. The law of the degradation of energy, in fact, does not bear essentially on magnitudes. No doubt its first idea was born, in Carnot's thought, of certain quantitative considerations on the efficiency of heat engines. No doubt too it was in mathematical terms that Clausius generalised it, and it was in the conception of a calculable magnitude, "entropy", that he ended. These precise determinations are necessary for applications. But the law would remain vaguely formulable, and could, at a pinch, have been formulated in broad terms, even if no one had ever thought of measuring the various energies of the physical world, even if the concept of energy had not been created. It expresses essentially, in fact, that all physical changes have a tendency to be degraded into heat, and that heat itself tends to be distributed uniformly among bodies. In this less precise form it becomes independent of all convention; it is the most metaphysical of the laws of physics, in that it points out to us with its finger, without interposed symbols, without artifices of measurement, the direction in which the world is going. It says that changes that are visible and heterogeneous to one another will be more and more diluted into changes that are invisible and homogeneous, and that the instability to which we owe the richness and variety of the changes taking place in our solar system will gradually give way to the relative stability of elementary vibrations which will repeat one another indefinitely. So a man might keep his strength but devote it less and less to acts, and end by employing it wholly in making his lungs breathe and his heart beat. Seen from this point of view, a world such as our solar system appears as exhausting at every moment something of the mutability it contains. At the beginning was the maximum possible utilisation of energy; this mutability has gone on ceaselessly diminishing. Whence does it come? We might first suppose that it came from some other point of space, but the difficulty would only be pushed back, and the same question would arise for this external source of mutability. It might be added, it is true, that the number of worlds capable of passing mutability on to one another is unlimited, that the sum of mutability contained in the universe is infinite, and that therefore there is no more reason to seek its origin than to foresee its end. A hypothesis of this kind is as irrefutable as it is indemonstrable; but to speak of an infinite universe is to admit a perfect coincidence of matter with abstract space, and consequently an absolute externality of all the parts of matter in relation to one another. I have seen above what we must think of this last thesis, and how difficult it is to reconcile with the idea of a reciprocal influence of all the parts of matter on one another, an influence to which appeal is precisely being made here. Finally, it might be supposed that the general instability has issued from a general state of stability, that the period in which we are, and during which utilisable energy is diminishing, was preceded by a period in which mutability was in process of increasing, and that, moreover, the alternations of increase and diminution succeed one another without end. This hypothesis is theoretically conceivable, as has been precisely shown in recent times; but, according to Boltzmann's calculations, it is of a mathematical improbability that passes all imagination and amounts, practically, to absolute impossibility1. In reality the problem is insoluble if we keep to the ground of physics, for the physicist is obliged to attach energy to extended particles, and, even if he sees in the particles only reservoirs of energy, he remains in space: he would be false to his role if he sought the origin of these energies in an extra-spatial process. Yet it is there, in my view, that it must be sought. Do we consider extension in general in abstracto? Extension appears only, I was saying, as a tension that is interrupted. Do we attach ourselves to the concrete reality that fills this extension? The order that reigns in it, and that manifests itself in the laws of nature, is an order that must be born of itself when the inverse order is suppressed: a relaxation of willing would produce precisely this suppression. Lastly, the direction in which this reality is moving now suggests to us the idea of a thing unmaking itself; therein, without any doubt, lies one of the essential features of materiality. What are we to conclude from this, if not that the process by which this thing makes itself is directed in the opposite way to physical processes, and that it is therefore, by its very definition, immaterial? Our vision of the material world is that of a falling weight; no image drawn from matter properly so called will give us an idea of the weight rising. But this conclusion will force itself upon us with still greater force if we press closer to concrete reality, if we consider no longer merely matter in general but, within this matter, living bodies. All our analyses show us, in fact, in life an effort to climb back up the slope that matter descends. In this way they let us glimpse the possibility, even the necessity, of a process inverse to materiality, creative of matter by its mere interruption. Certainly, the life that evolves on the surface of our planet is attached to matter. If it were pure consciousness, and still more if it were supra-consciousness, it would be pure creative activity. In fact, it is riveted to an organism that subjects it to the general laws of inert matter. But everything happens as if it were doing its utmost to free itself from these laws. It has not the power to reverse the direction of physical changes, as Carnot's principle determines it. At least it behaves absolutely as a force would behave which, left to itself, worked in the inverse direction. Unable to stop the course of material changes, it succeeds nevertheless in retarding it. The evolution of life continues, in fact, as I have shown, an initial impulsion; this impulsion, which determined the development of the chlorophyllian function in the plant and of the sensori-motor system in the animal, brings life to more and more efficacious acts through the manufacture and use of more and more powerful explosives. Now, what do these explosives represent if not a storing up of solar energy, energy whose degradation is thus provisionally suspended at some of the points where it was being poured out? The utilisable energy that the explosive conceals will be spent, no doubt, at the moment of explosion; but it would have been spent sooner if an organism had not happened to be there to arrest its dissipation, to retain it and add it up with itself. Such as it presents itself to our eyes today, at the point to which it has been brought by a splitting of the tendencies, complementary to one another, which it contained within itself, life is entirely suspended from the chlorophyllian function of the plant. That is to say that, considered in its initial impulsion, before any splitting, it was a tendency to accumulate in a reservoir, as the green parts of plants above all do, with a view to an efficacious instantaneous expenditure, such as the animal effects, something that would have flowed away without it. It is like an effort to raise the falling weight. It succeeds, it is true, only in retarding its fall. At least it can give us an idea of what the raising of the weight was1. Let us imagine, then, a vessel full of steam at a high tension, and here and there in the walls of the vessel a crack through which the steam escapes in a jet. The steam thrown into the air condenses almost entirely into droplets that fall back, and this condensation and this fall represent simply the loss of something, an interruption, a deficit. But a small part of the jet of steam subsists, uncondensed, for a few moments; this part makes an effort to raise the falling drops; it succeeds at most in slowing their fall. So from an immense reservoir of life jets must be ceaselessly springing out, each of which, falling back, is a world. The evolution of living species within this world represents what subsists of the primitive direction of the original jet, and of an impulsion that continues itself in the direction inverse to materiality. But let us not attach ourselves too much to this comparison. It would give us only a weakened and even misleading image of reality, for the crack, the jet of steam, the lifting of the droplets are necessarily determined, whereas the creation of a world is a free act, and life, within the material world, participates in this freedom. Let us think rather, then, of a gesture like that of an arm being raised; then let us suppose that the arm, left to itself, falls back, and that yet there subsists in it, striving to raise it again, something of the willing that animated it: with this image of a creative gesture unmaking itself we shall already have a more exact representation of matter. And we shall then see in vital activity what subsists of the direct movement in the inverted movement, a reality making itself through the one that is unmaking itself. Everything is obscure in the idea of creation if we think of things that would be created and of a thing that creates, as we habitually do, as the understanding cannot help doing. I shall show in my next chapter the origin of this illusion. It is natural to our intellect, an essentially practical function, made to represent to us things and states rather than changes and acts. But things and states are only views taken by our mind of becoming. There are no things, there are only actions. More particularly, if I consider the world in which we live, I find that the automatic and rigorously determined evolution of this well-knit whole is action unmaking itself, and that the unforeseen forms which life cuts out in it, forms capable of prolonging themselves in unforeseen movements, represent action in the making. Now, I have every reason to believe that the other worlds are analogous to ours, that things happen in them in the same way. And I know that they were not all constituted at the same time, since observation shows me, even today, nebulae in process of concentration. If everywhere it is the same kind of action that is being accomplished, whether it is unmaking itself or whether it is trying to remake itself, I am simply expressing this probable similitude when I speak of a centre from which worlds would shoot out like rockets from an immense bouquet, - provided, however, that I do not present this centre as a thing, but as a continuity of shooting out. God, thus defined, has nothing of the ready-made; he is unceasing life, action, freedom. Creation, so conceived, is not a mystery; we experience it in ourselves as soon as we act freely. That new things can be added to the things that exist is absurd, no doubt, since the thing results from a solidification performed by our understanding, and there are never any things other than those the understanding has constituted. To speak of things creating themselves would therefore amount to saying that the understanding gives itself more than it gives itself, - an assertion self-contradictory, an empty and vain representation. But that action swells as it advances, that it creates in proportion to its progress, is what each of us observes when he watches himself act. Things are constituted by the instantaneous cut that the understanding makes, at a given moment, in a flux of this kind, and what is mysterious when we compare the cuts with one another becomes clear when we refer back to the flux. Even the modalities of creative action, in so far as it is pursued in the organisation of living forms, are singularly simplified when taken from this angle. Before the complexity of an organism and the quasi-infinite multitude of interwoven analyses and syntheses that it presupposes, our understanding recoils disconcerted. That the pure and simple play of physical and chemical forces can work this marvel we find hard to believe. And if it is a profound science that is at work, how are we to understand the influence exerted on formless Matter by this matterless form? But the difficulty arises from our representing to ourselves, statically, ready-made material particles juxtaposed to one another, and, statically too, an external cause that would plaster a learned organisation upon them. In reality life is a movement, materiality is the inverse movement, and each of these two movements is simple, the matter that forms a world being an undivided flux, and undivided also the life that runs through it, cutting out living beings in it. Of these two currents the second runs counter to the first, but the first nevertheless obtains something from the second: there results between them a modus vivendi, which is precisely organisation. This organisation takes on, for our senses and for our intellect, the form of parts entirely external to parts in time and in space. Not only do we shut our eyes to the unity of the impetus which, passing through the generations, links individuals to individuals, species to species, and makes of the entire series of the living one single immense wave running over matter, but each individual itself appears to us as an aggregate, an aggregate of molecules and an aggregate of facts. The reason for this would be found in the structure of our intellect, which is made to act on matter from without and which succeeds in doing so only by making, in the flux of the real, instantaneous cuts each of which becomes, in its fixity, indefinitely decomposable. Perceiving in an organism only parts external to parts, the understanding has the choice only between two systems of explanation: either to hold the infinitely complicated (and thereby infinitely learned) organisation to be a fortuitous assemblage, or to refer it to the incomprehensible influence of an external force that has grouped its elements. But this complication is the work of the understanding, and this incomprehensibility is its work too. Let us try to see no longer with the eyes of the intellect alone, which grasps only the ready-made and which looks from without, but with the mind, I mean with that faculty of seeing which is immanent in the faculty of acting and which springs, in some sort, from the twisting of willing back upon itself. Everything will be set in motion again, and everything will be resolved into movement. Where the understanding, working on the image, supposed fixed, of action in progress, showed us infinitely manifold parts and an infinitely learned order, we shall divine a simple process, an action making itself through an action of the same kind unmaking itself, something like the path that the last rocket of a firework display cuts for itself among the debris falling back from the rockets that have burnt out. From this point of view the general considerations I presented on the evolution of life will be cleared up and completed. We shall bring out more distinctly what is accidental and what is essential in this evolution. The impetus of life of which I am speaking consists, in short, in a demand for creation. It cannot create absolutely, because it meets before it matter, that is to say the movement inverse to its own. But it seizes upon this matter, which is necessity itself, and tends to introduce into it the greatest possible amount of indetermination and freedom. How does it set about it? An animal high in the series may be represented roughly, I was saying, by a sensori-motor nervous system set upon digestive, respiratory, circulatory systems, etc. The role of these latter is to cleanse it, repair it, protect it, make it as independent as possible of external circumstances, but above all to supply it with the energy it will expend in movements. The growing complexity of the organism is therefore theoretically due (in spite of the innumerable exceptions owing to the accidents of evolution) to the necessity of complicating the nervous system. Each complication of any part whatever of the organism entails, moreover, many others, because this part itself must live, every change at one point of the body having its repercussion everywhere. The complication may therefore go on to infinity in all directions: but it is the complication of the nervous system that conditions the others by right, if not always in fact. Now, in what does the progress of the nervous system itself consist? In a simultaneous development of automatic activity and of voluntary activity, the first supplying the second with an appropriate instrument. Thus, in an organism such as ours, a considerable number of motor mechanisms are set up in the spinal cord and in the medulla, awaiting only a signal to release the corresponding act; the will is employed, in some cases, in setting up the mechanism itself, and, in others, in choosing the mechanisms to be released, the manner of combining them, the moment of release. The will of an animal is the more efficacious, and the more intense too, the greater the number of these mechanisms among which it has the choice, the more complicated the crossroads where all the motor paths cross, or, in other words, the more considerable the development its brain attains. Thus the progress of the nervous system ensures to the act a growing precision, a growing variety, a growing efficacy and independence. The organism behaves more and more like a machine for acting which would reconstruct itself entirely for each new action, as if it were made of india-rubber and could, at every instant, change the shape of all its parts. But before the appearance of the nervous system, before even the formation of an organism properly so called, this essential property of animal life was already manifesting itself in the undifferentiated mass of the Amoeba. The Amoeba deforms itself in varying directions; its whole mass therefore does what the differentiation of parts will localise in a sensori-motor system in the developed animal. Doing it only in a rudimentary manner, it is dispensed from the complication of the higher organisms: there is no need here for auxiliary elements to pass on to motor elements the energy to be spent; the undivided animal moves, and, undivided too, procures energy for itself by means of the organic substances it assimilates. Thus, whether we place ourselves at the bottom or at the top of the animal series, we always find that animal life consists (1) in procuring a supply of energy, (2) in spending it, by means of a matter as supple as possible, in varying and unforeseen directions. Now, whence comes the energy? From the food ingested, for food is a kind of explosive, which awaits only the spark to discharge the energy it stores up. Who has manufactured this explosive? The food may be the flesh of an animal that has fed on animals, and so on; but in the end we shall come to the plant. It alone truly gathers solar energy. Animals merely borrow it from the plant, either directly or by passing it on to one another. How has the plant stored up this energy? Chiefly by the chlorophyllian function, that is to say by a chemistry sui generis (of its own kind) to which we have not the key, and which probably does not resemble that of our laboratories. The operation consists in using solar energy to fix the carbon of carbonic acid, and thereby in storing up this energy as one would store up that of a water-carrier by using it to fill a raised reservoir: the water, once raised, will be able to set in motion, as one wishes and when one wishes, a mill or a turbine. Each atom of carbon fixed represents something like the raising of this weight of water, or like the tension of an elastic thread which would have united the carbon to the oxygen in the carbonic acid. The elastic will relax, the weight will fall back, the energy held in reserve will be recovered, in short, on the day when, by a simple release, the carbon is allowed to go and rejoin its oxygen. So that life as a whole, animal and vegetable, in what is essential to it, appears as an effort to accumulate energy and then to let it go into flexible, deformable channels, at the end of which it will perform infinitely varied kinds of work. That is what the vital impetus, passing through matter, would like to obtain all at once. It would succeed, no doubt, if its power were unlimited, or if some help could come to it from without. But the impetus is finite, and it has been given once for all. It cannot overcome all obstacles. The movement it imprints is sometimes deflected, sometimes divided, always opposed, and the evolution of the organised world is only the unrolling of this struggle. The first great splitting that had to take place was that of the two kingdoms, vegetable and animal, which thus happen to be complementary to each other, without, however, any agreement having been established between them. It is not for the animal that the plant accumulates energy, it is for its own consumption; but its own expenditure is less discontinuous, less concentrated, and therefore less efficacious, than the initial impetus of life required, directed as it essentially was towards free acts: the same organism could not sustain with equal force the two roles at once, of accumulating gradually and of utilising suddenly. That is why, of themselves, without any external intervention, by the mere effect of the duality of tendency implied in the original impetus and of the resistance offered by matter to this impetus, organisms leaned some in the first direction, others in the second. This splitting in two was followed by many others. Hence the divergent lines of evolution, at least in what is essential to them. But we must take account of regressions, of arrests, of accidents of every kind. And we must remember, above all, that each species behaves as if the general movement of life stopped at it instead of passing through it. It thinks only of itself, it lives only for itself. Hence the numberless struggles of which nature is the theatre. Hence a disharmony that is striking and shocking, but for which we must not hold the principle of life itself responsible. The part played by contingency in evolution is therefore great. Contingent, most often, are the forms adopted, or rather invented. Contingent, relative to the obstacles met with in such a place and at such a moment, is the dissociation of the primordial tendency into such and such complementary tendencies, which create divergent lines of evolution. Contingent the arrests and the setbacks; contingent, in large measure, the adaptations. Two things only are necessary: (1) a gradual accumulation of energy; (2) an elastic canalisation of this energy in variable and indeterminable directions, at the end of which are free acts. This twofold result has been obtained in a certain way on our planet. But it might have been obtained by quite other means. There was no necessity for life to fix its choice principally on the carbon of carbonic acid. What was essential for it was to store up solar energy; but instead of asking the Sun, for example, to pull apart atoms of oxygen and carbon, it might (theoretically at least, and setting aside difficulties of execution that are perhaps insurmountable) have proposed to it other chemical elements, which would then have had to be associated or dissociated by entirely different physical means. And if the element characteristic of the energy-giving substances of the organism had been other than carbon, the element characteristic of the plastic substances would probably have been other than nitrogen. The chemistry of living bodies would therefore have been radically different from what it is. There would have resulted living forms without analogy to those we know, whose anatomy would have been different, their physiology different. Only the sensori-motor function would have been preserved, if not in its mechanism, at least in its effects. It is therefore probable that life unfolds on other planets, in other solar systems too, under forms of which we have no idea, in physical conditions to which, from the point of view of our physiology, it seems to us absolutely repugnant. If its essential aim is to capture utilisable energy in order to spend it in explosive actions, it no doubt chooses in each solar system and on each planet, as it does on the earth, the means best fitted to obtain this result in the conditions offered it. That at least is what reasoning by analogy says, and it is to use this reasoning backwards to declare life impossible wherever conditions are offered it other than those on the earth. The truth is that life is possible wherever energy descends the slope indicated by Carnot's law and where a cause of inverse direction can retard the descent, - that is to say, no doubt, in all the worlds suspended from all the stars. Let us go further: it is not even necessary that life should concentrate itself and become precise in organisms properly so called, that is to say in definite bodies presenting to the flow of energy ready-made, though elastic, channels. It is conceivable (though one can hardly manage to imagine it) that energy might be held in reserve and then spent along variable lines running through a matter not yet solidified. All that is essential to life would be there, since there would still be slow accumulation of energy and sudden release. Between this vague and blurred vitality and the definite vitality we know there would be hardly more difference than there is, in our psychological life, between the state of dreaming and the waking state. Such may have been the condition of life in our nebula before the condensation of matter was complete, if it is true that life takes its flight at the very moment when, by the effect of an inverse movement, nebular matter appears. It is conceivable, then, that life might have assumed a quite different outward aspect and traced forms very different from those we know it to have. With another chemical substrate, in other physical conditions, the impulsion would have remained the same, but it would have split up very differently on the way, and, on the whole, another road would have been travelled, - less road perhaps, perhaps also more. In any case, of the entire series of the living, no term would have been what it is. Now, was it necessary that there should be a series and terms? Why should the single impetus not have been imprinted on a single body, which would have evolved indefinitely? This question arises, no doubt, when we compare life to an impetus. And we must compare it to an impetus, because there is no image, borrowed from the physical world, that can give a more approximate idea of it. But it is only an image. Life is in reality of the psychological order, and it is of the essence of the psychical to envelop a confused plurality of terms that interpenetrate. In space, and in space alone, no doubt, is distinct multiplicity possible: one point is absolutely external to another point. But pure and empty unity, too, is met with only in space: it is that of a mathematical point. Abstract unity and multiplicity are, as one pleases, determinations of space or categories of the understanding, spatiality and intellectuality being modelled on each other. But what is of a psychological nature cannot be laid exactly upon space, nor enter wholly into the frames of the understanding. Is my person, at a given moment, one or many? If I declare it one, inner voices arise and protest, those of the sensations, feelings, representations among which my individuality is divided. But if I make it distinctly many, my consciousness rebels just as strongly; it affirms that my sensations, my feelings, my thoughts are abstractions that I perform upon myself, and that each of my states implies all the others. I am, then - we must indeed adopt the language of the understanding, since the understanding alone has a language - a multiple unity and a unitary multiplicity1; but unity and multiplicity are only views taken of my personality by an understanding that turns its categories upon me: I enter neither into the one nor into the other nor into both at once, although the two, combined, may give an approximate imitation of that reciprocal interpenetration and that continuity which I find at the bottom of myself. Such is my inner life, and such too is life in general. If, in its contact with matter, life is comparable to an impulsion or an impetus, regarded in itself it is an immensity of virtuality, a mutual encroachment of thousands upon thousands of tendencies which will nevertheless be "thousands upon thousands" only once they have been externalised in relation to one another, that is to say spatialised. Contact with matter decides this dissociation. Matter effectively divides what was only virtually multiple, and, in this sense, individuation is in part the work of matter, in part the effect of what life carries within itself. Thus of a poetic feeling unfolding itself in distinct stanzas, in distinct lines, in distinct words, it may be said that it contained this multiplicity of individuated elements and that yet it is the materiality of language that creates it. But through the words, the lines and the stanzas runs the simple inspiration that is the whole of the poem. So, among the dissociated individuals, life still circulates: everywhere the tendency to individuate itself is opposed and at the same time completed by an antagonistic and complementary tendency to associate, as if the multiple unity of life, drawn in the direction of multiplicity, made all the more effort to draw itself back upon itself. No sooner is a part detached than it tends to reunite itself, if not with all the rest, at least with what is nearest to it. Hence, throughout the whole domain of life, a swaying between individuation and association. Individuals are juxtaposed in a society; but the society, hardly formed, would like to fuse the juxtaposed individuals into a new organism, so as itself to become an individual that may, in its turn, be an integral part of a new association. At the lowest degree of the scale of organisms we already find true associations, microbial colonies, and in these associations, if a recent work is to be believed, the tendency to individuate themselves by the constitution of a nucleus1. The same tendency is found again on a higher rung, in those Protophyta which, once they have issued from the mother cell by way of division, remain united to one another by the gelatinous substance surrounding their surface, as also in those Protozoa which begin by intermingling their pseudopodia and end by fusing together. The so-called "colonial" theory of the genesis of the higher organisms is well known. The Protozoa, consisting of a single cell, are supposed to have formed aggregates by juxtaposition, and these, coming together in their turn, to have given aggregates of aggregates: thus more and more complicated, and more and more differentiated, organisms would have been born from the association of barely differentiated and elementary organisms2. In this extreme form the thesis has met with grave objections; more and more the idea seems to be gaining ground that polyzoism is an exceptional and abnormal fact3. But it is none the less true that things happen as if every higher organism had been born of an association of cells which had divided the labour among themselves. Very probably it is not the cells that have made the individual by way of association; it is rather the individual that has made the cells by way of dissociation4. But this very fact reveals to us, in the genesis of the individual, a haunting of the social form, as if it could develop only on condition of splitting its substance into elements that themselves have an appearance of individuality and are united among themselves by an appearance of sociability. Numerous are the cases in which nature seems to hesitate between the two forms, and to ask itself whether it will constitute a society or an individual: the slightest impulsion then suffices to tip the balance to one side or the other. If we take a fairly large Infusorian, such as the Stentor, and cut it into two halves each containing a part of the nucleus, each of the two halves regenerates an independent Stentor; but if we perform the division incompletely, leaving a protoplasmic communication between the two halves, we see them carry out, each on its own side, perfectly synergic movements, so that here a thread kept or cut suffices for life to take on the social form or the individual form. Thus, in rudimentary organisms made of a single cell, we already observe that the apparent individuality of the whole is compounded of an undefined number of virtual individualities, virtually associated. But from the bottom to the top of the series of the living the same law manifests itself. And this is what I express by saying that unity and multiplicity are categories of inert matter, that the vital impetus is neither pure unity nor pure multiplicity, and that if the matter to which it communicates itself compels it to opt for one of the two, its option will never be definitive: it will leap indefinitely from the one to the other. The evolution of life in the twofold direction of individuality and association has therefore nothing accidental about it. It belongs to the very essence of life. Essential too is the march towards reflection. If my analyses are correct, it is consciousness, or rather supra-consciousness, that is at the origin of life. Consciousness or supra-consciousness is the rocket whose extinguished debris falls back as matter; consciousness again is what subsists of the rocket itself, passing through the debris and lighting it up into organisms. But this consciousness, which is a demand for creation, manifests itself to itself only where creation is possible. It falls asleep when life is condemned to automatism; it wakes up as soon as the possibility of a choice is reborn. That is why, in organisms devoid of a nervous system, it varies in proportion to the power of locomotion and deformation at the organism's disposal. And in animals with a nervous system it is proportional to the complication of the crossroads where the so-called sensory paths and the motor paths cross, that is to say of the brain. How is this solidarity between the organism and consciousness to be understood? I shall not dwell here on a point that I have gone into deeply in earlier works. Let me confine myself to recalling that the theory according to which consciousness is attached to certain neurones, for example, and is given off by their work like a phosphorescence, may be accepted by the scientist for the detail of analysis; it is a convenient way of expressing oneself. But it is nothing else. In reality a living being is a centre of action. It represents a certain sum of contingency entering the world, that is to say a certain quantity of possible action, - a quantity that varies with individuals and above all with species. The nervous system of an animal traces the flexible lines along which its action will run (although the potential energy to be released is accumulated in the muscles rather than in the nervous system itself); its nerve centres indicate, by their development and their configuration, the more or less extensive choice it will have among more or less numerous and complicated actions. Now, since the awakening of consciousness in a living being is the more complete the greater the latitude of choice left to it and the more considerable the sum of action allotted to it, it is clear that the development of consciousness will appear to be regulated by that of the nerve centres. On the other hand, since every state of consciousness is, from a certain side, a question put to motor activity and even the beginning of an answer, there is no psychological fact that does not imply the bringing into play of cortical mechanisms. Everything will therefore seem to happen as if consciousness sprang from the brain, and as if the detail of conscious activity were modelled on that of brain activity. In reality consciousness does not spring from the brain; but brain and consciousness correspond because they equally measure, the one by the complexity of its structure and the other by the intensity of its awakening, the quantity of choice at the living being's disposal. Precisely because a cerebral state expresses simply what there is of nascent action in the corresponding psychological state, the psychological state tells more than the cerebral state. The consciousness of a living being, as I have tried to prove elsewhere, is bound up with its brain in the sense in which a pointed knife is bound up with its point: the brain is the sharp point by which consciousness penetrates the compact tissue of events, but it is no more coextensive with consciousness than the point is with the knife. Thus, from the fact that two brains, such as that of the ape and that of man, closely resemble each other, we cannot conclude that the corresponding consciousnesses are comparable or commensurable with each other. But perhaps they resemble each other less than is supposed. How can we fail to be struck by the fact that man is capable of learning any exercise whatever, of manufacturing any object whatever, in short of acquiring any motor habit whatever, whereas the faculty of combining new movements is strictly limited in the best-endowed animal, even in the ape? Here lies the cerebral characteristic of man. The human brain is made, like every brain, to set up motor mechanisms and to let us choose among them, at any instant whatever, the one we shall set in motion by a trigger action. But it differs from other brains in that the number of mechanisms it can set up, and consequently the number of triggers among which it gives the choice, is indefinite. Now, from the limited to the unlimited there is all the distance between the closed and the open. It is not a difference of degree, but of nature. Radical too, consequently, is the difference between the consciousness of the animal, even the most intelligent, and human consciousness. For consciousness corresponds exactly to the power of choice at the living being's disposal; it is coextensive with the fringe of possible action that surrounds real action: consciousness is synonymous with invention and freedom. Now, in the animal, invention is never anything but a variation on the theme of routine. Shut up in the habits of the species, it succeeds no doubt in enlarging them by its individual initiative; but it escapes from automatism only for an instant, just long enough to create a new automatism; the doors of its prison close again as soon as they are opened; by pulling at its chain it succeeds only in lengthening it. With man, consciousness breaks the chain. In man, and in man alone, it sets itself free. The whole history of life until then had been that of an effort of consciousness to lift matter, and of a more or less complete crushing of consciousness by the matter that fell back upon it. The enterprise was paradoxical, - if indeed one may speak here, otherwise than by metaphor, of enterprise and effort. It was a matter of creating with matter, which is necessity itself, an instrument of freedom, of manufacturing a mechanics that should triumph over mechanism, and of using the determinism of nature to pass through the meshes of the net it had spread. But everywhere except in man consciousness has let itself be caught in the net whose meshes it wanted to pass through. It has remained captive to the mechanisms it had set up. Automatism, which it claimed to draw in the direction of freedom, winds itself around it and drags it along. It has not the strength to escape, because the energy it had laid in store for acts is employed almost wholly in maintaining the infinitely subtle, essentially unstable equilibrium into which it has brought matter. But man does not merely maintain his machine; he succeeds in using it as he pleases. He owes this no doubt to the superiority of his brain, which allows him to construct an unlimited number of motor mechanisms, ceaselessly to oppose new habits to the old, and, by dividing automatism against itself, to master it. He owes it to his language, which furnishes consciousness with an immaterial body in which to incarnate itself and thus dispenses it from resting exclusively on material bodies, whose flux would first sweep it along and soon swallow it up. He owes it to social life, which stores up and preserves efforts as language stores up thought, thereby fixes an average level to which individuals will have to raise themselves at the outset, and, by this initial stimulation, prevents the mediocre from falling asleep and drives the best to climb higher. But our brain, our society and our language are only the external and diverse signs of one and the same internal superiority. They tell, each in its own way, of the unique, exceptional success that life won at a given moment of its evolution. They translate the difference of nature, and not merely of degree, that separates man from the rest of animality. They let us divine that if, at the end of the broad springboard from which life had taken its leap, all the others came down, finding the rope stretched too high, man alone has jumped the obstacle. It is in this quite special sense that man is the "term" and the "goal" of evolution. Life, I have said, transcends finality as it transcends the other categories. It is essentially a current launched through matter and drawing from it what it can. There has therefore not been, properly speaking, any project or plan. On the other hand, it is only too evident that the rest of nature has not been referred to man: we struggle like the other species, we have struggled against the other species. Lastly, if the evolution of life had come up against different accidents on the way, if thereby the current of life had been divided differently, we should have been, physically and morally, rather different from what we are.
