In this sense the negation of dampness would be a thing as objective, as purely intellectual, as detached from every pedagogical intention as the affirmation. - But let us look closely: we shall see that the negative proposition "the ground is not damp" and the affirmative proposition "the ground is dry" have entirely different contents. The second implies that one knows the dry, that one has experienced the specific sensations, tactile or visual for example, which are at the base of this representation. The first requires nothing of the kind: it could just as well be formulated by an intelligent fish, which had never perceived anything but the damp. It would be necessary, it is true, that this fish should have raised itself to the distinction between the real and the possible, and that it should care to forestall the error of its fellows, who no doubt consider as alone possible the conditions of dampness in which they actually live. Keep strictly to the terms of the proposition "the ground is not damp", and you will find that it signifies two things: 1st, that one might believe that the ground is damp, 2nd, that the dampness is in fact replaced by a certain quality x. This quality is left in indetermination, either because one has no positive knowledge of it or because it has no present interest for the person to whom the negation is addressed. To deny, then, always consists in presenting in a truncated form a system of two affirmations, the one determinate, bearing on a certain possible, the other indeterminate, relating to the unknown or indifferent reality which supplants this possibility: the second affirmation is virtually contained in the judgement we pass on the first, a judgement which is negation itself. And what gives negation its subjective character is precisely that, in the observation of a replacement, it takes account only of what is replaced and does not concern itself with what replaces it. What is replaced exists only as a conception of the mind. In order to continue to see it, and consequently to speak of it, one must turn one's back on reality, which flows from the past to the present, from behind forwards. That is what one does when one denies. One observes the change, or more generally the substitution, as the route of the carriage would be seen by a traveller who looked backwards and wished to know at each instant only the point at which he had ceased to be; he would never determine his present position except in relation to the one he has just left, instead of expressing it as a function of itself. In sum, for a mind which followed purely and simply the thread of experience, there would be no void, no nothingness, even relative or partial, no possible negation. Such a mind would see facts succeed facts, states succeed states, things succeed things. What it would note at every moment are things which exist, states which appear, facts which occur. It would live in the actual and, if it were capable of judging, it would never affirm anything but the existence of the present. Let us endow this mind with memory and above all with the desire to dwell on the past. Let us give it the faculty of dissociating and distinguishing. It will no longer note only the present state of the passing reality. It will represent the passing to itself as a change, and consequently as a contrast between what has been and what is. And since there is no essential difference between a past one recalls and a past one imagines, it will soon have raised itself to the representation of the possible in general. It will thus be switched on to the track of negation. And above all it will be on the point of representing a disappearance to itself. It will not yet succeed in doing so, however. To represent to oneself that a thing has disappeared, it is not enough to perceive a contrast between the past and the present; one must further turn one's back on the present, dwell on the past, and think the contrast of the past with the present in terms of the past only, without letting the present figure in it. The idea of abolition is therefore not a pure idea; it implies that one regrets the past or conceives it as regrettable, that one has some reason for lingering over it. It arises when the phenomenon of substitution is cut in two by a mind which considers only the first half of it, because it is interested only in that. Suppress all interest, all affection: there remains nothing but the reality which flows, and the indefinitely renewed knowledge it impresses on us of its present state. From abolition to negation, which is a more general operation, there is now only one step. It suffices that one represents to oneself the contrast of what is, not only with what has been, but also with all that might have been. And one must express this contrast as a function of what might have been and not of what is; one must affirm the existence of the actual while looking only at the possible. The formula thus obtained no longer expresses simply a disappointment of the individual: it is made to correct or forestall an error, which one supposes rather to be the error of someone else. In this sense negation has a pedagogical and social character. Now, once negation has been formulated, it presents an aspect symmetrical with that of affirmation. It then seems to us that, if the latter affirmed an objective reality, the former must affirm a non-reality equally objective and, so to speak, equally real. In this we are at once wrong and right: wrong, since negation could not be objectified in what it has of the negative; right, however, in that the negation of a thing implies the latent affirmation of its replacement by another thing, which is systematically left aside. But the negative form of negation benefits from the affirmation which is at the bottom of it: astride the body of positive reality to which it is attached, this phantom objectifies itself. Thus is formed the idea of the void or of partial nothingness, a thing being replaced no longer by another thing, but by a void which it leaves, that is to say by the negation of itself. And since this operation can be performed on any thing whatever, we suppose it carried out on each thing in turn, and finally carried out on all things together. We thus obtain the idea of "absolute nothingness". If now we analyse this idea of Nothing, we find that it is, at bottom, the idea of All, with, in addition, a movement of the mind which leaps indefinitely from one thing to another, refuses to keep still, and concentrates all its attention on this refusal, never determining its present position except in relation to the one it has just left. It is therefore a pre-eminently comprehensive and full representation, as full and comprehensive as the idea of All, with which it has the closest kinship. How, then, can the idea of Nothing be opposed to that of All? Is it not seen that this is to oppose the full to the full, and that the question of knowing "why something exists" is consequently a question devoid of meaning, a pseudo-problem raised around a pseudo-idea? Yet I must say once more why this phantom of a problem haunts the mind with such obstinacy. In vain do I show that in the representation of an "abolition of the real" there is only the image of all realities driving one another out, indefinitely, in a circle. In vain do I add that the idea of non-existence is only that of the expulsion of an imponderable existence, or "merely possible" existence, by a more substantial existence, which would be the true reality. In vain do I find in the sui generis form of negation something extra-intellectual, negation being the judgement of a judgement, a warning given to someone else or to oneself, so that it would be absurd to attribute to it the power of creating representations of a new kind, ideas without content. Always the conviction persists that before things, or at least beneath things, there is nothingness. If one seeks the reason for this fact, one finds it precisely in the affective, social and, in a word, practical element which gives negation its specific form. The greatest philosophical difficulties arise, I said, from the fact that the forms of human action venture outside their proper domain. We are made for acting as much as, and more than, for thinking; - or rather, when we follow the movement of our nature, it is in order to act that we think. We must not be astonished, then, that the habits of action rub off on those of representation, and that our mind always perceives things in the very order in which we are accustomed to picture them when we set out to act on them. Now it is incontestable, as I pointed out above, that every human action has its starting-point in a dissatisfaction and, by that very fact, in a feeling of absence. One would not act if one did not set oneself an end, and one seeks a thing only because one feels the lack of it. Our action thus proceeds from "nothing" to "something", and its very essence is to embroider "something" on the canvas of "nothing". To tell the truth, the nothing in question here is not so much the absence of a thing as that of a utility. If I take a visitor into a room that I have not yet furnished, I warn him "that there is nothing in it". I know, however, that the room is full of air; but, since it is not on air that one sits, the room truly contains nothing of what, at this moment, for the visitor and for myself, counts for something. In a general way, human work consists in creating utility; and, so long as the work is not done, there is "nothing", - nothing of what one wished to obtain. Our life is thus spent in filling voids, which our intellect conceives under the extra-intellectual influence of desire and regret, under the pressure of vital necessities: and, if by void one understands an absence of utility and not of things, one can say, in this entirely relative sense, that we are constantly going from the empty to the full. Such is the direction in which our action moves. Our speculation cannot help doing the same, and, naturally, it passes from the relative sense to the absolute sense, since it is exercised on things themselves and not on the utility they have for us. Thus there takes root in us the idea that reality fills a void, and that nothingness, conceived as an absence of everything, pre-exists all things by right, if not in fact. It is this illusion that I have tried to dispel, by showing that the idea of Nothing, if one claims to see in it that of an abolition of all things, is a self-destructive idea and reduces itself to a mere word, - and that if, on the contrary, it is truly an idea, one finds in it as much matter as in the idea of All. This long analysis was necessary in order to show that a reality which is self-sufficient is not necessarily a reality foreign to duration. If one passes (consciously or unconsciously) through the idea of nothingness in order to arrive at that of Being, the Being one arrives at is a logical or mathematical essence, and hence timeless. And, that being so, a static conception of the real forces itself upon us: everything appears given at once, in eternity. But we must accustom ourselves to think Being directly, without making a detour, without first applying to the phantom of nothingness which interposes itself between it and us. We must try here to see for the sake of seeing, and no longer to see for the sake of acting. Then the Absolute reveals itself very near us and, in a certain measure, in us. It is psychological, and not mathematical or logical, in essence. It lives with us. Like us, but in certain respects infinitely more concentrated and more gathered up into itself, it endures. But do we ever think true duration? Here again a direct taking of possession will be necessary. One will not reach duration by a detour: one must install oneself in it straight away. That is what the intellect most often refuses to do, accustomed as it is to think the moving by means of the immobile. The role of the intellect is, in fact, to preside over actions. Now, in action, it is the result that interests us; the means matter little provided the end is attained. Hence it is that we strain our whole being towards the end to be realised, trusting it, most often, to turn itself from idea into act. And hence it is also that the term at which our activity will come to rest is alone explicitly represented to our mind: the movements constituting the action itself either escape our consciousness or reach it only confusedly. Let us consider a very simple act such as that of raising the arm. Where should we be if we had to imagine in advance all the elementary contractions and tensions it involves, or even to perceive them, one by one, while they are being accomplished? The mind transports itself at once to the goal, that is to say to the schematic and simplified vision of the act supposed accomplished. Then, if no antagonistic representation neutralises the effect of the first, the appropriate movements come of themselves to fill out the schema, drawn in, as it were, by the void of its interstices. The intellect therefore represents to activity only ends to be attained, that is to say points of rest. And, from one end attained to another end attained, from one rest to another rest, our activity is carried along by a series of leaps, during which our consciousness turns away as much as possible from the movement in course of accomplishment, so as to look only at the anticipated image of the movement accomplished. Now, in order that it may represent to itself, as immobile, the result of the act being accomplished, the intellect must perceive, as immobile too, the medium in which this result is framed. Our activity is inserted in the material world. If matter appeared to us as a perpetual flowing, we should assign a term to none of our actions. We should feel each of them dissolve as fast as it was accomplished, and we should not anticipate an ever-fleeing future. In order that our activity may leap from act to act, matter must pass from state to state, for it is only in a state of the material world that action can insert a result and consequently be accomplished. But is it indeed thus that matter presents itself? A priori, one may presume that our perception arranges itself so as to take matter from this angle. Sensory organs and motor organs are, in fact, co-ordinated with each other. Now, the former symbolise our faculty of perceiving, as the latter our faculty of acting. The organism thus reveals to us, in a visible and tangible form, the perfect accord of perception and action. If, then, our activity always aims at a result into which it is momentarily inserted, our perception must retain of the material world, at every instant, scarcely more than a state in which it provisionally settles. Such is the hypothesis that presents itself to the mind. It is easy to see that experience confirms it. From the first glance cast upon the world, even before we mark out bodies in it, we distinguish qualities in it. Colour succeeds colour, sound succeeds sound, resistance succeeds resistance, etc. Each of these qualities, taken separately, is a state which seems to persist as it is, immobile, until another replaces it. Yet each of these qualities resolves itself, on analysis, into an enormous number of elementary movements. Whether one sees vibrations in it or represents it in any other way, one fact is certain: every quality is change. In vain, moreover, does one look here, beneath the change, for the thing that changes; it is always provisionally, and to satisfy our imagination, that we attach the movement to a moving body. The moving body flees incessantly under the gaze of science; science never has to do with anything but mobility. In the smallest perceptible fraction of a second, in the quasi-instantaneous perception of a sensible quality, there may be trillions of oscillations repeating themselves: the permanence of a sensible quality consists in this repetition of movements, as the persistence of life is made of successive palpitations. The first function of perception is precisely to grasp a series of elementary changes in the form of a quality or of a simple state, by a work of condensation. The greater the power of acting allotted to an animal species, the more numerous, no doubt, are the elementary changes that its faculty of perceiving concentrates into one of its instants. And the progress must be continuous, in nature, from the beings that vibrate almost in unison with the ethereal oscillations up to those that immobilise trillions of these oscillations in the shortest of their simple perceptions. The former feel hardly anything but movements; the latter perceive quality. The former are very near to letting themselves be caught in the gearing of things; the others react, and the tension of their faculty of acting is no doubt proportional to the concentration of their faculty of perceiving. The progress continues into humanity itself. One is the more a "man of action" the greater the number of events one can embrace at a glance: it is the same reason that makes one perceive successive events one by one and let oneself be led by them, or grasp them as a block and dominate them. In sum, the qualities of matter are so many stable views that we take of its instability. Now, in the continuity of sensible qualities we mark out bodies. Each of these bodies changes, in reality, at every moment. First, it resolves itself into a group of qualities, and every quality, I said, consists in a succession of elementary movements. But even if one regards quality as a stable state, the body is still unstable in that it is ceaselessly changing qualities. The body par excellence, the one we are best justified in isolating in the continuity of matter, because it constitutes a relatively closed system, is the living body; it is for it, moreover, that we cut out the others in the whole. Now, life is an evolution. We concentrate a period of this evolution into a stable view which we call a form, and, when the change has become considerable enough to overcome the happy inertia of our perception, we say that the body has changed its form. But in reality the body is changing form at every instant. Or rather there is no form, since form is something immobile and reality is movement. What is real is the continual change of form: form is only a snapshot taken of a transition. Here again, therefore, our perception arranges itself so as to solidify the fluid continuity of the real into discontinuous images. When the successive images do not differ too much from one another, we regard them all as the waxing and waning of a single mean image, or as the deformation of this image in different directions. And it is of this mean that we are thinking when we speak of the essence of a thing, or of the thing itself. Finally, things, once constituted, manifest on the surface, by their changes of situation, the profound modifications that are being accomplished within the Whole. We then say that they act on one another. This action appears to us no doubt in the form of movement. But from the mobility of the movement we turn our gaze away as much as possible: what interests us is, as I said above, the immobile design of the movement rather than the movement itself. Is it a simple movement? We ask ourselves where it is going. It is by its direction, that is to say by the position of its provisional goal, that we represent it to ourselves at every moment. Is it a complex movement? We wish to know, before everything, what is going on, what the movement is doing, that is to say the result obtained or the intention that presides over it. Examine closely what you have in mind when you speak of an action in course of accomplishment. The idea of change is there, I grant, but it hides in the half-light. In full light there is the immobile design of the act supposed accomplished. It is by this, and by this alone, that the complex act is distinguished and defined. We should be very much at a loss to imagine the movements inherent in the actions of eating, drinking, fighting, etc. It is enough for us to know, in a general and indeterminate way, that all these acts are movements. Once in order on that side, we seek simply to represent to ourselves the overall plan of each of these complex movements, that is to say the immobile design that underlies them. Here again knowledge bears on a state rather than on a change. It is therefore with this third case as with the other two. Whether it is a matter of qualitative movement or of evolutionary movement or of extensive movement, the mind arranges itself so as to take stable views of instability. And it thus arrives, as I have just shown, at three kinds of representations: 1st, qualities; 2nd, forms or essences; 3rd, acts. To these three ways of seeing correspond three categories of words: adjectives, substantives and verbs, which are the primordial elements of language. Adjectives and substantives therefore symbolise states. But the verb itself, if one keeps to the illuminated part of the representation it calls up, expresses scarcely anything else. If now one sought to characterise more precisely our natural attitude towards becoming, here is what one would find. Becoming is infinitely varied. That which goes from yellow to green is not like that which goes from green to blue: they are different qualitative movements. That which goes from flower to fruit is not like that which goes from larva to nymph and from nymph to perfect insect: they are different evolutionary movements. The action of eating or of drinking is not like the action of fighting: they are different extensive movements. And these three kinds of movement themselves, qualitative, evolutionary, extensive, differ profoundly. The artifice of our perception, like that of our intellect, like that of our language, consists in extracting from these very varied becomings the single representation of becoming in general, an indeterminate becoming, a mere abstraction which by itself says nothing and of which, indeed, we rarely think. To this idea, always the same, and moreover obscure or unconscious, we then join, in each particular case, one or more clear images which represent states and which serve to distinguish all becomings from one another. It is this composition of a specific and determinate state with change in general and indeterminate that we substitute for the specificity of change. An indefinite multiplicity of becomings, diversely coloured, so to speak, passes before our eyes: we arrange things so as to see mere differences of colour, that is to say of state, beneath which there would flow in obscurity a becoming always and everywhere the same, invariably colourless. Suppose one wished to reproduce on a screen an animated scene, the march-past of a regiment for example. There would be a first way of going about it. It would be to cut out jointed figures representing the soldiers, to impart to each of them the movement of marching, a movement varying from individual to individual although common to the human species, and to project the whole on to the screen. One would have to spend a formidable amount of work on this little game, and one would, moreover, obtain only a rather mediocre result: how could one reproduce the suppleness and variety of life? Now, there is a second way of proceeding, much easier and at the same time more effective. It is to take a series of snapshots of the passing regiment, and to project these snapshots on to the screen in such a way that they replace one another very rapidly. This is what the cinematograph does. With photographs each of which represents the regiment in an immobile attitude, it reconstitutes the mobility of the passing regiment. It is true that, if we were dealing with the photographs alone, however much we looked at them, we should not see them come to life: with immobility, even indefinitely juxtaposed with itself, we shall never make movement. For the images to come to life, there must be movement somewhere. Movement does indeed exist here; it is in the apparatus. It is because the cinematographic film unrolls, bringing the various photographs of the scene in turn to continue one another, that each actor in this scene recovers his mobility: he strings all his successive attitudes on the invisible movement of the cinematographic film. The procedure has therefore consisted, in sum, in extracting from all the movements peculiar to all the figures an impersonal movement, abstract and simple, movement in general, so to speak, in putting it into the apparatus, and in reconstituting the individuality of each particular movement by the composition of this anonymous movement with the personal attitudes. Such is the artifice of the cinematograph. And such is also that of our knowledge. Instead of attaching ourselves to the inner becoming of things, we place ourselves outside them in order to recompose their becoming artificially. We take quasi-instantaneous views of the passing reality, and, since they are characteristic of this reality, it suffices for us to string them along an abstract, uniform, invisible becoming, situated at the back of the apparatus of knowledge, in order to imitate what is characteristic in this becoming itself. Perception, intellection, language in general proceed thus. Whether it is a matter of thinking becoming, or of expressing it, or even of perceiving it, we do hardly anything but set going a kind of inner cinematograph. One would therefore sum up all that precedes by saying that the mechanism of our ordinary knowledge is of a cinematographic nature. Of the entirely practical character of this operation there can be no doubt. Each of our acts aims at a certain insertion of our will into reality. It is, between our body and other bodies, an arrangement comparable to that of the pieces of glass which compose a kaleidoscopic figure. Our activity goes from an arrangement to a rearrangement, each time giving the kaleidoscope, no doubt, a new shake, but taking no interest in the shake and seeing only the new figure. The knowledge it gives itself of the operation of nature must therefore be exactly symmetrical with the interest it takes in its own operation. In this sense one might say, if it were not abusing a certain kind of comparison, that the cinematographic character of our knowledge of things is due to the kaleidoscopic character of our adaptation to them. The cinematographic method is therefore the only practical method, since it consists in regulating the general pace of knowledge on that of action, until the detail of each act is regulated in its turn on that of knowledge. In order that action may always be enlightened, the intellect must always be present in it; but the intellect, in order thus to accompany the progress of activity and ensure its direction, must begin by adopting its rhythm. Discontinuous is action, like every pulsation of life; discontinuous, therefore, will knowledge be. The mechanism of the faculty of knowing has been constructed on this plan. Essentially practical, can it serve, just as it is, for speculation? Let us try with it to follow reality in its windings, and let us see what is going to happen. Of the continuity of a certain becoming I have taken a series of views which I have linked together by "becoming" in general. But it is understood that I cannot stop there. What is not determinable is not representable: of "becoming in general" I have only a verbal knowledge. As the letter x designates a certain unknown, whatever it may be, so my "becoming in general", always the same, symbolises here a certain transition of which I have taken snapshots: of this transition itself it teaches me nothing. I am therefore going to concentrate myself wholly on the transition and, between two snapshots, seek what is happening. But, since I am applying the same method, I arrive at the same result; a third view will simply be inserted between the other two. Indefinitely I shall begin again, and indefinitely I shall juxtapose views with views, without obtaining anything else. The application of the cinematographic method will therefore lead here to a perpetual beginning again, in which the mind, never finding satisfaction and seeing nowhere to settle, no doubt persuades itself that by its instability it imitates the very movement of the real. But if, by training itself to vertigo, it ends by giving itself the illusion of mobility, its operation has not advanced it a single step, since it leaves it always as far from the goal. To advance with moving reality, it is within it that one would have to place oneself again. Install yourself in change, and you will grasp at once both change itself and the successive states in which it could at any instant be immobilised. But with these successive states, perceived from without as real and no longer virtual immobilities, you will never reconstitute movement. Call them, as the case may be, qualities, forms, positions or intentions; you may multiply their number as much as you please and thus bring two consecutive states indefinitely closer to each other: you will always experience, before the intermediate movement, the disappointment of the child who would like, by bringing his two open hands together, to crush smoke. The movement will slip through the interval, because every attempt to reconstitute change with states implies the absurd proposition that movement is made of immobilities. This is what philosophy perceived as soon as it opened its eyes. The arguments of Zeno of Elea, although they were formulated with a very different intention, say nothing else. Do we consider the flying arrow? At every instant, says Zeno, it is immobile, for it would have time to move, that is to say to occupy at least two successive positions, only if it were granted at least two instants. At a given moment, therefore, it is at rest at a given point. Immobile at every point of its course, it is, during the whole time it is moving, immobile. Yes, if we suppose that the arrow can ever be at a point of its course. Yes, if the arrow, which is something moving, ever coincided with a position, which is something immobile. But the arrow is never at any point of its course. At most one should say that it could be there, in the sense that it passes there and that it would be free to stop there. It is true that, if it stopped there, it would remain there, and that it would no longer be movement that we should be dealing with at that point. The truth is that, if the arrow leaves the point A to fall back at the point B, its movement AB is as simple, as indecomposable, in so far as it is movement, as the tension of the bow that shoots it. As the shrapnel, bursting before it touches the ground, covers the zone of explosion with an indivisible danger, so the arrow which goes from A to B displays at a single stroke, although over a certain extent of duration, its indivisible mobility. Suppose an elastic that you were to stretch from A to B; could you divide its extension? The course of the arrow is this very extension, as simple as it, undivided like it. It is one single leap. You fix a point C in the interval traversed, and you say that at a certain moment the arrow was at C. If it had been there, that would mean that it had stopped there, and you would no longer have a course from A to B, but two courses, one from A to C, the other from C to B, with an interval of rest. A single movement is entirely, by hypothesis, a movement between two stops: if there are intermediate stops, it is no longer a single movement. At bottom, the illusion comes from the fact that the movement, once effected, has laid down along its course an immobile trajectory on which one can count as many immobilities as one likes. From this one concludes that the movement, while being effected, laid down at each instant beneath it a position with which it coincided. One does not see that the trajectory is created all at once, although it needs a certain time for that, and that, if one can divide the trajectory at will once it has been created, one could not divide its creation, which is an act in progress and not a thing. To suppose that the moving body is at a point of its course is, by a cut of the scissors given at that point, to cut the course in two and to substitute two trajectories for the single trajectory one was considering at first. It is to distinguish two successive acts where, by hypothesis, there is only one. In short, it is to carry over to the very course of the arrow everything that can be said of the interval it has traversed, that is to say to admit a priori the absurdity that movement coincides with the immobile. I shall not dwell here on the three other arguments of Zeno. I have examined them elsewhere. Let me confine myself to recalling that they again consist in applying the movement along the line traversed and in supposing that what is true of the line is true of the movement. For example, the line can be divided into as many parts as one likes, of whatever size one likes, and it is always the same line. From this one will conclude that one has the right to suppose the movement articulated as one likes, and that it is always the same movement. One will thus obtain a series of absurdities which will all express the same fundamental absurdity. But the possibility of applying the movement to the line traversed exists only for an observer who, keeping outside the movement and envisaging at every instant the possibility of a stop, claims to recompose the real movement with these possible immobilities. It vanishes as soon as one adopts in thought the continuity of the real movement, the continuity of which each of us is conscious when he raises his arm or takes a step forward. We then feel clearly that the line traversed between two stops is described in a single indivisible stroke, and that one would seek in vain to make in the movement that traces it divisions corresponding, each to each, to the arbitrarily chosen divisions of the line once traced. The line traversed by the moving body lends itself to any mode of decomposition whatever because it has no internal organisation. But every movement is internally articulated. It is either an indivisible leap (which may, moreover, occupy a very long duration) or a series of indivisible leaps. Take the articulations of this movement into account, or else do not speculate on its nature, When Achilles pursues the tortoise, each of his steps must be treated as an indivisible, and each step of the tortoise likewise. After a certain number of steps, Achilles will have stridden past the tortoise. Nothing is simpler. If you insist on dividing the two movements further, distinguish on either side, in the course of Achilles and in that of the tortoise, submultiples of the step of each of them; but respect the natural articulations of the two courses. So long as you respect them, no difficulty will arise, because you will be following the indications of experience. But Zeno's artifice consists in recomposing the movement of Achilles according to an arbitrarily chosen law. Achilles is supposed to arrive with a first bound at the point where the tortoise was, with a second bound at the point to which it has moved while he was making the first, and so on. In that case Achilles would indeed always have a fresh bound to make. But it goes without saying that Achilles, in order to catch up with the tortoise, goes about it quite differently. The movement considered by Zeno would be the equivalent of the movement of Achilles only if one could treat the movement as one treats the interval traversed, decomposable and recomposable at will. Once one has subscribed to this first absurdity, all the others follow1. Nothing would be easier, moreover, than to extend Zeno's argument to qualitative becoming and to evolutionary becoming. We should find the same contradictions again. That the child becomes an adolescent, then a mature man, and finally an old man, is understandable when we consider that vital evolution is here reality itself. Childhood, adolescence, maturity, old age are mere views of the mind, possible stops imagined by us, from without, along the continuity of a progress. Let us on the contrary take childhood, adolescence, maturity and old age as integral parts of the evolution: they become real stops, and we can no longer conceive how evolution is possible, for juxtaposed rests will never be equivalent to a movement. How, with what is made, are we to reconstitute what is in the making? How, for example, once childhood has been posited as a thing, shall we pass to adolescence, when, by hypothesis, we have given ourselves childhood only? Look at it closely: you will see that our habitual way of speaking, which is modelled on our habitual way of thinking, leads us into veritable logical impasses, impasses into which we venture without uneasiness because we feel confusedly that we would always be at liberty to get out of them; all we should have to do, in fact, would be to renounce the cinematographic habits of our intellect. When we say "the child becomes a man", let us take care not to probe too deeply into the literal meaning of the expression. We should find that, when we posit the subject "child", the attribute "man" does not yet fit it, and that, when we state the attribute "man", it no longer applies to the subject "child". The reality, which is the transition from childhood to mature age, has slipped through our fingers. We have only the imaginary stops "child" and "man", and we are very near to saying that one of these stops is the other, just as the arrow of Zeno is, according to that philosopher, at all the points of its course. The truth is that, if language here were moulded on the real, we should not say "the child becomes a man", but "there is becoming from the child to the man". In the first proposition, "becomes" is a verb of indeterminate meaning, intended to mask the absurdity into which we fall when we attribute the state "man" to the subject "child". It behaves much like the movement, always the same, of the cinematographic film, a movement hidden in the apparatus whose role is to superpose the successive pictures on one another in order to imitate the movement of the real object. In the second, "becoming" is a subject. It comes to the foreground. It is reality itself: childhood and manhood are then no more than virtual stops, mere views of the mind: this time we are dealing with objective movement itself, and no longer with its cinematographic imitation. But the first way of expressing ourselves is the only one in conformity with our habits of language. To adopt the second, we should have to withdraw from the cinematographic mechanism of thought. We should have to abstract from it completely, in order to dispel at a single stroke the theoretical absurdities that the question of movement raises. All is obscurity, all is contradiction when we try to manufacture a transition out of states. The obscurity is dispelled, the contradiction falls away, as soon as we place ourselves along the transition, in order to distinguish states in it by making cross-sections in it in thought. The reason is that there is more in the transition than the series of states, that is to say, of possible sections, more in the movement than the series of positions, that is to say, of possible stops. Only, the first way of looking at things is in conformity with the procedures of the human mind; the second, on the contrary, requires us to climb back up the slope of intellectual habits. Is it surprising if philosophy at first recoiled before such an effort? The Greeks had confidence in nature, confidence in the mind left to its natural inclination, confidence above all in language, in so far as it externalises thought naturally. Rather than find fault with the attitude that thought and language adopt before the course of things, they preferred to find fault with the course of things. This is what the philosophers of the Eleatic school did, without scruple. Since becoming shocks the habits of thought and fits ill into the frames of language, they declared it unreal. In spatial movement and in change in general they saw nothing but pure illusion. One could soften this conclusion without changing the premisses, and say that reality changes, but that it ought not to change. Experience confronts us with becoming: that is sensible reality. But intelligible reality, that which ought to be, is more real still, and that reality, it will be said, does not change. Beneath qualitative becoming, beneath evolutionary becoming, beneath extensive becoming, the mind must seek what is refractory to change: the definable quality, the form or essence, the end. Such was the fundamental principle of the philosophy that developed throughout classical antiquity, the philosophy of Forms or, to use a term closer to the Greek, the philosophy of Ideas. The word eidos, which I here translate by Idea, has in fact this threefold sense. It denotes: 1st, the quality; 2nd, the form or essence; 3rd, the end or design of the act being accomplished, that is to say, at bottom, the drawing of the act supposed accomplished. These three points of view are those of the adjective, the substantive and the verb, and correspond to the three essential categories of language. After the explanations I gave a little above, I could, and perhaps should, translate eidos by "view" or rather by "moment". For eidos is the stable view taken of the instability of things: the quality, which is a moment of becoming; the form, which is a moment of evolution; the essence, which is the mean form above and below which the other forms are ranged as alterations of it; and finally the design inspiring the act being accomplished, which is nothing else, as I said, than the anticipated drawing of the action accomplished. To bring things back to Ideas therefore consists in resolving becoming into its principal moments, each of these being moreover withdrawn by hypothesis from the law of time and as it were plucked in eternity. That is to say, we arrive at the philosophy of Ideas when we apply the cinematographic mechanism of the intellect to the analysis of the real. But as soon as we set the immutable Ideas at the bottom of moving reality, a whole physics, a whole cosmology, even a whole theology, necessarily follow. Let us dwell on this point. It is not my intention to sum up in a few pages a philosophy as complex and as comprehensive as that of the Greeks. But since I have just described the cinematographic mechanism of the intellect, it is important that I show to what representation of the real the play of this mechanism leads. This representation is precisely, I believe, the one we find in ancient philosophy. The main lines of the doctrine that developed from Plato to Plotinus, passing through Aristotle (and even, in a certain measure, through the Stoics), have nothing accidental about them, nothing contingent, nothing that must be held to be a philosopher's fancy. They sketch the vision that a systematic intellect will form of universal becoming when it looks at it through views taken at intervals of its flowing. So that even today we shall philosophise in the manner of the Greeks, we shall rediscover, without needing to know them, this and that of their general conclusions, in the exact measure in which we trust to the cinematographic instinct of our thought. I said that there is more in a movement than in the successive positions attributed to the moving body, more in a becoming than in the forms passed through in turn, more in the evolution of form than the forms realised one after another. Philosophy will therefore be able to derive terms of the second kind from those of the first, but not the first from the second: it is from the first that speculation ought to start. But the intellect reverses the order of the two terms, and on this point ancient philosophy proceeds as the intellect does. It therefore installs itself in the immutable; it will give itself only Ideas. Yet there is becoming; that is a fact. How, having posited immutability by itself alone, shall we make change come out of it? It cannot be by the addition of something, since, by hypothesis, nothing positive exists outside the Ideas. It will therefore be by a diminution. At the bottom of ancient philosophy necessarily lies this postulate: there is more in the immobile than in the moving, and we pass, by way of diminution or attenuation, from immutability to becoming. It is therefore something negative, or at most a zero, that will have to be added to the Ideas to obtain change. In this consists the Platonic "non-being", the Aristotelian "matter", - a metaphysical zero which, attached to the Idea like the arithmetical zero to unity, multiplies it in space and in time. Through it the immobile and simple Idea is refracted into a movement indefinitely propagated. By right, there ought to be only immutable Ideas, immutably fitted into one another. In fact, matter comes to add its void to them and thereby unhooks universal becoming. It is the elusive nothing which, slipping in between the Ideas, creates endless agitation and eternal restlessness, like a suspicion insinuated between two loving hearts. Degrade the immutable Ideas: you thereby obtain the perpetual flux of things. The Ideas or Forms are no doubt the whole of intelligible reality, that is to say, of truth, in that they represent, taken together, the theoretical equilibrium of Being. As for sensible reality, it is an indefinite oscillation to either side of this point of equilibrium. Hence, throughout the philosophy of Ideas, a certain conception of duration, as also of the relation of time to eternity. To one who installs himself in becoming, duration appears as the very life of things, as the fundamental reality. The Forms, which the mind isolates and stores up in concepts, are then no more than views taken of changing reality. They are moments gathered along duration, and, precisely because the thread that bound them to time has been cut, they no longer endure. They tend to merge with their own definition, that is to say, with the artificial reconstruction and the symbolic expression that is their intellectual equivalent. They enter eternity, if you will; but what is eternal in them is one and the same with what is unreal in them. - If, on the contrary, we treat becoming by the cinematographic method, the Forms are no longer views taken of change; they are its constitutive elements, they represent all that is positive in becoming. Eternity no longer hovers above time as an abstraction; it grounds it as a reality. Such is precisely, on this point, the attitude of the philosophy of Forms or Ideas. It establishes between eternity and time the same relation as between the gold piece and small change, - change so small that payment goes on indefinitely without the debt ever being paid off: one would be quit at a single stroke with the gold piece. This is what Plato expresses in his magnificent language when he says that God, unable to make the world eternal, gave it Time, "a moving image of eternity"1. Hence also a certain conception of extension, which lies at the basis of the philosophy of Ideas, although it has not been brought out so explicitly. Let us again imagine a mind that places itself back along becoming and adopts its movement. Each successive state, each quality, each Form, in short, will appear to it as a mere section made by thought in universal becoming. It will find that form is essentially extended, inseparable as it is from the extensive becoming that has materialised it in the course of its flowing. Every form thus occupies space as it occupies time. But the philosophy of Ideas follows the inverse path. It starts from the Form; it sees in it the very essence of reality. It does not obtain form by a view taken of becoming; it gives itself forms in the eternal; of this immobile eternity duration and becoming are supposed to be only the degradation. Form thus posited, independent of time, is then no longer the form that is held in a perception; it is a concept. And since a reality of the conceptual order occupies no more extension than it has duration, the Forms must reside outside space as they hover above time. Space and time therefore necessarily have, in ancient philosophy, the same origin and the same value. It is the same diminution of being that is expressed by a distension in time and by an extension in space. Extension and distension then simply manifest the gap between what is and what ought to be. From the standpoint where ancient philosophy places itself, space and time can only be the field that an incomplete reality, or rather a reality strayed outside itself, gives itself in order to run about in it in search of itself. Only, it will have to be admitted here that the field is created as the race proceeds, and that the race deposits it, in a manner, beneath itself. Move an ideal pendulum, a mere mathematical point, from its position of equilibrium: an endless oscillation is produced, along which points are juxtaposed to points and instants succeed instants. The space and time that are thus born have no more "positivity" than the movement itself. They represent the gap between the position artificially given to the pendulum and its normal position, what it lacks in order to recover its natural stability. Bring it back to its normal position: space, time and movement contract into a mathematical point. In the same way, human reasonings continue in an endless chain, but they would be swallowed up all at once in truth grasped by intuition, for their extension and their distension are only a gap, so to speak, between our thought and the truth1. So it is with extension and duration in relation to the pure Forms or Ideas. The sensible forms are before us, always ready to recapture their ideality, always prevented by the matter they bear within them, that is to say, by their inner void, by the interval they leave between what they are and what they ought to be. Unceasingly they are on the point of recovering themselves, and unceasingly occupied in losing themselves. An inescapable law condemns them, like the rock of Sisyphus, to fall back just as they are about to reach the summit, and this law, which has launched them into space and time, is nothing else than the very constancy of their original insufficiency. The alternations of generation and decay, the evolutions ceaselessly reborn, the indefinitely repeated circular movement of the celestial spheres, all this simply represents a certain fundamental deficit in which materiality consists. Fill up this deficit: at the same stroke you abolish space and time, that is to say, the indefinitely renewed oscillations around a stable equilibrium always pursued, never attained. Things re-enter one another. What was relaxed in space is tensed again into pure form. And past, present and future contract into a single moment, which is eternity. This amounts to saying that the physical is the logical spoiled. In this proposition the whole philosophy of Ideas is summed up. And there too lies the hidden principle of the philosophy innate in our understanding. If immutability is more than becoming, form is more than change, and it is by a veritable fall that the logical system of Ideas, rationally subordinated and co-ordinated with one another, is scattered into a physical series of objects and events accidentally placed one after another. The generative idea of a poem develops into thousands of imaginings, which materialise in sentences that unfold into words. And the further we descend from the immobile idea, rolled up upon itself, to the words that unroll it, the more room is left to contingency and choice: other metaphors, expressed by other words, might have arisen; an image has been called up by an image, a word by a word. All these words now run one behind another, seeking in vain, by themselves, to render the simplicity of the generative idea. Our ear hears only the words; it therefore perceives only accidents. But our mind, by successive bounds, leaps from the words to the images, from the images to the original idea, and so climbs back, from the perception of the words, accidents called forth by accidents, to the conception of the Idea that posits itself. So proceeds the philosopher in face of the universe. Experience passes before his eyes phenomena which, they too, run one behind another in an accidental order, determined by the circumstances of time and place. This physical order, a veritable collapse of the logical order, is nothing else than the fall of the logical into space and time. But the philosopher, climbing back from the percept to the concept, sees all that the physical had of positive reality condense into the logical. His intellect, abstracting from the materiality that distends being, recaptures being in itself in the immutable system of Ideas. Thus is obtained Science, which appears to us complete and ready-made as soon as we put our intellect back in its true place, correcting the gap that separated it from the intelligible. Science, then, is not a human construction. It is prior to our intellect, independent of it, truly generative of things. And indeed, if one held the Forms to be mere views taken by the mind of the continuity of becoming, they would be relative to the mind that represents them to itself; they would have no existence in themselves. At most one could say that each of these Ideas is an ideal. But it is in the contrary hypothesis that we have placed ourselves. The Ideas must therefore exist by themselves. Ancient philosophy could not escape this conclusion. Plato formulated it, and it was in vain that Aristotle tried to evade it. Since movement is born of the degradation of the immutable, there would be no movement, and consequently no sensible world, if there were not, somewhere, immutability realised. And so, having begun by refusing the Ideas an independent existence, and yet unable to deprive them of it, Aristotle pressed them into one another, rolled them up into a ball, and placed above the physical world a Form which thus turned out to be the Form of Forms, the Idea of Ideas, or finally, to use his expression, the Thought of Thought. Such is the God of Aristotle, - necessarily immutable and a stranger to what happens in the world, since he is only the synthesis of all concepts in a single concept. It is true that none of the many concepts could exist apart, as it is, in the divine unity: it would be vain to look for the Ideas of Plato within the God of Aristotle. But it suffices to imagine the God of Aristotle refracting himself, or simply inclining towards the world, for the Platonic Ideas, implied in the unity of his essence, at once to seem to pour out of him: just so do the rays issue from the sun, which nevertheless did not contain them. It is doubtless this possibility of an outpouring of the Platonic Ideas from the Aristotelian God that is figured, in Aristotle's philosophy, by the active intellect, the nous that has been called poiètikos, - that is to say, by what is essential, and yet unconscious, in the human intellect. The nous poiètikos is integral Science, posited all at once, which the conscious, discursive intellect is condemned to reconstruct laboriously, piece by piece. There is therefore in us, or rather behind us, a possible vision of God, as the Alexandrians will say, a vision always virtual, never actually realised by the conscious intellect. In this intuition we should see God expand into Ideas. It is this that "makes all things1", playing in relation to the discursive intellect, in movement in time, the same role that the immobile Mover himself plays in relation to the movement of the heavens and the course of things. We should thus find, immanent in the philosophy of Ideas, a conception sui generis of causality, a conception which it is important to bring into full light, because it is the one at which each of us will arrive when he follows to the end, in order to climb back to the origin of things, the natural movement of the intellect. To tell the truth, the ancient philosophers never formulated it explicitly. They confined themselves to drawing its consequences, and in general they have pointed out to us points of view on it rather than presented it to us itself. Sometimes, indeed, we are told of an attraction, sometimes of an impulsion exerted by the first mover on the whole of the world. Both views are found in Aristotle, who shows us in the movement of the universe an aspiration of things towards the divine perfection, and consequently an ascent towards God, while elsewhere he describes it as the effect of a contact of God with the first sphere, and as descending, consequently, from God to things. The Alexandrians, moreover, only followed, I believe, this double indication when they spoke of procession and conversion: everything derives from the first principle and everything aspires to return to it. But these two conceptions of divine causality can be identified with each other only if we bring them both back to a third, which I hold to be fundamental, and which alone will make us understand not only why, in what sense, things move in space and in time, but also why there is space and time, why there is movement, why there are things. This conception, which shows through more and more beneath the reasonings of the Greek philosophers as we go from Plato to Plotinus, I would formulate thus: The positing of a reality implies the simultaneous positing of all the degrees of reality intermediate between it and pure nothingness. The principle is evident when it is a question of number: we cannot posit the number 10 without thereby positing the existence of the numbers 9, 8, 7..., etc., in short of the whole interval between 10 and zero. But our mind here passes naturally from the sphere of quantity to that of quality. It seems to us that, a certain perfection being given, the whole continuity of degradations is given also between this perfection on the one hand and, on the other, the nothingness that we imagine we conceive. Let us posit, then, the God of Aristotle, thought of thought, that is to say, thought turning in a circle, transforming itself from subject into object and from object into subject by an instantaneous, or rather eternal, circular process. Since, on the other hand, nothingness seems to posit itself, and since, these two extremities being given, the interval between them is given as well, it follows that all the descending degrees of being, from the divine perfection down to "absolute nothing", will be realised, so to speak, automatically as soon as God has been posited. Let us then run through this interval from top to bottom. First, the slightest diminution of the first principle suffices for being to be precipitated into space and time; but the duration and the extension that represent this first diminution will be as close as possible to the divine inextension and eternity. We must therefore picture this first degradation of the divine principle as a sphere turning upon itself, imitating by the perpetuity of its circular movement the eternity of the circulus of divine thought, creating moreover its own place and thereby place in general1, since nothing contains it and it does not change its place, creating also its own duration and thereby duration in general, since its movement is the measure of all the others1. Then, from degree to degree, we shall see perfection decrease down to our sublunary world, where the cycle of generation, growth and death imitates one last time, while spoiling it, the original circulus. So understood, the causal relation between God and the world appears as an attraction if we look from below, as an impulsion or an action by contact if we look from above, since the first heaven with its circular movement is an imitation of God, and imitation is the reception of a form. So, according as we look in one direction or the other, we perceive God as efficient cause or as final cause. And yet neither of these two relations is the definitive causal relation. The true relation is the one we find between the two sides of an equation, of which the first side is a single term and the second a summation of an indefinite number of terms. It is, if you will, the relation of the gold piece to its change, provided we suppose the change offering itself automatically as soon as the gold piece is presented. Only thus shall we understand that Aristotle demonstrated the necessity of a first immobile mover, not by basing himself on the fact that the movement of things must have had a beginning, but on the contrary by positing that this movement cannot have begun and must never end. If movement exists, or, in other words, if the change is being counted, it is because the gold piece is somewhere. And if the summation goes on without end, never having begun, it is because the single term that is its eminent equivalent is eternal. A perpetuity of mobility is possible only if it is backed by an eternity of immutability, which it unrolls in a chain without beginning or end. Such is the last word of Greek philosophy. I have not claimed to reconstruct it a priori. It has manifold origins. It is attached by invisible threads to all the fibres of the ancient soul. It would be vain to try to deduce it from a simple principle2. But if we eliminate from it all that came from poetry, from religion, from social life, as also from a physics and a biology that were still rudimentary, if we abstract from the friable materials that enter into the construction of this immense edifice, a solid framework remains, and this framework sketches the main lines of a metaphysics which is, I believe, the natural metaphysics of the human intellect. We arrive at a philosophy of this kind, in fact, as soon as we follow to the end the cinematographic tendency of perception and thought. For the continuity of evolutionary change our perception and our thought begin by substituting a series of stable forms which are supposed to be threaded in turn on the passage, like those rings that the children riding on wooden horses unhook with their stick as they go by. In what, then, will the passage consist, and on what will the forms be threaded? Since the stable forms have been obtained by extracting from change all that is definite in it, there remains, to characterise the instability on which the forms are laid, only a negative attribute: this will be indetermination itself. Such is the first step of our thought: it dissociates each change into two elements, the one stable, definable for each particular case, namely the Form, the other indefinable and always the same, which would be change in general. And such too is the essential operation of language. Forms are all that it is capable of expressing. It is reduced to leaving understood, or it confines itself to suggesting, a mobility which, precisely because it remains unexpressed, is supposed to remain the same in all cases. Then comes a philosophy that holds the dissociation thus effected by thought and language to be legitimate. What will it do but objectify the distinction with greater force, push it to its extreme consequences, reduce it to a system? It will therefore compose the real out of definite Forms or immutable elements on the one hand, and, on the other, a principle of mobility which, being the negation of form, will by hypothesis escape all definition and will be pure indeterminacy. The more it directs its attention to these forms that thought delimits and language expresses, the more it will see them rise above the sensible and become rarefied into pure concepts, capable of entering into one another and even of gathering themselves at last into a single concept, the synthesis of all reality, the completion of all perfection. The more, on the contrary, it descends towards the invisible source of universal mobility, the more it will feel it slip away beneath it and at the same time empty itself, be swallowed up in what it will call pure nothingness. Finally it will have, on one side, the system of Ideas logically co-ordinated with one another or concentrated into one, on the other a quasi-nothingness, the Platonic "non-being" or the Aristotelian "matter". But, having cut out, one must sew. The task now is to reconstitute the sensible world with supra-sensible Ideas and an infra-sensible non-being. This can be done only if one postulates a kind of metaphysical necessity, by virtue of which the bringing together of this Whole and this Zero is equivalent to the positing of all the degrees of reality that measure the interval between the two, just as an undivided number, as soon as we regard it as a difference between itself and zero, reveals itself as a certain sum of units and at the same stroke brings out all the lower numbers. That is the natural postulate. It is also the one we perceive at the bottom of Greek philosophy. It will then remain only, in order to explain the specific characters of each of these intermediate degrees of reality, to measure the distance that separates it from integral reality: each lower degree consists in a diminution of the higher, and what we perceive in it of sensible novelty would resolve itself, from the point of view of the intelligible, into a new quantity of negation that has been added to it. The smallest possible quantity of negation, the one already found in the highest forms of sensible reality, and consequently, a fortiori, in the lower forms, will be the one expressed by the most general attributes of sensible reality, extension and duration. By increasing degradations we shall obtain more and more special attributes. Here the philosopher's fancy will have free play, for it is by an arbitrary, or at least debatable, decree that we shall equate this or that aspect of the sensible world with this or that diminution of being. We shall not necessarily arrive, as Aristotle did, at a world made up of concentric spheres turning upon themselves. But we shall be led to an analogous cosmology, I mean to a construction whose pieces, though all different, will nonetheless have the same relations among themselves. And this cosmology will always be dominated by the same principle. The physical will be defined by the logical. Beneath the changing phenomena we shall be shown, as if by transparency, a closed system of concepts subordinated and co-ordinated with one another. Science, understood as the system of concepts, will be more real than sensible reality. It will be prior to human knowledge, which does no more than spell it out letter by letter, prior also to things, which clumsily try to imitate it. It would need only to be distracted from itself for an instant in order to come out of its eternity and thereby coincide with all this knowledge and with all these things. Its immutability is therefore indeed the cause of universal becoming. Such was the point of view of ancient philosophy on change and on duration. That modern philosophy, on many occasions, but above all at its beginnings, had a mind to change it, does not seem to me contestable. But an irresistible attraction brings the intellect back to its natural movement, and the metaphysics of the moderns to the general conclusions of Greek metaphysics. It is this last point that I shall now try to bring to light, in order to show by what invisible threads our mechanistic philosophy is attached to the ancient philosophy of Ideas, and how also it answers to the demands, practical above all, of our intellect. Modern science, like ancient science, proceeds by the cinematographic method. It cannot do otherwise; all science is subject to this law. It is of the essence of science, in fact, to manipulate signs that it substitutes for the objects themselves. These signs no doubt differ from those of language by their greater precision and their higher efficacy; they are nonetheless bound by the general condition of the sign, which is to note in a fixed form a fixed aspect of reality. To think movement, a ceaselessly renewed effort of the mind is required. Signs are made to dispense us from this effort by substituting for the moving continuity of things an artificial recomposition that is equivalent to it in practice and has the advantage of being manipulated without difficulty. But let us leave the procedures aside and consider only the result. What is the essential object of science? It is to increase our influence over things. Science may be speculative in its form, disinterested in its immediate ends: in other words, we may give it credit as long as it pleases. But however far the day of payment is put off, we must in the end be paid for our trouble. It is therefore always, in sum, practical utility that science will aim at. Even when it launches into theory, science is bound to adapt its procedure to the general configuration of practice. However high it rises, it must be ready to fall back into the field of action, and to land there at once on its feet. This would not be possible for it if its rhythm differed absolutely from that of action itself. Now action, I have said, proceeds by leaps. To act is to readapt oneself. To know, that is to say, to foresee in order to act, will therefore be to go from one situation to another, from an arrangement to a rearrangement. Science may consider rearrangements closer and closer to one another; it will thus increase the number of moments that it isolates, but it will always isolate moments. As for what happens in the interval, science is no more concerned with it than are common intellect, the senses and language: it bears not on the interval but on the extremities. The cinematographic method therefore imposes itself on our science, as it already imposed itself on that of the ancients. Where, then, is the difference between these two sciences? I indicated it when I said that the ancients brought the physical order back to the vital order, that is to say, laws to genera, whereas the moderns seek to resolve genera into laws. But it is important to consider it under another aspect, which is moreover only a transposition of the first. In what does the difference of attitude of these two sciences towards change consist? I would formulate it by saying that ancient science believes it knows its object sufficiently when it has noted certain privileged moments of it, whereas modern science considers it at any moment whatever. The forms or ideas of a Plato or an Aristotle correspond to privileged or salient moments in the history of things - those very ones, in general, that have been fixed by language. They are supposed, like the childhood or the old age of a living being, to characterise a period of which they are said to express the quintessence, all the rest of this period being filled by the passage, devoid of interest in itself, from one form to another. Is it a question of a falling body? We think we have grasped the fact closely enough when we have characterised it as a whole: it is a movement downwards, it is the tendency towards a centre, it is the natural movement of a body which, separated from the earth to which it belonged, is now going back to find its place there. We therefore note the final term or culminating point (telos, akmè), we set it up as the essential moment, and this moment, which language has retained to express the whole of the fact, suffices science also to characterise it. In the physics of Aristotle, it is by the concepts of up and down, of spontaneous and constrained motion, of proper place and alien place, that the movement of a body thrown into space or falling freely is defined. But Galileo judged that there was no essential moment, no privileged instant: to study the falling body is to consider it at any moment whatever of its course. The true science of gravity will be the one that determines, for any instant of time whatever, the position of the body in space. For this it will need, it is true, signs far more precise than those of language. We might therefore say that our physics differs from that of the ancients above all by the indefinite decomposition of time that it effects. For the ancients, time comprises as many undivided periods as our natural perception and our language cut out in it successive facts presenting a kind of individuality. That is why each of these facts admits, in their eyes, only of a global definition or description. If, in describing it, we are led to distinguish phases in it, we shall have several facts instead of one, several undivided periods instead of a single period; but time will always have been divided into determinate periods, and this mode of division will always have been imposed on the mind by apparent crises of the real, comparable to that of puberty, by the apparent release of a new form. For a Kepler or a Galileo, on the contrary, time is not divided objectively in one way or another by the matter that fills it. It has no natural articulations. We can, we must, divide it as we please. All instants are of equal worth. None of them has the right to set itself up as an instant representative of the others or dominating them. And consequently we know a change only when we are able to determine where it stands at any one of its moments. The difference is profound. It is even radical in a certain respect. But from the point of view from which I am considering it, it is a difference of degree rather than of kind. The human mind has passed from the first kind of knowledge to the second by gradual improvement, simply by seeking a higher precision. There is between these two sciences the same relation as between the noting of the phases of a movement by the eye and the far more complete recording of these phases by instantaneous photography. It is the same cinematographic mechanism in both cases, but in the second it attains a precision it cannot have in the first. Of a horse's gallop our eye perceives chiefly a characteristic attitude, essential or rather schematic, a form that seems to radiate over a whole period and so to fill a time of gallop: it is this attitude that sculpture has fixed on the friezes of the Parthenon. But instantaneous photography isolates any moment whatever; it puts them all in the same rank, and thus the gallop of a horse is scattered for it into as great a number of successive attitudes as we please, instead of gathering itself into a single attitude that would shine at a privileged instant and light up a whole period. From this original difference all the others follow. A science that considers undivided periods of duration in turn sees only phases succeeding phases, forms replacing forms; it is content with a qualitative description of objects, which it likens to organised beings. But when we seek what happens within one of these periods, at any moment whatever of time, we are aiming at something quite different: the changes that occur from one moment to another are no longer, by hypothesis, changes of quality; they are henceforth quantitative variations, either of the phenomenon itself or of its elementary parts. It has therefore rightly been said that modern science stands out from that of the ancients in that it bears on magnitudes and proposes, above all, to measure them. The ancients had already practised experimentation, and on the other hand Kepler did not experiment, in the proper sense of the word, in order to discover a law which is the very type of scientific knowledge as we understand it. What distinguishes our science is not that it experiments, but that it experiments, and more generally works, only with a view to measuring. That is why it has also rightly been said that ancient science bore on concepts, whereas modern science seeks laws, constant relations between variable magnitudes. The concept of circularity sufficed Aristotle to define the movement of the heavenly bodies. But even with the more exact concept of elliptical form, Kepler would not have believed he had accounted for the movement of the planets. He needed a law, that is to say, a constant relation between the quantitative variations of two or more elements of planetary movement. Yet these are only consequences, I mean differences that derive from the fundamental difference. It may have happened to the ancients accidentally to experiment with a view to measuring, as also to discover a law that stated a constant relation between magnitudes. The principle of Archimedes is a true experimental law. It takes into account three variable magnitudes: the volume of a body, the density of the liquid in which it is immersed, the upward thrust that it undergoes. And it does state, in sum, that one of these three terms is a function of the other two. The essential, original difference must therefore be sought elsewhere. It is the very one I pointed out at first. The science of the ancients is static. Either it considers the change it studies as a block, or, if it divides it into periods, it makes each of these periods a block in its turn: which amounts to saying that it takes no account of time. But modern science was constituted around the discoveries of Galileo and Kepler, which at once furnished it with a model. Now what do Kepler's laws say? They establish a relation between the areas described by the heliocentric radius vector of a planet and the times taken to describe them, between the major axis of the orbit and the time taken to travel round it. What was Galileo's chief discovery? A law linking the space traversed by a falling body to the time occupied by the fall. Let us go further. In what did the first of the great transformations of geometry in modern times consist? In introducing, in a veiled form, it is true, time and movement even into the consideration of figures. For the ancients, geometry was a purely static science. Its figures were given all at once, in the finished state, like the Platonic Ideas. But the essence of Cartesian geometry (although Descartes did not give it this form) was to consider every plane curve as described by the movement of a point on a moving straight line which is displaced, parallel to itself, along the axis of abscissae, - the displacement of the moving line being supposed uniform and the abscissa thus becoming representative of time. The curve will then be defined if we can state the relation that links the space traversed on the moving line to the time taken to traverse it, that is to say, if we are able to indicate the position of the moving point on the line it traverses at any moment whatever of its course. This relation will be nothing else than the equation of the curve. To substitute an equation for a figure consists, in sum, in seeing where we are in the tracing of the curve at any moment whatever, instead of envisaging this tracing all at once, gathered up in the single movement in which the curve is in the finished state. Such, then, was indeed the guiding idea of the reform by which both the science of nature and the mathematics that served it as instrument were renewed. Modern science is the daughter of astronomy; it came down from heaven to earth along Galileo's inclined plane, for it is through Galileo that Newton and his successors are linked to Kepler. Now how did the astronomical problem present itself to Kepler? The task was, knowing the respective positions of the planets at a given moment, to calculate their positions at any other moment. The same question henceforth arose for every material system.
