Each material point became a rudimentary planet, and the question par excellence, the ideal problem whose solution was to yield the key to all the others, was to determine the relative positions of these elements at any moment whatever, once their positions at a given moment were known. No doubt the problem is put in these precise terms only in very simple cases, for a schematised reality, for we never know the respective positions of the true elements of matter, supposing that there are real elements, and even if we knew them at a given moment, the calculation of their positions for another moment would most often require a mathematical effort exceeding human powers. But it is enough for us to know that these elements could be known, that their present positions could be recorded, and that a superhuman intellect could, by submitting these data to mathematical operations, determine the positions of the elements at any other moment of time. This conviction lies at the bottom of the questions we ask ourselves about nature, and of the methods we employ to solve them. That is why every law of static form appears to us as a provisional instalment, or as a particular point of view on a dynamic law which alone would give us integral and definitive knowledge. Let us conclude that our science is distinguished from ancient science not only in that it seeks laws, nor even in that its laws state relations between magnitudes. We must add that the magnitude to which we should like to be able to relate all the others is time, and that modern science must be defined above all by its aspiration to take time as an independent variable. But what time is in question? I have said it, and I cannot repeat it too often: the science of matter proceeds like ordinary knowledge. It perfects this knowledge, it increases its precision and its range, but it works in the same direction and brings the same mechanism into play. If, then, ordinary knowledge, by reason of the cinematographic mechanism to which it subjects itself, gives up following becoming in what is moving in it, the science of matter gives it up likewise. No doubt it distinguishes as great a number of moments as we please in the interval of time it considers. However small the intervals at which it has stopped, it authorises us to divide them further, if we need to. Unlike ancient science, which stopped at certain so-called essential moments, it concerns itself indifferently with any moment whatever. But always it considers moments, always virtual halts, always, in sum, immobilities. That is to say, real time, regarded as a flux or, in other words, as the very mobility of being, here escapes the grasp of scientific knowledge. I have already tried to establish this point in an earlier work. I touched on it again in the first chapter of this book. But it is important to come back to it one last time, in order to dispel misunderstandings. When positive science speaks of time, it is referring to the movement of a certain moving body T along its trajectory. This movement has been chosen by it as representative of time, and it is uniform by definition. Let us call T1, T2, T3, ... etc., points that divide the trajectory of the moving body into equal parts from its origin T0. We shall say that 1, 2, 3, ... units of time have elapsed when the moving body is at the points T1, T2, T3, ... of the line it traverses. Then, to consider the state of the universe at the end of a certain time t is to examine where it will be when the moving body T is at the point Tt of its trajectory. But of the flux itself of time, still less of its effect on consciousness, there is no question here; for what enters into the reckoning are points T1, T2, T3, ... taken on the flux, never the flux itself. We may narrow the time considered as much as we please, that is to say, decompose at will the interval between two consecutive divisions Tn and Tn+1; it is always with points, and with points only, that we shall be dealing. What we retain of the movement of the moving body T are positions taken on its trajectory. What we retain of the movement of all the other points of the universe are their positions on their respective trajectories. To each virtual halt of the moving body T at points of division T1, T2, T3, ... we make correspond a virtual halt of all the other moving bodies at the points they are passing. And when we say that a movement or any other change has occupied a time t, we mean by this that we have noted a number t of correspondences of this kind. We have therefore counted simultaneities; we have not concerned ourselves with the flux that goes from one to another. The proof of this is that I can, at my pleasure, vary the rapidity of the flux of the universe in regard to a consciousness that was independent of it and would notice the variation by the wholly qualitative feeling it would have of it: so long as the movement of T shared in this variation, I should have nothing to change in my equations or in the numbers that figure in them. Let us go further. Suppose that this rapidity of flux becomes infinite. Let us imagine, as I said in the first pages of this book, that the trajectory of the moving body T is given all at once, and that the whole history, past, present and future, of the material universe is spread out instantaneously in space. The same mathematical correspondences will subsist between the moments of the history of the world unfolded like a fan, so to speak, and the divisions T1, T2, T3, ... of the line which will be called, by definition, "the course of time". In the eyes of science nothing will have changed. But if, time being thus spread out into space and succession becoming juxtaposition, science has nothing to change in what it tells us, it is because, in what it was telling us, it took account neither of succession in what is specific in it nor of time in what is fluent in it. It has no sign to express what, of succession and of duration, strikes our consciousness. It no more applies to becoming, in what is moving in it, than the bridges thrown at intervals across the river follow the water that flows beneath their arches. Yet succession exists; I am conscious of it; it is a fact. When a physical process is accomplished before my eyes, it does not depend on my perception or my inclination to accelerate or slow it down. What matters to the physicist is the number of units of duration that the process fills: he need not trouble himself about the units themselves, and that is why the successive states of the world could be unfolded all at once in space without his science being changed by it and without his ceasing to speak of time. But for us, conscious beings, it is the units that matter, for we do not count extremities of intervals; we feel and live the intervals themselves. Now we are conscious of these intervals as determinate intervals. I always come back to my glass of sugared water1: why must I wait for the sugar to melt? If the duration of the phenomenon is relative for the physicist, in that it reduces to a certain number of units of time and the units themselves are whatever we please, this duration is an absolute for my consciousness, for it coincides with a certain degree of impatience which is itself rigorously determinate. Whence comes this determination? What is it that obliges me to wait, and to wait for a certain length of psychological duration that is imposed on me, over which I have no power? If succession, as distinct from mere juxtaposition, has no real efficacy, if time is not a kind of force, why does the universe unroll its successive states with a speed which, in regard to my consciousness, is a veritable absolute? why with this determinate speed rather than with any other? why not with an infinite speed? Whence comes it, in other words, that everything is not given all at once, as on the film of the cinematograph? The more I go into this point, the more it appears to me that, if the future is condemned to succeed the present instead of being given alongside it, it is because it is not altogether determined at the present moment, and that, if the time occupied by this succession is something other than a number, if it has, for the consciousness installed in it, an absolute value and reality, it is because there is ceaselessly being created in it, not indeed in this or that artificially isolated system, like a glass of sugared water, but in the concrete whole with which this system forms one body, something unforeseeable and new. This duration may not be the doing of matter itself, but that of the Life which climbs back up its course: the two movements are nonetheless bound up with each other. The duration of the universe must therefore be one and the same with the latitude for creation that can find place in it. When the child amuses himself by reconstituting a picture by putting together the pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, he succeeds more and more quickly the more he practises. The reconstitution, moreover, was instantaneous; the child found it ready-made when he opened the box on leaving the shop. The operation therefore does not require a determinate time, and even, theoretically, it requires no time at all. That is because its result is given. It is because the picture is already created, and to obtain it a work of recomposition and rearrangement suffices, - a work that we may suppose going faster and faster, and even infinitely fast, to the point of being instantaneous. But for the artist who creates a picture by drawing it from the depths of his soul, time is no longer an accessory. It is not an interval that can be lengthened or shortened without modifying its content. The duration of his work is an integral part of his work. To contract or to dilate it would be to modify at once the psychological evolution that fills it and the invention that is its outcome. The time of invention is here one and the same with the invention itself. It is the progress of a thought that changes as it takes body. In short, it is a vital process, something like the ripening of an idea. The painter is before his canvas, the colours are on the palette, the model is sitting; we see all this, and we know the painter's manner too: do we foresee what will appear on the canvas? We possess the elements of the problem; we know, with an abstract knowledge, how it will be solved, for the portrait will surely resemble the model and surely also the artist; but the concrete solution brings with it that unforeseeable nothing which is the whole of the work of art. And it is this nothing that takes time. A nothingness of matter, it creates itself as form. The germination and flowering of this form stretch out into an unshrinkable duration, which forms one body with them. So it is with the works of nature. What appears new in them issues from an inner thrust which is progress or succession, which confers on succession a virtue of its own or which holds all its virtue from succession, which, in any case, makes succession, or continuity of interpenetration in time, irreducible to a mere instantaneous juxtaposition in space. That is why the idea of reading in a present state of the material universe the future of living forms, and of unfolding their future history all at once, must contain a veritable absurdity. But this absurdity is difficult to bring out, because our memory is accustomed to line up in an ideal space the terms it perceives in turn, because it always represents past succession to itself in the form of juxtaposition. It can do so, moreover, precisely because the past is what has already been invented, what is dead, and no longer creation and life. Then, since the succession to come will end by being a past succession, we persuade ourselves that the duration to come admits of the same treatment as past duration, that it could be unrolled from this moment on, that the future is there, rolled up, already painted on the canvas. An illusion, no doubt, but a natural, ineradicable illusion, which will last as long as the human mind! Time is invention or it is nothing at all. But physics cannot take account of time-invention, bound as it is to the cinematographic method. It confines itself to counting the simultaneities between the events constitutive of this time and the positions of the moving body T on its trajectory. It detaches these events from the whole which at each instant puts on a new form and which communicates to them something of its novelty. It considers them in the abstract state, such as they would be outside the living whole, that is to say, in a time unrolled into space. It retains only the events or systems of events that can be thus isolated without subjecting them to too profound a distortion, because these alone lend themselves to the application of its method. Our physics dates from the day when it became possible to isolate such systems. In sum, if modern physics is distinguished from the old in that it considers any moment whatever of time, it rests entirely on a substitution of time-length for time-invention. It seems, then, that parallel to this physics a second kind of knowledge ought to have been constituted, which would have retained what physics let slip. On the very flux of duration science neither would nor could have any hold, attached as it was to the cinematographic method. One would have broken free of this method. One would have required the mind to renounce its dearest habits. It is into the interior of becoming that one would have transported oneself by an effort of sympathy. One would no longer have asked where a moving body will be, what configuration a system will take, through what state a change will pass at any moment whatever: the moments of time, which are only halts of our attention, would have been abolished; it is the flowing of time, it is the very flux of the real, that one would have tried to follow. The first kind of knowledge has the advantage of making us foresee the future and of making us, in a certain measure, masters of events; in return, it retains of moving reality only eventual immobilities, that is to say, views taken of it by our mind: it symbolises the real and transposes it into the human rather than expressing it. The other knowledge, if it is possible, will be practically useless; it will not extend our empire over nature; it will even run counter to certain natural aspirations of the intellect; but, if it succeeded, it is reality itself that it would embrace in a definitive clasp. In this way we should not only complete the intellect and its knowledge of matter, by accustoming it to install itself in the moving: by developing also another faculty, complementary to that one, we should open for ourselves a perspective on the other half of the real. For as soon as we find ourselves again in the presence of true duration, we see that it signifies creation, and that, if what is unmaking itself endures, it can only be through its solidarity with what is in the making. Thus the necessity of a continual growth of the universe would appear, I mean of a life of the real. And from then on we should regard under a new aspect the life we meet with on the surface of our planet, a life directed in the same direction as that of the universe and inverse to materiality. To the intellect, in short, we should join intuition. The more we reflect on it, the more we shall find that this conception of metaphysics is the one that modern science suggests. For the ancients, indeed, time is theoretically negligible, because the duration of a thing manifests only the degradation of its essence: it is with this immobile essence that science concerns itself. Change being only the effort of a Form towards its own realisation, the realisation is all that it matters to us to know. No doubt this realisation is never complete: that is what ancient philosophy expresses by saying that we perceive no form without matter. But if we consider the changing object at a certain essential moment, at its apogee, we can say that it brushes against its intelligible form. Of this intelligible form, ideal and, so to speak, limiting, our science takes possession. And when it thus possesses the gold piece, it holds eminently that small change which change is. Change is less than being. The knowledge that took it for object, supposing such knowledge possible, would be less than science. But for a science that places all the instants of time in the same rank, that admits no essential moment, no culminating point, no apogee, change is no longer a diminution of essence, nor duration a dilution of eternity. The flux of time here becomes reality itself, and what is studied are the things that flow. It is true that of the reality that flows we confine ourselves to taking snapshots. But precisely for this reason, scientific knowledge ought to call for another knowledge that would complete it. Whereas the ancient conception of scientific knowledge ended by making time a degradation, and change the diminution of a Form given from all eternity, on the contrary, by following the new conception to the end, we should have come to see in time a progressive growth of the absolute, and in the evolution of things a continual invention of new forms. It is true that this would have meant breaking with the metaphysics of the ancients. They perceived only one way of knowing definitively. Their science consisted in a scattered and fragmentary metaphysics, their metaphysics in a concentrated and systematic science: they were at most two species of one and the same genus. On the contrary, in the hypothesis in which we are placing ourselves, science and metaphysics would be two opposed, though complementary, ways of knowing, the first retaining only instants, that is to say, what does not endure, the second bearing on duration itself. It was natural that there should be hesitation between so new a conception of metaphysics and the traditional conception. The temptation must even have been great to begin over again with the new science what had been attempted with the old, to suppose our scientific knowledge of nature at once completed, to unify it completely, and to give this unification, as the Greeks had already done, the name of metaphysics. Thus, beside the new path that philosophy could open up, the old one remained open. It was the very one along which physics was travelling. And since physics retained of time only what could just as well be spread out all at once in space, the metaphysics that took this direction necessarily had to proceed as if time created and annihilated nothing, as if duration had no efficacy. Bound, like the physics of the moderns and the metaphysics of the ancients, to the cinematographic method, it arrived at this conclusion, implicitly admitted at the outset and immanent in the method itself: All is given. That metaphysics at first hesitated between the two paths does not seem to me contestable. The oscillation is visible in Cartesianism. On the one hand, Descartes affirms universal mechanism: from this point of view movement would be relative1, and since time has just as much reality as movement, past, present and future would have to be given from all eternity. But on the other hand (and that is why the philosopher did not go as far as these extreme consequences) Descartes believes in the free will of man. He superposes on the determinism of physical phenomena the indeterminism of human actions, and consequently on time-length a duration in which there is invention, creation, true succession. This duration he backs with a God who ceaselessly renews the creative act and who, being thus tangent to time and becoming, sustains them, necessarily communicates to them something of his absolute reality. When he places himself at this second point of view, Descartes speaks of movement, even spatial movement, as of an absolute2. He therefore set out in turn on the one path and on the other, resolved to follow neither of the two to the end. The first would have led him to the denial of free will in man and of true willing in God. It meant the suppression of all efficacious duration, the assimilation of the universe to a given thing that a superhuman intellect would embrace all at once, in the instantaneous or in the eternal. By following the second, on the contrary, one arrived at all the consequences that the intuition of true duration implies. Creation no longer appeared simply as continued, but as continuous. The universe, regarded as a whole, truly evolved. The future was no longer determinable as a function of the present; at most could one say that once realised it could be found again in its antecedents, as the sounds of a new language can be expressed with the letters of an old alphabet: one then dilates the value of the letters, one attributes to them retroactively sounds that no combination of the old sounds could have led one to foresee. Finally, mechanistic explanation could remain universal in that it would have extended to as many systems as one might have wished to cut out of the continuity of the universe; but mechanism then became a method rather than a doctrine. It expressed that science must proceed in the cinematographic manner, that its role is to scan the rhythm of the flowing of things and not to insert itself into it. Such were the two opposed conceptions of metaphysics that offered themselves to philosophy. It was towards the first that philosophy turned. The reason for this choice lies no doubt in the mind's tendency to proceed according to the cinematographic method, a method so natural to our intellect, so well adjusted too to the demands of our science, that one must be doubly sure of its speculative impotence to renounce it in metaphysics. But the influence of ancient philosophy also counted for something in it. Artists for ever admirable, the Greeks created a type of supra-sensible truth, as of sensible beauty, whose attraction it is difficult not to undergo. As soon as one inclines to make metaphysics a systematisation of science, one slides in the direction of Plato and Aristotle. And once one has entered the zone of attraction in which the Greek philosophers move, one is drawn into their orbit. Thus were constituted the doctrines of Leibniz and of Spinoza. I do not fail to recognise the treasures of originality they contain. Spinoza and Leibniz poured into them the content of their soul, rich with the inventions of their genius and the acquisitions of the modern mind. And there are in both of them, in Spinoza above all, thrusts of intuition that make the system crack. But if we eliminate from the two doctrines what gives them animation and life, if we retain only their skeleton, we have before us the very image we should obtain by looking at Platonism and Aristotelianism through Cartesian mechanism. We are in the presence of a systematisation of the new physics, a systematisation built on the model of the old metaphysics. What, indeed, could the unification of physics be? The inspiring idea of this science was to isolate, within the universe, systems of material points such that, the position of each of these points being known at a given moment, it could then be calculated for any moment whatever. Since, moreover, the systems thus defined were the only ones on which the new science had a hold, and since one could not say a priori whether a system did or did not satisfy the required condition, it was useful to proceed always and everywhere as if the condition were fulfilled. Here was a methodological rule plainly indicated, and so evident that it was not even necessary to formulate it. Plain good sense tells us, in fact, that when we are in possession of an efficacious instrument of research, and do not know the limits of its applicability, we must act as if this applicability were without limit: there will always be time to lower our claims. But the temptation must have been great for the philosopher to hypostatise this hope, or rather this impetus, of the new science, and to convert a general rule of method into a fundamental law of things. One then transported oneself to the limit; one supposed physics completed and embracing the totality of the sensible world. The universe became a system of points whose position was rigorously determined at each instant in relation to the preceding instant, and theoretically calculable for any moment whatever. One arrived, in a word, at universal mechanism. But it was not enough to formulate this mechanism; it had to be grounded, that is to say, its necessity proved and its reason given. And since the essential affirmation of mechanism is that of a mathematical solidarity of all the points of the universe with one another, of all the moments of the universe with one another, the reason for mechanism had to be found in the unity of a principle in which all that is juxtaposed in space, all that is successive in time, was contracted. From then on the totality of the real was supposed given all at once. The reciprocal determination of the appearances juxtaposed in space was due to the indivisibility of true being. And the rigorous determinism of the phenomena successive in time simply expressed that the whole of being is given in the eternal. The new philosophy was therefore to be a recommencement, or rather a transposition, of the old. The latter had taken each of the concepts in which a becoming is concentrated or in which its apogee is marked; it supposed them all known and gathered them up into a single concept, form of forms, idea of ideas, like the God of Aristotle. The former was to take each of the laws which condition one becoming in relation to others and which are as it were the permanent substratum of phenomena; it would suppose them all known and would gather them up into a unity which expressed them, it too, eminently, but which, like the God of Aristotle and for the same reasons, had to remain immutably shut up within itself. It is true that this return to ancient philosophy did not come about without great difficulties. When a Plato, an Aristotle or a Plotinus fuses all the concepts of his science into a single one, he thereby embraces the totality of the real, for concepts represent things themselves and possess at least as much positive content as they do. But a law, in general, expresses only a relation, and physical laws in particular express only quantitative relations between concrete things. So that if a modern philosopher operates on the laws of the new science as ancient philosophy did on the concepts of the old, if he makes all the conclusions of a physics supposed omniscient converge upon a single point, he leaves aside what is concrete in phenomena: the perceived qualities, the perceptions themselves. His synthesis comprehends, it seems, only a fraction of reality. In fact, the first result of the new science was to cut the real into two halves, quantity and quality, of which one was put down to the account of bodies and the other to that of souls. The ancients had raised no such barriers either between quality and quantity or between soul and body. For them, mathematical concepts were concepts like the others, akin to the others and fitting quite naturally into the hierarchy of ideas. Neither was body then defined by geometrical extension, nor soul by consciousness. If the psukhè of Aristotle, entelechy of a living body, is less spiritual than our "soul", it is because his sôma, already imbued with idea, is less corporeal than our "body". The scission between the two terms was therefore not yet irremediable. It has become so, and from then on a metaphysics which aimed at an abstract unity had to resign itself either to comprehending in its synthesis only one half of the real, or, on the contrary, to taking advantage of the absolute irreducibility of the two halves to each other in order to regard the one as a translation of the other. Different sentences will say different things if they belong to one and the same language, that is to say if they have a certain kinship of sound with one another. On the contrary, if they belong to two different languages, they may, precisely because of their radical diversity of sound, express the same thing. So with quality and quantity, with soul and body. It is for having cut every tie between the two terms that philosophers were led to establish between them a rigorous parallelism, of which the ancients had not dreamed, to hold them for translations, and not inversions, of one another, and finally to give their duality a fundamental identity as substratum. The synthesis to which they had risen thus became capable of embracing everything. A divine mechanism made the phenomena of thought correspond, each to each, to those of extension, qualities to quantities and souls to bodies. It is this parallelism that we find both in Leibniz and in Spinoza, in different forms, it is true, because of the unequal importance they attach to extension. In Spinoza, the two terms Thought and Extension are placed, in principle at least, on the same rank. They are therefore two translations of one and the same original or, as Spinoza says, two attributes of one and the same substance, which must be called God. And these two translations, as also an infinity of others in languages which we do not know, are called for and even required by the original, just as the essence of the circle is translated automatically, so to speak, both by a figure and by an equation. For Leibniz, on the contrary, extension is indeed still a translation, but it is thought that is the original, and thought could do without translation, the translation being made only for us. In positing God, we necessarily posit also all the possible views of God, that is to say the monads. But we can always imagine that a view has been taken from a point of view, and it is natural to an imperfect mind like ours to classify views, qualitatively different, according to the order and position of points of view, qualitatively identical, from which the views would have been taken. In reality the points of view do not exist, for there are only views, each given in an indivisible block and representing, in its own way, the whole of reality, which is God. But we need to translate by the multiplicity of these points of view, external to one another, the plurality of views dissimilar to one another, as also to symbolise by the relative situation of these points of view to one another, by their nearness or their distance, that is to say by a magnitude, the more or less close kinship of the views with one another. This is what Leibniz expresses in saying that space is the order of coexistents, that the perception of extension is a confused perception (that is to say, relative to an imperfect mind), and that there are only monads, meaning thereby that the real Whole has no parts, but that it is repeated to infinity, each time integrally (though diversely), within itself, and that all these repetitions are complementary to one another. Thus the visible relief of an object is equivalent to the totality of the stereoscopic views that one might take of it from every point, and instead of seeing in the relief a juxtaposition of solid parts one might just as well regard it as made of the reciprocal complementarity of these integral views, each given in a block, each indivisible, each different from the others and yet representative of the same thing. The Whole, that is to say God, is this very relief for Leibniz, and the monads are these plane views complementary to one another: that is why he defines God as "the substance which has no point of view", or again as "the universal harmony", that is to say the reciprocal complementarity of the monads. In short, Leibniz differs here from Spinoza in that he regards the universal mechanism as an aspect which reality takes on for us, whereas Spinoza makes it an aspect which reality takes on for itself. It is true that, having concentrated the totality of the real in God, they found it difficult to pass from God to things, from eternity to time. The difficulty was even much greater for these philosophers than for an Aristotle or a Plotinus. The God of Aristotle, indeed, had been obtained by the compression and reciprocal compenetration of the Ideas which represent, in their completed state or at their culminating point, the things that change in the world. He was therefore transcendent to the world, and the duration of things was juxtaposed to his eternity, of which it was a weakening. But the principle to which we are led by the consideration of the universal mechanism, and which must serve it as substratum, no longer condenses within itself concepts or things, but laws or relations. Now a relation does not exist separately. A law connects terms which change; it is immanent in what it governs. The principle in which all these relations come to be condensed, and which grounds the unity of nature, can therefore no longer be transcendent to sensible reality; it is immanent in it, and we must suppose at one and the same time that it is in time and outside time, gathered up in the unity of its substance and yet condemned to unroll it in a chain without beginning or end. Rather than formulate so shocking a contradiction, the philosophers were bound to be led to sacrifice the weaker of the two terms, and to hold the temporal aspect of things for a pure illusion. Leibniz says so in so many words, for he makes of time, as of space, a confused perception. If the multiplicity of his monads expresses only the diversity of the views taken of the whole, the history of an isolated monad seems hardly to be anything else, for this philosopher, than the plurality of the views that a monad can take of its own substance: so that time would consist in the totality of the points of view of each monad upon itself, as space in the totality of the points of view of all the monads upon God. But the thought of Spinoza is much less clear, and it seems that this philosopher sought to establish between eternity and that which endures the same difference as Aristotle made between essence and accidents: an undertaking difficult above all others, for the hulè of Aristotle was no longer there to measure the gap and explain the passage from the essential to the accidental, Descartes having eliminated it for ever. However that may be, the more deeply we go into the Spinozist conception of the "inadequate" in its relations with the "adequate", the more we feel ourselves moving in the direction of Aristotelianism, just as the Leibnizian monads, the more clearly they take shape, the more they tend to draw near to the Intelligibles of Plotinus1. The natural slope of these two philosophies brings them back to the conclusions of ancient philosophy. To sum up, the resemblances of this new metaphysics to that of the ancients come from the fact that both suppose ready-made, the latter above the sensible and the former in the very bosom of the sensible, a Science one and complete, with which whatever reality the sensible contains would coincide. For both, reality, like truth, would be integrally given in eternity. Both are averse to the idea of a reality which would create itself as it went along, that is to say, at bottom, of an absolute duration. That, moreover, the conclusions of this metaphysics, sprung from science, have rebounded right into the interior of science by a sort of ricochet, could be shown without difficulty. The whole of our so-called empiricism is still pervaded by them. Physics and chemistry study only inert matter; biology, when it treats the living being physically and chemically, considers only its side of inertia. Mechanistic explanations, then, in spite of their development, take in only a small part of the real. To suppose a priori that the totality of the real is resolvable into elements of this kind, or at least that mechanism could give an integral translation of what happens in the world, is to opt for a certain metaphysics, the very one whose principles a Spinoza and a Leibniz laid down and whose consequences they drew. Certainly, a psychophysiologist who affirms the exact equivalence of the cerebral state and the psychological state, who pictures the possibility, for some superhuman intellect, of reading in the brain what is going on in consciousness, believes himself very far from the metaphysicians of the seventeenth century, and very close to experience. Yet experience pure and simple tells us nothing of the sort. It shows us the interdependence of the physical and the mental, the necessity of a certain cerebral substratum for the psychological state, nothing more. From the fact that one term is bound up with another term, it does not follow that there is equivalence between the two. Because a certain nut is necessary to a certain machine, because the machine works when the nut is left in and stops when it is taken out, we shall not say that the nut is the equivalent of the machine. For the correspondence to be equivalence, it would be necessary that to any part whatever of the machine there should correspond a determinate part of the nut, – as in a literal translation in which each chapter renders a chapter, each sentence a sentence, each word a word. Now, the relation of the brain to consciousness seems to be quite another thing. Not only does the hypothesis of an equivalence between the psychological state and the cerebral state imply a real absurdity, as I have tried to prove in an earlier work, but the facts, questioned without bias, seem clearly to indicate that the relation of the one to the other is precisely that of the machine to the nut. To speak of an equivalence between the two terms is simply to truncate – while rendering it well-nigh unintelligible – the Spinozist or Leibnizian metaphysics. This philosophy is accepted, just as it is, on the side of Extension, but it is mutilated on the side of Thought. With Spinoza, with Leibniz, the unifying synthesis of the phenomena of matter is supposed complete: everything in it would be explained mechanically. But, for conscious facts, the synthesis is no longer pushed through to the end. We stop half-way. We suppose consciousness coextensive with this or that part of nature, and no longer with nature as a whole. We thus end up sometimes in an "epiphenomenalism" which attaches consciousness to certain particular vibrations and places it here and there in the world, in a sporadic state, sometimes in a "monism" which scatters consciousness into as many little grains as there are atoms. But, in either case, it is to an incomplete Spinozism or Leibnizianism that we come back. Between this conception of nature and Cartesianism, moreover, we should find the historical intermediaries again. The philosophical physicians of the eighteenth century, with their narrowed Cartesianism, had a great deal to do with the genesis of contemporary "epiphenomenalism" and "monism". These doctrines thus turn out to lag behind the Kantian critique. Certainly, the philosophy of Kant is imbued, it too, with the belief in a science one and integral, embracing the totality of the real. Indeed, viewed from a certain side, it is only a prolongation of the metaphysics of the moderns and a transposition of the ancient metaphysics. Spinoza and Leibniz had, following the example of Aristotle, hypostatised the unity of knowledge in God. The Kantian critique, on one of its sides at least, consisted in asking whether the whole of this hypothesis was necessary to modern science as it had been to ancient science, or whether a part only of the hypothesis would not suffice. For the ancients, indeed, science bore on concepts, that is to say on kinds of things. In compressing all concepts into a single one, they therefore necessarily arrived at a being, which might be called Thought, no doubt, but which was rather thought-object than thought-subject: when Aristotle defined God as the noèseôs noèsis, it is probably on noèseôs, and not on noèsis, that he laid the stress. God was here the synthesis of all concepts, the idea of ideas. But modern science turns on laws, that is to say on relations. Now, a relation is a connection established by a mind between two or more terms. A relation is nothing outside the intellect which relates. The universe can therefore be a system of laws only if phenomena pass through the filter of an intellect. No doubt this intellect might be that of a being infinitely superior to man, who would ground the materiality of things at the same time as he connected them with one another: such was the hypothesis of Leibniz and of Spinoza. But it is not necessary to go so far, and, for the effect that is to be obtained here, the human intellect suffices: such is precisely the Kantian solution. Between the dogmatism of a Spinoza or a Leibniz and the critique of Kant, there is just the same distance as between "it must be that" and "it suffices that". Kant halts this dogmatism on the slope which was making it slide too far towards Greek metaphysics; he reduces to the strict minimum the hypothesis that has to be made in order to suppose the physics of Galileo indefinitely extensible. It is true that, when he speaks of the human intellect, it is neither yours nor mine that is in question. The unity of nature would indeed come from the human understanding which unifies, but the unifying function which operates here is impersonal. It communicates itself to our individual consciousnesses, but it goes beyond them. It is much less than a substantial God; it is a little more, however, than the isolated work of a man or even than the collective work of humanity. It does not exactly form part of man; it is rather man who is in it, as in an atmosphere of intellectuality which his consciousness would breathe. It is, if you will, a formal God, something which is not yet divine in Kant, but which tends to become so. This was seen with Fichte. However that may be, its principal role, in Kant, is to give to the whole of our science a relative and human character, although of a humanity already somewhat deified. The critique of Kant, viewed from this standpoint, consisted above all in limiting the dogmatism of his predecessors, accepting their conception of science and reducing to the minimum what it implied of metaphysics. But it is otherwise with the Kantian distinction between the matter of knowledge and its form. In seeing in the intellect, above all, a faculty of establishing relations, Kant attributed to the terms between which the relations are established an extra-intellectual origin. He affirmed, against his immediate predecessors, that knowledge is not entirely resolvable into terms of intellect. He reinstated in philosophy, but modifying it, transporting it on to another plane, that essential element of the philosophy of Descartes which had been abandoned by the Cartesians. In this way he opened the road to a new philosophy, which might have established itself in the extra-intellectual matter of knowledge by a higher effort of intuition. Coinciding with this matter, adopting the same rhythm and the same movement, could not consciousness, by two efforts of inverse direction, raising itself and lowering itself by turns, grasp from within, and no longer perceive from without, the two forms of reality, body and mind? Would not this double effort make us, as far as possible, live the absolute over again? As, moreover, in the course of this operation, we should see the intellect arise of itself, cut itself out within the whole of mind, intellectual knowledge would then appear as it is, limited, but no longer relative. Such was the direction that Kantianism could point out to a revivified Cartesianism. But Kant himself did not set out in this direction. He would not set out in it, because, while assigning to knowledge an extra-intellectual matter, he believed this matter either coextensive with the intellect or narrower than the intellect. From then on, he could no longer think of cutting the intellect out within it, nor consequently of retracing the genesis of the understanding and its categories. The frames of the understanding and the understanding itself had to be accepted as they were, ready-made. Between the matter presented to our intellect and this intellect itself there was no kinship. The agreement between the two came from the intellect's imposing its form on matter. So that not only did the intellectual form of knowledge have to be posited as a kind of absolute and all attempt to give its genesis renounced, but the very matter of this knowledge seemed too much ground down by the intellect for one to be able to hope to reach it in its original purity. It was not the "thing in itself", it was only its refraction through our atmosphere. If now we ask why Kant did not believe that the matter of our knowledge overflowed its form, this is what we find. The critique that Kant instituted of our knowledge of nature consisted in disentangling what our mind must be and what nature must be, if the claims of our science are justified; but of these claims themselves Kant made no critique. I mean that he accepted without discussion the idea of a science that is one, capable of grasping with the same force all the parts of the given and of coordinating them into a system presenting on every side an equal solidity. He did not judge, in his Critique of Pure Reason, that science became less and less objective, more and more symbolic, in proportion as it went from the physical to the vital, from the vital to the psychical. Experience does not move, in his eyes, in two different and perhaps opposite senses, the one conforming to the direction of the intellect, the other contrary to it. There is for him only one experience, and the intellect covers its whole extent. This is what Kant expresses in saying that all our intuitions are sensible, or, in other words, infra-intellectual. And this is what we should indeed have to admit, if our science presented in all its parts an equal objectivity. But let us suppose, on the contrary, that science is less and less objective, more and more symbolic, in proportion as it goes from the physical to the psychical, passing through the vital. Then, since one must indeed perceive a thing in some fashion in order to come to symbolise it, there would be an intuition of the psychical, and more generally of the vital, which the intellect would no doubt transpose and translate, but which would none the less go beyond the intellect. There would be, in other words, a supra-intellectual intuition. If this intuition exists, a taking possession of the mind by itself is possible, and no longer merely an external and phenomenal knowledge. What is more: if we have an intuition of this kind, I mean ultra-intellectual, sensible intuition is no doubt continuous with it through certain intermediaries, as the infra-red with the ultra-violet. Sensible intuition will therefore itself be raised up. It will no longer reach merely the phantom of an unseizable thing in itself. It is (provided certain indispensable corrections are made) into the absolute again that it would introduce us. So long as we saw in it the sole matter of our science, there rebounded upon all science something of the relativity which strikes a scientific knowledge of mind; and from then on the perception of bodies, which is the beginning of the science of bodies, itself appeared relative. Relative, then, sensible intuition seemed to be. But it is no longer so if we make distinctions between the various sciences, and if we see in the scientific knowledge of mind (and so also of the vital) the more or less artificial extension of a certain way of knowing which, applied to bodies, was not at all symbolic. Let us go further: if there are thus two intuitions of different order (the second, moreover, being obtained by a reversal of the sense of the first), and if it is towards the side of the second that the intellect naturally tends, there is no essential difference between the intellect and this intuition itself. The barriers are lowered between the matter of sensible knowledge and its form, as also between the "pure forms" of sensibility and the categories of the understanding. We see the matter and the form of intellectual knowledge (restricted to its proper object) engendering each other by a reciprocal adaptation, the intellect modelling itself on corporeity and corporeity on the intellect. But this duality of intuition Kant neither would nor could admit. To admit it, he would have had to see in duration the very stuff of reality, and consequently to distinguish between the substantial duration of things and time scattered in space. He would have had to see in space itself, and in the geometry immanent in it, an ideal term in the direction of which material things develop, but in which they are not developed. Nothing could be more contrary to the letter, and perhaps also to the spirit, of the Critique of Pure Reason. No doubt knowledge is presented to us here as a list always open, experience as a thrust of facts which goes on indefinitely. But, according to Kant, these facts are scattered, as they come, upon a plane; they are external to one another and external to the mind. Of a knowledge from within, which would grasp them in their very springing forth instead of taking them once sprung, which would thus dig beneath space and spatialised time, there is never any question. And yet it is indeed beneath this plane that our consciousness places us; there lies true duration. On this side too, Kant is fairly close to his predecessors. Between the timeless and time scattered in distinct moments, he admits no middle term. And as there is no intuition which transports us into the timeless, every intuition thus turns out to be sensible, by definition. But between physical existence, which is scattered in space, and a timeless existence, which could only be a conceptual and logical existence like that of which metaphysical dogmatism spoke, is there not room for consciousness and for life? Yes, incontestably. We perceive it as soon as we place ourselves in duration in order to go from there to the moments, instead of starting from the moments in order to bind them together into duration. Yet it was towards a timeless intuition that the immediate successors of Kant turned in order to escape from Kantian relativism. Certainly, the ideas of becoming, of progress, of evolution, seem to occupy a large place in their philosophy. But does duration really play a part in it? Real duration is that in which each form derives from the previous forms, while adding something to them, and is explained by them in so far as it can be explained. But to deduce this form directly from the global Being which it is supposed to manifest is to return to Spinozism. It is, like Leibniz and like Spinoza, to deny duration all efficacious action. Post-Kantian philosophy, however severe it may have been towards mechanistic theories, accepts from mechanism the idea of a science that is one, the same for every kind of reality. And it is nearer to that doctrine than it imagines; for if, in its consideration of matter, life and thought, it replaces the successive degrees of complication which mechanism supposed by degrees of realisation of an Idea or by degrees of objectification of a Will, it still speaks of degrees, and these degrees are those of a scale which being would traverse in a single direction. In short, it disentangles in nature the same articulations as mechanism disentangled in it; from mechanism it retains the whole design; it simply puts other colours on it. But it is the design itself, or at least one half of the design, that has to be done over again. For that, it is true, one would have to renounce the method of construction, which was that of Kant's successors. One would have to appeal to experience, – to a purified experience, I mean one freed, where necessary, from the frames that our intellect has built up in step with the progress of our action on things. An experience of this kind is not a timeless experience. It seeks only, beyond the spatialised time in which we believe we perceive continual rearrangements among the parts, the concrete duration in which a radical recasting of the whole is unceasingly going on. It follows the real in all its windings. It does not lead us, like the method of construction, to higher and higher generalities, storeys superimposed upon a magnificent edifice. But at least it leaves no play between the explanations it suggests to us and the objects to be explained. It is the detail of the real that it claims to illuminate, and no longer merely the whole. That the thought of the nineteenth century called for a philosophy of this kind, withdrawn from the arbitrary, capable of descending to the detail of particular facts, is not in doubt. Incontestably too, it felt that this philosophy ought to establish itself in what we call concrete duration. The advent of the moral sciences, the progress of psychology, the growing importance of embryology among the biological sciences, all this was bound to suggest the idea of a reality which endures inwardly, which is duration itself. So, when a thinker arose who announced a doctrine of evolution, in which the progress of matter towards perceptibility would be retraced together with the advance of mind towards rationality, in which the complication of the correspondences between the external and the internal would be followed from degree to degree, in which change would at last become the very substance of things, towards him all eyes turned. The powerful attraction that Spencerian evolutionism has exercised on contemporary thought comes from that. However far removed Spencer may seem to be from Kant, however ignorant he may moreover have been of Kantianism, he none the less felt, at his first contact with the biological sciences, in what direction philosophy might continue to advance while taking account of the Kantian critique. But no sooner had he set out on the road than he turned off short. He had promised to retrace a genesis, and lo, he was doing something quite different. His doctrine did indeed bear the name of evolutionism; it claimed to go up and down the course of universal becoming. In reality, there was no question in it either of becoming or of evolution. I need not enter into a thorough examination of this philosophy. Let me say simply that the usual artifice of Spencer's method consists in reconstructing evolution out of fragments of the evolved. If I paste a picture on a card and then cut the card into pieces, I can, by grouping the little cards properly, reproduce the picture. And the child who works in this way on the pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, who juxtaposes shapeless fragments of picture and ends by obtaining a fine coloured drawing, no doubt imagines that he has produced drawing and colour. Yet the act of drawing and painting has no relation to that of putting together the fragments of a picture already drawn, already painted. In the same way, by combining with one another the simplest results of evolution, you will imitate after a fashion its most complex effects; but of neither the one nor the other will you have retraced the genesis, and this addition of the evolved to the evolved will not at all resemble the movement of evolution itself. Such, however, is Spencer's illusion. He takes reality in its present form, he breaks it, he scatters it in fragments which he throws to the wind, then he "integrates" these fragments and "dissipates their motion". Having imitated the Whole by a work of mosaic, he imagines that he has retraced its design and given its genesis. Is it a question of matter? The diffused elements which he integrates into visible and tangible bodies look very much like the very particles of simple bodies, which he supposes at first scattered through space. They are, in any case, "material points" and consequently invariable points, veritable little solids: as if solidity, being what is nearest to us and most manipulable by us, could be at the very origin of materiality! The more physics progresses, the more it shows the impossibility of picturing the properties of the ether or of electricity, the probable basis of all bodies, on the model of the properties of the matter we perceive. But philosophy goes back further still than the ether, a mere schematic figuration of the relations grasped by our senses between phenomena. It knows well that what is visible and tangible in things represents our possible action on them. It is not by dividing the evolved that we shall reach the principle of what evolves. It is not by recomposing the evolved with itself that we shall reproduce the evolution of which it is the term. Is it a question of mind? By compounding reflex with reflex, Spencer believes he generates in turn instinct and rational will. He does not see that the specialised reflex, being a terminal point of evolution in the same right as the consolidated will, cannot be supposed at the start. That the first of the two terms reached its definitive form more quickly than the other is very probable; but both are deposits of the evolutionary movement, and the evolutionary movement itself can no more be expressed as a function of the first alone than of the second alone. One would have to begin by mixing the reflex and the voluntary together. One would then have to go in search of the fluid reality which is precipitated in this double form and which, no doubt, partakes of both without being either. At the lowest degree of the animal scale, in living beings which are reduced to an undifferentiated protoplasmic mass, the reaction to stimulus does not yet bring into play a determinate mechanism, as in the reflex; it does not yet have the choice between several determinate mechanisms, as in the voluntary act; it is therefore neither voluntary nor reflex, and yet it heralds both. We experience in ourselves something of the true original activity when we perform semi-voluntary and semi-automatic movements to escape a pressing danger: and even this is only a very imperfect imitation of the primitive procedure, for we are then dealing with a mixture of two activities already constituted, already localised in a brain and in a spinal cord, whereas the primary activity is a simple thing, which diversifies itself through the very production of mechanisms like those of the spinal cord and the brain. But to all this Spencer shuts his eyes, because it is of the essence of his method to recompose the consolidated with the consolidated, instead of rediscovering the gradual work of consolidation, which is evolution itself. Is it a question, finally, of the correspondence between mind and matter? Spencer is right to define the intellect by this correspondence. He is right to see in it the term of an evolution. But when he comes to retrace this evolution, he again integrates the evolved with the evolved, without noticing that he is thus taking useless trouble: in granting himself the least fragment of the presently evolved, he posits the whole of the present evolved, and it is in vain that he would then claim to give its genesis. For Spencer, indeed, the phenomena which succeed one another in nature project into the human mind images which represent them. To the relations between phenomena, therefore, there correspond, symmetrically, relations between representations. And the most general laws of nature, in which the relations between phenomena are condensed, are thus found to have engendered the guiding principles of thought, in which the relations between representations have been integrated. Nature, then, is reflected in mind. The inmost structure of our thought corresponds, piece by piece, to the very framework of things. I grant it; but, for the human mind to be able to represent relations between phenomena, there must first be phenomena, that is to say distinct facts, cut out in the continuity of becoming. And as soon as we grant ourselves this special mode of decomposition, such as we perceive it today, we grant ourselves also the intellect, such as it is today, for it is in relation to the intellect, and to it alone, that the real is decomposed in this manner. Does anyone think that the Mammal and the Insect note the same aspects of nature, trace in it the same divisions, disarticulate the whole in the same manner? And yet the Insect, in so far as it is intelligent, already has something of our intellect. Each being decomposes the material world along the very lines that its action is to follow in it: it is these lines of possible action which, in crossing one another, trace out the network of experience of which each mesh is a fact. No doubt a town is composed exclusively of houses, and the streets of the town are only the intervals between the houses: in the same way, one may say that nature contains only facts, and that, once the facts are posited, the relations are simply the lines that run between the facts. But, in a town, it is the gradual division of the ground into lots that has determined at once the place of the houses, their configuration, and the direction of the streets; it is to this division into lots that we must refer in order to understand the particular mode of subdivision which makes each house be where it is, each street go where it goes. Now, Spencer's fundamental error is to grant himself experience already divided into lots, whereas the true problem is to know how the division into lots came about. I grant that the laws of thought are only the integration of the relations between facts. But, as soon as I posit the facts with the configuration they have today for me, I suppose my faculties of perception and intellection such as they are today in me, for it is they that divide the real into lots, they that cut out the facts in the whole of reality. From then on, instead of saying that the relations between facts have engendered the laws of thought, I can just as well claim that it is the form of thought that has determined the configuration of the facts perceived, and consequently their relations to one another. The two ways of expressing oneself are equivalent. They say, at bottom, the same thing. With the second, it is true, we give up speaking of evolution. But with the first we merely speak of it; we think of it no more for that. For a true evolutionism would set itself to find out by what gradually attained modus vivendi the intellect has adopted its plan of structure, and matter its mode of subdivision. This structure and this subdivision mesh with each other. They are complementary to each other. They must have progressed together. And, whether we posit the present structure of the mind or grant ourselves the present subdivision of matter, in either case we remain within the evolved: we are told nothing of what evolves, nothing of evolution. Yet it is this evolution that would have to be rediscovered. Already, in the domain of physics itself, the scientists who carry the deepening of their science furthest incline to believe that we cannot reason about the parts as we reason about the whole, that the same principles are not applicable to the origin and to the term of a progress, that neither creation nor annihilation, for example, is inadmissible when it is a question of the corpuscles that constitute the atom. In this way they tend to place themselves in concrete duration, the only duration in which there is generation, and not merely composition of parts. It is true that the creation and annihilation of which they speak concern movement or energy, and not the imponderable medium through which energy and movement are supposed to circulate. But what can remain of matter when we take away from it everything that determines it, that is to say, precisely, energy and movement? The philosopher must go further than the scientist. Making a clean sweep of what is only an imaginative symbol, he will see the material world resolve itself into a simple flux, a continuity of flowing, a becoming. And he will thus prepare himself to rediscover real duration where it is still more useful to rediscover it, in the domain of life and of consciousness. For, so long as it is a question of inert matter, we can neglect the flowing without committing a serious error: matter, as I have said, is weighted with geometry, and it endures, this reality which descends, only through its solidarity with what ascends. But life and consciousness are this very ascent. Once we have grasped them in their essence by adopting their movement, we understand how the rest of reality derives from them. Evolution appears, and, within this evolution, the progressive determination of materiality and of intellectuality by the gradual consolidation of the one and the other. But it is then into the evolutionary movement that we insert ourselves, in order to follow it right into its present results, instead of artificially recomposing these results with fragments of themselves. Such seems to me to be the proper function of philosophy. So understood, philosophy is not only the return of mind to itself, the coincidence of human consciousness with the living principle from which it emanates, a taking of contact with the creative effort. It is the deepening of becoming in general, the true evolutionism, and consequently the true prolongation of science, – provided that by this last word we understand a body of truths established or demonstrated, and not a certain new scholasticism which grew up during the second half of the nineteenth century around the physics of Galileo, as the old one did around Aristotle.
